## src/components/Three/character/index.tsx

```tsx
/**
 * @license
 * SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
 */

import { useEffect, useRef } from 'react';
import type * as THREE from 'three';
import {
  AUTHORED_ATTACHMENTS, AUTHORED_SKELETON,
  LEGACY_ATTACHMENTS, LEGACY_SKELETON,
  V2_ATTACHMENTS, V2_SKELETON,
} from '../../../constants/characterRig';
import { applyCharacterSurface } from './bodySurface';
import { AuthoredCharacterModel } from './AuthoredCharacterModel';
import { CharacterModelV2 } from './CharacterModelV2';
import { LegacyCharacterModel } from './legacy';
import { hasAuthoredParts } from './slots';
import type { CharacterModelDefinition, CharacterModelId, CharacterOutfit, CharacterRig } from './types';

/**
 * THE MODEL REGISTRY — every character model the game can draw, and the single point at
 * which one is chosen.
 *
 * Adding a model is adding an entry here. Nothing in the controller, the camera, the
 * collision system or the wardrobe changes, because none of them can see this file: they
 * see the rig and the skeleton, and both are the same shape for every entry.
 */
export const CHARACTER_MODELS: Record<CharacterModelId, CharacterModelDefinition> = {
  legacy: {
    id: 'legacy',
    label: '原始模型',
    skeleton: LEGACY_SKELETON,
    attachments: LEGACY_ATTACHMENTS,
    wearsWardrobe: true,
    Component: LegacyCharacterModel,
  },
  v2: {
    id: 'v2',
    label: '新模型 v2（無服裝）',
    skeleton: V2_SKELETON,
    attachments: V2_ATTACHMENTS,
    // Bare by design until the wardrobe is refitted to this skull — see CharacterModelV2.
    wearsWardrobe: false,
    Component: CharacterModelV2,
  },
  authored: {
    id: 'authored',
    label: '自製 3D 模型',
    skeleton: AUTHORED_SKELETON,
    attachments: AUTHORED_ATTACHMENTS,
    // Every unregistered part falls back to its legacy counterpart, and those DO wear the
    // wardrobe. A part that cannot host it declares so itself — see AuthoredPart.
    wearsWardrobe: true,
    Component: AuthoredCharacterModel,
  },
};

export function getCharacterModelDefinition(id: CharacterModelId): CharacterModelDefinition {
  return CHARACTER_MODELS[id] ?? CHARACTER_MODELS.legacy;
}

/**
 * Draws the active character model. The ONE thing Avatar.tsx renders for the body.
 *
 * Note what does not happen here: no branch on the model id, no per-model special case, no
 * transform. The definition supplies a skeleton, sockets and a component, and this mounts
 * them. That is the whole model layer at runtime — everything else about swapping models is
 * a matter of which entry got picked, which is why a new model cannot break the old one.
 */
export function CharacterModel({
  modelId,
  rig,
  outfit,
}: {
  modelId: CharacterModelId;
  rig: CharacterRig;
  outfit: CharacterOutfit;
}) {
  const model = getCharacterModelDefinition(modelId);
  const { Component } = model;
  const root = useRef<THREE.Group>(null);

  /**
   * 角色表面 — the shading treatment, applied to whatever the model turned out to be.
   *
   * Deliberately no dependency array. It has to re-run whenever this subtree may have CHANGED,
   * and what changes it is React adding or removing a wearable — which is precisely a render of
   * this component. The traversal is idempotent and each material is patched once (see
   * bodySurface.ts), so the repeat cost is a walk of ~100 objects and one property read each; a
   * dependency list would instead be a list of everything a wearable might key off, kept correct
   * by hand, failing silently as a hat that is lit differently from the head under it.
   *
   * It lives HERE, at the registry, rather than in Avatar: this is the one point every character
   * in the game passes through, so the island, the house and the dressing room are all covered by
   * one call, and a model that has not been written yet is covered too.
   */
  useEffect(() => {
    applyCharacterSurface(root.current);
  });

  return (
    <group ref={root}>
      <Component
        rig={rig}
        skeleton={model.skeleton}
        attachments={model.attachments}
        // A model that has not been fitted with the wardrobe is given a BARE outfit rather
        // than being trusted to ignore the one it was handed. Two reasons it is enforced here
        // instead of in each model: a new model gets the safe behaviour for free, and the
        // colours still come through, so a bare character is still the right skin tone.
        outfit={model.wearsWardrobe ? outfit : bareOutfit(outfit)}
      />
    </group>
  );
}

/** Strips every worn item, keeping only the colours. */
function bareOutfit(outfit: CharacterOutfit): CharacterOutfit {
  return {
    ...outfit,
    hair: null,
    hat: null,
    outfit: null,
    pants: null,
    shoes: null,
    necklaceId: null,
    earring: null,
    hasGlasses: false,
    hasMask: false,
    hasShellNecklace: false,
    hasSkirt: false,
    hasSwimsuit: false,
    hasShirt: false,
    hasFallbackShirt: false,
    hasSleeves: false,
    specials: [],
  };
}

export { hasAuthoredParts };
export type { CharacterModelDefinition, CharacterModelId, CharacterOutfit, CharacterRig };
```

## src/components/Three/character/legacy/hairShading.ts

```ts
/**
 * How a hairstyle is SHADED, as opposed to where its pieces sit.
 *
 * ============================================================================
 * WHY THIS FILE EXISTS
 * ============================================================================
 *
 * constants/hair.ts solved the shape problem: every piece is fitted to a skull
 * frame and clamped into an envelope, so no hairstyle can land on the face any
 * more. Nothing solved the SURFACE problem, and it was the whole of what was left
 * between this hair and illustrated hair:
 *
 *   1. FLAT FILL. Every piece was one `meshStandardMaterial color={...}` - the
 *      style's single hex, root to tip, crown to nape. Real hair is darkest where
 *      it leaves the scalp (light never reaches in there, and the strands are
 *      packed tightest) and lightest at the cut ends. A constant fill throws away
 *      the one cue that says "this is a mass of strands" rather than "this is a
 *      moulded plastic shell", which is why the short styles read as helmets even
 *      after they got their occiput back.
 *   2. NO HIGHLIGHT. The only relief in the shop was `shadeHairColor(color, tint)`
 *      on strand locks plus a roughness flip - a per-PIECE shade, so the lightest
 *      thing on a head was a whole lock being slightly paler than its neighbour.
 *      Illustrated hair does the opposite: it runs one bright band ACROSS the
 *      pieces, at a constant height, and lets it cut whichever locks it crosses.
 *      That band is the single most recognisable feature of drawn hair and there
 *      was no machinery in the renderer that could produce one.
 *   3. NO SILHOUETTE SEPARATION. Dark hair against a dark background was a hole.
 *
 * So this file is the missing half: a material factory that shades a piece ALONG
 * ITS OWN LENGTH instead of filling it. Shape still comes from constants/hair.ts
 * and nothing here moves a vertex - `npm run audit:hair` measures geometry, and
 * geometry is exactly what this leaves alone.
 *
 * ============================================================================
 * HOW A PIECE KNOWS WHERE ITS ROOT IS - AND WHY IT IS uv.y AND NOT A UNIFORM
 * ============================================================================
 *
 * Everything below needs one number per fragment: `t`, 0 at the root and 1 at the
 * tip. The obvious way to get it is to hand each mesh its own axis extent as a
 * uniform - and it is the wrong way, because there are sixty-odd pieces on a head
 * and each distinct extent would be its own material.
 *
 * Every primitive the hair is built from - capsule, cylinder, cone - already
 * carries that number: three.js runs `uv.y` from 0 at the bottom of the axis to 1
 * at the top, whatever the piece's radius or length. A lock is placed with its
 * root at local +Y (see `hangCapsule`: `position` is the capsule's midpoint, and
 * `LockGeometry` puts the FULL radius at `radiusTop`), so `t = 1 - uv.y` is the
 * root-to-tip parameter for free, on shared geometry, with no per-piece uniform.
 *
 * `t` is really "how deep into the mass am I", and two kinds of piece measure it
 * from the other end of uv.y - cones, whose apex is their +Y, and the scalp shell,
 * whose occluded end is its tucked rim rather than its crown. Both say so with
 * `flip`; see there.
 *
 * The scalp shell is a hand-built BufferGeometry rather than a primitive, so it
 * has no UVs of its own; `scalpGeometry` in wardrobe.tsx now writes them, running
 * v from 1 at the crown to 0 at the rim.
 *
 * `USE_UV` is what makes `vUv` reach the fragment shader. It is normally switched
 * on by having a texture, which this hair does not; setting the define by hand is
 * the supported way to ask for the varying alone, and it costs one interpolator.
 *
 * ============================================================================
 * WHY THE MATERIALS ARE CACHED AND WHY THAT IS CHEAP
 * ============================================================================
 *
 * `HairPiece` is deliberately hook-free - `scripts/audit-hair.ts` calls it as a
 * plain function - so there is no `useMemo` to hang a material off, and a fresh
 * material per render would leak a GPU program every time an outfit changed. They
 * are therefore cached at module scope on their own parameters, exactly as
 * SCALP_GEOMETRY is.
 *
 * The cache holds a handful of materials per style rather than one per piece,
 * because `t` comes from UVs: two locks of different lengths shade identically and
 * share an entry. And every one of them shares a single compiled PROGRAM - three
 * keys its program cache on `onBeforeCompile.toString()`, and every material here
 * is built by the same function object, so the GLSL below is compiled once for the
 * whole shop no matter how many materials exist.
 */
import * as THREE from 'three';

/**
 * The key light, world space.
 *
 * Restated from Scene.tsx's `<directionalLight position={[20, 20, 10]} />`, which
 * aims at the origin, so the direction from a surface toward the light is that
 * position normalised. The highlight band has to agree with the scene's main light
 * or it reads as a painted-on stripe rather than as a shine - a band sitting on
 * the shadowed side of the head is the classic tell of faked hair specular.
 *
 * A constant rather than a lookup because the band is an ART effect with a
 * deliberately wide, soft falloff, not a physical specular lobe: it wants the
 * scene's light DIRECTION, which is fixed, not its per-frame intensity, which the
 * day/night cycle drives through the light itself.
 */
const KEY_LIGHT_DIR = new THREE.Vector3(20, 20, 10).normalize();

/** Wraps a hue back into 0..1 after an offset has pushed it out. */
const wrapHue = (h: number) => h - Math.floor(h);

/**
 * The four colours a base hex is shaded into.
 *
 * Every one is DERIVED, never authored, which is the rule `shadeHairColor` already
 * follows: a style declares one colour and the shop thumbnail and the model both
 * work from it, so a new hairstyle gets the full treatment by existing rather than
 * by someone remembering to pick four more hexes for it.
 *
 * The moves are the ones an illustrator makes by hand, and they are HUE moves, not
 * just value moves - which is the part a plain darken() cannot do and the reason
 * the old flat fill looked plastic. A shadow that is only the base colour turned
 * down is grey; a shadow that also rotates toward violet and gains saturation
 * reads as hair in shade. Likewise the tips warm as they thin out.
 */
export function hairPalette(hex: string) {
  const base = new THREE.Color(hex);
  const hsl = { h: 0, s: 0, l: 0 };
  base.getHSL(hsl, THREE.SRGBColorSpace);

  /** Roots: deeper, cooler, MORE saturated - packed strands with no light in them. */
  const root = new THREE.Color().setHSL(
    wrapHue(hsl.h - 0.035),
    Math.min(1, hsl.s * 1.3 + 0.05),
    Math.max(0.03, hsl.l * 0.64),
    THREE.SRGBColorSpace,
  );

  /** Tips: lighter and a touch warmer, where the mass thins toward single strands. */
  const tip = new THREE.Color().setHSL(
    wrapHue(hsl.h + 0.014),
    Math.max(0, hsl.s * 0.9),
    Math.min(0.96, hsl.l * 1.34 + 0.09),
    THREE.SRGBColorSpace,
  );

  /**
   * The band. Lifted hard and desaturated toward the light's own colour, because a
   * highlight is the light source seen in the hair rather than the hair lit up - a
   * band that keeps the hair's saturation reads as a paler stripe of hair.
   *
   * `l * 1.75 + 0.3` rather than a fixed near-white, so a bleached style gets a
   * subtle sheen instead of a blown-out slab while the near-black styles - which is
   * where the effect matters most, a dark mass with nothing else to catch - get the
   * full lift.
   */
  const band = new THREE.Color().setHSL(
    wrapHue(hsl.h + 0.03),
    Math.max(0, hsl.s * 0.55),
    Math.min(0.95, hsl.l * 1.75 + 0.3),
    THREE.SRGBColorSpace,
  );

  /**
   * Rim. A fixed cool sky tone rather than a shift of the hair's own hue, because
   * that is what it physically is: the sky wrapping round the silhouette. Keeping
   * it independent of the style is also what makes it work as SEPARATION - it
   * cannot come out the same colour as the background the hair is being lifted off.
   */
  const rim = new THREE.Color().setHSL(
    0.58,
    0.35,
    Math.min(0.92, hsl.l * 0.55 + 0.45),
    THREE.SRGBColorSpace,
  );

  return { root, tip, band, rim };
}

/**
 * Where the two highlight bands sit along `t`, how wide they are, and how hard.
 *
 * TWO of them, not one, because a single band reads as a hoop and real drawn hair
 * has a bright primary with a fainter echo below it. The primary sits at 0.3 -
 * high on the mass, just below the crown, which is where the head's curvature
 * turns fastest and a real shine actually lands - and the secondary at 0.66 with
 * under half the strength, close enough to the tips to travel with them when the
 * hanging pieces sway.
 */
export interface BandSpec {
  center: number;
  width: number;
  strength: number;
}

/** Locks, bangs, curtains, bundles - anything measured from a root at t = 0. */
export const HAIR_BANDS: readonly [BandSpec, BandSpec] = [
  { center: 0.3, width: 0.13, strength: 1 },
  { center: 0.66, width: 0.1, strength: 0.36 },
];

/**
 * The scalp shell, whose `t` runs the other way - 0 at the tucked rim, 1 at the
 * crown - so the primary has to sit HIGH to land in the same place on the head.
 *
 * Wider than a lock's, too: the dome is one broad surface rather than a bundle of
 * thin ones, so the same band drawn at a lock's width reads as a drawn-on hoop
 * instead of as a sheen.
 */
export const SCALP_BANDS: readonly [BandSpec, BandSpec] = [
  { center: 0.68, width: 0.13, strength: 0.72 },
  { center: 0.34, width: 0.1, strength: 0.26 },
];

/**
 * The HANGING pieces - the curtain and the locks that fall below the mass.
 *
 * The secondary band is nearly gone, and that is the point. On the scalp the two
 * bands sit on one continuous surface and read as a sheen with an echo. On a
 * hanging bundle the second band lands down in the last third of every strand -
 * i.e. exactly at the hem - and lights up each of twenty-five separate rods at its
 * own end, which is the opposite of the hem reading as one mass of hair. What is
 * left of it is a suggestion, and the tips get {@link HANG_TIP_SHADE} instead.
 *
 * The primary is WIDE and WEAK where the scalp's is narrow and strong, and that is
 * a consequence of the locks having been widened to close the hem: a band tuned for
 * a 2.6mm rod, drawn on a 5.8mm one, stops being a sheen along a strand and becomes
 * a lit rectangle - and nine lit rectangles side by side read as a collar of plates
 * bolted round the head. Spread over more than twice the length at under half the
 * strength it goes back to being light falling down the hair.
 */
export const HANG_BANDS: readonly [BandSpec, BandSpec] = [
  { center: 0.24, width: 0.28, strength: 0.4 },
  { center: 0.62, width: 0.08, strength: 0.1 },
];

/**
 * How dark the very root goes, as a multiplier on the root colour, and how far
 * down the strand that darkening has faded out.
 *
 * This is contact shading, and it is what stops a lock reading as a rod resting
 * ON the scalp: the last few millimetres before a strand disappears under the
 * mass above it get almost no light, so a piece that stays full brightness right
 * up to where it vanishes looks stuck on rather than growing out.
 */
const ROOT_AO = 0.74;
const ROOT_AO_FADE = 0.3;

/** Fresnel exponent and strength for the rim. */
const RIM_POWER = 2.6;
const RIM_STRENGTH = 0.2;

/**
 * How far the last stretch of a hanging strand falls back toward the root colour,
 * and where that fall starts.
 *
 * ============================================================================
 * WHY THE ENDS ARE NOT THE BRIGHTEST PART
 * ============================================================================
 *
 * A two-stop root-to-tip ramp is right for one strand in isolation and wrong for
 * a hem made of twenty-five of them. Lifting every tip lights up every rod at its
 * own free end, and since those ends are what stands against the background, the
 * hem stopped reading as a mass of hair and started reading as a picket fence -
 * which is exactly what 「髮尾不協調」 is.
 *
 * The fix is the third stop an illustrator actually paints: dark at the roots,
 * brightest through the middle where the band runs, and then SETTLING again into
 * the ends. That is not a stylisation, it is what a hem does - the ends gather,
 * overlap and shadow one another, so the last stretch of long hair is darker than
 * the length above it, not lighter. It also closes the gaps for free: dark tips
 * sit much closer in value to the background showing between them, so the comb
 * teeth stop being individually legible and the hem softens into one shape.
 *
 * Only the hanging pieces take it. A bang is short, isolated against the face and
 * genuinely does thin to a lit point, so it settles far less.
 */
export const HANG_TIP_SHADE = 0.62;
export const FRINGE_TIP_SHADE = 0.25;
const TIP_SHADE_START = 0.55;

export interface HairMaterialOptions {
  /** The style's own colour, or a piece's `shadeHairColor`-derived tint of it. */
  color: string;
  roughness: number;
  /**
   * The slice of the WHOLE strand this piece covers, 0..1.
   *
   * Only `segmentedLock` ever passes anything but [0, 1], and it has to: it breaks
   * one lock into a chain of capsules, and each of those has its own uv.y running
   * the full 0..1. Shading them independently would restart the root-to-tip ramp
   * at every join, so a wave would come out as a stack of separately-shaded beads -
   * the exact striping the chain exists to avoid. Mapping each segment onto its own
   * share of the parent strand makes the gradient and the highlight bands run
   * continuously down the whole lock, across the seams.
   */
  span?: readonly [number, number];
  /**
   * Which end of `uv.y` is the DARK, occluded end - the end `t = 0` has to land on.
   *
   * Default (false) is a lock: its root is at local +Y, so uv.y = 1 is the buried
   * end and `t = 1 - uv.y`. Two kinds of piece are the other way round, for
   * unrelated reasons that come out at the same place:
   *
   *   CONES. three.js puts a cone's apex at +Y, so a spike's uv.y = 1 is its free
   *   tip and its dark end is the base it grows out of.
   *   THE SCALP SHELL. Its dark end is not a root at all - it is the RIM, which
   *   tucks under the skull and sits beneath whatever hair hangs over it, while
   *   the crown is the most exposed surface on the whole head. Shading the crown
   *   as a root is the one thing that fights the key light instead of agreeing
   *   with it, and it reads immediately: a head with its brightest lighting and
   *   its darkest pigment in the same place just looks muddy.
   */
  flip?: boolean;
  /**
   * Where the two highlight bands sit along `t`. Defaults to {@link HAIR_BANDS}.
   *
   * The scalp overrides them because flipping its ramp also flips where a `t` sits
   * on the head: measured from the rim upward, the ring an illustrator draws is
   * high on the dome, not a third of the way up it.
   */
  bands?: readonly [BandSpec, BandSpec];
  /**
   * Rim strength as a multiple of {@link RIM_STRENGTH}. 1 by default; the hanging
   * pieces turn it nearly off.
   *
   * A fresnel rim is a silhouette effect, and it is only ever as good as the
   * silhouette it is drawn on. On the scalp shell - ONE broad surface whose outline
   * is the outline of the head - it is the thing that lifts near-black hair off a
   * near-black background. On a bundle of thin locks it fires on every rod's edge,
   * so instead of lighting the hem's outline it draws twenty-five outlines INSIDE
   * the hem, and the mass comes apart into rods. Same effect, opposite result,
   * decided entirely by whether the piece IS the silhouette or is one strand of it.
   */
  rim?: number;
  /**
   * How far this piece's tip settles back toward the root colour, 0..1.
   * See {@link HANG_TIP_SHADE}.
   */
  tipShade?: number;
  /**
   * How much of the band's brightness is handed over to the piece's own break
   * profile, 0..1.
   *
   * Only the scalp asks for it, and only the scalp supplies the profile: it stores
   * a 0..1 dash value per column in `uv.x` (see `scalpGeometry`), because on a dome
   * the band is one continuous ring and a perfectly even ring is the giveaway that
   * it was computed rather than drawn - an illustrator breaks it into an uneven
   * dashed run.
   *
   * The hanging pieces leave this at 0, which is why `uv.x` meaning something else
   * on them (a capsule's circumferential coordinate) is harmless: at breakup 0 the
   * shader never reads it. They need no help anyway - they are already separate
   * locks at slightly different heights, so the band arrives broken for free, and
   * breaking it up WITHIN one thin lock would just be stripes down a strand.
   */
  breakup?: number;
  side?: THREE.Side;
  /**
   * The mohawk's blade glows, and that is a property of the ITEM rather than of
   * hair, so it is passed straight through to the standard material underneath
   * instead of being folded into the palette. The gradient and the bands still
   * apply on top of it - a lit crest is still hair.
   */
  emissive?: string;
  emissiveIntensity?: number;
}

const MATERIALS = new Map<string, THREE.MeshStandardMaterial>();

/**
 * Declarations injected ahead of the standard fragment shader's own.
 *
 * `hairT` folds the three axis conventions into one number: which end of uv.y is
 * the root (`uHairFlip`), and which slice of the parent strand this piece is
 * (`uHairSpan`).
 */
const HAIR_PARS = /* glsl */ `
uniform vec3 uHairRoot;
uniform vec3 uHairTip;
uniform vec3 uHairBand;
uniform vec3 uHairRimColor;
uniform vec2 uHairSpan;
uniform float uHairFlip;
uniform float uHairBreakup;
uniform vec3 uHairKeyDir;
uniform vec4 uHairBand1;
uniform vec4 uHairBand2;
uniform float uHairRimScale;
uniform float uHairTipShade;

float hairT() {
  float axis = mix(1.0 - vUv.y, vUv.y, uHairFlip);
  return clamp(mix(uHairSpan.x, uHairSpan.y, clamp(axis, 0.0, 1.0)), 0.0, 1.0);
}
`;

/**
 * The gradient, applied BEFORE lighting so it behaves like pigment rather than
 * like a decal: a root in shadow is a dark colour that is then also unlit, which
 * is what gives the mass its depth.
 *
 * `diffuseColor.rgb` is REPLACED rather than multiplied. Both ends of the ramp are
 * already derived from `material.color` by `hairPalette`, so multiplying would
 * apply the style's colour twice and drag every style toward black.
 */
const HAIR_GRADIENT = /* glsl */ `
{
  float t = hairT();
  vec3 shade = mix(uHairRoot, uHairTip, smoothstep(0.0, 1.0, t));
  // The third stop: the ends gather and shadow each other, so they settle back
  // toward the root colour instead of being the brightest thing on the head.
  shade = mix(shade, uHairRoot, uHairTipShade * smoothstep(${TIP_SHADE_START.toFixed(3)}, 1.0, t));
  shade *= mix(${ROOT_AO.toFixed(3)}, 1.0, smoothstep(0.0, ${ROOT_AO_FADE.toFixed(3)}, t));
  diffuseColor.rgb = shade;
}
`;

/**
 * The bands and the rim, added AFTER lighting.
 *
 * Deliberately not fed through the BRDF. A physical specular lobe on a surface
 * this lumpy comes out as scattered glints on whichever locks happen to face the
 * light, and the whole point of the band is that it is ONE shape crossing many
 * pieces - it has to be placed by where a fragment is along the hair, which is a
 * drawing decision, not a lighting one.
 *
 * It is still gated on the real light: `lit` kills the band on the shadowed side
 * of the head, and the half-vector term concentrates it toward where a shine
 * genuinely would be, so the band travels correctly as the character turns instead
 * of being painted at a fixed spot on the mesh.
 *
 * WHERE this goes in the chunk order is not free. It is added just before
 * `<tonemapping_fragment>`, which is the last point at which `gl_FragColor` is
 * still LINEAR: one chunk later `<colorspace_fragment>` has encoded it to sRGB,
 * and adding a linear colour to an encoded one double-brightens the band and
 * clips it. Injecting at `<dithering_fragment>`, the obvious end-of-shader hook,
 * is on the wrong side of exactly that line.
 */
const HAIR_HIGHLIGHT = /* glsl */ `
{
  float t = hairT();
  vec3 N = normalize(normal);
  vec3 V = normalize(vViewPosition);
  vec3 L = normalize((viewMatrix * vec4(uHairKeyDir, 0.0)).xyz);

  float lit = smoothstep(0.0, 0.55, dot(N, L));
  float shine = pow(max(dot(N, normalize(L + V)), 0.0), 10.0);

  float dash = mix(1.0, 0.34 + 0.66 * vUv.x, uHairBreakup);

  float b1 = (1.0 - smoothstep(0.0, uHairBand1.y, abs(t - uHairBand1.x))) * uHairBand1.z;
  float b2 = (1.0 - smoothstep(0.0, uHairBand2.y, abs(t - uHairBand2.x))) * uHairBand2.z;
  float ring = (b1 + b2) * dash * lit * (0.4 + 0.6 * shine);

  float fresnel = pow(1.0 - clamp(abs(dot(N, V)), 0.0, 1.0), ${RIM_POWER.toFixed(2)});

  gl_FragColor.rgb += uHairBand * ring + uHairRimColor * (fresnel * ${RIM_STRENGTH.toFixed(3)} * uHairRimScale);
}
`;

/**
 * ONE function, shared by every material this file hands out.
 *
 * Three calls this as a method, so `this` is the material being compiled, which is
 * what lets a single function serve materials with different palettes: the values
 * are read back off `userData` rather than closed over. That matters because
 * three's program cache key for a patched material is `onBeforeCompile.toString()`
 * - one function means one key means ONE compiled program for the whole shop,
 * however many materials the cache below ends up holding.
 */
function patchHairShader(
  this: THREE.MeshStandardMaterial,
  shader: THREE.WebGLProgramParametersWithUniforms,
) {
  Object.assign(shader.uniforms, this.userData.hairUniforms);
  shader.fragmentShader = shader.fragmentShader
    // Anchored on the UV declarations and NOT on `<common>`, which is the obvious
    // spot and three lines too early: three declares `varying vec2 vUv` in
    // `<uv_pars_fragment>`, which follows `<common>`, so a block injected after
    // `<common>` reads the varying before it exists and the whole shader fails to
    // compile with `'vUv' : undeclared identifier`. A hairstyle whose fragment
    // shader will not build is not a subtle bug - the mesh draws nothing at all.
    .replace('#include <uv_pars_fragment>', `#include <uv_pars_fragment>\n${HAIR_PARS}`)
    .replace('#include <color_fragment>', `#include <color_fragment>\n${HAIR_GRADIENT}`)
    .replace(
      '#include <tonemapping_fragment>',
      `${HAIR_HIGHLIGHT}\n#include <tonemapping_fragment>`,
    );
}

/**
 * A shaded hair material for one kind of piece.
 *
 * Returns a SHARED instance - callers must not mutate what comes back.
 */
export function hairMaterial(options: HairMaterialOptions): THREE.MeshStandardMaterial {
  const {
    color,
    roughness,
    span = [0, 1] as const,
    flip = false,
    breakup = 0,
    side = THREE.FrontSide,
    emissive,
    emissiveIntensity,
    bands = HAIR_BANDS,
    rim = 1,
    tipShade = 0,
  } = options;

  const key = [
    color,
    roughness.toFixed(2),
    span[0].toFixed(3),
    span[1].toFixed(3),
    flip ? 1 : 0,
    breakup.toFixed(2),
    side,
    emissive ?? '',
    emissiveIntensity ?? '',
    bands[0].center.toFixed(2),
    bands[1].center.toFixed(2),
    rim.toFixed(2),
    tipShade.toFixed(2),
  ].join('|');

  const cached = MATERIALS.get(key);
  if (cached) return cached;

  const palette = hairPalette(color);
  const material = new THREE.MeshStandardMaterial({
    color,
    roughness,
    side,
    ...(emissive === undefined ? {} : { emissive, emissiveIntensity }),
  });

  // Asks for `vUv` alone. Every chunk that reads it guards on `defined(USE_UV)`,
  // and none of the map transforms this would normally arrive with are involved,
  // so the varying is the entire cost.
  material.defines = { ...(material.defines ?? {}), USE_UV: '' };

  material.userData.hairUniforms = {
    uHairRoot: { value: palette.root },
    uHairTip: { value: palette.tip },
    uHairBand: { value: palette.band },
    uHairRimColor: { value: palette.rim },
    uHairRimScale: { value: rim },
    uHairTipShade: { value: tipShade },
    uHairSpan: { value: new THREE.Vector2(span[0], span[1]) },
    uHairFlip: { value: flip ? 1 : 0 },
    uHairBreakup: { value: breakup },
    uHairKeyDir: { value: KEY_LIGHT_DIR },
    uHairBand1: {
      value: new THREE.Vector4(bands[0].center, bands[0].width, bands[0].strength, 0),
    },
    uHairBand2: {
      value: new THREE.Vector4(bands[1].center, bands[1].width, bands[1].strength, 0),
    },
  };

  material.onBeforeCompile = patchHairShader;

  MATERIALS.set(key, material);
  return material;
}
```

## src/components/Three/character/legacy/index.tsx

```tsx
/**
 * @license
 * SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
 */

import { useMemo } from 'react';
import * as THREE from 'three';
import { PantsModel } from '../../Pants';
import { ShoeModel } from '../../Shoes';
import { JacketCuff } from '../../Outfits';
import { PANTS_PALETTES } from '../../../../constants/pants';
import { CHARACTER_ROOT_SCALE, LEG_LENGTHEN, LEGACY_TORSO_SHAPE, LEGACY_WEARABLE_FIT } from '../../../../constants/characterRig';
import type { CharacterAttachments, CharacterSkeleton } from '../../../../constants/characterRig';
import { CosmeticSlot } from '../../effects';
import { BodyForm } from '../bodyForm';
import { Attachment } from '../Attachment';
import { TorsoFit } from '../bodyFit';
import type { CharacterModelProps, CharacterOutfit, CharacterRig } from '../types';
import { GRASS_SKIRT_WAIST_R, GrassSkirt, HAT_CROWN_RING, HairPiece, LegacyEarring, LegacyGlasses, LegacyHat, LegacyTorsoWear, TribalMask, hairCrownRing, hairPinOnHair } from './wardrobe';

/**
 * THE LEGACY CHARACTER MODEL — the procedural chibi that ships today.
 *
 * Moved out of Avatar.tsx with its geometry untouched: every radius, offset and material
 * below is the number that was there before, so the shipped character is the same character.
 * What changed is only WHERE it lives and WHAT it is allowed to know.
 *
 * ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 * WHY IT IS FOUR PARTS AND NOT ONE COMPONENT
 * ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 *
 * Section 六 of the brief: a future model may arrive as separate head / torso / arm / leg
 * assets rather than one mesh, and it may arrive ONE PART AT A TIME. So each part below is
 * a standalone export, and `AuthoredCharacterModel` composes imported parts with these as
 * the fallback for whatever has not been made yet. That is what lets an authored head walk
 * around on legacy legs on day one instead of waiting for the whole body.
 *
 * ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 * WHAT EACH PART MAY AND MAY NOT DO
 * ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 *
 * MAY: choose its own geometry, materials, and — for the limbs — where its joint sits,
 *      since the controller writes rotation only there.
 * MAY NOT: hold state, run useFrame, read input, or set `position.y` on the head/torso
 *      joints. The controller re-asserts those from the skeleton every frame.
 *
 * Each part binds exactly one rig joint, at the joint's origin. Geometry inside a part is
 * PART-LOCAL — measured from that joint, not from the character's feet — which is the
 * convention an imported mesh's pivot has to match. See constants/characterRig.ts.
 */

/** Both legs are the same model mirrored, so the side is a parameter, not a copy. */
type Side = 'left' | 'right';

// ===========================================================================
// HEAD
// ===========================================================================

/**
 * Binds `rig.head`. HEAD-LOCAL: the origin is the head joint, which for this model is also
 * the centre of the skull sphere — a coincidence of a spherical head, and NOT something a
 * future head may assume, which is why the wearables mount through anchors rather than
 * off the sphere's centre.
 *
 * The hat, mask and earrings used to be children of the head MESH and the glasses/eyes/
 * mouth/blush siblings of it, an inconsistency with no meaning behind it. They are all
 * anchor-mounted now; the rendered result is identical because the mesh sat at the group's
 * own origin untransformed.
 */
export function LegacyHead({
  rig,
  skeleton,
  attachments,
  outfit,
}: {
  rig: CharacterRig;
  skeleton: CharacterSkeleton;
  attachments: CharacterAttachments;
  outfit: CharacterOutfit;
}) {
  return (
    <group ref={rig.head} position={[0, skeleton.head.y, 0]}>
      <mesh castShadow>
        <sphereGeometry args={[0.26, 32, 32]} />
        <meshStandardMaterial color={outfit.skinColor} roughness={0.7} />
      </mesh>

      <LegacyHeadWearables rig={rig} attachments={attachments} outfit={outfit} />

      {/* Expressive Eyes. Each is a GROUP holding the eyeball, so the controller's blink
          (scale.y) and squint (position.y) drive a transform rather than a mesh - which is
          what lets a future head make an eye out of something other than one sphere. */}
      <group position={[0, 0.035, 0.225]}>
        <group ref={rig.eyeL} position={[-0.104, 0, 0]}>
          <mesh castShadow={false}>
            <sphereGeometry args={[0.036, 16, 16]} />
            <meshStandardMaterial color="#0d1117" roughness={0.1} />
          </mesh>
        </group>
        <group ref={rig.eyeR} position={[0.104, 0, 0]}>
          <mesh castShadow={false}>
            <sphereGeometry args={[0.036, 16, 16]} />
            <meshStandardMaterial color="#0d1117" roughness={0.1} />
          </mesh>
        </group>
      </group>

      {/* Smile Mouth (Subtle mascot smile, shallow upward curve, centered horizontally and slightly below eye line) */}
      <group ref={rig.mouth} position={[0, -0.045, 0.255]}>
        <mesh rotation={[0, 0, Math.PI * 1.275]}>
          <torusGeometry args={[0.036, 0.0043, 8, 24, Math.PI * 0.45]} />
          <meshStandardMaterial color="#0d1117" roughness={0.5} />
        </mesh>
      </group>

      {/* Rose Blush (Cheeks) */}
      {/* Deeply embedded blush spheres to prevent protrusion from side views while maintaining cute front-view color */}
      <mesh position={[-0.122, -0.029, 0.180]}>
        <sphereGeometry args={[0.056, 16, 16]} />
        <meshStandardMaterial color="#fda4af" transparent opacity={0.3} roughness={0.9} />
      </mesh>
      <mesh position={[0.122, -0.029, 0.180]}>
        <sphereGeometry args={[0.056, 16, 16]} />
        <meshStandardMaterial color="#fda4af" transparent opacity={0.3} roughness={0.9} />
      </mesh>
    </group>
  );
}

/**
 * Everything worn ON the head, with no joint group of its own.
 *
 * Split out of LegacyHead so an IMPORTED head can host the same wardrobe: the authored model
 * renders this inside its own joint when its head part declares `wearsWardrobe`, which is what
 * keeps hats, hair, glasses, masks, earrings and the head cosmetics working the day a new
 * skull is dropped in, rather than only after every one of them is re-modelled. The sockets do
 * the fitting — see AUTHORED_ATTACHMENTS in constants/characterRig.ts.
 *
 * It takes `rig` for one thing only: `rig.hairSway`, which the HAIRSTYLE binds, not the head.
 */
export function LegacyHeadWearables({
  rig,
  attachments,
  outfit,
}: {
  rig: CharacterRig;
  attachments: CharacterAttachments;
  outfit: CharacterOutfit;
}) {
  /**
   * The wreath ring, re-aimed at whatever is actually outermost on this head.
   *
   * Composed here rather than in either half, because neither half can do it alone: the
   * MODEL owns `attachments.crown` (v2's is scaled 0.81 for its smaller skull), while the
   * HAT and the HAIRSTYLE each own where their own surface is. A bare head, or a hat with
   * no entry, falls through to the plain socket and nothing changes.
   *
   * Hat first, and not because it is more important: the crown ring sits high on the skull,
   * where a hat is the outermost surface and the hair under it has been pressed flat against
   * the head (see HairPiece and constants/hair.ts). So when both are on, the hat's own band
   * is what the wreath has to ring. See HAT_CROWN_BAND and hairCrownRing for the clash.
   */
  const crownPoint = useMemo(() => {
    const ring = outfit.hat
      ? HAT_CROWN_RING[outfit.hat]
      : outfit.hair
        ? hairCrownRing(outfit.hair)
        : null;
    if (!ring) return attachments.crown;
    const base = attachments.crown;
    const baseScale = base.scale ?? 1;
    return {
      position: [
        base.position[0] + ring.position[0] * baseScale,
        base.position[1] + ring.position[1] * baseScale,
        base.position[2] + ring.position[2] * baseScale,
      ] as const,
      rotation: ring.rotation ?? base.rotation,
      scale: baseScale * (ring.scale ?? 1),
    };
  }, [attachments.crown, outfit.hat]);

  const hairPinPoint = useMemo(
    () => hairPinOnHair(outfit.hair, attachments.hairPin, outfit.hat),
    [attachments.hairPin, outfit.hair, outfit.hat],
  );

  return (
    <>
      {outfit.hat && (
        <Attachment point={attachments.hat}>
          <LegacyHat kind={outfit.hat} />
        </Attachment>
      )}

      {/* Hairstyle - one spec in, one hairpiece out. See constants/hair.ts. */}
      <Attachment point={attachments.hair}>
        <HairPiece spec={outfit.hair} hat={outfit.hat} swayRef={rig.hairSway} />
      </Attachment>

      {/* Mask - see TribalMask for the 原住民 carving it now wears. It is told whether a hat
          is on for the same reason HairPiece is: both are authored around the whole skull,
          and a hat takes the top of that skull away. */}
      {outfit.hasMask && (
        <Attachment point={attachments.mask}>
          <TribalMask
            underHat={outfit.hat !== null}
            browOffset={(attachments.hat.position[1] - attachments.mask.position[1]) / (attachments.mask.scale ?? 1)}
          />
        </Attachment>
      )}

      {/* Earrings. One socket, mirrored - see Attachment. */}
      {outfit.earring && (
        <>
          <Attachment point={attachments.ear}>
            <LegacyEarring kind={outfit.earring} />
          </Attachment>
          <Attachment point={attachments.ear} mirror>
            <LegacyEarring kind={outfit.earring} />
          </Attachment>
        </>
      )}

      {outfit.hasGlasses && (
        <Attachment point={attachments.glasses}>
          <LegacyGlasses />
        </Attachment>
      )}

      {/* Special cosmetics — the ornaments that move (constants/cosmeticEffects.ts).
          The head declares only that it CAN host a pin and a wreath; which ones, what they
          look like and how they animate are the catalog's business, so a new star clip never
          reaches this file. See Three/effects/. */}
      {/* ...and the same composition for the pin socket, for the same reason and by the same
          rule: the model owns where the socket is, the HAIRSTYLE owns where its own surface is,
          and only this file has both. See hairPinOnHair. */}
      <CosmeticSlot
        socket="hairPin"
        cosmetics={outfit.specials}
        point={hairPinPoint}
        rootScale={CHARACTER_ROOT_SCALE}
      />
      <CosmeticSlot
        socket="crown"
        cosmetics={outfit.specials}
        point={crownPoint}
        rootScale={CHARACTER_ROOT_SCALE}
      />
      {/* Hovering above the crown, not on it. Under the HEAD joint, so a halo nods with the
          head-turn the controller writes — which is what keeps it reading as attached to this
          character rather than as a marker floating at a fixed height above them. */}
      <CosmeticSlot
        socket="halo"
        cosmetics={outfit.specials}
        point={attachments.halo}
        rootScale={CHARACTER_ROOT_SCALE}
      />
    </>
  );
}

// ===========================================================================
// TORSO
// ===========================================================================

/**
 * Binds `rig.torso`. TORSO-LOCAL, origin at the torso's centre.
 *
 * The joint is a GROUP wrapping the capsule rather than being the capsule. Same rendered
 * result — the mesh sits at the group's origin untransformed — but it separates the
 * transform the controller animates (rotation, the idle bob, the landing squash) from the
 * geometry the model owns, so an imported torso can be a whole GLB node here.
 */
export function LegacyTorso({
  rig,
  skeleton,
  attachments,
  outfit,
}: {
  rig: CharacterRig;
  skeleton: CharacterSkeleton;
  attachments: CharacterAttachments;
  outfit: CharacterOutfit;
}) {
  return (
    <group ref={rig.torso} position={[0, skeleton.torso.y, 0]}>
      <mesh castShadow>
        <capsuleGeometry args={[0.135, 0.08, 4, 16]} />
        <meshStandardMaterial color={outfit.bodyColor} roughness={0.7} />
      </mesh>

      {/* 身體銜接 — the shoulder yoke and the pelvis (constants/characterForm.ts).
          The capsule above tapers to a point at both ends, which is where the head is sunk in
          and where the legs come out; these two fills are what stop those being creases between
          primitives. Declared as data per MODEL, so an imported torso that has its own shoulders
          modelled in simply declares none and this draws nothing. */}
      <BodyForm modelId="legacy" joint="torso" outfit={outfit} />

      <LegacyTorsoWearables attachments={attachments} outfit={outfit} />
    </group>
  );
}

/**
 * Everything worn on the TORSO, with no joint group of its own — the sibling of
 * {@link LegacyHeadWearables}, split out for the same reason and mounted the same way by the
 * authored model.
 */
export function LegacyTorsoWearables({
  attachments,
  outfit,
}: {
  attachments: CharacterAttachments;
  outfit: CharacterOutfit;
}) {
  return (
    <>
      {/* Layered clothing. A model that states its torso's SHAPE gets the garments warped onto
          it rather than scaled — the socket scale can only fix size, and a chest that is shallower
          than it is wide wore every top as a bib standing off it. See character/bodyFit.tsx. */}
      {attachments.torsoShape ? (
        <group position={[...attachments.torso.position]}>
          <TorsoFit shape={attachments.torsoShape}>
            <LegacyTorsoWear outfit={outfit} withSkirt={false} />
          </TorsoFit>
          {/* The skirt is placed against the HIPS and the top's HEM rather than warped with the
              chest. Its hem keeps legacy's distance below the hip joint, so it ends at the same
              point on the thigh; its waistband sits on the line where every top now ends, so it
              covers that seam instead of riding up the chest as a dress. Warped, its flare was
              carried out past the dressed hem and it stood off like a lampshade. */}
          {outfit.hasSkirt && (() => {
            const shape = attachments.torsoShape;
            const hem = shape.hem ?? { y: shape.hipY, halfX: shape.halfX, halfZ: shape.halfZ };
            const ease = GRASS_SKIRT_WAIST_R - LEGACY_TORSO_SHAPE.halfX;
            return (
              <GrassSkirt
                top={hem.y + ease}
                hem={shape.hipY + (-0.205 - LEGACY_TORSO_SHAPE.hipY)}
                waistX={hem.halfX + ease / 2}
                waistZ={hem.halfZ + ease / 2}
              />
            );
          })()}
        </group>
      ) : (
        <Attachment point={attachments.torso}>
          <LegacyTorsoWear outfit={outfit} />
        </Attachment>
      )}

      {/* Pendant charms — see the hairPin/crown note in LegacyHead. */}
      <CosmeticSlot
        socket="pendant"
        cosmetics={outfit.specials}
        point={attachments.charm}
        rootScale={CHARACTER_ROOT_SCALE}
      />

      {/* Back wearables — capes, wings. Under the TORSO joint rather than the root, so they
          inherit the idle bob, the walk lean and the landing squash the controller writes
          there; a back wearable that ignored those would slide against the body on every
          step. Same one-line declaration as every other slot: the torso says it can host a
          back item and never learns which one. */}
      <CosmeticSlot
        socket="back"
        cosmetics={outfit.specials}
        point={attachments.back}
        rootScale={CHARACTER_ROOT_SCALE}
      />
    </>
  );
}

// ===========================================================================
// ARMS
// ===========================================================================

/**
 * Binds `rig.leftArm` / `rig.rightArm`. ARM-LOCAL, origin at the SHOULDER — the point the
 * controller rotates. The upper arm therefore hangs at negative y.
 *
 * How much longer the arms are than the original build, LOCAL. ~2 cm on the same
 * 1 world unit = ~0.8 m scale LEG_LENGTHEN derives, so 0.025 world and 0.0111 local.
 *
 * Simpler than the legs because an arm hangs free: nothing downstream has to be paid back,
 * so the upper-arm capsule just grows downward from a fixed shoulder and the fist follows it.
 * The sleeve does NOT move - it caps the shoulder end, which hasn't gone anywhere.
 */
const ARM_LENGTHEN = 0.0111;

export function LegacyArm({
  side,
  rig,
  skeleton,
  attachments,
  outfit,
}: {
  side: Side;
  rig: CharacterRig;
  skeleton: CharacterSkeleton;
  attachments: CharacterAttachments;
  outfit: CharacterOutfit;
}) {
  const x = side === 'left' ? -skeleton.shoulder.x : skeleton.shoulder.x;
  return (
    <group ref={side === 'left' ? rig.leftArm : rig.rightArm} position={[x, skeleton.shoulder.y, 0]}>
      <mesh position={[0, -0.07 - ARM_LENGTHEN / 2, 0]} castShadow>
        <capsuleGeometry args={[0.040, 0.10 + ARM_LENGTHEN, 4, 16]} />
        <meshStandardMaterial color={outfit.skinColor} roughness={0.7} />
      </mesh>
      {/* The deltoid, at the pivot the controller rotates — so the shoulder keeps the same
          silhouette through the whole swing instead of the capsule's end sweeping across the
          ribs. See constants/characterForm.ts. */}
      <BodyForm modelId="legacy" joint="arm" outfit={outfit} side={side} />
      <LegacyArmWearables attachments={attachments} outfit={outfit} />
      {/* Cute fist hand */}
      <mesh position={[0, -0.16 - ARM_LENGTHEN, 0]}>
        <sphereGeometry args={[0.08, 16, 16]} />
        <meshStandardMaterial color={outfit.skinColor} roughness={0.7} />
      </mesh>
    </group>
  );
}

/**
 * The sleeve, with no joint group of its own.
 *
 * The only wearable an arm has, and the one that WRAPS the limb rather than resting against a
 * point on it: a capsule drawn around the top of the upper arm, with the arm it was drawn for
 * baked into its radius and its height. On any other arm both of those are wrong, in the two
 * ways a sleeve can be — too narrow and the arm comes through its side, sat too low and the
 * shoulder stands bare above it.
 *
 * So it is socket-mounted like everything else now, on `attachments.sleeve`, which is legacy's
 * identity and the imported model's fit. The cuff goes inside the same socket rather than
 * beside it: it is a ring ON the sleeve, so it has to travel and resize with it or it ends up
 * banding a bare forearm.
 *
 * The authored model additionally renders this inside the arm's `transform`, so an imported arm
 * that hangs at an angle does not wear a sleeve pointing straight down through it.
 */
/**
 * The sleeve's shape: a shoulder dome, a straight tube, and an OPEN hem with a small turn-back.
 *
 * It used to be a closed capsule, and a capsule's lower cap is the wrong way to end a sleeve: it
 * curves in until it meets the arm, and the line where it does is a shallow intersection of two
 * faceted surfaces — which renders as a sawtooth of skin through cloth around the whole arm, and
 * on an arm not quite centred in it (the authored arm sits ~9 mm off the sleeve's axis) a lopsided
 * one. A real sleeve stops at a hem that stands off the arm; so does this one. Its outer radius
 * and its extent are legacy's capsule to the millimetre, so everything sized off
 * LEGACY_WEARABLE_FIT (the audit, the authored socket, the jacket's cuff) still holds.
 *
 * Built once at module scope: it is the same for every arm, and nothing else owns it.
 */
const SLEEVE_GEOMETRY = (() => {
  const { radius: r, length, y } = LEGACY_WEARABLE_FIT.sleeve;
  const top = y + length / 2;
  // The hem: where legacy's cap met the arm, so the sleeve does not get longer or shorter.
  const hemY = y - length / 2 - 0.0265;
  const profile: THREE.Vector2[] = [
    // Turn-back inside the hem, so looking up the sleeve shows a folded edge, not a raw tube.
    new THREE.Vector2(r * 0.96, hemY + 0.006),
    new THREE.Vector2(r * 1.04, hemY),
    new THREE.Vector2(r * 1.035, hemY + 0.005),
    new THREE.Vector2(r, hemY + 0.02),
    new THREE.Vector2(r, top),
  ];
  const DOME = 8;
  for (let i = 1; i <= DOME; i++) {
    const a = (i / DOME) * (Math.PI / 2);
    profile.push(new THREE.Vector2(i === DOME ? 0 : r * Math.cos(a), top + r * Math.sin(a)));
  }
  return new THREE.LatheGeometry(profile, 20);
})();

export function LegacyArmWearables({
  attachments,
  outfit,
}: {
  attachments: CharacterAttachments;
  outfit: CharacterOutfit;
}) {
  if (!outfit.hasSleeves) return null;
  return (
    <Attachment point={attachments.sleeve}>
      <mesh geometry={SLEEVE_GEOMETRY}>
        <meshStandardMaterial color={outfit.bodyColor} roughness={0.6} side={THREE.DoubleSide} />
      </mesh>
      {/* Knitted cuff closing the end of a flight-jacket sleeve. */}
      {outfit.outfit === 'jacket' && <JacketCuff />}
    </Attachment>
  );
}

// ===========================================================================
// LEGS
// ===========================================================================

/**
 * Binds `rig.leftLeg` / `rig.rightLeg`. LEG-LOCAL, origin at the HIP pivot, which is nested
 * up inside the torso so the thigh can swing without opening a gap at the seam.
 *
 * The trouser and the shoe are the two wearables that are NOT anchor-mounted with a plain
 * offset: both are lathed against this leg's own capsule (Pants.tsx and Shoes.tsx share
 * `LEG_RADIUS` and the derived ground height with it), so they take `legLengthen` and do
 * their own fitting. An imported leg will need those two refitted — which is exactly why
 * `attachments.foot` states where the sole is, so a shoe can be placed without re-deriving
 * it from a capsule that no longer exists.
 */
export function LegacyLeg({
  side,
  rig,
  skeleton,
  attachments,
  outfit,
}: {
  side: Side;
  rig: CharacterRig;
  skeleton: CharacterSkeleton;
  attachments: CharacterAttachments;
  outfit: CharacterOutfit;
}) {
  const x = side === 'left' ? -skeleton.hip.x : skeleton.hip.x;
  return (
    <group ref={side === 'left' ? rig.leftLeg : rig.rightLeg} position={[x, skeleton.hip.y, 0]}>
      {/* Grows downward only: dropping the centre by half of what the straight section
          gains holds the capsule's TOP at a constant -0.10 + (0.14/2 + 0.055) = 0.025
          above the hip pivot, which is what preserves the torso seam (see LEG_LENGTHEN). */}
      <mesh position={[0, -0.10 - LEG_LENGTHEN / 2, 0]} castShadow>
        <capsuleGeometry args={[0.055, 0.14 + LEG_LENGTHEN, 4, 16]} />
        <meshStandardMaterial
          color={
            // The LINING, not the garment: PantsModel lathes the actual trouser over this.
            // It stays trouser-coloured rather than reverting to skin so that a crease
            // displaced inward, or the gap under a wide hem, can never flash bare leg.
            //
            // The colours themselves used to be spelled out here, once per leg, and
            // disagreed with the shop icon on five cuts out of six - buy a near-white
            // 寬褲, wear a dark slate one. They now come from constants/pants.ts, which
            // both this and QVersionIcon read.
            //
            // Deliberately no shoe branch: a shoe now models its own upper, and a boot its
            // shaft, so the leg underneath is just the leg. Tinting it by shoe is what used
            // to turn a bare-legged avatar in sandals into one solid brown stick.
            outfit.pants ? PANTS_PALETTES[outfit.pants].body : outfit.skinColor
          }
          roughness={0.7}
        />
      </mesh>

      {/* Nothing declared on the leg today — the knee and the ankle both sit under the trousers'
          2.5 mm clearance, so there is no room for a fill there (see constants/characterForm.ts).
          Mounted anyway so a model that DOES declare one gets it without editing this file. */}
      <BodyForm modelId="legacy" joint="leg" outfit={outfit} side={side} />

      <LegacyLegWearables side={side} attachments={attachments} outfit={outfit} />
    </group>
  );
}

/**
 * Everything worn on a LEG, with no joint group of its own.
 *
 * The trousers and the shoe are the two wearables that still measure the body rather than
 * asking a socket: both are lathed against `LEG_RADIUS = 0.055` in Pants.tsx / Shoes.tsx. They
 * survive the imported leg by luck rather than by design — its thigh comes out at 0.0554 after
 * the splitter's unit fix — so this is the pair to look at first if a new export makes the
 * legs thicker. `attachments.foot` is the part that IS derived, which is what keeps a shoe on
 * the ground when the leg length changes.
 */
export function LegacyLegWearables({
  side,
  attachments,
  outfit,
}: {
  side: Side;
  attachments: CharacterAttachments;
  outfit: CharacterOutfit;
}) {
  return (
    <>
      {outfit.pants && (
        /* side -1 is the left leg, so its pockets and zips face -x, away from the body.
           See the LOCAL SPACE note in Pants.tsx. */
        <Attachment point={attachments.leg}>
          <PantsModel
            cut={outfit.pants}
            side={side === 'left' ? -1 : 1}
            legLengthen={LEG_LENGTHEN}
            rise={attachments.trouserRise}
            overBoots={outfit.shoes === 'boots'}
          />
        </Attachment>
      )}
      {outfit.shoes && (
        /* Anchored on the sole rather than the hip: `attachments.foot` lands the shoe's own
           origin on the leg capsule's bottom cap, which is the foot's ground contact. */
        <Attachment point={attachments.foot}>
          <ShoeModel type={outfit.shoes} skinColor={outfit.skinColor} />
        </Attachment>
      )}

      {/* Anklets. Rendered by the LEG, so one catalog row puts a band on both legs and each one
          swings with the leg it is on — the pair is out of step for free, because the walk cycle
          already moves the two joints separately. */}
      <CosmeticSlot
        socket="ankle"
        cosmetics={outfit.specials}
        point={attachments.ankle}
        rootScale={CHARACTER_ROOT_SCALE}
      />
    </>
  );
}

/**
 * The ground cosmetics, which belong to the FLOOR rather than to any body part — so they hang
 * off the character ROOT, and every model has to render them itself.
 *
 * Extracted for the same reason as the other four: so the authored model can mount the same
 * one line instead of quietly dropping every ground aura the moment a part is imported.
 */
export function LegacyGroundWearables({
  attachments,
  outfit,
}: {
  attachments: CharacterAttachments;
  outfit: CharacterOutfit;
}) {
  return (
    <CosmeticSlot
      socket="aura"
      cosmetics={outfit.specials}
      point={attachments.aura}
      rootScale={CHARACTER_ROOT_SCALE}
    />
  );
}

// ===========================================================================
// THE ASSEMBLED MODEL
// ===========================================================================

/**
 * The four parts hung off the character root. Note there is no transform here at all: the
 * root is the controller's, and every part places itself from the skeleton, so this
 * component is pure assembly.
 */
export function LegacyCharacterModel({ rig, skeleton, attachments, outfit }: CharacterModelProps) {
  return (
    <>
      <LegacyHead rig={rig} skeleton={skeleton} attachments={attachments} outfit={outfit} />
      <LegacyTorso rig={rig} skeleton={skeleton} attachments={attachments} outfit={outfit} />
      <LegacyArm side="left" rig={rig} skeleton={skeleton} attachments={attachments} outfit={outfit} />
      <LegacyArm side="right" rig={rig} skeleton={skeleton} attachments={attachments} outfit={outfit} />
      <LegacyLeg side="left" rig={rig} skeleton={skeleton} attachments={attachments} outfit={outfit} />
      <LegacyLeg side="right" rig={rig} skeleton={skeleton} attachments={attachments} outfit={outfit} />

      {/* Ground cosmetics. The one slot mounted at the ROOT rather than under a body part,
          because what it hangs off is the floor: the root origin is the ground contact point,
          so this anchor is (0,0,0) and the runtime takes it from there — see GroundSpec. */}
      <LegacyGroundWearables attachments={attachments} outfit={outfit} />
    </>
  );
}
```
