## src/components/Three/character/outfit.ts

```ts
/**
 * @license
 * SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
 */

import type { ItemDefinition } from '../../../constants/items';
import { ItemCategory } from '../../../types';
import { AVATAR_SKIN_COLOR, resolveHairSpec } from '../../../constants/hair';
import { OUTFIT_HAS_SLEEVES, OUTFIT_SHELL_COLOR } from '../Outfits';
import type { OutfitType } from '../Outfits';
import type { PantsCut } from '../../../constants/pants';
import type { ShoeType } from '../Shoes';
import { resolveSpecialCosmetics } from '../../../constants/cosmeticEffects';
import type { CharacterOutfit, EarringKind, HatKind } from './types';

/**
 * WHAT the player is wearing, resolved from the equipped item list.
 *
 * Lifted out of Avatar.tsx unchanged — same name matching, same precedence, same colours.
 * It is here rather than in the controller because it is neither controller logic nor
 * model geometry: it is the translation between the two, and both a model and the dressing
 * room preview need the same answer out of it.
 *
 * Pure and synchronous on purpose. Every model gets the identical `CharacterOutfit`, so two
 * models cannot disagree about whether a 貝雷帽 is a hat, and a new model gets the whole
 * wardrobe resolved for free the moment it can draw it.
 */
export function resolveCharacterOutfit(equipped: readonly ItemDefinition[]): CharacterOutfit {
  const wearing = (needle: string) => equipped.some(item => item.name.includes(needle));

  // --- Tops ---
  const hasSkirt = wearing('草裙');
  const hasShirt = wearing('襯衫');
  const hasSurf = wearing('衝浪運動裝');
  const hasSwim = wearing('沙灘泳衣');
  const hasExplorerSuit = wearing('探險套裝');
  const hasVest = wearing('探險背心');
  const hasCaptain = wearing('船長制服');
  const hasDiving = wearing('潛水服');
  const hasShawl = wearing('披肩');
  const hasJacket = wearing('夾克');
  // Kept for the equipped-anything checks below, which only care that SOME top is on.
  const hasAdventure = hasExplorerSuit || hasVest;

  /**
   * Exactly one torso garment is drawn. Ordered most-covering first: a captain's coat over a
   * shawl has to win, or the two shells fight over the same few millimetres of torso surface
   * and z-fight. Beach swimwear is not in here - it keeps its own separate model.
   */
  const outfit: OutfitType | null =
    hasCaptain ? 'captain' :
    hasDiving ? 'diving' :
    hasSurf ? 'surf' :
    hasJacket ? 'jacket' :
    hasExplorerSuit ? 'explorer' :
    hasVest ? 'vest' :
    hasShawl ? 'shawl' :
    null;

  // --- Hats ---
  const hat: HatKind | null =
    equipped.some(item => item.name === '草帽') ? 'straw' :
    wearing('漁夫帽') ? 'bucket' :
    wearing('貝雷帽') ? 'beret' :
    wearing('毛帽') ? 'beanie' :
    wearing('平板帽') ? 'snapback' :
    null;

  // --- Necklaces ---
  const jewellery = equipped.filter(
    item => item.category === ItemCategory.NECKLACE && !item.name.includes('貝殼'),
  );

  // --- Earrings ---
  const earring: EarringKind | null =
    wearing('藍寶石') ? 'jewel' :
    wearing('花環耳飾') ? 'flower' :
    wearing('珍珠耳環') ? 'pearl' :
    wearing('金質耳環') ? 'gold' :
    wearing('珊瑚飾品') ? 'coral' :
    wearing('海星耳釘') ? 'star' :
    null;

  /**
   * Exactly one shoe is drawn. Two shoe items can be equipped at once, so without a single
   * winner the foot would try to wear both models at the same time. Most-covering first:
   * a boot's shaft would swallow anything picked under it anyway.
   *
   * MATCHED BY ID, unlike every garment above it, and that is not a style preference — it is
   * the one place where the name matching had already broken. 運動/休閒鞋's own 運動 is also
   * inside 衝浪運動裝, so `wearing('運動')` put a pair of trainers on the feet of anyone
   * wearing the surf suit; and because sport outranks sandals and flip-flops in this chain,
   * it also took those OFF a player who had actually bought a pair. A substring cannot tell
   * a garment from a shoe, so this rung of the ladder does not ask it to.
   */
  const wearingId = (id: string) => equipped.some(item => item.id === id);
  const shoes: ShoeType | null =
    wearingId('shoes-boots') ? 'boots' :
    wearingId('shoes-heels') ? 'heels' :
    wearingId('shoes-leather') ? 'leather' :
    wearingId('shoes-sport') ? 'sport' :
    wearingId('shoes-sandals') ? 'sandals' :
    // 'shoes-flats' is the 夾腳拖's id: it kept the old id so that players who had already
    // bought it did not lose it when the item changed. See constants/items.ts.
    wearingId('shoes-flats') ? 'flipflops' :
    null;

  // --- Pants ---
  const hasStraightPants = wearing('直筒褲');
  const hasWidePants = wearing('寬褲');
  const hasCargoPants = wearing('工裝褲');
  const hasSkinnyPants = wearing('窄管') || wearing('緊身褲');
  const hasTaperedPants = wearing('錐形') || wearing('蘿蔔褲');
  const hasDenimPants = wearing('牛仔褲');

  // Fallback Outfit System Check
  const isAnyShirtEquipped = hasShirt || hasSurf || hasSwim || hasAdventure || hasCaptain || hasDiving || hasShawl || hasJacket;
  const hasFallbackShirt = !isAnyShirtEquipped;

  const isAnyPantsEquipped = hasStraightPants || hasWidePants || hasCargoPants || hasSkinnyPants || hasTaperedPants || hasDenimPants || hasSkirt || hasSwim;
  const isFallbackPantsActive = !isAnyPantsEquipped;

  /**
   * Which trouser to build, resolved once from the flags above instead of at each leg.
   *
   * Null means "do not put trousers on this avatar at all", which is NOT the same as the
   * fallback pair: a 草裙 or a 沙灘泳衣 is already the bottom half of the outfit, so it counts
   * as pants being equipped (see isAnyPantsEquipped) and must not get a trouser leg lathed
   * over it. Only a genuinely bare-legged avatar wears the fallback.
   */
  const pants: PantsCut | null =
    hasStraightPants ? 'straight' :
    hasTaperedPants ? 'tapered' :
    hasWidePants ? 'wide' :
    hasSkinnyPants ? 'skinny' :
    hasCargoPants ? 'cargo' :
    hasDenimPants ? 'denim' :
    isFallbackPantsActive ? 'fallback' :
    null;

  const skinColor = AVATAR_SKIN_COLOR;
  let bodyColor = skinColor;
  if (hasShirt) bodyColor = '#38bdf8'; // Sky 400
  else if (hasSwim) bodyColor = '#f43f5e'; // Rose 500
  // Single source of truth with the 3D garment itself, so the sleeves and the torso under
  // the shell can never disagree with the shell - or with the shop icon it was taken from.
  else if (outfit) bodyColor = OUTFIT_SHELL_COLOR[outfit];
  else if (hasFallbackShirt) bodyColor = '#718096'; // Gray fallback shirt color

  return {
    // Hairstyles - exactly one spec, so two styles can never render on one head.
    hair: resolveHairSpec(equipped),
    hat,
    outfit,
    pants,
    shoes,
    necklaceId: jewellery.length > 0 ? jewellery[0].id : null,
    earring,
    hasGlasses: wearing('墨鏡'),
    hasMask: wearing('面具'),
    hasShellNecklace: wearing('貝殼項鍊'),
    hasSkirt,
    hasSwimsuit: hasSwim,
    hasShirt,
    hasFallbackShirt,
    hasSleeves: hasShirt || hasFallbackShirt || (outfit !== null && OUTFIT_HAS_SLEEVES[outfit]),
    /**
     * Special cosmetics, resolved by ITEM ID.
     *
     * Note the contrast with every line above it. This function matches on substrings of
     * Chinese item names because it predates stable ids, and that is a debt to contain
     * rather than a pattern to extend: `wearing('星星髮飾')` would also match a future
     * 小星星髮飾, and the wrong one would silently win. A catalog keyed on id cannot do that.
     *
     * Pet cosmetics are filtered out here by their socket, so an equipped 蘑菇帽 never ends
     * up on the player's head — the catalog's own SOCKET_WEARER table is what decides, not a
     * naming convention.
     */
    specials: resolveSpecialCosmetics(equipped.map(item => item.id), 'player'),
    skinColor,
    bodyColor,
  };
}
```

## src/components/Three/character/partLoader.tsx

```tsx
/**
 * @license
 * SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
 */

import { Component, useLayoutEffect, useMemo } from 'react';
import type { ErrorInfo, ReactNode } from 'react';
import * as THREE from 'three';
import { useGLTF } from '@react-three/drei';
import { CHARACTER_MODEL_BUDGET } from '../../../constants/characterAssets';
import type { CharacterOutfit, CharacterRig } from './types';

/**
 * LOADING A HAND-MADE PART — the file that turns a .glb on disk into something the rig can
 * drive, and the file that makes a broken .glb a message instead of a black screen.
 *
 * Three jobs, in the order they matter:
 *
 *   1. NEVER take the game down. A model that 404s, arrives truncated, or throws inside the
 *      parser must degrade to the procedural part, not to an error screen. See
 *      {@link CharacterPartBoundary}.
 *   2. Say what is wrong, in dev, in terms of the thing that is actually wrong. See
 *      {@link validateCharacterPart}.
 *   3. Load the thing. See {@link GlbPart}.
 *
 * None of this assumes anything about how the finished model is built: no bone name is
 * required or looked for, no rig is expected, no part count is fixed. Everything the
 * validator checks is either structural (is there geometry at all, is the bounding box a real
 * number) or a comparison against a number the project already states about itself.
 */

// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
// FAILURE — the fallback path
// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

/**
 * Catches anything thrown while a character part loads or renders, and shows the fallback
 * part instead — which in practice is the procedural part that has always been there.
 *
 * WHY THIS IS NOT OPTIONAL. `Suspense` handles a part that is still ARRIVING; it does nothing
 * for a part that arrives broken. `useGLTF` throws on a 404, on malformed binary, and on an
 * unsupported extension, and without a boundary here that throw unwinds all the way to the
 * app-level one in main.tsx — so a single mistyped filename replaces the ENTIRE GAME with an
 * error screen, in a project where models are meant to be dropped in and tried one at a time.
 * The blast radius of a bad asset should be that one limb.
 *
 * The fallback is a thunk for the same reason it is one in AuthoredCharacterModel: the
 * procedural part binds a rig ref, and handing a single element to both the normal path and
 * the fallback would bind that ref from two places at once.
 */
export class CharacterPartBoundary extends Component<
  { label: string; fallback: () => ReactNode; children: ReactNode },
  { failed: boolean }
> {
  state = { failed: false };

  static getDerivedStateFromError() {
    return { failed: true };
  }

  componentDidCatch(error: Error, info: ErrorInfo) {
    // Loud in dev, and still recorded in production. A player never sees this, but a part
    // quietly falling back to the old one is exactly the kind of thing that otherwise gets
    // noticed weeks later as "the new head sometimes doesn't show up".
    console.error(
      `[character] the "${this.props.label}" part failed to load and has fallen back to the ` +
        `procedural part. The character is complete and playable; only this part is not the ` +
        `imported one.\n` +
        `  Check: the file exists under public/models/character/, the path in ` +
        `constants/characterAssets.ts matches it, and the export is glTF-Binary (.glb).`,
      error,
      info.componentStack,
    );
  }

  render() {
    return this.state.failed ? this.props.fallback() : this.props.children;
  }
}

// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
// VALIDATION — dev only
// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

/** What one part costs, kept so the budget can be judged on the WHOLE character. */
interface PartCost {
  triangles: number;
  meshes: number;
  materials: number;
  maxTexture: number;
}

const loadedCosts = new Map<string, PartCost>();

export interface PartValidationContext {
  /** What to call this part in messages — the slot id, e.g. `head`. */
  label: string;
  /**
   * The character's total height in LOCAL units (see constants/characterRig.ts). The unit
   * check compares the part against this rather than against a hardcoded figure, so it keeps
   * working if the character is ever re-proportioned.
   */
  bodyLocalHeight: number;
}

/**
 * Checks a loaded part and reports to the console. Dev only, and it NEVER throws: a model
 * that fails every check still renders, because seeing what is wrong beats not seeing it.
 *
 * WHAT IT DELIBERATELY DOES NOT CHECK: bone names, bone counts, whether a skeleton exists at
 * all, how many parts there are, or the part's proportions. None of that is decided yet, and
 * a validator that guessed would be quietly enforcing a rig nobody agreed to. Skeleton and
 * animation content is REPORTED, never required.
 */
export function validateCharacterPart(root: THREE.Object3D, ctx: PartValidationContext): void {
  if (!import.meta.env.DEV) return;

  const errors: string[] = [];
  const warnings: string[] = [];
  const notes: string[] = [];

  // --- Geometry, material, skeleton, cost -----------------------------------
  let meshes = 0;
  let triangles = 0;
  let vertices = 0;
  let missingMaterial = 0;
  let skinnedMeshes = 0;
  let maxTexture = 0;
  const materials = new Set<THREE.Material>();
  const bones: string[] = [];

  root.traverse((node) => {
    if ((node as THREE.Bone).isBone) bones.push(node.name || '(unnamed)');

    const mesh = node as THREE.Mesh;
    if (!mesh.isMesh) return;
    meshes += 1;
    if ((mesh as unknown as THREE.SkinnedMesh).isSkinnedMesh) skinnedMeshes += 1;

    const geom = mesh.geometry;
    const pos = geom?.getAttribute?.('position');
    if (pos) {
      vertices += pos.count;
      triangles += geom.index ? geom.index.count / 3 : pos.count / 3;
    }

    const mats = Array.isArray(mesh.material) ? mesh.material : [mesh.material];
    for (const mat of mats) {
      if (!mat) {
        missingMaterial += 1;
        continue;
      }
      materials.add(mat);
      for (const value of Object.values(mat as unknown as Record<string, unknown>)) {
        const tex = value as THREE.Texture;
        // `Texture.image` is `any`-shaped in three's types (it can be an ImageBitmap, a canvas,
        // a video or a plain data object), so the dimensions are read through a narrow cast
        // rather than trusted. A source without them simply contributes nothing to the max.
        const img = tex?.isTexture ? (tex.image as { width?: number; height?: number } | null) : null;
        if (img) maxTexture = Math.max(maxTexture, img.width ?? 0, img.height ?? 0);
      }
    }
  });

  if (meshes === 0) {
    errors.push(
      'contains no mesh at all. The file loaded, so this is an export problem rather than a ' +
        'path problem — usually exporting with nothing selected, or exporting only an armature.',
    );
  } else if (vertices === 0) {
    errors.push('has meshes but no vertices — the geometry did not survive the export.');
  }
  if (missingMaterial > 0) {
    errors.push(`has ${missingMaterial} mesh(es) with no material; they render as default white.`);
  }

  // --- Bounding box: finite, real, and the right ORDER OF MAGNITUDE ---------
  //
  // The units mistake is the one import bug that is both near-certain to happen and invisible
  // in the modelling tool: a model authored at human scale looks perfectly correct right up
  // until it is dropped into a world measured in LOCAL units. Catching it here turns "the
  // character is a skyscraper" into a line saying exactly what to multiply by.
  const box = new THREE.Box3().setFromObject(root);
  const size = box.getSize(new THREE.Vector3());
  const largest = Math.max(size.x, size.y, size.z);
  const finite = [box.min, box.max].every(
    (v) => Number.isFinite(v.x) && Number.isFinite(v.y) && Number.isFinite(v.z),
  );

  if (meshes > 0 && !finite) {
    errors.push(
      'has a non-finite bounding box (NaN vertex data). It will not appear, and it can poison ' +
        'anything that measures the scene.',
    );
  } else if (meshes > 0 && largest <= 1e-6) {
    errors.push('has a zero-sized bounding box — every vertex is at the same point.');
  } else if (meshes > 0) {
    const body = ctx.bodyLocalHeight;
    if (largest > body * 1.5) {
      warnings.push(
        `is ${largest.toFixed(3)} units across against a character only ${body.toFixed(3)} tall ` +
          `— about ${(largest / body).toFixed(1)}x too big. This is the units mistake: the part ` +
          `was almost certainly authored at real-world scale. Fix it in the EXPORT (scale ` +
          `${(body / largest).toFixed(4)}), not with a transform here.`,
      );
    } else if (largest < body / 50) {
      warnings.push(
        `is only ${largest.toFixed(4)} units across against a ${body.toFixed(3)}-tall character, ` +
          `so it will be invisible. Likely authored in millimetres.`,
      );
    }

    // Where the ORIGIN sits relative to the geometry. A part authored about its joint has its
    // origin on or inside its own bounds; one authored about the world origin, or about its own
    // centre when it should be about the shoulder, sits off to one side. A warning rather than
    // an error, because how far off the joint should sit genuinely depends on the part.
    const centre = box.getCenter(new THREE.Vector3());
    if (centre.length() > largest * 1.5) {
      warnings.push(
        `sits ${centre.length().toFixed(3)} units away from its own origin. A part is authored ` +
          `about its JOINT — the point it rotates about — so the origin belongs on or inside the ` +
          `geometry. An arm pivoting about its centre instead of its shoulder looks correct ` +
          `standing still and detaches the moment the character walks.`,
      );
    }
    notes.push(
      `bounds ${size.x.toFixed(3)}x${size.y.toFixed(3)}x${size.z.toFixed(3)}, ` +
        `origin offset ${centre.length().toFixed(3)}`,
    );
  }

  // --- Skeleton and animation: reported, never required ---------------------
  if (skinnedMeshes > 0 || bones.length > 0) {
    notes.push(
      `${skinnedMeshes} skinned mesh(es), ${bones.length} bone(s): ` +
        `${bones.slice(0, 12).join(', ')}${bones.length > 12 ? ', …' : ''}`,
    );
  } else {
    notes.push('no skeleton (rigid part) — fine: the controller animates the joint group above it');
  }

  // --- Performance, judged on the whole character ---------------------------
  loadedCosts.set(ctx.label, { triangles, meshes, materials: materials.size, maxTexture });
  const total = [...loadedCosts.values()].reduce<PartCost>(
    (acc, c) => ({
      triangles: acc.triangles + c.triangles,
      meshes: acc.meshes + c.meshes,
      materials: acc.materials + c.materials,
      maxTexture: Math.max(acc.maxTexture, c.maxTexture),
    }),
    { triangles: 0, meshes: 0, materials: 0, maxTexture: 0 },
  );

  const over: string[] = [];
  if (total.triangles > CHARACTER_MODEL_BUDGET.triangles) {
    over.push(`${Math.round(total.triangles)} triangles (budget ${CHARACTER_MODEL_BUDGET.triangles})`);
  }
  if (total.meshes > CHARACTER_MODEL_BUDGET.meshes) {
    over.push(
      `${total.meshes} meshes (budget ${CHARACTER_MODEL_BUDGET.meshes}) — each is a draw call, ` +
        `merge them in the modelling tool`,
    );
  }
  if (total.materials > CHARACTER_MODEL_BUDGET.materials) {
    over.push(`${total.materials} materials (budget ${CHARACTER_MODEL_BUDGET.materials})`);
  }
  if (total.maxTexture > CHARACTER_MODEL_BUDGET.textureSize) {
    over.push(`${total.maxTexture}px texture (budget ${CHARACTER_MODEL_BUDGET.textureSize}px)`);
  }
  if (over.length > 0) {
    warnings.push(`the character as a whole is now over budget: ${over.join('; ')}.`);
  }

  notes.push(
    `cost ${Math.round(triangles)} tris / ${meshes} mesh / ${materials.size} mat` +
      `${maxTexture ? ` / ${maxTexture}px tex` : ''} ` +
      `(character total ${Math.round(total.triangles)} tris, ${total.meshes} mesh)`,
  );

  // --- Report ---------------------------------------------------------------
  const head = `[character] "${ctx.label}"`;
  for (const e of errors) console.error(`${head} ${e}`);
  for (const w of warnings) console.warn(`${head} ${w}`);
  console.info(
    `${head}${errors.length === 0 && warnings.length === 0 ? ' loaded OK —' : ''} ${notes.join(' | ')}`,
  );
}

// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
// THE LOADER
// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

/**
 * Loads a .glb part and drops its scene in at the joint.
 *
 * `clone` is deliberate: `useGLTF` caches one scene per URL, so mounting the same asset twice
 * (both arms from one file, or the dressing-room preview alongside the world avatar — the
 * dressing room renders the SAME Avatar component) would otherwise have the two instances
 * fight over one Object3D's parent.
 *
 * The shadow pass is deliberate too. glTF has no concept of `castShadow`, so an imported mesh
 * arrives with it false while every procedural part sets it true — leaving exactly one piece
 * of the character not casting a shadow, which reads as that piece floating and gets blamed on
 * the model rather than on the loader.
 */
/**
 * The props are exactly `AuthoredPartProps` plus a `url`, and deliberately so: it is what lets
 * a registration in slots.tsx be the single line
 *
 *     head: { Component: (p) => <GlbPart url={CHARACTER_MODEL_FILES.head} {...p} /> }
 *
 * with no destructuring and no adapter. They are spelled structurally rather than imported from
 * slots.tsx to keep the dependency pointing one way — the registry knows about the loader, the
 * loader knows nothing about the registry. `outfit` is accepted and ignored: a plain imported
 * mesh has no colours to apply, and a part that DOES need them writes its own component instead
 * of using this one.
 */
export function GlbPart({
  url,
  partId,
  bodyLocalHeight,
}: {
  url: string;
  partId: string;
  bodyLocalHeight: number;
}) {
  return <primitive object={usePreparedGlb(url, partId, bodyLocalHeight)} />;
}

/**
 * A part that takes its colour from what is being WORN, the way the procedural part it replaces
 * always has.
 *
 * Legacy never had a separate "bare body" colour: its torso capsule is drawn in
 * `outfit.bodyColor` (skin, or the shirt's, the swimsuit's, the outfit shell's), and its leg
 * capsule in the trousers' lining colour or skin. Several garments lean on that. The 沙灘泳衣 is
 * a strap and a band over a torso that is itself rose; the leg under a wide hem is the trousers'
 * lining, not skin. An imported part with its colours baked in dropped all of it — a swimsuit
 * became a red ribbon across a bare chest, and every bare-legged outfit (swimsuit, grass skirt)
 * stood on the grey legs the source file was exported with.
 *
 * So the part's materials are CLONED for this instance and recoloured from `tint(outfit)`.
 * Cloned, because `useGLTF` shares one material between both legs and the dressing-room preview.
 * The clone drops the character-surface mark it may have copied, so bodySurface.ts patches it
 * again — `Material.copy` does not carry `onBeforeCompile` over.
 */
export function GlbTintedPart({
  url,
  partId,
  bodyLocalHeight,
  outfit,
  tint,
}: {
  url: string;
  partId: string;
  bodyLocalHeight: number;
  outfit: CharacterOutfit;
  tint: (outfit: CharacterOutfit) => string;
}) {
  const prepared = usePreparedGlb(url, partId, bodyLocalHeight);
  const materials = useMemo(() => {
    const owned: THREE.MeshStandardMaterial[] = [];
    prepared.traverse((child) => {
      const mesh = child as THREE.Mesh;
      if (!mesh.isMesh) return;
      const source = mesh.material as THREE.MeshStandardMaterial;
      if (!source?.isMeshStandardMaterial) return;
      const material = source.clone();
      delete material.userData.characterSurface;
      mesh.material = material;
      owned.push(material);
    });
    return owned;
  }, [prepared]);

  const color = tint(outfit);
  useLayoutEffect(() => {
    for (const material of materials) material.color.set(color);
  }, [materials, color]);

  useLayoutEffect(() => () => {
    for (const material of materials) material.dispose();
  }, [materials]);

  return <primitive object={prepared} />;
}

/**
 * The shared half of {@link GlbPart}: load, clone, fix shadows, validate.
 *
 * Split out so a part that needs to do something MORE with the loaded scene — bind a node to
 * the rig, tint a material, hide a mesh for an outfit — does not have to re-implement the
 * loading rules and quietly drop the clone or the shadow pass while doing it.
 */
function usePreparedGlb(url: string, partId: string, bodyLocalHeight: number): THREE.Object3D {
  const { scene } = useGLTF(url);
  return useMemo(() => {
    const root = scene.clone(true);
    root.traverse((child) => {
      const mesh = child as THREE.Mesh;
      if (mesh.isMesh) mesh.castShadow = true;
    });
    validateCharacterPart(root, { label: partId, bodyLocalHeight });
    return root;
  }, [scene, partId, bodyLocalHeight]);
}

/**
 * A head part, plus the one thing a head has that no other part does: EYES the controller
 * drives.
 *
 * `rig.eyeL` / `rig.eyeR` take `scale.y` for the blink and squint and an absolute `position.y`
 * for the squint lift (see CharacterRig). Both are transforms about the eye's own centre, so
 * each eye has to be its OWN node — an eye left inside the head mesh would blink by scaling
 * the whole skull about the neck. The part file therefore ships an `Eye_L` and an `Eye_R`
 * group sitting at each eye, which `npm run split:character` builds; this binds them.
 *
 * Bound imperatively rather than through a React `ref` because the nodes come out of a loaded
 * file rather than out of JSX. Everything about it is optional: a head with no eye nodes — an
 * early export, a masked character, a model that simply has no face — leaves the refs unbound,
 * and the controller null-checks every one of them. The face stops blinking; nothing breaks.
 */
export function GlbHeadPart({
  url,
  partId,
  bodyLocalHeight,
  rig,
}: {
  url: string;
  partId: string;
  bodyLocalHeight: number;
  rig: CharacterRig;
}) {
  const prepared = usePreparedGlb(url, partId, bodyLocalHeight);

  useLayoutEffect(() => {
    const left = prepared.getObjectByName('Eye_L') ?? null;
    const right = prepared.getObjectByName('Eye_R') ?? null;
    if (import.meta.env.DEV && !left && !right) {
      console.info(
        `[character] "${partId}" has no Eye_L/Eye_R nodes, so this face will not blink. ` +
          `That is only a problem if it was meant to — see GlbHeadPart.`,
      );
    }
    rig.eyeL.current = left as THREE.Group | null;
    rig.eyeR.current = right as THREE.Group | null;
    return () => {
      // Released on unmount so a model swap cannot leave the controller writing into the
      // previous head's eyes — which would keep an unmounted scene graph alive for as long as
      // the avatar lives.
      if (rig.eyeL.current === left) rig.eyeL.current = null;
      if (rig.eyeR.current === right) rig.eyeR.current = null;
    };
  }, [prepared, partId, rig]);

  return <primitive object={prepared} />;
}
```

## src/components/Three/character/slots.tsx

```tsx
/**
 * @license
 * SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
 */

import type { ReactElement } from 'react';
import { CHARACTER_MODEL_FILES } from '../../../constants/characterAssets';
import { AUTHORED_ARM_REST_Z } from '../../../constants/characterRig';
import type { AttachmentPoint } from '../../../constants/characterRig';
import { PANTS_PALETTES } from '../../../constants/pants';
import { GlbHeadPart, GlbPart, GlbTintedPart } from './partLoader';
import type { CharacterOutfit, CharacterRig } from './types';

/**
 * THE PART SLOTS — where hand-made 3D assets get plugged in.
 *
 * This is the file to edit when a real model part is finished. Nothing else has to change:
 * not Avatar.tsx, not the camera, not collision, not the wardrobe. Register a part here,
 * select the `authored` model, and it appears on the character.
 *
 * ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 * THE RULE THAT MAKES PARTIAL IMPORT WORK
 * ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 *
 * Every slot is INDEPENDENTLY optional. A slot with no entry falls back to the legacy
 * procedural part, so the character is always complete and always walkable — an authored head
 * can be tested on legacy legs the day it is finished, months before the legs exist.
 *
 * The same mechanism covers the OTHER shape the finished model might take. If it turns out to
 * be one whole body rather than six parts, register that single mesh in the `head` slot's
 * place with a `transform` that re-bases it on the root, or add a `whole` slot here — the
 * controller cannot tell the difference, because it only ever drives joint GROUPS and never
 * asks how many meshes are underneath them. Nothing in this design requires the six-part
 * split; the six slots are the finest granularity that is supported, not a required shape.
 *
 * ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 * WHAT A PART MUST DO
 * ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 *
 * A part renders PART-LOCAL geometry and nothing else. It does NOT create the joint group,
 * set the joint position, or bind the rig ref — `AuthoredCharacterModel` does all three, so a
 * part cannot accidentally move a joint the animation depends on.
 *
 * PART-LOCAL means the origin is the JOINT, +Y up, +Z out of the character's face:
 *
 *   head       origin at the neck pivot. The crown must land at `crownRise` above it.
 *   torso      origin at the torso's centre, not its base.
 *   arm        origin at the SHOULDER, so the mesh hangs at negative y.
 *   leg        origin at the HIP, so the sole lands at `attachments.foot`.
 *
 * Authoring an arm about its own centre instead of its shoulder is the single most common
 * import bug: it looks right standing still and detaches the moment the character walks,
 * because the animation rotates about the joint and the mesh is not centred on it. The loader
 * warns about this specifically — see validateCharacterPart. If an export cannot be
 * re-pivoted in the modelling tool, `transform` below is the escape hatch.
 */

/** The six body parts, each replaceable on its own. */
export type CharacterPartId =
  | 'head'
  | 'torso'
  | 'leftArm'
  | 'rightArm'
  | 'leftLeg'
  | 'rightLeg';

/** What a part receives. Small on purpose — a part draws itself and knows nothing else. */
export interface AuthoredPartProps {
  /** Skin/body colours and what is being worn, in case the part tints or hides for it. */
  outfit: CharacterOutfit;
  /** Which slot this part is filling. Used only to name it in loader messages. */
  partId: CharacterPartId;
  /**
   * The character's total height in LOCAL units, passed down so the loader can sanity-check
   * an imported part's scale against the character it is joining rather than against a
   * number copied into the loader. See constants/characterRig.ts.
   */
  bodyLocalHeight: number;
  /**
   * The joints, for the one thing a part legitimately needs them for: binding a node the
   * controller animates but does not own the geometry of — today, the eyes (see GlbHeadPart).
   *
   * A part still MUST NOT bind its own body joint. `AuthoredCharacterModel` owns every one of
   * those, which is what stops an imported limb from moving a pivot the walk cycle depends on;
   * the face targets are different in kind, because they are transforms INSIDE a part rather
   * than the part's own place on the skeleton.
   */
  rig: CharacterRig;
}

export interface AuthoredPart {
  /** Renders PART-LOCAL geometry. See the note above on what that means. */
  Component: (props: AuthoredPartProps) => ReactElement | null;
  /**
   * Correction applied between the joint and the mesh, for an asset whose export pivot or
   * unit scale cannot be fixed at source. Prefer fixing it in the modelling tool: a correction
   * here is invisible to whoever opens the .glb next and wonders why it does not line up.
   * Omit when the asset is authored correctly.
   */
  transform?: AttachmentPoint;
  /**
   * Whether this part hosts the existing wardrobe. Defaults to false: a new head does not
   * automatically fit the legacy hats, and drawing them on it before they are refitted
   * produces a hat floating beside a skull rather than an honest bare head.
   */
  wearsWardrobe?: boolean;
}

/**
 * The arm's rest splay, as a part transform.
 *
 * The angle itself is measured off the source model and stated once in characterRig.ts; what
 * is decided HERE is that it is a transform on the part rather than geometry inside it. See
 * AUTHORED_ARM_REST_Z for why it cannot be either the joint's rotation (the controller
 * overwrites that every frame) or the mesh's (the sleeve would not follow).
 *
 * The two sides are one number and its negative, so the arms cannot end up splayed by
 * different amounts.
 */
const armRest = (side: 'left' | 'right'): AttachmentPoint => ({
  position: [0, 0, 0],
  rotation: [0, 0, side === 'left' ? AUTHORED_ARM_REST_Z : -AUTHORED_ARM_REST_Z],
});

/**
 * THE REGISTRY — the six parts of the hand-made model, all present.
 *
 * The files are cut from ONE Blender source by `npm run split:character`; do not hand-edit
 * them, and do not hand-edit the numbers they produced in characterRig.ts. See
 * docs/character-authored-model.md for the whole pipeline.
 *
 * `wearsWardrobe` is true on every part, which is the claim that the EXISTING wardrobe still
 * fits this body — and it does, because nothing about the wardrobe was changed: the sockets
 * were re-fitted instead (AUTHORED_ATTACHMENTS), so a hat modelled for the old 0.26 skull
 * arrives at this one's 0.2294 by the socket's own scale. The one place that is fit by luck
 * rather than by a socket is trousers and shoes, which lathe against a hard-coded leg radius —
 * see LegacyLegWearables.
 *
 * Any single part can still be commented out to fall back to its procedural counterpart, which
 * is the fastest way to answer "is this the model or the rig?". A part that fails to LOAD does
 * that on its own and logs why; it cannot take the game down — see CharacterPartBoundary.
 */
/**
 * The colours the procedural torso and leg are drawn in — see GlbTintedPart for why an imported
 * part has to take them too. Same expressions as LegacyTorso / LegacyLeg, so the two models
 * cannot disagree about what colour a swimsuit or a trouser lining is.
 */
const torsoTint = (outfit: CharacterOutfit) => outfit.bodyColor;
const legTint = (outfit: CharacterOutfit) =>
  outfit.pants ? PANTS_PALETTES[outfit.pants].body : outfit.skinColor;

export const AUTHORED_PARTS: Partial<Record<CharacterPartId, AuthoredPart>> = {
  // The head is the one part with its own loader: it binds the eye nodes so the controller can
  // still blink and squint a face it did not draw. See GlbHeadPart.
  head: { Component: (p) => <GlbHeadPart url={CHARACTER_MODEL_FILES.head} {...p} />, wearsWardrobe: true },
  torso: {
    Component: (p) => <GlbTintedPart url={CHARACTER_MODEL_FILES.torso} tint={torsoTint} {...p} />,
    wearsWardrobe: true,
  },
  leftArm: {
    Component: (p) => <GlbPart url={CHARACTER_MODEL_FILES.leftArm} {...p} />,
    transform: armRest('left'),
    wearsWardrobe: true,
  },
  rightArm: {
    Component: (p) => <GlbPart url={CHARACTER_MODEL_FILES.rightArm} {...p} />,
    transform: armRest('right'),
    wearsWardrobe: true,
  },
  leftLeg: {
    Component: (p) => <GlbTintedPart url={CHARACTER_MODEL_FILES.leftLeg} tint={legTint} {...p} />,
    wearsWardrobe: true,
  },
  rightLeg: {
    Component: (p) => <GlbTintedPart url={CHARACTER_MODEL_FILES.rightLeg} tint={legTint} {...p} />,
    wearsWardrobe: true,
  },
};

/** True once at least one real part exists, which is what the model picker keys its label off. */
export const hasAuthoredParts = () => Object.keys(AUTHORED_PARTS).length > 0;

/**
 * All three are IMPORTED above rather than re-exported straight through, which matters more
 * than it looks: `export { GlbPart } from './partLoader'` would forward the name without
 * binding it in this module's scope, so a registration written against it would not compile —
 * and the one promise this file makes is that registering a part is a one-line edit needing no
 * other change. Re-exported as well so anything else that wants the loader can take it from
 * here, next to the registry it belongs to.
 */
export { CHARACTER_MODEL_FILES, GlbHeadPart, GlbPart, GlbTintedPart };
```

## src/components/Three/character/types.ts

```ts
/**
 * @license
 * SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
 */

import type { RefObject } from 'react';
import type * as THREE from 'three';
import type { CharacterAttachments, CharacterSkeleton } from '../../../constants/characterRig';
import type { OutfitType } from '../Outfits';
import type { PantsCut } from '../../../constants/pants';
import type { ShoeType } from '../Shoes';
import type { HairSpec } from '../../../constants/hair';
import type { SpecialCosmeticDef } from '../../../constants/cosmeticEffects';

/**
 * THE MODEL INTERFACE — what the controller hands a character model, and what it expects back.
 *
 *   Character Logic (Avatar.tsx)
 *         ↓  CharacterRig + CharacterModelProps    ← this file
 *   Character Model
 *         ├── LegacyCharacterModel     the procedural chibi that ships today
 *         ├── CharacterModelV2         the procedural remodel
 *         └── AuthoredCharacterModel   imported GLB/GLTF parts, one slot at a time
 *
 * The rule that makes a model swappable: A MODEL OWNS GEOMETRY AND NOTHING ELSE. It holds
 * no state, runs no useFrame, reads no input and never touches playerBus. Everything that
 * moves is driven through the rig below by the controller's single animation loop, so two
 * models cannot drift out of sync — there is only one loop.
 */

/**
 * The joints, as refs the controller writes to every frame.
 *
 * Every one is a `Group` rather than a `Mesh`, and that is the load-bearing decision in
 * this file: it means a joint is a TRANSFORM the controller owns, not a piece of geometry
 * the model owns. A model can hang a single mesh under a joint (as legacy does), or a
 * loaded GLB node, or five meshes, or nothing at all — the animation cannot tell the
 * difference, because all it ever touches is the group's transform.
 *
 * A model MUST bind every joint. An unbound joint is not a crash — the controller null-checks
 * each one — but the part it drives will not animate, which reads as a limb frozen mid-walk.
 *
 * WHAT THE CONTROLLER WRITES, measured from Avatar.tsx's useFrame rather than assumed:
 *
 *   head          rotation (look/idle/crawl) and position.y (bob), re-asserted from the
 *                 skeleton every frame — see CharacterSkeleton on why the model cannot own it
 *   torso         rotation, position.y, and scale (the landing squash)
 *   limbs         ROTATION ONLY — 94 writes, zero position, zero scale. This is why a model
 *                 is free to put its shoulders and hips wherever its proportions want them.
 *   eyeL/eyeR     scale.y (blink, squint) and position.y (squint lift)
 *   mouth         scale (the smile widening on a happy reaction)
 *   hairSway      rotation, for hair long enough to swing. Bound by the HAIR, not the model.
 */
export interface CharacterRig {
  head: RefObject<THREE.Group | null>;
  torso: RefObject<THREE.Group | null>;
  leftArm: RefObject<THREE.Group | null>;
  rightArm: RefObject<THREE.Group | null>;
  leftLeg: RefObject<THREE.Group | null>;
  rightLeg: RefObject<THREE.Group | null>;
  /** Face expression targets. A model with no face may leave these unbound. */
  eyeL: RefObject<THREE.Group | null>;
  eyeR: RefObject<THREE.Group | null>;
  mouth: RefObject<THREE.Group | null>;
  /** Swing target for long hair. Bound by HairPiece, not by the body model. */
  hairSway: RefObject<THREE.Group | null>;
}

/**
 * WHAT the character is wearing — never WHERE it goes.
 *
 * Resolved once by the controller from the player's equipped items (item names in, types
 * out), so no model repeats that parsing and two models cannot disagree about whether a
 * given item counts as a hat. Where each of these lands is the MODEL's answer, given
 * through its `CharacterAttachments` — which is the split section 十一 of the brief asks
 * for: the wardrobe systems stop knowing about the old meshes and start knowing about
 * named sockets.
 */
export interface CharacterOutfit {
  hair: HairSpec | null;
  hat: HatKind | null;
  outfit: OutfitType | null;
  pants: PantsCut | null;
  shoes: ShoeType | null;
  necklaceId: string | null;
  earring: EarringKind | null;
  hasGlasses: boolean;
  hasMask: boolean;
  hasShellNecklace: boolean;
  hasSkirt: boolean;
  hasSwimsuit: boolean;
  /** The plain sky-blue 襯衫, which predates the OutfitModel system and keeps its own model. */
  hasShirt: boolean;
  /** The grey stand-in worn when no top at all is equipped. */
  hasFallbackShirt: boolean;
  /** Whichever sleeve state the equipped top implies, resolved once for both arms. */
  hasSleeves: boolean;
  /**
   * Special cosmetics — the ornaments that MOVE. See constants/cosmeticEffects.ts.
   *
   * Rows of catalog data, not flags, and that is the difference that matters: every other
   * field here is a hand-added boolean or enum, so a new hat is a new line in three files.
   * A new special cosmetic is a row in the catalog and nothing else, because this field
   * carries the whole definition through rather than a name the model has to interpret.
   *
   * A model that cannot host them simply does not render a `CosmeticSlot`, exactly like any
   * other wearable it has not been fitted for.
   */
  specials: SpecialCosmeticDef[];
  /** Skin, and the torso colour the equipped top implies. */
  skinColor: string;
  bodyColor: string;
}

export type HatKind = 'straw' | 'bucket' | 'beret' | 'beanie' | 'snapback';

export type EarringKind = 'jewel' | 'flower' | 'pearl' | 'gold' | 'coral' | 'star';

/**
 * What every character model receives. Deliberately small: a rig to bind, a skeleton to
 * place itself by, sockets to hang wearables on, and what to wear.
 *
 * Note what is ABSENT — movement state, velocity, the swim state machine, the terrain, the
 * camera, playerBus. A model that needed any of those would be a model that had started
 * doing the controller's job.
 */
export interface CharacterModelProps {
  rig: CharacterRig;
  skeleton: CharacterSkeleton;
  attachments: CharacterAttachments;
  outfit: CharacterOutfit;
}

/**
 * A registered model. `id` is what `?character=` and the persisted setting store.
 *
 * `wearsWardrobe` is the honest flag that keeps the dressing room from lying: a model that
 * has not yet had the wardrobe fitted to it renders bare, and the UI needs to be able to
 * say so rather than leaving the player to wonder why their hat vanished.
 */
export interface CharacterModelDefinition {
  id: CharacterModelId;
  /** Shown in the model picker. */
  label: string;
  skeleton: CharacterSkeleton;
  attachments: CharacterAttachments;
  /** Whether hair/hats/outfits/shoes render on this model. */
  wearsWardrobe: boolean;
  Component: (props: CharacterModelProps) => React.ReactElement;
}

/**
 * `legacy`  the shipped procedural chibi. The default, and the only model the whole
 *           wardrobe is authored against.
 * `v2`      the procedural remodel. Opt-in, renders bare.
 * `authored` the slot-based model for hand-made 3D assets: each body part is either an
 *           imported mesh or, until one is registered, the legacy part. This is the one to
 *           select while importing Head → Torso → Arms → Legs one at a time.
 */
export type CharacterModelId = 'legacy' | 'v2' | 'authored';

```
