## src/components/Three/effects/particleShapes.ts

```ts
/**
 * @license
 * SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
 */

import * as THREE from 'three';

/**
 * THE PARTICLE SHAPES — every silhouette a special cosmetic can emit.
 *
 * ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 * WHY THESE ARE MESHES AND NOT SPRITES
 * ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 *
 * The obvious build for this system is a `<points>` cloud with a soft round texture, which
 * is what Fireflies.tsx correctly uses — a firefly IS a blur of light, and it is 40 of them
 * at 30 units away. These are not that. A leaf coming off a flower crown is a small solid
 * object a metre from the camera, and a billboarded blob at that distance reads as a smudge
 * on the lens, not as a leaf. The brief's whole point ("Low Poly / 動態優先 / 不寫實") is
 * that the effect must be made of the same stuff as the world it is in.
 *
 * So: one InstancedMesh per shape, and every shape below is 4 to 20 triangles. The eight of
 * them together are 8 draw calls and ~100 triangles for the entire effect system, which is
 * less than one piece of furniture.
 *
 * ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 * WHY MOST OF THEM ARE FLATTENED PLATONIC SOLIDS
 * ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 *
 * A tetrahedron squashed on one axis is a shard; an octahedron squashed is a four-pointed
 * star or, squashed differently, a leaf; an icosahedron is a ball at 20 triangles. Scaling
 * is baked into the geometry here rather than applied per instance because the instance
 * matrix is already carrying the particle's own size, rotation and position — folding the
 * shape's proportions in at build time keeps the per-frame write to one `compose()`.
 *
 * Every geometry is a UNIT shape (radius 1) so the runtime can drive size purely by scale.
 */

export type ParticleShape =
  /** Four-pointed sparkle. Starlight, and the bond burst. */
  | 'star'
  /** Pointed lens. Leaves. */
  | 'leaf'
  /** Rounded flat chip. Flower petals. */
  | 'petal'
  /** Faceted ball, drawn translucent. Bubbles. */
  | 'bubble'
  /** Sharp shard. Embers. */
  | 'spark'
  /** Tiny soft ball. Mushroom spores, pollen. */
  | 'spore'
  /** An actual heart, extruded. Pet affection. */
  | 'heart'
  /** Featureless mote, for anything that just needs a speck of light. */
  | 'mote'
  /** Long, narrow quill. Wings — and the only shape meant to be SEEN falling. */
  | 'feather'
  /**
   * A flat annulus lying in the GROUND PLANE. Ripples, expanding halos, shockwaves.
   *
   * The first shape here that is not a small solid object, and the first whose orientation
   * carries meaning: every other shape reads correctly from any angle, so the runtime is free
   * to give it a random tumble. A ring that tumbles is an ellipse flapping about, so this one
   * has to declare itself — see {@link SHAPE_FLAT}.
   */
  | 'ring'
  /** A quaver. The only shape in the set that MEANS something rather than just looking like it. */
  | 'note'
  /**
   * A long double-pointed shard. Ice, and anything that wants to read as CUT rather than grown.
   *
   * Deliberately not a second `spark`: an ember is a stubby wedge that reads as a fleck of
   * burning matter, and a crystal is a narrow spike with a point at BOTH ends, which is the
   * silhouette of something that grew out of a facet. At 4 cm those two are still told apart,
   * and giving frost the ember's shape would have made two series look like one emitter.
   */
  | 'crystal'
  /** A six-armed flake. The one shape whose whole job is to be recognised at a glance. */
  | 'snow'
  /**
   * A teardrop, point UP.
   *
   * The second {@link SHAPE_FLAT} shape, and for the same reason as the ring: a drop that
   * tumbles is not a drop, it is a seed. Rain, splashes and anything shed by water.
   */
  | 'drop'
  /**
   * A soft flattened puff, drawn very faint and usually with `grow`.
   *
   * The only shape in the set that is meant to be looked THROUGH rather than at — mist, smoke,
   * cloud vapour, frost haze. It is the answer to "this effect needs air around it" that would
   * otherwise be reached for by turning an emitter's count up.
   */
  | 'wisp';

export const PARTICLE_SHAPES: ParticleShape[] = [
  'star', 'leaf', 'petal', 'bubble', 'spark', 'spore', 'heart', 'mote', 'feather', 'ring', 'note',
  'crystal', 'snow', 'drop', 'wisp',
];

/**
 * Shapes authored in a FIXED world orientation, which the runtime must never rotate.
 *
 * Not the same question as `tumble: 0`. A particle with no tumble still gets one random
 * orientation at spawn (that is what stops eight stars in a burst looking like eight copies of
 * one sprite), so "does not spin" and "keeps the orientation it was drawn in" are different
 * things, and a ring needs the second one. Stated per shape rather than per emitter because it
 * is a property of the GEOMETRY: no config should be able to make a ground ripple stand on its
 * edge.
 */
export const SHAPE_FLAT: Record<ParticleShape, boolean> = {
  star: false,
  leaf: false,
  petal: false,
  bubble: false,
  spark: false,
  spore: false,
  heart: false,
  mote: false,
  feather: false,
  ring: true,
  // A note read edge-on or upside down is not a note — but it must still tumble a little, or a
  // row of them along a path reads as printed sheet music rather than as something drifting.
  // So it is not flat, and the emitter that uses it keeps its tumble very low instead.
  note: false,
  crystal: false,
  // Flakes flutter as they fall, and a flake frozen square to the camera reads as a decal. The
  // emitters that use it pair a very low tumble with `wobble` instead.
  snow: false,
  // THE SECOND FIXED-ORIENTATION SHAPE. A drop has an up: the point leads and the belly follows.
  // Given a random spawn orientation like every other shape, a third of a rain burst falls
  // sideways and another third falls blunt-end first, and what that draws is a shower of seeds.
  drop: true,
  wisp: false,
};

/**
 * How many of each shape may exist at once, across every wearer in the scene.
 *
 * This is the SECOND of the two caps — the first is `maxAlive` per emitter in
 * constants/cosmeticEffects.ts. Both exist because they fail differently: the per-emitter
 * cap keeps one cosmetic tasteful, and this one keeps a crowd of wearers from adding up.
 * A spawn that would exceed this is dropped, never queued.
 *
 * The numbers are the worst case the prototype set can produce with a comfortable margin:
 * the heaviest shape is `star` (a player hairpin at 3 + a pet collar at 2 + bond bursts),
 * and 32 leaves room for roughly ten wearers of the heaviest possible loadout.
 */
export const SHAPE_POOL_SIZE: Record<ParticleShape, number> = {
  star: 58,
  leaf: 43,
  petal: 43,
  bubble: 50,
  spark: 36,
  spore: 43,
  heart: 29,
  mote: 58,
  // Lower than leaf despite doing a similar job: a feather is the flagship's trail, and one
  // wearer's emitter is capped at 4. 20 is five such wearers on screen at once, which is more
  // than the island has ever had.
  feather: 36,
  // The smallest pool in the file. A ring is the one shape that grows — it ends its life many
  // times the size it started — so it is also the one where "a few too many" is immediately
  // a screen full of overlapping circles rather than a slightly busier sparkle.
  ring: 22,
  note: 29,
  crystal: 40,
  snow: 46,
  drop: 46,
  // Small for the same reason `ring` is: a wisp is drawn large and grows larger, so its cost is
  // overdraw rather than geometry, and overdraw is the one thing a crowd of wearers must not be
  // able to multiply. A dozen alive across the whole scene is already a haze.
  wisp: 26,
};

/**
 * Per-shape alpha multiplier, folded in on top of whatever opacity the emitter asks for.
 *
 * A bubble is glass and reads wrong at the same opacity as a petal, and a spore is nearly
 * air. Putting that in the SHAPE rather than in every emitter's config means "a bubble"
 * cannot be configured into "a solid blue ball" by a future cosmetic.
 *
 * There is no blending mode here, and that is a decision rather than an omission: every
 * particle in this system uses normal alpha blending. Additive blending is precisely the
 * 閃光 the brief rules out — it blows out to white wherever two particles overlap and it
 * glows straight through the character's own head.
 */
export const SHAPE_ALPHA: Record<ParticleShape, number> = {
  star: 1,
  leaf: 1,
  petal: 1,
  // Raised across the board in the visibility pass. These numbers are multiplied by the emitter's
  // own opacity AND by the fade curve, so three sub-1 factors were stacking: a 0.55 emitter using
  // the old 0.75 bubble peaked at 0.41 and averaged well under that over its life. A bubble still
  // wants to be the most transparent thing in the set — it is glass — it just cannot be a ghost.
  bubble: 0.88,
  spark: 1,
  spore: 0.95,
  heart: 1,
  mote: 1,
  feather: 1,
  // A ring is drawn large and is the only shape a player looks THROUGH, so it wants LESS than
  // an opaque chip — but not much less. 0.5 was the first guess and it composited to grey
  // against the night ground, which is the opposite of the one thing a ripple has to say.
  ring: 0.8,
  note: 1,
  crystal: 0.92,
  snow: 1,
  // Water, so a step below solid — but a rain drop still has to be visible against the ground it
  // is falling toward, and the ground on this island is a mid-value green.
  drop: 0.86,
  // THE LOWEST IN THE FILE BY A LONG WAY, and that is the shape's entire character. A wisp is
  // meant to be several overlapping ones reading as one soft mass; at any alpha where a single
  // wisp is clearly visible, three overlapping ones are a white blob.
  wisp: 0.34,
};

/**
 * A thin flat annulus lying in the ground plane. 12 segments = 24 triangles.
 *
 * Wide band (0.78 → 1.0) rather than a hairline: a ring one or two pixels thick shimmers as it
 * expands, and at the sizes this is drawn a thin ring simply disappears at the far end of its
 * growth. The band is what stays legible from 0.1 to 0.5 world units.
 */
function ringGeometry(): THREE.BufferGeometry {
  // 20 segments, not 12. A ring is the one shape that GROWS — it ends its life several times
  // the size it started — so its silhouette is the only one in the set that gets bigger than
  // the faceting can carry. At 0.6 world units a 12-gon reads as a stop sign.
  const geo = new THREE.RingGeometry(0.78, 1, 20);
  geo.rotateX(-Math.PI / 2);
  return geo;
}

/**
 * A quaver: a head and a stem, extruded as one geometry.
 *
 * TWO SHAPES IN ONE ExtrudeGeometry, which is the trick that makes this affordable. A note is
 * not a single closed contour, and drawing it as one would mean hand-authoring the join between
 * a round head and a straight stem as one path. ExtrudeGeometry accepts an ARRAY of shapes and
 * welds the result into one buffer, so the pool still gets exactly one geometry and one draw
 * call while the source stays two obvious primitives.
 *
 * The flag is deliberately absent. At the 3-4 cm these are drawn it is two or three pixels, and
 * what it actually adds is a spike that reads as noise; a head-and-stem silhouette is already
 * unmistakably a note.
 */
function noteGeometry(): THREE.BufferGeometry {
  // Tilted ellipse head, the way a note head is actually drawn.
  const head = new THREE.Shape();
  head.absellipse(-0.26, -0.52, 0.44, 0.34, 0, Math.PI * 2, false, -0.35);

  const stem = new THREE.Shape();
  stem.moveTo(0.05, -0.5);
  stem.lineTo(0.19, -0.5);
  stem.lineTo(0.19, 1);
  stem.lineTo(0.05, 1);
  stem.lineTo(0.05, -0.5);

  const geo = new THREE.ExtrudeGeometry([head, stem], {
    depth: 0.2,
    bevelEnabled: false,
    curveSegments: 5,
  });
  geo.center();
  // Normalised to roughly a unit tall like every other shape here, so a size of 0.05 keeps
  // meaning the same thing across the whole catalog.
  geo.scale(0.66, 0.66, 0.66);
  return geo;
}

/** A heart, drawn once as a 2D outline and extruded thin. ~40 triangles, the priciest shape. */
function heartGeometry(): THREE.BufferGeometry {
  const s = new THREE.Shape();
  // Standard heart bezier, authored around the origin at roughly unit size.
  s.moveTo(0, -0.9);
  s.bezierCurveTo(0.9, 0.05, 0.75, 1.0, 0, 0.55);
  s.bezierCurveTo(-0.75, 1.0, -0.9, 0.05, 0, -0.9);
  const geo = new THREE.ExtrudeGeometry(s, {
    depth: 0.28,
    bevelEnabled: false,
    // 6 segments per curve. This said 4 and "any more is invisible at 3-5 cm" — true when hearts
    // were drawn at 0.035; after the visibility pass they start at 0.042 and the lobes were
    // reading as a pair of corners.
    curveSegments: 6,
  });
  geo.center();
  return geo;
}

/**
 * A six-armed flake: a twelve-point star outline, extruded thin.
 *
 * Drawn as ONE contour rather than as three crossed bars, which is the cheaper build and the
 * wrong one — three bars meeting at the centre triple the geometry exactly where it is least
 * visible, and their ends are square. The alternating radii here (1 and 0.38) are what put a
 * notch between the arms, and the notch is the whole of what says "flake" instead of "asterisk".
 */
function snowGeometry(): THREE.BufferGeometry {
  const s = new THREE.Shape();
  const ARMS = 6;
  for (let i = 0; i < ARMS * 2; i++) {
    const a = (i / (ARMS * 2)) * Math.PI * 2;
    // 0.38, not the 0.5 a star outline usually takes: a flake's arms are thin spurs off a small
    // hub, and at 0.5 the hub swells until the silhouette is a cog.
    const r = i % 2 === 0 ? 1 : 0.38;
    const x = Math.cos(a) * r;
    const y = Math.sin(a) * r;
    if (i === 0) s.moveTo(x, y); else s.lineTo(x, y);
  }
  s.closePath();
  // Thinner than the note (0.2) and the heart (0.28). A flake is a plate of ice; any depth that
  // is visible from the side turns it into a bolt head.
  const geo = new THREE.ExtrudeGeometry(s, { depth: 0.09, bevelEnabled: false, curveSegments: 1 });
  geo.center();
  return geo;
}

/**
 * A teardrop with the point UP, lathed from a profile.
 *
 * Six radial segments over five profile spans — 60 triangles, the priciest shape here, and the
 * reason it is worth it is that a drop is the one particle players have an exact mental picture
 * of. A flattened ball (which is what `bubble` gives at this size) reads as a bead of water
 * sitting on a surface; the taper is what makes it a drop in the AIR.
 *
 * Authored so the point sits at y = +1 like every other shape's extreme, which keeps `size`
 * meaning the same thing across the whole catalog.
 */
function dropGeometry(): THREE.BufferGeometry {
  const profile = [
    new THREE.Vector2(0.004, 1),
    new THREE.Vector2(0.12, 0.42),
    new THREE.Vector2(0.29, -0.06),
    new THREE.Vector2(0.34, -0.44),
    new THREE.Vector2(0.22, -0.76),
    new THREE.Vector2(0.004, -0.9),
  ];
  return new THREE.LatheGeometry(profile, 6);
}

/**
 * Builds every shape's geometry, once per Canvas.
 *
 * Returned as a plain record rather than module-level constants so the caller owns disposal:
 * a geometry is GPU memory attached to a specific renderer, and the dressing room mounts its
 * own Canvas. See EffectField's unmount cleanup.
 */
export function createParticleGeometries(): Record<ParticleShape, THREE.BufferGeometry> {
  const scaled = (geo: THREE.BufferGeometry, x: number, y: number, z: number) => {
    geo.scale(x, y, z);
    return geo;
  };

  return {
    // Octahedron flattened on Z: seen face-on this is the classic four-pointed ✦ sparkle,
    // and seen edge-on it thins out instead of vanishing the way a flat quad would.
    star: scaled(new THREE.OctahedronGeometry(1, 0), 1, 1, 0.32),
    // Narrow and flat: a pointed lens. The 0.12 depth is what catches a highlight as it
    // tumbles, which is what stops a falling leaf reading as a falling sticker.
    leaf: scaled(new THREE.OctahedronGeometry(1, 0), 0.55, 1, 0.12),
    // Rounded and flat — a petal is a chip, not a shard, so this starts from the 20-face
    // icosahedron rather than the 8-face octahedron.
    petal: scaled(new THREE.IcosahedronGeometry(1, 0), 1, 0.22, 0.85),
    // Detail 1 on the three shapes that are meant to be ROUND. They were 8-face solids on the
    // reasoning that faceting is invisible at 2 cm and is the island's visual language anyway —
    // the first half of which stopped being true when the visibility pass took sizes up to 4.5 cm
    // and raised their alpha. At that size a bubble reads as a cut crystal. The flattened solids
    // (star, leaf, petal, spark, feather) stay at detail 0: there the faceting IS the silhouette.
    bubble: new THREE.IcosahedronGeometry(1, 1),
    // Four triangles, stretched along Y so an ember reads as a rising streak.
    spark: scaled(new THREE.TetrahedronGeometry(1, 0), 0.7, 1.3, 0.7),
    spore: new THREE.IcosahedronGeometry(1, 1),
    heart: heartGeometry(),
    mote: new THREE.IcosahedronGeometry(1, 1),
    // Narrower and thinner than `leaf` (0.55/0.12), which is the entire difference between
    // the two silhouettes at 4 cm: a leaf is a lens, a feather is a stroke. Thin enough to
    // catch the light edge-on as it tumbles, which is what a falling feather does.
    feather: scaled(new THREE.OctahedronGeometry(1, 0), 0.26, 1, 0.09),
    // Outer radius 1 like every other shape, so `size` still means "how big is this". Laid
    // into the XZ plane here rather than at spawn — RingGeometry is authored in XY, and baking
    // the quarter-turn into the geometry is what lets the runtime write an IDENTITY rotation
    // for flat shapes instead of a special-case quaternion.
    ring: ringGeometry(),
    note: noteGeometry(),
    // A NARROW double-pointed spike, against `spark`'s stubby wedge (0.7/1.3/0.7 on a
    // tetrahedron). Both are "a small sharp thing"; the proportions are the whole difference,
    // and they have to be this far apart because frost and fire are on the same shelf.
    crystal: scaled(new THREE.OctahedronGeometry(1, 0), 0.4, 1, 0.4),
    snow: snowGeometry(),
    drop: dropGeometry(),
    // Flattened, and detail 1 so the silhouette is round. A wisp's job is to have no edges — an
    // 8-face ball at 0.34 alpha still shows its facets as value steps, which reads as a shard of
    // fog rather than as fog.
    wisp: scaled(new THREE.IcosahedronGeometry(1, 1), 1, 0.52, 1),
  };
}
```

## src/components/Three/floorMaterial.ts

```ts
/**
 * @license
 * SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
 */

import * as THREE from 'three';

import { NOISE_GLSL } from './proceduralNoise';

/**
 * Procedural materials for the five interior floor styles.
 *
 * Every one of these used to be a single flat colour plus a gloss setting, which
 * is why none of them looked like what it was called: "復刻花紋磚" had no pattern,
 * "奢華大理石" had no veining, and "溫潤橡木地板" was one unbroken sheet of brown
 * with no planks in it. At the interior camera's distance a floor is one of the
 * largest things on screen, so a flat fill reads as "unfinished", not "minimal".
 *
 * Each style is drawn in the fragment shader from world XZ - NOT from the mesh's
 * own UVs. Rooms are separate 12x12 plane meshes laid edge to edge, so UV-space
 * patterns would restart at every room boundary and put a seam down the middle
 * of the house; keying off world position lets planks, grout lines and tile
 * motifs run continuously from one room into the next, which is what makes it
 * look laid rather than wallpapered.
 *
 * All of it is arithmetic - no texture files, matching the rest of the project's
 * fully-procedural art.
 */

/**
 * Per-style body. Each sets `vec3 col` and `float gloss` (0 = matte, 1 = mirror)
 * from `vec2 P`, the world XZ of the fragment.
 */
const PATTERNS: Record<string, string> = {
  // 溫潤橡木地板 - staggered oak boards. The stagger is the whole trick: a plank
  // floor with aligned end joints reads as a grid, not as a floor.
  'floor-oak': `
    const float PW = 0.34;   // plank width
    const float PL = 2.6;    // plank length
    float row = floor(P.y / PW);
    // Each row starts at its own offset, so end joints never line up.
    float stagger = fHash(vec2(row, 7.3)) * PL;
    float alongRaw = P.x + stagger;
    float plank = floor(alongRaw / PL);
    vec2 cell = vec2(fract(alongRaw / PL), fract(P.y / PW));
    float tone = fHash(vec2(plank, row));

    // Board colour: warm oak, each board a little lighter or darker than its
    // neighbours, which is what stops a wood floor looking printed.
    vec3 light = vec3(0.780, 0.560, 0.320);
    vec3 dark  = vec3(0.510, 0.320, 0.155);
    col = mix(dark, light, 0.35 + 0.5 * tone);

    // Grain: noise stretched hard along the board so it becomes long fibres
    // rather than blobs, plus a few darker cathedral arcs.
    float grain = fFbm(vec2(alongRaw * 1.4, P.y * 34.0 + tone * 40.0));
    col *= 0.86 + 0.24 * grain;
    float arc = fFbm(vec2(alongRaw * 0.55, P.y * 6.0 + tone * 30.0));
    col *= 0.90 + 0.16 * smoothstep(0.35, 0.75, arc);
    // Occasional knot.
    float knot = fHash(vec2(plank * 3.1, row * 5.7));
    if (knot > 0.86) {
      vec2 kp = vec2(cell.x - 0.5, (cell.y - 0.5) * (PW / PL) * 3.0);
      col *= 1.0 - 0.45 * (1.0 - smoothstep(0.0, 0.045, length(kp)));
    }

    // Chamfered seams - a dark micro-bevel at every board edge. Widths are in
    // cell space, so they are converted back to world units to stay even.
    float seamL = fLine(min(cell.x, 1.0 - cell.x) * PL, 0.006, 0.010);
    float seamW = fLine(min(cell.y, 1.0 - cell.y) * PW, 0.005, 0.008);
    float seam = max(seamL, seamW);
    col *= 1.0 - 0.55 * seam;
    // Satin lacquer, dulled slightly in the seams where it pools.
    gloss = 0.72 - 0.5 * seam;
  `,

  // 亮白瓷磚 - a seamless poured-look white surface.
  //
  // DELIBERATELY NO GRID. This did have tile joints, which is what porcelain
  // really has, but the name is "亮白" - bright white - and a grout grid works
  // against that twice over: the lines are the darkest thing on an otherwise
  // white floor, and a repeating grid across a whole house reads as busy rather
  // than bright. Without it the floor is one continuous sheet of white and the
  // only thing left to look at is the light moving over it, which is the point.
  'floor-white-tile': `
    col = vec3(0.972, 0.988, 1.000);

    // Everything below is at single-digit-percent strength: enough that the
    // surface is not a dead flat fill under a moving camera, never enough to
    // read as dirt or pattern on what is supposed to be pure white.
    col *= 0.988 + 0.014 * fFbm(P * 2.2);
    // Very faint large-scale sheen banding, like light across polished stone.
    col *= 0.994 + 0.010 * fFbm(P * 0.5 + 9.0);
    // A rare glint in the glaze.
    col += 0.020 * smoothstep(0.990, 1.0, fHash(floor(P * 190.0)));

    gloss = 0.96;
  `,

  // 工業風水泥 - a single seamless pour of dark polished concrete.
  //
  // NO CONTROL JOINTS, and much darker than the first pass. Those saw-cut joints
  // were technically right - a real slab has to have them - but they put a 3m
  // grid across the floor, and a grid is the opposite of what this style is for.
  // Industrial minimalism is about an uninterrupted surface; the interest has to
  // come from the material itself, not from lines drawn on it. So everything
  // here is depth *within* the pour: broad tonal drift, a trowel-burnished
  // sheen that moves with it, and aggregate just under the surface.
  //
  // The near-black base does the rest. Mid-grey concrete under a warm ceiling
  // light comes out beige and reads as "unpainted floor"; at this value it
  // reads as a deliberate finish, and it lets the furniture above it pop.
  'floor-industrial-concrete': `
    vec3 base = vec3(0.052, 0.060, 0.076);

    // Broad pour variation, then a finer trowel swirl riding on top of it.
    float broad = fFbm(P * 0.30);
    float swirl = fFbm(P * 1.5 + vec2(broad * 2.4));
    col = base * (0.70 + 0.68 * broad) * (0.90 + 0.20 * swirl);

    // Burnished patches: where the power trowel passed, the surface is both
    // slightly lighter and markedly glossier. Tying colour and gloss to the same
    // field is what makes it read as one polished floor catching the light
    // unevenly, rather than as a grey texture with a separate shine on top.
    float burnish = smoothstep(0.36, 0.74, fFbm(P * 0.55 + 4.0));
    col *= 1.0 + 0.22 * burnish;

    // Aggregate ground just proud of the surface - the pale specks are the
    // giveaway that this is polished concrete and not painted board.
    float spec = fHash(floor(P * 78.0));
    col += 0.055 * smoothstep(0.964, 1.0, spec);
    col += 0.030 * smoothstep(0.930, 1.0, fHash(floor(P * 150.0) + 8.3));
    col -= 0.022 * smoothstep(0.975, 1.0, fHash(floor(P * 78.0) + 31.7));

    // Occasional tiny pinhole from the pour.
    col -= 0.05 * smoothstep(0.994, 1.0, fHash(floor(P * 42.0) + 57.1));

    gloss = 0.30 + 0.34 * burnish;
  `,

  // 復刻花紋磚 - encaustic cement tile. A real one is a hand-poured geometric
  // motif in flat, unshaded colour, so this is built from hard-edged distance
  // fields rather than noise: crisp shapes are the point of the style.
  'floor-vintage-pattern': `
    const float TS = 0.98;
    vec2 id = floor(P / TS);
    vec2 cell = fract(P / TS);
    vec2 q = (cell - 0.5) * 2.0;           // -1..1 within the tile
    float r = length(q);

    vec3 cream    = vec3(0.918, 0.878, 0.780);
    vec3 teal     = vec3(0.106, 0.400, 0.400);
    vec3 terracot = vec3(0.760, 0.376, 0.235);
    vec3 ink      = vec3(0.129, 0.192, 0.204);

    col = cream;

    // Corner quarter-discs. Four tiles meeting make one full circle, which is
    // what makes an encaustic floor read as a continuous pattern instead of a
    // grid of separate stamps.
    float corner = length(abs(q) - vec2(1.0));
    col = mix(col, terracot, 1.0 - smoothstep(0.50, 0.53, corner));
    col = mix(col, cream, 1.0 - smoothstep(0.33, 0.36, corner));

    // Central four-petal rosette, from a polar-modulated radius.
    float a = atan(q.y, q.x);
    float petal = 0.40 + 0.20 * cos(4.0 * a);
    col = mix(col, teal, 1.0 - smoothstep(petal, petal + 0.03, r));
    // Small cream eye at the centre.
    col = mix(col, cream, 1.0 - smoothstep(0.11, 0.135, r));
    // Ink hairline around the rosette.
    col = mix(col, ink, fLine(r - petal - 0.055, 0.012, 0.012));

    // Diagonal ties from the rosette out to each corner disc.
    float diag = min(abs(abs(q.x) - abs(q.y)), 1.0);
    float tie = fLine(diag, 0.030, 0.020) * smoothstep(0.44, 0.58, r) * (1.0 - smoothstep(0.74, 0.86, r));
    col = mix(col, teal, tie);

    // Age: cement tile is porous and never perfectly even.
    col *= 0.93 + 0.11 * fFbm(P * 5.0 + fHash(id) * 30.0);
    col *= 0.96 + 0.06 * fHash(id);

    // Thin grout between tiles.
    vec2 e = min(cell, 1.0 - cell) * TS;
    float grout = max(fLine(e.x, 0.010, 0.007), fLine(e.y, 0.010, 0.007));
    col = mix(col, vec3(0.700, 0.672, 0.600), grout);
    // Waxed cement - a low sheen, not a glaze.
    gloss = 0.34 - 0.2 * grout;
  `,

  // 奢華大理石 - big book-matched Calacatta slabs.
  'floor-luxury-marble': `
    const float SS = 2.9;    // slab size
    vec2 id = floor(P / SS);
    vec2 cell = fract(P / SS);

    // Book-matching: mirror alternate slabs so the veins run into each other at
    // the joint the way a real cut-and-opened block does. This is the detail
    // that separates "marble" from "grey noise".
    vec2 m = cell;
    if (mod(id.x, 2.0) > 0.5) m.x = 1.0 - m.x;
    if (mod(id.y, 2.0) > 0.5) m.y = 1.0 - m.y;
    vec2 W = (id * 0.0 + m) * SS;

    col = vec3(0.945, 0.945, 0.936);

    // Domain-warped fbm: warping is what turns round noise blobs into the long
    // wandering fissures marble actually has.
    vec2 warp = vec2(fFbm(W * 0.55), fFbm(W * 0.55 + 5.2));
    float v = fFbm(W * 0.85 + warp * 2.6);

    // Primary grey veins - thin, dark, high contrast.
    float vein = 1.0 - smoothstep(0.0, 0.055, abs(v - 0.5));
    col = mix(col, vec3(0.360, 0.380, 0.415), vein * 0.85);
    // Secondary soft grey drift either side of them.
    col = mix(col, vec3(0.800, 0.812, 0.828), smoothstep(0.42, 0.62, v) * 0.35);
    // A few warm gold seams, the Calacatta signature.
    float gold = 1.0 - smoothstep(0.0, 0.022, abs(fFbm(W * 0.42 + warp * 1.4 + 17.0) - 0.52));
    col = mix(col, vec3(0.760, 0.610, 0.330), gold * 0.55);

    // Very fine crystalline sparkle in the stone itself.
    col += 0.025 * smoothstep(0.985, 1.0, fHash(floor(P * 160.0)));

    // Tight, pale joints - a luxury slab floor is butted almost closed.
    vec2 e = min(cell, 1.0 - cell) * SS;
    float joint = max(fLine(e.x, 0.008, 0.006), fLine(e.y, 0.008, 0.006));
    col = mix(col, vec3(0.855, 0.855, 0.850), joint);
    gloss = 0.98 - 0.4 * joint;
  `,
};

/** Base PBR settings per style, before the pattern's own gloss modulation. */
const BASE_PROPS: Record<string, { roughness: number; metalness: number; clearcoat: number; clearcoatRoughness: number }> = {
  'floor-oak': { roughness: 0.34, metalness: 0.0, clearcoat: 0.55, clearcoatRoughness: 0.22 },
  'floor-white-tile': { roughness: 0.12, metalness: 0.0, clearcoat: 0.9, clearcoatRoughness: 0.08 },
  'floor-industrial-concrete': { roughness: 0.62, metalness: 0.0, clearcoat: 0.35, clearcoatRoughness: 0.42 },
  'floor-vintage-pattern': { roughness: 0.5, metalness: 0.0, clearcoat: 0.25, clearcoatRoughness: 0.35 },
  'floor-luxury-marble': { roughness: 0.09, metalness: 0.02, clearcoat: 1.0, clearcoatRoughness: 0.05 },
};

const DEFAULT_PROPS = { roughness: 0.4, metalness: 0.1, clearcoat: 0.3, clearcoatRoughness: 0.25 };

/**
 * Builds the material for one floor style.
 *
 * Call through {@link getFloorMaterial} rather than directly - these are shared
 * and cached, because there is one of these per style, not one per room.
 */
function createFloorMaterial(floorId: string, fallbackColor: string): THREE.MeshPhysicalMaterial {
  const pattern = PATTERNS[floorId];
  const props = BASE_PROPS[floorId] ?? DEFAULT_PROPS;

  const material = new THREE.MeshPhysicalMaterial({
    color: pattern ? '#ffffff' : fallbackColor,
    ...props,
  });

  if (!pattern) return material;

  material.onBeforeCompile = (shader) => {
    shader.vertexShader = shader.vertexShader
      .replace('void main() {', 'varying vec3 vFloorW;\nvoid main() {')
      .replace(
        '#include <begin_vertex>',
        '#include <begin_vertex>\n\tvFloorW = (modelMatrix * vec4(transformed, 1.0)).xyz;'
      );

    shader.fragmentShader = shader.fragmentShader
      .replace(
        'void main() {',
        `varying vec3 vFloorW;
         ${NOISE_GLSL}
         void main() {
           // Declared here so the roughness patch further down can read the
           // gloss the pattern decided on - grout and seams have to be duller
           // than the tile face or the whole floor reads as one plastic sheet.
           float floorGloss = 0.5;`
      )
      .replace(
        '#include <color_fragment>',
        `#include <color_fragment>
         {
           vec2 P = vFloorW.xz;
           vec3 col = diffuseColor.rgb;
           float gloss = 0.5;
           ${pattern}
           diffuseColor.rgb = col;
           floorGloss = clamp(gloss, 0.0, 1.0);
         }`
      )
      .replace(
        '#include <roughnessmap_fragment>',
        // Pattern-driven roughness. Without this the grout lines are only a
        // colour change and still mirror the ceiling lights exactly like the
        // tile does, which instantly gives away that it is a painted-on grid.
        `#include <roughnessmap_fragment>
         roughnessFactor = clamp(mix(0.95, 0.04, floorGloss), 0.02, 1.0);`
      );
  };

  // three keys its shader cache on onBeforeCompile's SOURCE TEXT, which is
  // identical for every style built by this one factory - without a distinct
  // key, all five floors would be handed whichever program compiled first.
  material.customProgramCacheKey = () => `floor|${floorId}`;

  return material;
}

const cache = new Map<string, THREE.MeshPhysicalMaterial>();

/**
 * The shared material for a floor style. Cached per style: a house can have
 * eight rooms on the same floor, and they should be one material and one
 * compiled program, not eight.
 */
export function getFloorMaterial(floorId: string, fallbackColor: string): THREE.MeshPhysicalMaterial {
  const key = `${floorId}|${fallbackColor}`;
  let material = cache.get(key);
  if (!material) {
    material = createFloorMaterial(floorId, fallbackColor);
    cache.set(key, material);
  }
  return material;
}

/** True when this style draws a procedural pattern (rather than a flat colour). */
export function hasFloorPattern(floorId: string): boolean {
  return floorId in PATTERNS;
}
```

## src/components/Three/glowTexture.ts

```ts
/**
 * @license
 * SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
 */

import * as THREE from 'three';

/**
 * 一張徑向漸層的光暈貼圖 —— 中心白、往外淡到全透明。
 *
 * 加法混合的球體看起來還是像球體：邊緣是硬的，因為它就是一顆球。「光」的樣子是中心亮、邊緣
 * 沒有邊緣，而那只能由一張中間到外面連續變透明的貼圖來給。房間裡每一個會發光的東西 —— 燭火、
 * 開關上那顆找得到位置的小指示燈 —— 用的都是這同一張。
 *
 * 一張、全域共用、只做一次。它跟顏色無關（材質的 `color` 會乘上去），所以不需要每種顏色一張。
 */
let cached: THREE.CanvasTexture | null = null;

export function getGlowTexture(): THREE.CanvasTexture {
  if (cached) return cached;

  const size = 128;
  const canvas = document.createElement('canvas');
  canvas.width = size;
  canvas.height = size;
  const ctx = canvas.getContext('2d')!;

  const c = size / 2;
  const g = ctx.createRadialGradient(c, c, 0, c, c, c);
  // 四個停點而不是兩個：一條直線的漸層看起來像一個有邊界的圓盤，因為亮度在中間就已經掉了一半。
  // 前段掉得慢、後段拖長的尾巴，才是光真正的衰減形狀。
  g.addColorStop(0, 'rgba(255,255,255,1)');
  g.addColorStop(0.18, 'rgba(255,255,255,0.82)');
  g.addColorStop(0.45, 'rgba(255,255,255,0.26)');
  g.addColorStop(1, 'rgba(255,255,255,0)');
  ctx.fillStyle = g;
  ctx.fillRect(0, 0, size, size);

  const tex = new THREE.CanvasTexture(canvas);
  tex.colorSpace = THREE.SRGBColorSpace;
  cached = tex;
  return tex;
}
```

## src/components/Three/groundMaterial.ts

```ts
/**
 * @license
 * SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
 */

/**
 * 地面材質 —— the island's surfaces, as a procedural material instead of a fill.
 *
 * The sibling of `floorMaterial.ts` and `wallMaterial.ts`, built the same way and for the same
 * reason those two exist: a surface that is one of the largest things on screen cannot be a
 * single colour without reading as unfinished. Indoors that was solved a while ago — the oak
 * floor has planks, grain and knots. Outdoors the plateau was still two greens graded by radius,
 * which is why the island read as a flat green disc with props standing on it.
 *
 * ## What this does NOT do
 *
 * It does not replace the colours. `PLATEAU_INNER_COLOR` / `PLATEAU_OUTER_COLOR` / `MOUND_COLOR`
 * still arrive as `diffuseColor` (as a vertex colour on the plateau, as `material.color` on the
 * mounds) and everything below MODULATES that. The island is the same green it has always been;
 * it just stops being exactly one green everywhere. Keeping the base outside the shader is also
 * what lets one program serve the plateau, the mounds, the body skirt and the sand cone.
 *
 * It also does not move a single vertex. The plateau is the surface `getTerrainInfo` promises is
 * flat at `ISLAND_SURFACE_Y`, and displacing it would put the drawn ground somewhere the walk
 * height is not — the exact class of bug `constants/terrain.ts` exists to prevent. The relief
 * here is entirely in the NORMAL (see the bump note below), which lighting reads and collision
 * cannot.
 *
 * ## The three scales, and why the finest one fades with distance
 *
 * A ground texture has to answer two questions that pull in opposite directions: 「走近看有沒有
 * 細節」 and 「拉遠看乾不乾淨」. Drawing the fine grain everywhere answers the first and fails the
 * second — worse than failing it, because high-frequency noise on a surface being minified into
 * a few pixels ALIASES, and a lawn that fizzes as the camera moves is a far more obvious defect
 * than a lawn that is slightly plain.
 *
 * So the three scales are spent at three distances:
 *
 *   BROAD   the shared field (lib/groundField.ts). Metres across. Always drawn — this is what
 *           the tufts are scattered by, so it must be visible at every distance or the lawn's
 *           dense patches would have nothing under them.
 *   MID     ~1.5 cycles per unit. Always drawn. Clump-sized mottle; too coarse to alias.
 *   FINE    ~7 cycles per unit, faded out between 9 and 26 units from the camera. This is the
 *           close-up grain, gone by the time the surface is small enough to sparkle.
 *
 * `CameraController` orbits between 10 and 35 units, so at a normal gameplay framing the fine
 * grain is already mostly faded and the island reads clean; bringing the camera in for a close
 * look brings it back. That is the whole of 「近景有細節、遠景乾淨」, and it costs one
 * `smoothstep` on a value the standard shader already has to hand.
 */

import * as THREE from 'three';

import { NOISE_GLSL } from './proceduralNoise';
import { GROUND_FIELD_UV_SCALE, getGroundFieldTexture } from '../../lib/groundField';
import { ISLAND_TERRAIN } from '../../constants/terrain';

/**
 * How wide the grass-to-sand grade is, in LOCAL island units, and the colour it lands on.
 *
 * 1.1 is a little wider than the grass's own thinning band (0.82, see `RIM_FADE_START` in
 * lib/groundField.ts), on purpose: the soil has to START turning before the last tuft goes, or
 * the two transitions stack into one visible step instead of overlapping into a beach.
 *
 * The colour is `SandEdge`'s own dry-sand hex (#fef08a) pulled well down toward the soil, because
 * this is damp sand under the last of the turf rather than the bright dry sand of the beach
 * proper — landing exactly on the beach colour would make the plateau look like it has a painted
 * border.
 */
const EDGE_SAND_WIDTH = 1.1;
const EDGE_SAND_COLOR: readonly [number, number, number] = [0.706, 0.647, 0.396];

/**
 * The island's XZ scale, shared by every material this module hands out.
 *
 * The field is authored in LOCAL island units (see lib/groundField.ts) while a fragment shader
 * only knows world position, so the shader has to divide — and the divisor is the territory
 * level's scale, which changes at runtime. It lives here, as one uniform object shared by every
 * terrain material, because there is exactly one island: a per-material copy would be four
 * copies of one fact, kept in step by hand.
 */
const islandScaleUniform = { value: 1 };

/** Called by Island.tsx whenever the territory level changes. */
export function setTerrainIslandScale(scale: number): void {
  islandScaleUniform.value = scale;
}

/**
 * Which grading a surface takes.
 *
 *   plateau  the lawn. Full lushness grading, full bump.
 *   mound    the raised ground. Same treatment, read a little drier — a rise catches more light
 *            and dries out faster, and that one number is what stops the mound looking like a
 *            disc of a different green set down on the lawn.
 *   shore    the sand cone and the island's own skirt. GRAIN ONLY: no lushness, no wear, no
 *            bump, so their authored gradients come through untouched and merely stop being
 *            perfectly smooth.
 */
export type TerrainSurface = 'plateau' | 'mound' | 'shore';

const SURFACES: Record<TerrainSurface, {
  /** How far lushness may move the colour. */
  lushGain: number;
  /** How far a worn patch may expose earth. */
  wearGain: number;
  /** Fine (close-range) grain strength. */
  grainGain: number;
  /** Mid (clump-scale) mottle strength. */
  midGain: number;
  /** Normal tilt from the field's own gradient — see the bump note in `patchTerrainShader`. */
  bumpGain: number;
  /**
   * How far the surface's own colour gives way to sand over the last stretch before the plateau's
   * rim. 0 leaves the edge alone.
   *
   * The other half of the shoreline fix. `lib/groundField.ts` already thins the GRASS to nothing
   * by r 5.6, but thinning the plants only removes what stands ON the ground — the ground itself
   * still ended at its own geometric edge as a hard circle of dark green against beige sand, and
   * a lawn that stops at a drawn line is exactly 「草地與其他地面材質銜接生硬」.
   *
   * The two are tuned to overlap: the grass is gone before the colour has fully turned, so the
   * sequence reading outward is grass on green, thinning grass on paling green, bare sand-tinted
   * soil, then the sand cone itself. That is a beach.
   */
  edgeSand: number;
  /** Deep, slightly blue-shifted green a fully lush patch leans toward. */
  lushTint: readonly [number, number, number];
  /** Pale, yellower green a thin patch leans toward. */
  dryTint: readonly [number, number, number];
  /** Bare soil under a worn patch. */
  earth: readonly [number, number, number];
  roughBase: number;
}> = {
  plateau: {
    /**
     * Both gains are deliberately modest, and that is a tuning lesson worth keeping.
     *
     * The first pass ran the dry end at 0.5 toward a khaki and the island came out the colour of
     * dry hay. The field's mean sits near 0.5, so a grading that strong is not "variation around
     * the island's green" — it is a NEW base colour with the old one showing through in patches.
     * The rule these numbers follow: a mid-field spot must still read as PLATEAU_INNER_COLOR.
     */
    lushGain: 0.4,
    wearGain: 0.34,
    grainGain: 0.085,
    midGain: 0.1,
    bumpGain: 0.55,
    edgeSand: 0.62,
    lushTint: [0.208, 0.396, 0.055],
    dryTint: [0.435, 0.478, 0.173],
    earth: [0.376, 0.302, 0.184],
    roughBase: 0.88,
  },
  mound: {
    // Graded HARDER than the plateau, not softer. The mound is a 5 m disc of one flat colour
    // sitting inside a lawn that now has variation, and the eye finds an unbroken surface
    // instantly however small it is — so the raised ground needs at least as much breakup as the
    // ground around it, not less.
    lushGain: 0.46,
    wearGain: 0.3,
    grainGain: 0.085,
    midGain: 0.16,
    bumpGain: 0.5,
    edgeSand: 0,
    lushTint: [0.271, 0.447, 0.078],
    dryTint: [0.502, 0.545, 0.216],
    earth: [0.408, 0.333, 0.2],
    roughBase: 0.9,
  },
  shore: {
    lushGain: 0,
    wearGain: 0,
    grainGain: 0.07,
    midGain: 0.055,
    bumpGain: 0,
    edgeSand: 0,
    lushTint: [0.545, 0.596, 0.212],
    dryTint: [0.545, 0.596, 0.212],
    earth: [0.545, 0.478, 0.318],
    roughBase: 0.92,
  },
};

/**
 * ONE patch function for every surface, so three's program cache (keyed on
 * `onBeforeCompile.toString()`, exactly as hairShading.ts documents) compiles this GLSL once for
 * the whole island rather than once per surface. The per-surface numbers arrive as uniforms,
 * read back off `this.userData` the same way.
 */
function patchTerrainShader(
  this: THREE.MeshStandardMaterial,
  shader: THREE.WebGLProgramParametersWithUniforms,
) {
  Object.assign(shader.uniforms, this.userData.terrainUniforms);

  shader.vertexShader = shader.vertexShader
    .replace(
      'void main() {',
      'varying vec3 vTerrainW;\nvarying vec3 vTerrainN;\nvoid main() {',
    )
    .replace(
      '#include <begin_vertex>',
      `#include <begin_vertex>
       vTerrainW = (modelMatrix * vec4(transformed, 1.0)).xyz;
       vTerrainN = normalize(mat3(modelMatrix) * objectNormal);`,
    );

  shader.fragmentShader = shader.fragmentShader
    .replace(
      'void main() {',
      `varying vec3 vTerrainW;
       varying vec3 vTerrainN;
       uniform sampler2D uGroundField;
       uniform float uIslandScale;
       uniform vec4 uTerrainGain;     // lush, wear, fine grain, mid grain
       uniform vec3 uTerrainEdge;     // sand strength, fade start radius, fade width
       uniform vec3 uTerrainSand;
       uniform float uTerrainBump;
       uniform vec3 uTerrainLush;
       uniform vec3 uTerrainDry;
       uniform vec3 uTerrainEarth;
       uniform float uTerrainRough;
       ${NOISE_GLSL}
       void main() {
         // Filled in by the <color_fragment> block below and read again by
         // <normal_fragment_begin>, which three runs later in the same main().
         float terrainRough = uTerrainRough;
         vec2 terrainUv = vec2(0.5);`,
    )
    .replace(
      '#include <color_fragment>',
      `#include <color_fragment>
       {
         // Local island XZ — the frame lib/groundField.ts is authored in.
         vec2 L = vTerrainW.xz / max(uIslandScale, 0.0001);
         terrainUv = L * ${GROUND_FIELD_UV_SCALE.toFixed(6)} + 0.5;
         vec2 field = texture2D(uGroundField, terrainUv).rg;
         float lush = field.r;
         float wear = field.g;

         vec3 col = diffuseColor.rgb;

         // Lushness moves the base green between a dry pale and a deep saturated one. Both moves
         // are anchored so that a MID-field spot keeps almost exactly the colour the island
         // already had — the grading adds variation without shifting the island's overall hue.
         col = mix(col, uTerrainDry, uTerrainGain.x * (1.0 - smoothstep(-0.15, 0.72, lush)));
         col = mix(col, uTerrainLush, uTerrainGain.x * smoothstep(0.4, 1.05, lush));

         // Worn earth, and only where there is no grass to hide it.
         float bare = wear * (1.0 - 0.55 * lush);
         col = mix(col, uTerrainEarth, uTerrainGain.y * bare);

         // The shoreline. The last stretch of lawn before the plateau's own rim turns to sand, so
         // the disc does not end as a drawn circle of green against beige.
         float edge = smoothstep(${(0).toFixed(1)}, 1.0, (length(L) - uTerrainEdge.y) / max(uTerrainEdge.z, 0.0001));
         col = mix(col, uTerrainSand, edge * uTerrainEdge.x);

         // MID grain: clump-sized mottle, safe at any distance.
         float mid = fFbm(L * 1.5) - 0.5;
         col *= 1.0 + uTerrainGain.w * mid * 2.0;

         // FINE grain: faded out with distance so it cannot alias when the surface is minified.
         // vViewPosition is the fragment-to-camera vector the standard shader already carries.
         float nearness = 1.0 - smoothstep(9.0, 26.0, length(vViewPosition));
         float fine = fFbm(L * 7.0 + 13.0) - 0.5;
         col *= 1.0 + uTerrainGain.z * fine * 2.0 * nearness;

         diffuseColor.rgb = col;
         // Lush grass scatters; bare compacted earth is a touch tighter.
         terrainRough = clamp(uTerrainRough + 0.06 * lush - 0.12 * bare, 0.25, 1.0);
       }`,
    )
    .replace(
      '#include <roughnessmap_fragment>',
      '#include <roughnessmap_fragment>\n\troughnessFactor = terrainRough;',
    )
    .replace(
      '#include <normal_fragment_begin>',
      `#include <normal_fragment_begin>
       #ifdef USE_TERRAIN_BUMP
       {
         // THE ONLY RELIEF ON A SURFACE THAT MUST STAY FLAT.
         //
         // The plateau is the ground the character walks on and getIslandSurfaceY swears it is
         // flat, so its geometry may not move. Tilting the NORMAL by the lushness field's own
         // gradient gives the lighting something to grade across — the lawn picks up soft rises
         // and hollows — while every collision, placement and walk-height query is untouched.
         //
         // Keyed on the same field the tufts are scattered by, so a "hollow" is also where the
         // grass is deepest, which is what makes it read as terrain rather than as a stain.
         //
         // Low frequency by construction (the field is ~0.12 local units per texel, linearly
         // filtered), so unlike a noise-based bump this cannot shimmer when minified.
         const float E = 0.006;
         float hx = texture2D(uGroundField, terrainUv + vec2(E, 0.0)).r
                  - texture2D(uGroundField, terrainUv - vec2(E, 0.0)).r;
         float hz = texture2D(uGroundField, terrainUv + vec2(0.0, E)).r
                  - texture2D(uGroundField, terrainUv - vec2(0.0, E)).r;
         // Only surfaces that face upward get it: a vertical skirt has no "slope" to express and
         // tilting its normal sideways would just make the cliff face wobble.
         float up = clamp(vTerrainN.y, 0.0, 1.0);
         vec3 tiltW = vec3(-hx, 0.0, -hz) * uTerrainBump * up;
         normal = normalize(normal + (viewMatrix * vec4(tiltW, 0.0)).xyz);
       }
       #endif`,
    );
}

const cache = new Map<string, THREE.MeshStandardMaterial>();

/**
 * The shared material for one terrain surface.
 *
 * Cached per surface AND per base colour: the plateau passes white because its colour arrives as
 * a vertex attribute, the mounds pass their own green. Two mounds are one material and one
 * program.
 *
 * `vertexColors` is decided by the caller rather than sniffed, because the plateau and the sand
 * cone both carry a `color` attribute and the mounds do not — and a material with `vertexColors`
 * on over a geometry without the attribute renders black (see instanceColor.ts for the same trap
 * one layer down).
 */
export function getTerrainMaterial(
  surface: TerrainSurface,
  color: string,
  vertexColors = false,
): THREE.MeshStandardMaterial {
  const key = `${surface}|${color}|${vertexColors}`;
  const hit = cache.get(key);
  if (hit) return hit;

  const spec = SURFACES[surface];
  const material = new THREE.MeshStandardMaterial({
    color,
    vertexColors,
    roughness: spec.roughBase,
  });

  material.userData.terrainUniforms = {
    uGroundField: { value: getGroundFieldTexture() },
    uIslandScale: islandScaleUniform,
    uTerrainGain: {
      value: new THREE.Vector4(spec.lushGain, spec.wearGain, spec.grainGain, spec.midGain),
    },
    uTerrainEdge: {
      // Start and width in LOCAL island units. Deliberately reaching all the way to the plateau's
      // own rim: this is the ground's half of the shoreline, and it has to finish exactly where
      // the geometry does or it would leave a sliver of untreated green at the very edge.
      value: new THREE.Vector3(
        spec.edgeSand,
        ISLAND_TERRAIN.plateauRadius - EDGE_SAND_WIDTH,
        EDGE_SAND_WIDTH,
      ),
    },
    uTerrainSand: { value: new THREE.Vector3(...EDGE_SAND_COLOR) },
    uTerrainBump: { value: spec.bumpGain },
    uTerrainLush: { value: new THREE.Vector3(...spec.lushTint) },
    uTerrainDry: { value: new THREE.Vector3(...spec.dryTint) },
    uTerrainEarth: { value: new THREE.Vector3(...spec.earth) },
    uTerrainRough: { value: spec.roughBase },
  };
  // A define rather than a `uTerrainBump > 0` branch, so the two extra texture fetches are not
  // even compiled into the shore's program.
  if (spec.bumpGain > 0) material.defines = { ...material.defines, USE_TERRAIN_BUMP: '' };
  material.onBeforeCompile = patchTerrainShader;
  // three keys its shader cache on onBeforeCompile's source text, which is identical for every
  // surface built by this one factory — and the surfaces differ by a DEFINE, which the cache key
  // must therefore include or all four would be handed whichever program compiled first.
  material.customProgramCacheKey = () => `terrain|${surface}|${vertexColors}`;

  cache.set(key, material);
  return material;
}
```

## src/components/Three/instanceColor.ts

```ts
/**
 * @license
 * SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
 */

import * as THREE from 'three';

/**
 * What an InstancedMesh needs before `setColorAt` does anything at all.
 *
 * three writes `instanceColor` into `vColor`, but `vColor` is only *read* in the fragment shader
 * under `USE_COLOR` — which comes from `material.vertexColors`, not from the instance colours. So
 * a per-instance tint on a material that has not opted in is silently ignored: every instance
 * renders in the material's own colour, `setColorAt` looks broken, and nothing warns.
 *
 * Turning `vertexColors` on then creates the opposite trap. It makes three declare
 * `attribute vec3 color`, and WebGL feeds an unbound attribute (0, 0, 0), so a geometry without
 * one renders every instance BLACK. A flat white attribute makes the per-vertex term a no-op and
 * leaves `instanceColor` in sole control.
 *
 * Both halves are one requirement, so they live in one call. This was discovered twice
 * independently — once for the wildflower field (Three/IslandDecorations.tsx) and once for the
 * shoal (Three/Fish.tsx), each of which grew its own private copy — which is exactly why it is
 * extracted here rather than copied a third time for the offline overgrowth.
 */
export function tintableInstances<T extends THREE.BufferGeometry>(geometry: T): T {
  const count = geometry.attributes.position.count;
  geometry.setAttribute('color', new THREE.BufferAttribute(new Float32Array(count * 3).fill(1), 3));
  return geometry;
}

```
