## src/constants/environmentMaps.ts

```ts
/**
 * Environment (IBL) maps, served from this project's own `public/` folder.
 *
 * drei's `<Environment preset="..." />` is a convenience wrapper that fetches the
 * matching HDR from `raw.githubusercontent.com/pmndrs/drei-assets` at runtime.
 * That host rate-limits by IP and answers with a 429 once the limit is hit, and
 * because `<Environment>` loads through Suspense the rejected fetch is rethrown
 * during render - React unwinds to the nearest error boundary and the ENTIRE
 * game goes to the crash screen. A third party's rate limiter must not be able
 * to decide whether this game boots, so the three presets in use are vendored
 * into `public/hdri/` and referenced by path instead:
 *
 *   preset="sunset"    -> venice_sunset_1k.hdr
 *   preset="apartment" -> lebombo_1k.hdr
 *   preset="city"      -> potsdamer_platz_1k.hdr
 *
 * These are the exact files the presets resolved to, so the lighting is
 * unchanged. Paths are absolute (`/hdri/...`) because Vite serves `public/`
 * from the site root in dev and copies it to `dist/` on build - see server.ts,
 * which hands `dist/` to express.static in production.
 *
 * To add another preset: look up its filename in drei's `presetsObj`, download
 * it into `public/hdri/`, and add it here. Never reach for `preset=` again.
 */

/** Outdoor golden-hour light. Used by the island scene. */
export const HDRI_SUNSET = '/hdri/venice_sunset_1k.hdr';

/** Soft indoor light. Used by building interiors. */
export const HDRI_APARTMENT = '/hdri/lebombo_1k.hdr';

/** Neutral overcast street light. Used by the fitness demo figure. */
export const HDRI_CITY = '/hdri/potsdamer_platz_1k.hdr';
```

## src/constants/fragments.ts

```ts
/**
 * @license
 * SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
 */

import type { UserProfile } from '../types';
import { ALL_ITEMS, getItemById, type ItemDefinition } from './items';
import { isInChannel } from './distribution';
import { isStackableItem } from '../utils/inventory';

/**
 * 商品碎片 — the game's second way to own something, and the only one that is EARNED rather than
 * paid for.
 *
 * ## The one rule that shapes everything else
 *
 * A fragment belongs to exactly one product. There is no shared 通用碎片, no per-rarity pool and no
 * per-category pool, because every one of those turns「我還差多少」into a question the player cannot
 * answer by looking at the thing they want. A fragment stack is keyed by the item's own catalog id
 * ({@link UserProfile.itemFragments}), so 「珊瑚吊燈碎片」 is a real, distinct object in the save and
 * can never be spent on anything but 珊瑚吊燈.
 *
 * That also means this file never has to police mixing: the data model makes it impossible rather
 * than the code making it forbidden.
 *
 * ## Where they come from
 *
 *  - 運動結算 (components/FitnessView.tsx) — the everyday source, scaled by how much work was done.
 *  - 每日簽到 (components/UI/DailyLoginPanel.tsx) — the round's 主打商品, one item for the whole
 *    seven days so a week of logins adds up to something instead of scattering.
 *  - 幸運轉盤 (constants/luckyWheel.ts) — five of its ten wedges. It settles through the SAME pure
 *    functions the other two do ({@link settleFragmentGain}), and folds the result into its own
 *    single write because it also has to charge a 抽獎券 in the same breath — see
 *    context/useWheelActions.ts. Adding it moved no rule out of this file.
 *
 * ## Where they go
 *
 * {@link FRAGMENTS_TO_UNLOCK} of one item's fragments unlocks that item, free. A stack never grows
 * past that number: anything over the line is 多出來的碎片 and is settled by
 * {@link settleFragmentGain} into 抽獎券 instead, which is what stops a maxed-out item from
 * silently eating every drop it is handed. See {@link FRAGMENTS_PER_TICKET}.
 */

/** How many of an item's own fragments unlock it. The one number the whole feature is priced on. */
export const FRAGMENTS_TO_UNLOCK = 200;

/**
 * How many 多出來的碎片 make one 抽獎券.
 *
 * The overflow rate is deliberately coarse. Fragments over the line are a *consolation*, not a
 * second currency the player is meant to farm — if the rate were fine enough to make maxing an item
 * out and then feeding it profitable, the unlock itself would stop being the thing worth walking to.
 *
 * It does not divide evenly, so the remainder is CARRIED on the profile
 * ({@link UserProfile.raffleTicketProgress}) rather than dropped. Without the carry, five overflow
 * fragments would pay nothing and a player who overflows five at a time would be paid nothing ever,
 * while watching the number go up — the carry is what makes 「多出來的碎片會變成抽獎券」 true for
 * every amount instead of only for multiples of 20.
 */
export const FRAGMENTS_PER_TICKET = 20;

/**
 * 新玩家（和每一個在抽獎券存在之前就開好的存檔）拿到的第一張券。
 *
 * 一張，不是十張：它要買的是「知道轉盤是什麼」，不是一段免費的遊玩。轉一次會看到整個獎品階梯、
 * 拿到一份碎片，然後下一張券要自己來 —— 這正是要讓玩家知道的那件事（多出來的碎片會變成券，
 * 商店也買得到）。
 *
 * 發放的條件是「存檔裡完全沒有 `raffleTickets` 這個欄位」而不是一個新的旗標欄位（見
 * context/AppContext.tsx 的載入修補）。這樣寫有兩個好處：不必為了一次性的發放在
 * firestore.rules 上開一個新欄位（新欄位在部署到正式規則之前一律寫入失敗，見
 * docs/FIRESTORE_RULES.md），而且它天生只會發生一次 —— 寫完之後欄位就存在了。
 */
export const WELCOME_RAFFLE_TICKETS = 1;

/**
 * Whether this catalog entry has a fragment of its own.
 *
 * Everything the player buys with gold in the ordinary 商店 does. The exclusions are not
 * categories — they are the things that are not *a purchase you can make on that shelf*:
 *
 *  - an 經驗值 item (`xpUnlock`, utils/unlock.ts) is already earned rather than bought, and giving it
 *    a second earning track would mean two progress bars racing for the same card;
 *  - a `price: 0` entry is not on sale at all (毛胚屋 — see constants/houseStyles.ts), so there is
 *    nothing for 200 fragments to stand in for;
 *  - anything the ordinary shop does not stock (constants/distribution.ts). 商品碎片 are collected
 *    ON a shop card and redeemed FROM one: the meter, the 免費解鎖 button and the whole flow live
 *    on `PurchaseDialog`. A 限時商店 exclusive has no such card, so fragments collected toward it
 *    could never be spent — a bar filling toward an unlock the player cannot reach. Better that
 *    they are never minted. (Whatever a save already holds is not lost: buying that accessory in
 *    the 限時商店 settles the stranded stack into 抽獎券 through the same
 *    `fragmentPatchForPurchase` the ordinary shop uses — see context/useLimitedShop.ts.)
 */
export function isFragmentItem(item: ItemDefinition | string | null | undefined): boolean {
  const def = typeof item === 'string' ? getItemById(item) : item;
  if (!def) return false;
  if (!isInChannel(def, 'main-shop')) return false;
  // 抽獎券（`grantsTickets`，見 constants/items.ts）是第三種例外，而且是最不能少的一種：它買到
  // 的不是一個物件而是一個餘額，所以「集滿 200 個碎片免費解鎖它」會在背包裡放進一筆什麼都不做
  // 的資料 —— 而且那是一個迴圈，多出來的碎片本來就會自動變成券。
  if (def.grantsTickets) return false;
  return !def.xpUnlock && def.price > 0;
}

/**
 * Whether owning one of these leaves the fragment stack ALIVE.
 *
 * This is the split the shop card was missing. 「有沒有擁有」 and 「還要不要繼續收集碎片」 used to be
 * the same boolean in four different places — {@link canUnlockWithFragments} refused on `owned`,
 * the meter hid itself on `owned`, the purchase dialog hid the meter on `ownedCount > 0`, and
 * `fragmentPatchForPurchase` DELETED the stack on any purchase at all. For a hat all four are
 * right: there is exactly one of it, so once it is in the wardrobe its fragments can never buy
 * anything again.
 *
 * For a sofa all four are wrong. A placeable STACKS — one inventory entry per copy bought
 * (utils/inventory.ts) — and 特殊卡牌 stack the same way, so 「已擁有」 on those two kinds means
 * 「你有一件」, not 「這條路結束了」. The fragments a player is holding are still valid for the NEXT
 * one. Hiding the bar told them otherwise, and deleting the stack then made it true.
 *
 * Delegates to {@link isStackableItem} rather than re-deriving 「可不可以再買一件」 from the category:
 * that question already has exactly one answer in this codebase, and a second copy of it is free to
 * drift. Note it takes an ITEM and never a profile — this file still does not read ownership (see
 * {@link canUnlockWithFragments}); it only asks what KIND of thing the item is.
 */
export function isRepeatableFragmentItem(item: ItemDefinition | string | null | undefined): boolean {
  const def = typeof item === 'string' ? getItemById(item) : item;
  if (!def) return false;
  return isFragmentItem(def) && isStackableItem(def.id);
}

/**
 * Whether this item is still collecting fragments — the question every progress surface should be
 * asking instead of 「已擁有嗎」.
 *
 * Yes for an item not yet owned, and yes for an owned one that can be bought again. Ownership is
 * passed in for the same reason it is passed to {@link canUnlockWithFragments}: this file has no
 * business knowing how utils/inventory.ts counts copies.
 *
 * It deliberately does NOT cover the leftover-stack case — an own-once item that somehow still holds
 * fragments. That is the meter's own concern, because a stack which should not exist is a save to be
 * reported, not a state to design for.
 */
export function collectsFragments(itemId: string, owned: boolean): boolean {
  if (!isFragmentItem(itemId)) return false;
  return !owned || isRepeatableFragmentItem(itemId);
}

/**
 * Every item that has a fragment, in catalog order.
 *
 * This is the drop pool for every source. Computed once: `ALL_ITEMS` is a module-level constant and
 * re-filtering it per workout would be re-deriving the same list a few hundred times a session.
 */
export const FRAGMENT_ITEMS: readonly ItemDefinition[] = ALL_ITEMS.filter(isFragmentItem);

/** The fragment's own name, in the player's words: 「珊瑚吊燈碎片」. */
export function fragmentName(item: ItemDefinition | string | null | undefined): string {
  const def = typeof item === 'string' ? getItemById(item) : item;
  return def ? `${def.name}碎片` : '商品碎片';
}

/** How many of that item's fragments the save is holding. */
export function getFragmentCount(
  profile: UserProfile | null | undefined,
  itemId: string,
): number {
  const stored = profile?.itemFragments?.[itemId];
  return typeof stored === 'number' && Number.isFinite(stored) ? Math.max(0, Math.floor(stored)) : 0;
}

/** How many more are needed before {@link FRAGMENTS_TO_UNLOCK} is reached. 0 once it is. */
export function getFragmentsRemaining(
  profile: UserProfile | null | undefined,
  itemId: string,
): number {
  return Math.max(0, FRAGMENTS_TO_UNLOCK - getFragmentCount(profile, itemId));
}

/** Progress toward the unlock as 0–1 — the fill of the bar on the shop card. */
export function getFragmentProgress(
  profile: UserProfile | null | undefined,
  itemId: string,
): number {
  return Math.min(1, getFragmentCount(profile, itemId) / FRAGMENTS_TO_UNLOCK);
}

/**
 * Whether the fragment route is open on this item right now: it has a fragment, the stack is full,
 * and it is still collecting ({@link collectsFragments}).
 *
 * That last clause is the behaviour change. This used to be a flat `!owned`, so a player who filled
 * a second 200 toward a sofa they already owned was shown a full bar with no way to spend it. A
 * repeatable item's fragments buy the NEXT copy.
 *
 * Ownership is passed in rather than read here, so this file never has to know about
 * utils/inventory.ts's stacking rules — see the call in context/useFragmentActions.ts.
 */
export function canUnlockWithFragments(
  profile: UserProfile | null | undefined,
  itemId: string,
  owned: boolean,
): boolean {
  return collectsFragments(itemId, owned) && getFragmentCount(profile, itemId) >= FRAGMENTS_TO_UNLOCK;
}

/** 抽獎券 in hand. What the 幸運轉盤 charges one of per spin (constants/luckyWheel.ts). */
export function getRaffleTickets(profile: UserProfile | null | undefined): number {
  const held = profile?.raffleTickets;
  return typeof held === 'number' && Number.isFinite(held) ? Math.max(0, Math.floor(held)) : 0;
}

/** Overflow fragments already banked toward the next ticket, 0…{@link FRAGMENTS_PER_TICKET}-1. */
export function getTicketProgress(profile: UserProfile | null | undefined): number {
  const carry = profile?.raffleTicketProgress;
  const value = typeof carry === 'number' && Number.isFinite(carry) ? Math.max(0, Math.floor(carry)) : 0;
  return value % FRAGMENTS_PER_TICKET;
}

/**
 * Whether 多餘碎片轉換成抽獎券 is on for this save.
 *
 * Defaults to ON for a profile that predates the setting — `undefined` has to mean *something*, and
 * the alternative is a player whose overflow is silently thrown away by a switch they have never
 * seen. See {@link settleFragmentGain} for what OFF actually does.
 */
export function isOverflowConversionEnabled(
  settings: { fragmentOverflowToTickets?: boolean } | null | undefined,
): boolean {
  return settings?.fragmentOverflowToTickets !== false;
}

/**
 * What one grant of fragments actually does to the save — the whole overflow rule, as a pure
 * function.
 *
 * It is pure and it is in this file rather than inside the write path because it is the piece every
 * surface has to agree on: the settlement screen previews it before the write, the daily panel
 * announces its result after the write, and the shop card renders what it left behind. Three
 * screens re-deriving 「200 減掉現有的，剩下的除以 20」 is three chances to be off by one.
 *
 * `convert: false` (the setting turned off) does not bank the overflow somewhere else — it drops it.
 * That is the honest reading of turning the conversion off, and it is why the setting's copy says so
 * outright rather than describing itself as a preference.
 */
export interface FragmentSettlement {
  /** The item's stack after the grant. Never above {@link FRAGMENTS_TO_UNLOCK}. */
  stored: number;
  /** How many of the incoming fragments actually landed on the item. */
  kept: number;
  /** How many had nowhere to go — the 多出來的碎片. */
  overflow: number;
  /** Whole 抽獎券 minted from that overflow. 0 when the conversion is off. */
  tickets: number;
  /** The fraction of a ticket left over, to be carried on the profile. */
  carry: number;
}

export function settleFragmentGain({
  current,
  amount,
  carry = 0,
  convert = true,
}: {
  /** The item's stack before this grant. */
  current: number;
  /** How many fragments are being granted. */
  amount: number;
  /** {@link getTicketProgress} — overflow already banked toward the next ticket. */
  carry?: number;
  /** {@link isOverflowConversionEnabled}. */
  convert?: boolean;
}): FragmentSettlement {
  const held = Math.max(0, Math.floor(current));
  const incoming = Math.max(0, Math.floor(amount));
  const kept = Math.min(incoming, Math.max(0, FRAGMENTS_TO_UNLOCK - held));
  const overflow = incoming - kept;

  if (!convert || overflow === 0) {
    return { stored: held + kept, kept, overflow, tickets: 0, carry: carry % FRAGMENTS_PER_TICKET };
  }

  const pool = (carry % FRAGMENTS_PER_TICKET) + overflow;
  return {
    stored: held + kept,
    kept,
    overflow,
    tickets: Math.floor(pool / FRAGMENTS_PER_TICKET),
    carry: pool % FRAGMENTS_PER_TICKET,
  };
}

/**
 * What a whole stack is worth when the item is bought with gold instead.
 *
 * The second half of 「多出來的碎片」, and the one that is easy to miss: a player who was 180/200 of
 * the way to a lamp and then simply buys the lamp has 180 fragments that can never unlock anything
 * again, because the only thing they were ever valid for is now owned. Left alone they would sit in
 * the save forever as a number the player cannot act on. This converts the lot at the same rate the
 * overflow uses, so the two paths to a dead fragment pay the same.
 */
export function settleFragmentsOnPurchase({
  stored,
  carry = 0,
  convert = true,
}: {
  stored: number;
  carry?: number;
  convert?: boolean;
}): { tickets: number; carry: number; converted: number } {
  const held = Math.max(0, Math.floor(stored));
  if (!convert || held === 0) return { tickets: 0, carry: carry % FRAGMENTS_PER_TICKET, converted: 0 };
  const pool = (carry % FRAGMENTS_PER_TICKET) + held;
  return {
    tickets: Math.floor(pool / FRAGMENTS_PER_TICKET),
    carry: pool % FRAGMENTS_PER_TICKET,
    converted: held,
  };
}

// --- Where a drop lands ------------------------------------------------------

/** One grant, of one item's fragments. The shape every source hands to the write path. */
export interface FragmentGrant {
  itemId: string;
  amount: number;
}

/**
 * ## 每日登入的碎片曾經住在這裡 (2026-09-17)
 *
 * There used to be a `featuredFragmentItem(cycleId)` and a `DAILY_FRAGMENT_LADDER` here: one 主打
 * 商品 per round, and a seven-step ladder of how many of its fragments each day paid. The round no
 * longer works that way — every day is now its own draw and a fragment day picks its own item from
 * the 普通／稀有 shelf — so both moved to constants/dailyLoginPrizes.ts, which is where the round's
 * prizes live. Nothing about the fragment RULES moved with them: the cap, the overflow conversion
 * and the carry are still the pure functions above, and the new roller calls them exactly as the
 * old one did.
 *
 * The seeded pick they were built on is in constants/seed.ts now, shared with the wheel and the
 * 限時商店 rotation rather than hand-rolled here a second time.
 */

/**
 * What a finished workout pays in fragments, from the reps counted.
 *
 * Floored rather than proportional-all-the-way-down so a short session is still worth something, and
 * capped so a very long one cannot outpace the daily ladder — 運動 is the steady source, not the
 * fast one.
 */
export const WORKOUT_FRAGMENT_MIN = 3;
export const WORKOUT_FRAGMENT_MAX = 40;

export function fragmentsForWorkout(reps: number): number {
  const counted = Math.max(0, Math.floor(reps));
  if (counted === 0) return 0;
  return Math.min(WORKOUT_FRAGMENT_MAX, Math.max(WORKOUT_FRAGMENT_MIN, Math.floor(counted * 0.6)));
}

/**
 * Which item a workout's fragments are for.
 *
 * Weighted toward what is still collectible and already started, in that order:
 *
 *  1. a stack that is part-way there and still collecting — finishing something the player can see
 *     themselves finishing is the whole appeal of a fragment;
 *  2. any item not yet owned, so the pool keeps opening new ones;
 *  3. anything still collecting, once everything is owned — which for a stackable item means a
 *     second copy, a real reward rather than a consolation;
 *  4. anything at all, so the fragments are never worth nothing: they settle into 抽獎券 on arrival
 *     (see {@link settleFragmentGain}).
 *
 * ## Why tier 1 is no longer 「未擁有 AND 收集中」
 *
 * It used to filter on `!isOwned` at the top, which had a consequence the shop card then blamed on
 * the UI: an owned-but-repeatable item could not receive a fragment from the everyday source, so a
 * bar drawn for it would have been a bar that could never move. Drawing the bar (the point of
 * {@link collectsFragments}) and being able to fill it are the same feature — fixing one without
 * the other just moves the lie from 「進度不見了」 to 「進度不會動」.
 *
 * `random` is injected rather than called here so a caller (or a test) can make the roll
 * deterministic without stubbing a global.
 */
export function rollWorkoutFragmentItem(
  profile: UserProfile | null | undefined,
  isOwned: (itemId: string) => boolean,
  random: () => number = Math.random,
): ItemDefinition | null {
  if (FRAGMENT_ITEMS.length === 0) return null;

  const collecting = FRAGMENT_ITEMS.filter(item => collectsFragments(item.id, isOwned(item.id)));
  const started = collecting.filter(item => {
    const held = getFragmentCount(profile, item.id);
    return held > 0 && held < FRAGMENTS_TO_UNLOCK;
  });
  // Something brand new still outranks a second copy of something owned, so an unowned item is its
  // own tier rather than being folded into `collecting`.
  const fresh = collecting.filter(item => !isOwned(item.id));

  // 65% onto a stack already going, when there is one. Not 100%: a player who has one part-finished
  // item would otherwise never be shown a second one, and the pool would close behind them.
  const pool = started.length > 0 && random() < 0.65
    ? started
    : fresh.length > 0
      ? fresh
      : collecting.length > 0
        ? collecting
        : FRAGMENT_ITEMS;

  return pool[Math.floor(random() * pool.length) % pool.length];
}
```

## src/constants/furnitureInteractions.ts

```ts
/**
 * @license
 * SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
 */

import type { CharacterSkeleton } from './characterRig';
import { toWorld } from './characterRig';
import { getItemById } from './items';
import type { SuspendedMotionId } from './outdoorAnimation';
import {
  PostureAnchoring,
  PostureId,
  getPosture,
} from './interactionPostures';

/**
 * WHAT A PIECE OF FURNITURE LETS THE PLAYER DO — the one vocabulary the interaction system
 * speaks, and the sibling of constants/placement.ts.
 *
 * ## Why this file exists
 *
 * Before it, "can the player do something with this?" was answered by two hard-coded lists
 * inside the character controller (Three/Avatar.tsx):
 *
 *   `if (item.name === '吊床')`                    — the one piece you could lie on
 *   `INTERACTIVE_DECOR_NAMES = ['木製鞦韆', …]`     — the five that played an animation
 *
 * Both were keyed on the item's Chinese NAME, both lived in the file that animates the body,
 * and neither could be extended without editing that file. Indoors there was no third list —
 * every piece of furniture in the house was scenery, however obviously it was a seat.
 *
 * So the CAPABILITY ("this is something you sit on") existed nowhere as data. This module makes
 * it a declared property of the item, exactly as `placement`, `standable` and `tabletop` already
 * are: adding 鞦韆, 吊床, 浴缸, 鋼琴, 書桌 or 望遠鏡 behaviour is one field in the catalog, and
 * the controller, the prompt and the UI all follow from it without learning a single item name.
 *
 * ## The split this file used to be missing
 *
 * It originally held BOTH halves of an interaction — the verb and the body — in one table, and
 * that is what made every non-seat interaction in the game look the same. Its `pose` column had
 * exactly two values, `'sit'` and `'lie'`; every other kind left it undefined, and undefined was
 * routed to one shared two-arm reach. 泡澡, 烹飪, 觀星, 洗手, 許願 and 閱讀 were the same
 * animation with different captions, because there was nowhere to say otherwise.
 *
 * The two halves are now separate files:
 *
 *   THIS FILE                        the VERB — what the prompt offers, and where on the piece
 *                                    the body goes.
 *   constants/interactionPostures.ts the BODY — what the whole skeleton does, as joint targets.
 *
 * A kind names a posture; an item may override that posture; and nothing downstream branches on
 * either. See {@link INTERACTION_KINDS}.
 *
 * ## What IS here and what is NOT
 *
 * HERE: the verb, the posture it selects, and — for a posture that puts the body ON the piece —
 * WHERE ON THE PIECE it goes, stated in the piece's own local frame so it rides the placement's
 * position, rotation and scale. Nothing is ever expressed in world coordinates.
 *
 * NOT HERE: how big the piece is, how far away the player may stand, where the prompt floats.
 * All three are measured off the model (lib/furniturePlacement.ts) and resolved in
 * lib/furnitureInteraction.ts, for the same reason placement carries no sizes: a table of
 * dimensions can disagree with the thing on screen, and eventually does.
 */

/**
 * Which icon the touch prompt shows. A short closed set rather than a lucide name, so the
 * catalog never has to know which icon library the HUD is drawn with — UI/InteractionPrompt.tsx
 * maps these to components.
 */
export type InteractionIcon =
  | 'sit' | 'lie' | 'bath'
  | 'hand' | 'door' | 'panel' | 'cook' | 'droplet' | 'eye' | 'book' | 'sparkle' | 'flame'
  | 'brush' | 'push';

export interface InteractionKindSpec {
  /** What the prompt offers: 「E 坐下」. */
  verb: string;
  /** What it offers once the player is already on the piece. Occupying postures only. */
  exitVerb?: string;
  /**
   * THE JOIN between the verb and the body (constants/interactionPostures.ts).
   *
   * This one field is what the whole rework turns on. It used to be `pose?: 'sit' | 'lie'`,
   * where "absent" meant "no pose" and no pose meant one shared hand-wave; it is now a
   * required name from a table of fourteen full-body postures, so 「泡澡」 selects a body in a
   * bathtub rather than selecting nothing.
   */
  posture: PostureId;
  icon: InteractionIcon;
}

/**
 * The verbs. Adding one is a row here plus a member of the union — and, if no existing body
 * language fits it, a row in the posture table. Nothing downstream branches on the kind itself;
 * every consumer reads these fields.
 */
export type InteractionKind =
  | 'sit' | 'lie' | 'rest' | 'bathe' | 'swing'
  | 'use' | 'open' | 'operate' | 'cook' | 'wash' | 'observe' | 'read' | 'wish' | 'tend'
  | 'groom' | 'push' | 'play';

export const INTERACTION_KINDS: Record<InteractionKind, InteractionKindSpec> = {
  // --- the body goes onto or into the piece -----------------------------------
  sit: { verb: '坐下', exitVerb: '起身', posture: 'sit', icon: 'sit' },
  lie: { verb: '躺下', exitVerb: '起身', posture: 'lie', icon: 'lie' },
  // Same body as `lie`, different offer. A bed you sleep in and a hammock you rest in are one
  // posture and two verbs, which is exactly the separation this table now expresses.
  rest: { verb: '休息', exitVerb: '起身', posture: 'lie', icon: 'lie' },
  bathe: { verb: '泡澡', exitVerb: '起身', posture: 'bathe', icon: 'bath' },
  /**
   * 盪鞦韆. An OCCUPYING verb, and that is the whole of the swing rework.
   *
   * It used to be `push` — an ACTING verb, so the player stood beside the swing and played a
   * shove while the seat swung on a timer of its own. Nothing was wrong with that animation; the
   * problem was the category. A swing is a thing you get ON, and once it says so, every piece of
   * behaviour the brief asks for falls out of machinery that already existed: the controller
   * walks the body to the anchor, squares it up, holds it there until 「下來」, and eases it off
   * afterwards — the same code a sofa uses.
   */
  swing: { verb: '盪鞦韆', exitVerb: '下來', posture: 'swing', icon: 'sit' },

  // --- the body acts AT the piece and is handed back --------------------------
  use: { verb: '使用', posture: 'reach', icon: 'hand' },
  open: { verb: '打開', posture: 'open', icon: 'door' },
  operate: { verb: '操作', posture: 'operate', icon: 'panel' },
  cook: { verb: '烹飪', posture: 'cook', icon: 'cook' },
  wash: { verb: '清洗', posture: 'wash', icon: 'droplet' },
  observe: { verb: '觀看', posture: 'observe', icon: 'eye' },
  read: { verb: '閱讀', posture: 'read', icon: 'book' },
  wish: { verb: '許願', posture: 'wish', icon: 'sparkle' },
  tend: { verb: '照料', posture: 'tend', icon: 'flame' },
  groom: { verb: '整理儀容', posture: 'groom', icon: 'brush' },
  push: { verb: '推動', posture: 'push', icon: 'push' },
  play: { verb: '玩耍', posture: 'reach', icon: 'sparkle' },
};

/**
 * Which side of the piece an ACTING posture is played from.
 *
 *   `front`    the piece's own local +Z face — the front of every model in this catalog. What
 *              a fridge, a hob, a sink, a wardrobe and a desk all want: there is one side you
 *              use them from and the rest are their back and their sides.
 *   `nearest`  whichever side the player already happens to be on. What a campfire, a well and
 *              a telescope want: they have no front, and marching the player around to an
 *              arbitrary face of them would look worse than letting them stay put.
 *
 * Note what is NOT here: how far out to stand. That is measured off the piece's own box at
 * runtime, so it is right for a 2.5-unit bed and a 0.6-unit stool without a number being typed.
 */
export type ApproachSide = 'front' | 'nearest';

/**
 * One thing a piece of furniture lets the player do.
 *
 * ### The anchor (occupying postures only)
 *
 * `surfaceY`, `lateral`, `forward` and `facing` describe the Interaction Point — the seat point,
 * the lie point, the spot in the tub — in the PIECE'S OWN LOCAL FRAME, at the scale the piece is
 * drawn. They are never world coordinates: the runtime turns them by the placement's rotation
 * and adds its position, so a sofa rotated to face any wall carries its seat around with it.
 *
 * The body's own height on that anchor is NOT stated here. It is derived from the character rig
 * (constants/characterRig.ts) by {@link poseRootHeight}, so a remodel that changes the
 * character's proportions moves every seated body in the game with it and no catalog row has to
 * be retuned. What the catalog states is a fact about the FURNITURE — where its cushion is —
 * which is measurable, checkable (`npm run audit:interactions`) and cannot go stale in silence.
 */
export interface FurnitureInteraction {
  kind: InteractionKind;
  /**
   * Overrides the kind's posture.
   *
   * The escape hatch that keeps the kind table from having to grow a row for every shade of
   * meaning: a piece whose verb is 「使用」 but whose body language is a crouch says
   * `posture: 'tend'` rather than earning a kind of its own. Use it for a piece that is unusual;
   * a kind of interaction that recurs should become a kind.
   */
  posture?: PostureId;
  /** Overrides {@link INTERACTION_KINDS}'s verb — 「觀星」 on a telescope, 「演奏」 on a piano. */
  verb?: string;
  /** Overrides the exit verb. Occupying postures only. */
  exitVerb?: string;
  /** Overrides the icon, when a shared kind wants a more specific badge. */
  icon?: InteractionIcon;
  /** Acting postures only: which face of the piece it is used from. Defaults to `front`. */
  approach?: ApproachSide;
  /**
   * Occupying postures only, and required for them: the height of the surface the body rests
   * on — a cushion's top face, a mattress's top face, a hammock's fabric, a tub's inner floor —
   * measured from the piece's own base (its local y = 0, which is the floor it stands on).
   */
  surfaceY?: number;
  /**
   * Where the body sits ACROSS the piece — along the axis at right angles to the direction the
   * occupant faces. 0 is the piece's centre; for the usual `facing: 0` this is the piece's own
   * local X, which is what every row in the catalog states it in.
   */
  lateral?: number;
  /**
   * Where along the piece's local Z the body sits. + is toward the piece's local +Z.
   *
   * NOT for a posture whose legs hang over an edge (`reachFloor`) — those state
   * {@link seatFront} instead and have this DERIVED, for the reason set out there. The audit
   * fails an interaction that declares both.
   */
  forward?: number;
  /**
   * THE SEAT'S OWN FRONT LIP — the edge the legs hang over, measured along the direction the
   * occupant faces, from the piece's own origin, at the scale the piece is drawn.
   *
   * ## Why the anchor for a seat is derived from this rather than typed directly
   *
   * This character has no knee. Its leg is ONE straight segment from the hip to the sole, and
   * `poseRootHeight` puts that hip exactly ON the surface the catalog names. So a leg hanging
   * from a hip anywhere behind the seat's front edge is inside the seat — not by a little, and
   * not fixably by choosing a better angle: for any swing at all, the leg is below the top face
   * from the first millimetre, and it stays inside the piece until it has travelled forward as
   * far as the lip. That is a fact about a knee-less leg, not a tuning problem, and the leg
   * solver could not see it because the only thing it was told about the piece was how far the
   * whole BOUNDING BOX reached ahead — which is the armrests, the rocking runners, the L-sofa's
   * chaise and the camp chair's splayed frame, none of which is the cushion.
   *
   * The consequences were both visible in the game. On a deep, high seat (奢華沙發) the box
   * reached 0.26 ahead, the solver put the FOOT just past that, and the whole shin ran 47 cm
   * down through the sofa and came out of its front panel. On a piece whose box reached further
   * ahead than the leg is long (藤編單人沙發, L 型布沙發, 棉麻懶骨頭, 原木搖椅, 小型露營椅)
   * the `asin` saturated and both legs pegged STRAIGHT OUT horizontal, which is the mannequin
   * pose in five of the twelve seats in the catalog.
   *
   * So the one number the catalog states is the one thing a bounding box cannot tell us — where
   * the SEAT stops — and the body's own place on it is derived from the rig by
   * {@link seatHipInset}, exactly as its HEIGHT is already derived from `surfaceY` by
   * {@link poseRootHeight}. A remodelled character with a different build sits correctly on
   * every seat in the game without a catalog row being retyped; a redrawn sofa needs one number
   * re-measured, and `npm run audit:interactions` says so when it does not match the model.
   */
  seatFront?: number;
  /**
   * The body's yaw RELATIVE to the piece's own rotation, radians.
   *
   * 0 means the player faces the piece's local +Z, which is the front of every model in this
   * catalog (a sofa's backrest and a bed's headboard are both at -Z). A lying body extends
   * BACKWARDS from its anchor — the root origin is at the feet — so a bed whose headboard is at
   * -Z wants `facing: 0` and an anchor toward the foot of the mattress. A bathtub is long in X
   * and shallow in Z, so its occupant is turned a quarter turn to lie along it.
   */
  facing?: number;
  /**
   * Lie only: how far the body settles INTO the surface, 0..1. A hammock's fabric sags around
   * whoever is in it (~0.8); a mattress compresses a little (~0.25); a bench does not give at
   * all (0). Scales the body's own half-thickness — see {@link poseRootHeight}.
   */
  give?: number;
  /**
   * The piece MOVES under whoever is on it, and which way it moves.
   *
   * This was `sway?: boolean` — "rock the occupant a bit" — and the boolean is why the hammock
   * was never actually in sync with itself. A flag can say THAT something moves; it cannot say
   * how far, how fast, about what pivot, or for how long after the rider leaves, so the numbers
   * ended up written into the one file that happened to need them (Three/Avatar.tsx nudged the
   * BODY on a `sin(t * 1.5)` in WORLD space, while the hammock's own model did not move at all —
   * so a hammock rotated in build mode rocked its occupant sideways across the cloth).
   *
   * It now names a row in constants/outdoorAnimation.ts, and the model, the character controller
   * and the exit all resolve the same row. A bed still says nothing and still does not move.
   */
  sway?: SuspendedMotionId;
  /**
   * How far outside the piece's measured collision box the player may stand and still be
   * offered this, in world units. Defaults to {@link DEFAULT_INTERACTION_REACH}.
   */
  reach?: number;
}

/**
 * Distance from the piece's own measured box, not from its centre — so one number works for a
 * 2.5-unit bed and a 0.6-unit chair, and goes on working when either is rotated.
 *
 * Roughly an arm's length past where the player is stopped by the piece (they collide at
 * PLAYER_PHYSICAL_RADIUS, 0.35), so walking up to something puts you in range of it and
 * stepping away drops you out of it.
 */
export const DEFAULT_INTERACTION_REACH = 0.9;

/** How high above the piece's own top face the floating prompt badge is anchored. */
export const PROMPT_ANCHOR_CLEARANCE = 0.45;

/**
 * How far clear of a piece's own box an acting posture stands, on top of the player's radius.
 *
 * Small: the point is to be AT the hob, not near it. The player's own radius already keeps the
 * body out of the collider, so this is only the gap between a shoulder and a worktop.
 */
export const ACTION_STAND_CLEARANCE = 0.12;

const NO_INTERACTIONS: readonly FurnitureInteraction[] = [];

/** Every interaction this item declares, in priority order. Empty for ordinary scenery. */
export function getFurnitureInteractions(itemId: string): readonly FurnitureInteraction[] {
  return getItemById(itemId)?.interactions ?? NO_INTERACTIONS;
}

/**
 * The one the prompt offers.
 *
 * A piece may declare several (`[sit, store]`, `[lie, sleep]`) and the data model has always
 * allowed it — what the PLAYER has is one action key, so the first entry is what that key does
 * and the rest are there for the surface that will one day offer a choice. Order in the catalog
 * is therefore meaningful: put the thing someone walking up to the piece expects first.
 */
export function getPrimaryInteraction(itemId: string): FurnitureInteraction | null {
  return getFurnitureInteractions(itemId)[0] ?? null;
}

export function hasFurnitureInteraction(itemId: string): boolean {
  return getFurnitureInteractions(itemId).length > 0;
}

/**
 * WHICH BODY this interaction puts the player in — the item's own override if it has one, else
 * the one its verb selects.
 *
 * This function replaced `interactionPose`, whose answer was `'sit' | 'lie' | null` and whose
 * `null` was the single most consequential value in the old system: it meant "this piece does
 * not move the player", which meant "play the shared arm-wave", which is why a bathtub and a
 * fridge were animated identically.
 */
export function interactionPosture(interaction: FurnitureInteraction): PostureId {
  return interaction.posture ?? INTERACTION_KINDS[interaction.kind].posture;
}

/** Does this interaction hold the player until they get up, or play once and hand them back? */
export function interactionOccupies(interaction: FurnitureInteraction): boolean {
  return getPosture(interactionPosture(interaction)).occupies;
}

/** How the body's root height comes off the anchor — see PostureAnchoring. */
export function interactionAnchoring(interaction: FurnitureInteraction): PostureAnchoring {
  return getPosture(interactionPosture(interaction)).anchoring;
}

/** Which face of the piece an acting posture is played from. */
export function interactionApproach(interaction: FurnitureInteraction): ApproachSide {
  return interaction.approach ?? 'front';
}

export function interactionVerb(interaction: FurnitureInteraction): string {
  return interaction.verb ?? INTERACTION_KINDS[interaction.kind].verb;
}

export function interactionExitVerb(interaction: FurnitureInteraction): string {
  return interaction.exitVerb ?? INTERACTION_KINDS[interaction.kind].exitVerb ?? '離開';
}

export function interactionIcon(interaction: FurnitureInteraction): InteractionIcon {
  return interaction.icon ?? INTERACTION_KINDS[interaction.kind].icon;
}

// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
// THE BODY ON THE FURNITURE — derived from the rig, never typed into the catalog
// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

/**
 * How far a lying body's head sits ABOVE horizontal, radians — and why the recline is not a flat
 * quarter turn.
 *
 * This character is a chibi: the skull is 0.26 across against a 0.135 body, so a body laid
 * perfectly flat rests its torso on the mattress and buries a third of its head in it. The
 * amount of lift that fixes that is not a taste call — it is exactly the difference between the
 * two radii, seen from the head joint — so it is computed rather than tuned, and a model with a
 * smaller head automatically lies flatter.
 *
 * The hammock's hand-tuned pitch (-PI/2.1, 85.7 deg) was this same idea applied by eye to one
 * piece of furniture. On the legacy skeleton this returns 79.7 deg, which raises that hammock's
 * head by ~10cm and is the whole visible difference.
 */
export function lieHeadRise(skeleton: CharacterSkeleton): number {
  // Scale-free: every term is LOCAL, so `toWorld` would cancel out of the ratio.
  const excess = skeleton.head.crownRise - skeleton.torso.halfWidth;
  return Math.asin(Math.max(0, Math.min(0.5, excess / skeleton.head.y)));
}

/** The body's pitch while lying — negative tips the chest backwards. See {@link lieHeadRise}. */
export function liePitch(skeleton: CharacterSkeleton): number {
  return -(Math.PI / 2 - lieHeadRise(skeleton));
}

/**
 * Where the character's ROOT ORIGIN — its ground contact point, see constants/characterRig.ts —
 * has to be for the body to rest properly on a surface at `surfaceY`.
 *
 * Two different geometries, one function, because both are statements about the RIG rather than
 * about any particular piece or posture:
 *
 *   `hips`  The body's weight is on its HIP JOINT — sitting on a cushion, and sitting on the
 *           floor of a bathtub. Putting the hip on the surface puts the root exactly one
 *           hip-height below it, which is why a model with longer legs sits correctly on the
 *           same sofa without a single catalog row changing.
 *   `side`  The body is turned on its side about its own feet, so all of it ends up at the
 *           root's height and what rests on the surface is the body's SIDE. The root therefore
 *           rises by half the body's thickness, less however much the surface gives under it.
 *   `stand` No anchor at all: an acting posture is played on the floor the player is standing
 *           on, so the surface height is not consulted.
 */
export function poseRootHeight(
  anchoring: PostureAnchoring,
  surfaceY: number,
  skeleton: CharacterSkeleton,
  give = 0,
): number {
  if (anchoring === 'stand') return 0;
  if (anchoring === 'hips') return surfaceY - toWorld(skeleton.hip.y);
  return surfaceY + toWorld(skeleton.torso.halfWidth) * (1 - clamp01(give));
}

/**
 * How far a lying body reaches from its anchor, world units — the length that has to fit on the
 * mattress, and what `npm run audit:interactions` checks every lie point against. A shade less
 * than the character's height, because {@link lieHeadRise} holds the head a few degrees up.
 */
export function lieBodyReach(skeleton: CharacterSkeleton): number {
  const height = toWorld(skeleton.head.y + skeleton.head.crownRise - skeleton.soleY);
  return height * Math.cos(lieHeadRise(skeleton));
}

/**
 * HOW FAR BEHIND A SEAT'S FRONT LIP THE HIP JOINT GOES, world units — the whole of the
 * alignment rule for a seated body, and a rig measurement rather than a preference.
 *
 * The leg is a capsule about the hip's own axis. `hip.x` is the rig's statement of how far that
 * axis sits from the body's centreline, and on every skeleton in this project it is within a
 * couple of centimetres of the leg's own radius (legacy: hip.x 0.065 against LEG_RADIUS 0.055,
 * both LOCAL). So putting the hip ONE of these back from the lip is putting the leg's near
 * surface ON the lip: the leg grazes the seat's front face instead of crossing it, and every
 * millimetre of it below the lip is in open air.
 *
 * Any larger and the leg starts inside the piece — the bug this exists to end. Any smaller and
 * the body is perched on the very edge with nothing under its weight. The audit checks the
 * consequence rather than the number ({@link seatLegClearance} is what it hands the leg solver),
 * so a future rig where the two measurements diverge fails loudly instead of quietly clipping.
 */
export function seatHipInset(skeleton: CharacterSkeleton): number {
  return toWorld(skeleton.hip.x);
}

/**
 * WHERE ON THE PIECE THE BODY GOES, in the piece's own local frame — one function, so that
 * "the catalog says it" and "the rig says it" cannot be answered differently in two places.
 *
 * A seat whose legs hang over an edge states {@link FurnitureInteraction.seatFront} and has its
 * anchor derived; everything else states `forward` and keeps it. `lateral` is the same in both:
 * the position ACROSS the piece.
 *
 * The projection is written out in full rather than assuming `facing: 0` — the frame the anchor
 * is stated in is the OCCUPANT'S, so a seat turned to face along the piece's local X (nothing in
 * the catalog does today; a corner unit would) resolves without this function changing.
 */
export function interactionAnchorLocal(
  interaction: FurnitureInteraction,
  skeleton: CharacterSkeleton,
): { x: number; z: number } {
  const lateral = interaction.lateral ?? 0;
  if (interaction.seatFront === undefined) {
    return { x: lateral, z: interaction.forward ?? 0 };
  }
  const facing = interaction.facing ?? 0;
  const along = interaction.seatFront - seatHipInset(skeleton);
  // facing 0 gives (x, z) = (lateral, along), which is what every existing row means.
  return {
    x: Math.sin(facing) * along + Math.cos(facing) * lateral,
    z: Math.cos(facing) * along - Math.sin(facing) * lateral,
  };
}

/**
 * What the leg solver has to clear — the distance from the anchor to the lip the legs hang
 * over, or null for an interaction that never declared one.
 *
 * By construction this is exactly {@link seatHipInset}: the anchor was derived by stepping back
 * from the lip by it. It is a function rather than a constant at the call site so that the
 * relationship stays visible — the leg is cleared against the SEAT, and the seat is where the
 * catalog says it is, never where the bounding box happens to end.
 */
export function seatLegClearance(
  interaction: FurnitureInteraction,
  skeleton: CharacterSkeleton,
): number | null {
  return interaction.seatFront === undefined ? null : seatHipInset(skeleton);
}

/**
 * How far a body sitting on an anchor reaches AHEAD of it, world units — hip joint to sole,
 * with the legs straight out.
 *
 * The bathtub check: a body whose legs extend forward has to have somewhere to put them, and
 * `npm run audit:interactions` uses this to confirm the feet land inside the tub rather than
 * through its far end.
 */
export function seatedLegReach(skeleton: CharacterSkeleton): number {
  return toWorld(skeleton.hip.y - skeleton.soleY);
}

function clamp01(v: number): number {
  return v < 0 ? 0 : v > 1 ? 1 : v;
}
```

```ts
/**
 * WHICH 3D MODEL A PRODUCT IS — the one name the shop, the inventory and the world all mean.
 *
 * ## The bug this file ends
 *
 * A placed item used to find its model by SUBSTRING OF ITS NAME. `FurnitureItem.tsx` held an
 * ordered list of forty-odd `n.includes('…')` tests, and the first one that hit won:
 *
 * \`\`\`
 * { match: (n) => n.includes('裝飾台') || n.includes('燈'), Component: DecorLampModel },
 * \`\`\`
 *
 * That single line was the model for EIGHT different products — 貝殼裝飾台, 復古提燈, 石製路燈,
 * 螢光石燈 and all four pendant lights — because every one of their names contains 燈 (or 裝飾台).
 * Each of the eight has its own hand-drawn shop icon: a glass dome over a golden shell, a brass
 * carry-lantern, a stone post lamp, four distinct chandeliers. All eight put down the SAME grey
 * cube with a glowing ball on top. That is the 「圖片很精緻，實際模型完全不同」 report, and it was
 * not a bug in any one product — it was the addressing scheme.
 *
 * Three more collisions came from the same cause (兩張地毯, 手電筒/收音機, 兩支火把), and the
 * failure mode is open-ended: naming a new product 「工作桌」 silently hands it the 書桌 model,
 * and nothing anywhere reports it, because a name substring hitting is indistinguishable from a
 * name substring being *meant* to hit.
 *
 * ## The rule now
 *
 * A product NAMES its model. `ItemDefinition.model` (constants/items.ts) holds one of the ids
 * below, `FURNITURE_MODELS` (components/Three/FurnitureItem.tsx) is a
 * `Record<FurnitureModelId, Component>`, and resolution is one lookup with no ordering and no
 * fuzziness. Three things follow, and all three are compile- or audit-enforced rather than
 * conventions:
 *
 *  1. **Every id has a model.** `Record<FurnitureModelId, …>` is exhaustive, so adding an id here
 *     without writing its component is a TypeScript error, not a blue placeholder box in
 *     someone's living room.
 *  2. **Every model is reachable.** No rule can shadow another, because there are no rules —
 *     renaming a product cannot change what it looks like.
 *  3. **Two products cannot quietly share one model.** `npm run audit:shop` fails when an id is
 *     used twice unless the pair is listed in {@link SHARED_FURNITURE_MODELS} with a reason. That
 *     is the check that would have caught all eight lamps on day one.

  | 'pet-bed'
  | 'pet-dog-cabin'
  | 'pet-dog-tent'
  | 'pet-dog-basket'
  | 'pet-cat-donut'
  | 'pet-cat-yarn'
  | 'pet-cat-tower'
  | 'pet-bird-cage'
  | 'pet-bird-perch'
  | 'pet-bird-nest';

/**
 * The model ids two or more products are ALLOWED to share, and why.
 *
 * `npm run audit:shop` fails on any other repeat. The point is not that sharing is wrong — it is
 * that sharing must be a decision someone wrote down, because the failure it looks identical to
 * (eight lamps accidentally collapsing onto one grey box) is invisible from inside the code and
 * obvious to a player the moment they buy the second one.
 *
 * Keep this list short. If two products want to look different, they need two models, not a
 * shared one and a note.
 */
export const SHARED_FURNITURE_MODELS: Record<string, string> = {
  torch:
    '火把 (室外) 與 部落火把 (室內) 是同一支火把，差別只在它站在哪裡與尺寸 — TorchModel 讀 item.id 放大室外那一支。',
};

/**
 * 家具風格系列 —— 一組在材質與設計語言上刻意一致的家具，讓玩家可以整套搭。
 *
 * 這是一個**選配的標籤**，不是第三層分類。一件家具屬於哪個貨架仍然由 `shopCategory` 決定
 * (utils/categoryUtils.ts)，系列只影響卡片上多一個 chip 與同系列的辨識度 — 所以「全部家具都要
 * 隸屬某個系列」從來不是目標，獨立的特色商品（科技馬桶、工業風景觀窗、水晶吊燈）刻意不掛系列。
 *
 * 為什麼是資料而不是命名慣例：靠名字裡有沒有「原木」來認系列，就是這個檔案開頭在講的那個 bug
 * 換一個地方重演。
 */
export type FurnitureSeries = 'oak' | 'cottage' | 'island' | 'minimal' | 'cozy';

export interface FurnitureSeriesMeta {
  id: FurnitureSeries;
  /** 卡片 chip 上顯示的字。 */
  label: string;
  /** 這個系列在講什麼 — 商店的系列說明用。 */
  description: string;
  /** 系列的代表色，給 chip 與未來的系列頁使用。取自該系列模型實際用的木色/布色。 */
  accent: string;
}

export const FURNITURE_SERIES: readonly FurnitureSeriesMeta[] = [
  {
    id: 'oak',
    label: '原木系列',
    description: '直紋實木、外露的榫接與圓潤倒角。溫暖、厚實，木頭本身就是裝飾。',
    accent: '#b98a52',
  },
  {
    id: 'cottage',
    label: '鄉村系列',
    description: '刷白的木作、車枳腳與格紋布。手作感重，線條刻意不完全對稱。',
    accent: '#d9c3a5',
  },
  {
    id: 'island',
    label: '海島系列',
    description: '藤編、淺色漂流木與植物元素。輕、透氣，看得見編織的縫隙。',
    accent: '#cfa96b',
  },
  {
    id: 'minimal',
    label: '簡約系列',
    description: '細腳、平整的面與柔和的低彩度配色。少一點裝飾，多一點留白。',
    accent: '#98a8ad',
  },
  {
    id: 'cozy',
    label: '可愛生活系列',
    description: '圓角、軟墊與一堆生活小物。上面總是放著沒收好的東西。',
    accent: '#e8a09a',
  },
];

const SERIES_BY_ID = new Map(FURNITURE_SERIES.map((s) => [s.id, s]));

/** The series' display metadata, or undefined for an item that deliberately belongs to none. */
export function getFurnitureSeries(id?: FurnitureSeries): FurnitureSeriesMeta | undefined {
  return id ? SERIES_BY_ID.get(id) : undefined;
}
```

## src/constants/groundCover.ts

```ts
/**
 * @license
 * SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
 */

/**
 * 地被層 —— what grows on the island's lawn, as data.
 *
 * The lawn used to be one thing: 520 identical boxes, one colour, one size, spread evenly over
 * the whole plateau. Everything wrong with it follows from that sentence — no near/mid/far
 * reading, no clumping, no variation, and no way to add any of those without editing the
 * component that draws it.
 *
 * So the field is described here instead, as a LIST OF LAYERS, and Three/GroundCover.tsx draws
 * whatever is in the list. Adding a new kind of ground plant is a row; retuning density is a
 * number. Neither is a code change, which is the 「建立可擴充的設定或共用系統」 half of the brief.
 *
 * ## The three layers are three DISTANCES, not three plants
 *
 * This is the part that is easy to get wrong by adding "more stuff". A field reads as deep when
 * it has something to offer at each of the distances the camera actually sits at, and the island
 * camera sits between 10 and 35 units out:
 *
 *   tuft    the carpet. Small, dense, everywhere the field is lush. Alone it is what the lawn
 *           had before — at 25 units it averages out into a texture, which is its job.
 *   clump   the MID-ground mass. Ten times fewer, ten times bigger, and the only layer that
 *           casts a shadow. These are what give the lawn silhouette and relief from across the
 *           island; without them a field of tufts is a flat green rug however dense it is.
 *   frond   the accent. Taller and sparser still, biased hard toward the lushest spots, so the
 *           eye finds a few tall things standing where the grass is deepest.
 *
 * ## Density is a FIELD, not a count
 *
 * Every layer states how it reads `lib/groundField.ts` rather than how many instances to put
 * where. `lushThreshold` is where it starts growing at all, `lushExponent` how hard it crowds
 * into the good spots, `wearPenalty` how much a worn patch drives it off. That is what produces
 * 「合理的密度分布」 without a single hand-placed position: the layers agree with each other and
 * with the ground material because all four are reading one field.
 */

export interface GroundCoverLayer {
  /** Stable id. Used as the material/program cache key, so it must be unique. */
  id: 'tuft' | 'clump' | 'frond';

  /* --- how many ------------------------------------------------------------------------ */

  /** Instances on a territory-level-1 island. */
  baseCount: number;
  /**
   * Hard cap however far the territory grows.
   *
   * Instance count wants to follow AREA (islandScale²) to hold density constant, and area on a
   * level-5 island is nearly seven times level 1. The cap is what stops that being seven times
   * the triangles: past the point where the cap bites the lawn thins slightly, which is both
   * invisible (the camera has pulled back to fit a bigger island in frame) and the correct
   * trade — see the budget note in Three/GroundCover.tsx.
   */
  maxCount: number;

  /* --- where -------------------------------------------------------------------------- */

  /** Below this lushness the layer does not grow at all. */
  lushThreshold: number;
  /** Acceptance is `lush^exponent`; higher crowds the layer into the lushest spots. */
  lushExponent: number;
  /** How much a fully worn patch suppresses this layer, 0..1. */
  wearPenalty: number;
  /**
   * Minimum gap between two instances OF THIS LAYER, in world units. 0 turns the check off.
   *
   * Off for the tufts on purpose: they are supposed to crowd, and an O(n²) spacing pass over
   * fifteen hundred of them is the one part of the scatter that would actually cost something.
   * The two sparse layers do enforce it, which is what keeps a clump from standing inside
   * another clump.
   */
  spacing: number;

  /* --- what it looks like -------------------------------------------------------------- */

  /** Uniform scale range. The instance's own scale is drawn uniformly between these. */
  scale: readonly [number, number];
  /**
   * The layer's colours, BEFORE the field grades them.
   *
   * A palette rather than one colour because instance colour is free (one attribute, no extra
   * draw) and because a single green is exactly what made the old lawn read as plastic. Every
   * entry is then pushed toward the deep or the dry end by the lushness at that instance's own
   * spot, so two tufts of the same palette colour standing ten metres apart still differ.
   */
  colors: readonly string[];
  /** Deep green a fully lush spot pulls the palette colour toward. */
  lushTint: string;
  /** Pale, yellower green a thin spot pulls it toward. */
  dryTint: string;
  /** How dark the base of the plant is relative to its tip — the mass's own occlusion. */
  rootShade: number;

  /* --- how it moves -------------------------------------------------------------------- */

  /**
   * Horizontal travel of the TOP of the plant at full wind, in world units.
   *
   * A displacement rather than an angle, and that is deliberate: the bend is applied in the
   * vertex shader as a translation weighted by height², so the plant's base cannot move. A
   * rotation about the root would be equivalent for a thin blade and visibly wrong for a clump,
   * whose bottom would swing out of the ground.
   */
  bend: number;
  /** Sway rate multiplier — small plants flutter, big ones lumber. */
  bendRate: number;

  /**
   * Whether this layer writes the shadow map.
   *
   * Only the clumps do. The directional light's 2048² map covers 40 world units, i.e. ~2 cm per
   * texel, and a grass blade is 3 cm wide — a tuft casting into that map is one texel of noise
   * per blade, which costs a second full pass over every instance to produce shadow acne. A
   * clump is 35 cm across and lands on ~17 texels, which is a real soft shadow and the thing
   * that actually stops the lawn reading as flat.
   */
  castShadow: boolean;
}

export const GROUND_COVER_LAYERS: readonly GroundCoverLayer[] = [
  {
    id: 'tuft',
    baseCount: 1150,
    maxCount: 1300,
    lushThreshold: 0.08,
    lushExponent: 1.2,
    wearPenalty: 0.8,
    spacing: 0,
    scale: [0.7, 1.45],
    // Three greens spanning the plateau's own range, so the carpet sits INSIDE the ground's
    // colour rather than on top of it. The old single '#65a30d' was lighter than the plateau it
    // stood on at every point, which is why the blades read as separate objects.
    colors: ['#5c8f16', '#6fa524', '#4d7c1c'],
    lushTint: '#3f7a12',
    dryTint: '#93a03a',
    rootShade: 0.52,
    bend: 0.075,
    bendRate: 1.0,
    castShadow: false,
  },
  {
    id: 'clump',
    baseCount: 110,
    maxCount: 150,
    lushThreshold: 0.42,
    lushExponent: 2.1,
    wearPenalty: 0.95,
    spacing: 0.55,
    scale: [0.72, 1.25],
    colors: ['#578a22', '#4a7c1a', '#639429'],
    lushTint: '#3f7314',
    dryTint: '#8a9638',
    rootShade: 0.58,
    bend: 0.035,
    bendRate: 0.55,
    castShadow: true,
  },
  {
    id: 'frond',
    baseCount: 46,
    maxCount: 80,
    lushThreshold: 0.46,
    lushExponent: 2.2,
    wearPenalty: 1,
    spacing: 0.78,
    scale: [0.78, 1.32],
    colors: ['#3f6b18', '#4d7c1c', '#5c8f16'],
    lushTint: '#2f5c10',
    dryTint: '#8a9432',
    rootShade: 0.44,
    bend: 0.14,
    bendRate: 0.8,
    castShadow: false,
  },
];

/**
 * How far a ground plant stays off a stepping stone.
 *
 * Smaller than the overgrowth's own 0.85 (lib/islandOvergrowth.ts) because these are grass, not
 * weeds: a path with grass growing right up to the edge of its slabs is a path, while a path with
 * a metre of clearance round every stone is a paved area. It only has to be wider than the slab
 * itself (radius 0.5 in Three/IslandDecorations.tsx) plus a little.
 */
export const GROUND_COVER_PATH_CLEARANCE = 0.62;

/**
 * How far a ground plant stays outside the Home's solid box.
 *
 * Grass may grow right up against a wall — that is what a wall looks like — so this is small and
 * positive rather than the 0.6 the placement solver gives furniture. It exists only so a tuft
 * cannot stand half inside the shell, where the floor would slice it.
 */
export const GROUND_COVER_HOME_MARGIN = 0.12;
```
