## src/constants/hairRibbon.ts

```ts
/**
 * A hair BUNDLE as a swept ribbon, rather than as a stack of rods.
 *
 * ============================================================================
 * WHY A NEW PRIMITIVE AT ALL
 * ============================================================================
 *
 * Everything hanging off the head in constants/hair.ts is built from three.js
 * primitives - a cone for the curtain, capsules and cylinders for the locks. That
 * choice is what every complaint about the back of the head has actually been
 * about, and no amount of tuning could reach it:
 *
 *   1. A CONE IS A SKIRT. The curtain is one cone around the whole head, so the
 *      silhouette it draws is a tube. Real hair falling to the shoulders is not a
 *      surface of revolution - it parts, it gathers, it has a heavier side.
 *   2. A ROD IS A ROD. A lock is a capsule or a tapered cylinder, so it reads as a
 *      rod at every width. Thin, a set of them is a comb; thick, a set of them is
 *      a collar of fins. Both readings were reached experimentally, from opposite
 *      directions, and neither is hair.
 *   3. NOTHING RUNS ROOT TO TIP. A wave is emitted as a CHAIN of capsules, so the
 *      one thing a bundle of hair must do - leave the scalp and stay one object all
 *      the way to its end - was the one thing the geometry could not express.
 *
 * So this file adds the missing primitive: a flattened tube swept along a curve.
 * A bundle roots ON the skull surface, hugs it while it is still on the head, then
 * leaves it tangentially and falls to the nape - one continuous surface, with a
 * width that swells and then gathers to a soft point.
 *
 * ============================================================================
 * WHY A FLATTENED TUBE AND NOT A FLAT CARD
 * ============================================================================
 *
 * The obvious way to draw a hair bundle is a ribbon of zero thickness - a hair
 * card, as a game would texture it. Untextured, in a chibi renderer, that is a
 * paper edge: it vanishes at grazing angles and shows its own back face from the
 * other side, which is the 「懸浮、斷裂」 this is supposed to remove.
 *
 * The cross-section here is therefore a CLOSED ellipse - wide across the head,
 * shallow through it - so a bundle is a solid with a silhouette from every angle
 * and no interior to see into, while still reading as a broad sheet rather than as
 * a rod. Width and thickness are independent, which is exactly the axis the
 * primitives lacked: a capsule's only knob makes it fatter in both directions at
 * once.
 *
 * ============================================================================
 * PURE ARITHMETIC, ON PURPOSE
 * ============================================================================
 *
 * This file imports nothing. It returns vertex positions and the renderer uploads
 * them, exactly as `scalpVertex` does for the scalp shell - which is what lets
 * `npm run audit:hair` measure what is actually drawn without a renderer, and what
 * keeps the drawn mesh and the audited layout the same object seen twice.
 */

export type Vec3 = [number, number, number];

export interface RibbonInput {
  /** Azimuth of the bundle's centre line. 0 faces +Z (the face). */
  yaw: number;
  /** Polar angle on the shell where the bundle roots, from the crown. */
  rootTheta: number;
  /** Polar angle at which it stops hugging the shell and begins to fall. */
  leaveTheta: number;
  /** The shell it is fitted to. */
  shellRadius: number;
  shellOriginY: number;
  /** Where the tip ends up. */
  bottomY: number;
  /** Radius the tip settles to - smaller than the shell's pulls it toward the body. */
  hemRadius: number;
  /** Half-width, in metres of arc, at the bundle's widest. */
  halfWidth: number;
  /** How far the bundle stands off its own surface - its depth through the head. */
  thickness: number;
  /** Extra standoff, so an outer layer sits clear of the one behind it. */
  standoff?: number;
  /** S-curve down the fall. */
  waves?: number;
  waveDepth?: number;
  /** Phase for this bundle's own wave, so neighbours disagree. */
  phase?: number;
  /**
   * Width at the very tip, as a fraction of the widest. Defaults to {@link HEM_TIP}.
   *
   * A HEM must not come to a point - nine points is the jellyfish this file's own
   * comment on `widthAt` is about. A SPIKE is the one piece that must: it is a
   * bundle gathered to a tip on purpose, and drawing it with a hem's ending gives a
   * flat-ended paddle. Same sweep, opposite ending, so it is a parameter.
   */
  tipWidth?: number;
}

/** Stations down the sweep. Enough that the fall reads as a curve, not a chain. */
export const RIBBON_STATIONS = 26;
/** Points around the cross-section. Closed, so the last wraps onto the first. */
export const RIBBON_AROUND = 10;

/**
 * Where the bundle is wide.
 *
 * Narrow where it leaves the scalp (hair gathers at the root and the bundles have
 * to sit side by side up there without piling into each other), widest through the
 * middle where the mass is, then gathering to a soft point. The taper is the
 * 髮尾自然收束: it never reaches zero, because a bundle that closes to a true point
 * makes a spike, and spikes are what the icicles were.
 */
export const HEM_TIP = 0.62;

function widthAt(u: number, tipWidth: number): number {
  if (u < 0.28) return 0.52 + 0.48 * (u / 0.28);
  const v = (u - 0.28) / 0.72;
  // Taper to 0.62, NOT to a point. At 0.18 - the obvious reading of 收束 - each
  // bundle narrowed faster than its neighbours closed in, so the hem opened into a
  // row of tapered fingers with daylight between them: a jellyfish, which is the
  // same 「破碎、分離」 defect the rods had, reached from the opposite direction.
  // A hem gathers, it does not come to nine points.
  return 1 - (1 - tipWidth) * v * v;
}

/**
 * One bundle's centre line, and the flattened tube swept along it.
 *
 * `u` runs 0 at the root to 1 at the tip. The first stretch is ON the shell - the
 * bundle is part of the head there, which is what stops a gap opening at the
 * hairline - and it leaves tangentially rather than at an angle, so there is no
 * crease where the two meet.
 */
export function buildRibbon(input: RibbonInput): {
  positions: Vec3[];
  uvs: [number, number][];
} {
  const {
    yaw, rootTheta, leaveTheta, shellRadius, shellOriginY, bottomY, hemRadius,
    halfWidth, thickness, standoff = 0, waves = 0, waveDepth = 0, phase = 0,
    tipWidth = HEM_TIP,
  } = input;

  // Where the shell hands over. Everything below this is a free fall.
  const leaveY = shellOriginY + shellRadius * Math.cos(leaveTheta);
  const leaveR = shellRadius * Math.sin(leaveTheta) + standoff;
  /**
   * How much of the sweep is spent on the head.
   *
   * Proportional to how far the bundle actually has to travel on each side, so a
   * short style (whose fall is barely longer than its scalp run) does not spend
   * twenty of its twenty-six stations on the skull and then jump to the tip.
   */
  const onHead = Math.abs(leaveTheta - rootTheta) * shellRadius;
  /**
   * Signed, so a bundle can rise as well as fall.
   *
   * A spiked style is the same sweep read the other way up: the bundle roots LOW at
   * the temple, runs up over the skull, and leaves the surface still climbing.
   * Forcing this positive - which is all that stopped it before - meant the only
   * hair the file could express was hair that hangs, and spikes had to be separate
   * cones stuck on a smooth cap because of it.
   */
  const drop = leaveY - bottomY;
  // Capped at 0.78 rather than 0.55. A SHORT cut is mostly scalp run and barely any
  // fall - 短髮's bundles travel 36cm over the skull and then drop 9 - so a cap tuned
  // for long hair spent nearly half the stations on that 9cm and left the long run
  // over the skull described by a handful of segments. That is a faceted shell, and
  // a faceted shell under a smooth scalp dome is the 「生硬拼接」 seam.
  const attach = Math.max(0.12, Math.min(0.78, onHead / (onHead + Math.abs(drop) + 1e-6)));

  const positions: Vec3[] = [];
  const uvs: [number, number][] = [];

  for (let s = 0; s <= RIBBON_STATIONS; s++) {
    const u = s / RIBBON_STATIONS;

    let cy: number;
    let cr: number;
    if (u <= attach) {
      // On the skull: walk the shell from the root down to where it lets go.
      const theta = rootTheta + (leaveTheta - rootTheta) * (u / attach);
      cy = shellOriginY + shellRadius * Math.cos(theta);
      cr = shellRadius * Math.sin(theta) + standoff;
    } else {
      const v = (u - attach) / (1 - attach);
      cy = leaveY - drop * v;
      // Eased rather than linear so the bundle leaves the skull along the shell's
      // own tangent and only then curves in toward the body - a straight line from
      // the last shell point is a visible kink at the changeover.
      const ease = v * v * (3 - 2 * v);
      cr = leaveR + (hemRadius - leaveR) * ease;
      if (waves > 0 && waveDepth > 0) {
        // The S. Grows toward the tip, where a wave in real hair is deepest, and
        // rides ON the radius so it swings out and back through the fall rather
        // than displacing the whole bundle sideways.
        cr += Math.sin(v * Math.PI * waves + phase) * waveDepth * v;
      }
    }

    const w = halfWidth * widthAt(u, tipWidth);
    const t = thickness * (0.55 + 0.45 * widthAt(u, tipWidth));
    // Arc half-width converted to an azimuth at this station's own radius, so a
    // bundle keeps its WIDTH as it falls instead of fanning out with the radius.
    const dYaw = w / Math.max(0.02, cr);

    for (let k = 0; k < RIBBON_AROUND; k++) {
      const phi = (k / RIBBON_AROUND) * Math.PI * 2;
      const az = yaw + dYaw * Math.cos(phi);
      const r = cr + t * Math.sin(phi);
      positions.push([Math.sin(az) * r, cy, Math.cos(az) * r]);
      // v = 1 at the root so the shading's `1 - uv.y` comes out 0 there, matching
      // every other hanging piece. u is unused (these never ask for `breakup`).
      uvs.push([k / RIBBON_AROUND, 1 - u]);
    }
  }

  return { positions, uvs };
}

/**
 * Triangle indices for the grid `buildRibbon` returns.
 *
 * Shared rather than rebuilt per bundle: every ribbon has the same topology, so
 * this is one buffer the whole shop can point at.
 */
export function ribbonIndices(): number[] {
  const index: number[] = [];
  for (let s = 0; s < RIBBON_STATIONS; s++) {
    for (let k = 0; k < RIBBON_AROUND; k++) {
      // The cross-section is a closed loop, so the last column wraps onto the
      // first rather than onto a copy of it - a copy is two vertices in one place
      // averaging only their own side into a normal, i.e. a lit seam down the
      // length of every bundle.
      const a = s * RIBBON_AROUND + k;
      const b = s * RIBBON_AROUND + ((k + 1) % RIBBON_AROUND);
      const c = a + RIBBON_AROUND;
      const d = b + RIBBON_AROUND;
      index.push(a, c, b, b, c, d);
    }
  }
  return index;
}
```

## src/constants/hats.ts

```ts
// Colours for the five hats, shared between the 3D model the player wears
// (components/Three/Avatar.tsx) and the shop thumbnail (components/QVersionIcon.tsx).
//
// WHY THIS FILE EXISTS. The thumbnail is a promise about what you are buying, and
// before this the two ends disagreed outright: the 3D 漁夫帽 is slate blue-grey
// (#475569) while its shop icon was drawn in `bg-stone-300`, a light warm grey. A
// player picked a pale hat off the shelf and got a dark one. That is not a tuning
// mistake anyone can be blamed for - it is what happens when the same fact is
// written down twice.
//
// So the icon no longer authors colour at all; it reads it from here, exactly as
// every hairstyle thumbnail reads its colour from HAIR_SPECS. Only flat-art shading
// (highlights, stitching, straw lines) is authored in the icon, and all of that is
// derived from these values rather than picked.
//
// Shape is still authored at both ends - the 3D builds from three.js primitives and
// the icon from SVG paths - so the comments below record which primitive each part
// corresponds to, and that is what a future edit should keep in step.

export interface HatPalette {
  /** Main body: crown/dome. */
  body: string;
  /** Secondary structural part - brim, visor, cuff. Defaults to `body` when absent. */
  trim?: string;
  /** The one contrasting accent that identifies the hat at thumbnail size. */
  accent?: string;
}

export const HAT_PALETTES: Record<string, HatPalette> = {
  // 草帽: wide flat brim (r 0.45) under a tapered crown, with a red ribbon at the base.
  'item-5': { body: '#d97706', accent: '#b91c1c' },
  // 漁夫帽: straight cylinder crown, brim flaring DOWN all the way round (0.28 -> 0.42).
  'hat-bucket': { body: '#475569' },
  // 貝雷帽: one puffed dome worn tilted, plus the little stalk on the crown.
  'hat-beret': { body: '#450a0a' },
  // 毛帽: dome, darker folded cuff, white pompom.
  'hat-beanie': { body: '#1d4ed8', trim: '#1e3a8a', accent: '#ffffff' },
  // 平板帽: dome, flat straight visor, and the snap strap the style is named for.
  'hat-snapback': { body: '#1e293b', trim: '#334155', accent: '#0f172a' },
};

export function getHatPalette(id: string): HatPalette | undefined {
  return HAT_PALETTES[id];
}
```

## src/constants/houseStyles.ts

```ts
/**
 * @license
 * SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
 */

import type { Rarity } from './rarity';

/**
 * House Styles — the single source of truth for what the player's Home looks like AND how big
 * it is physically.
 *
 * A style is pure data. Adding 新房屋外觀 means appending one entry to HOUSE_STYLES below and
 * nothing else: the 3D model (components/Three/HouseModel.tsx), the shop tab, collision,
 * placement rules, the pet dog's avoidance box and rain roof-splash all read this table.
 *
 * This replaces four independent hardcoded descriptions of the same two houses that used to
 * drift apart: inline meshes in IslandDecorations, GrassHutModel/StoneHutModel in
 * FurnitureItem, per-name half-extents in characterMovement's resolveCollisions, and
 * getVisualBounds/getCollisionBounds in placementRules.
 */

/**
 * Roof silhouettes the parametric HouseModel knows how to build.
 *
 * ELEVEN kinds for TWELVE styles, and that ratio is the point. 「不要只是同一個房屋模型＋換不同
 * 顏色」 is enforced by construction rather than by taste: every style pairs a roof with a wall
 * treatment and no two styles use the same PAIR (`npm run audit:outdoor` checks it, and fails the
 * build if two houses are only a repaint of each other). A player who owns two houses is looking
 * at two different buildings from across the island, before any colour is read.
 */
export type RoofKind =
  /** Two stacked square cones with a bound ridge — thatch huts. */
  | 'thatch'
  /** Stacked flat slabs on corbels with a parapet — masonry cottages. */
  | 'slab'
  /** Single steep pitch with barge boards and rafter tails — timber cabins. */
  | 'gable'
  /** Shallow wide hip with corner brackets — coastal cottages. */
  | 'hip'
  /** Barn-style double pitch, steep below and shallow above — log cabins. */
  | 'gambrel'
  /** A hip with a small cross-gable projecting over the door — garden cottages. */
  | 'cottage'
  /**
   * Two-tier tropical pyramid: a wide low skirt on outriggers, a ventilation gap, then a steep
   * upper cap with a carved finial. The tallest, most layered silhouette on the shelf.
   */
  | 'pavilion'
  /** Steep gable with a dormer window pushing out of its front slope — country cottages. */
  | 'dormer'
  /** A true flat roof: parapet, coping, a roof terrace railing and a cantilevered eave band. */
  | 'flat'
  /** Asymmetric gable — short front pitch, long rear pitch sweeping down to a low eave. */
  | 'saltbox'
  /** A pitched roof turned 90°, so the gable TRIANGLE is what faces you over the door. */
  | 'gablefront';

/** Wall surface treatment — drives the trim/panel detailing on the walls. */
export type WallKind =
  /** Flat painted/plastered box: corner trim, a string course and a top plate. */
  | 'plain'
  /** Half-timbering — corner posts, a mid rail and diagonal braces. */
  | 'timber'
  /** Stone quoins, a capstone band and proud stones scattered over the face. */
  | 'masonry'
  /** Horizontal lapped siding boards with corner boards. */
  | 'plank'
  /** Stacked round logs whose ends cross at the corners. */
  | 'log'
  /** Vertical bamboo/reed poles lashed to two horizontal bands. */
  | 'bamboo'
  /** Board-and-batten: wide vertical boards with a narrow batten over every seam. */
  | 'batten'
  /** Large smooth panels separated by recessed reveal joints, plus one full-height accent bay. */
  | 'panel'
  /** Overlapping wood shakes in staggered courses. */
  | 'shingle';

/**
 * How much glass a style carries — the difference between 「小木屋的窗」 and 「大型窗戶」.
 *
 * A third axis of variation after roof and wall, and the one the brief asks for by name. It is a
 * TIER rather than a size in world units for the same reason the footprint is shared: a style says
 * what kind of building it is, and the model works out what that means against the wall it has.
 *
 *  - `cottage`   — one modest opening per elevation. The default, and what every original style wears.
 *  - `wide`      — landscape openings, and a SECOND window on the front so the façade is symmetrical
 *                  about the door instead of having a blank half.
 *  - `panoramic` — tall openings that run most of the wall's height, with a mullion down the middle.
 */
export type GlazingKind = 'cottage' | 'wide' | 'panoramic';

export interface HouseStylePalette {
  /** Main body / exterior wall. */
  wall: string;
  /** Corner posts, quoins, capstone band. */
  trim: string;
  /** Roof primary (lower layer / main slope). */
  roof: string;
  /** Roof secondary (upper cap / ridge). */
  roofAccent: string;
  /** Door leaf. */
  door: string;
  /** Door + window frames, beams. */
  frame: string;
  /** Window glass; also the colour of the warm light spilling out. */
  glass: string;
  /** Foundation plinth. */
  plinth: string;
}

/**
 * Physical footprint of a Home, in **world units**, measured from its centre.
 *
 * This is the single dimensional authority for the whole house system. The 3D mesh
 * (HouseModel.tsx) is built directly from these numbers at scale 1, the solid walk-collision box
 * is these numbers plus the player's radius (getHomeSolidHalfExtents), the entry trigger is
 * derived from them, and placement/pet/rain all read the same values. Model, collider and trigger
 * therefore agree by construction rather than by three people keeping three sets of magic numbers
 * in sync — and because there is exactly one footprint, every House Style is guaranteed to share
 * one proportion spec and one collision rule.
 */
export interface HouseStyleFootprint {
  /** Half-width along local X of the solid body. */
  halfWidth: number;
  /** Half-depth along local Z of the solid body. */
  halfDepth: number;
  /**
   * Vertical size parameter of the building. The walls take WALL_HEIGHT_RATIO of it above the
   * plinth and every other vertical feature (roof rise, door, window, chimney) is a fraction of
   * it, so this single number sets how tall the house reads.
   */
  height: number;
  /**
   * Half-width of the doorway *opening* on the +Z face — the door leaf, its jambs and the
   * keep-clear approach lane are all sized from it.
   *
   * NOT a hole in the collider. The house is a fully solid box (see resolveHomeCollision) and is
   * entered only through the "進入我的家" interaction, so this drives geometry and placement
   * rules, never walk-through.
   */
  doorLaneWidth: number;
  /**
   * Local +Z offset of the door's interaction anchor. Derived to sit *outside* the front wall
   * (halfDepth + approach clearance) — an anchor inside the shell gets occluded by the house's
   * own mesh and the "進入我的家" prompt never appears.
   */
  doorOffsetZ: number;
}

/**
 * Clearance between the front wall and the door's interaction anchor.
 *
 * Must exceed the player's physical radius (0.35), since the house is solid: the player is
 * stopped at halfDepth + 0.35, so a smaller value would put the anchor *behind* the closest point
 * they can stand and the entry prompt could never be approached. At 0.9 they end up 0.55 from it.
 */
const DOOR_APPROACH = 0.9;

/**
 * Half-depth, hoisted so doorOffsetZ can be *derived* from it rather than repeating the literal.
 * The two must move together — an anchor that no longer clears the front wall is invisible.
 */
const HOUSE_HALF_DEPTH = 1.7;

/**
 * The one size every House Style is built to.
 *
 * Deliberately shared rather than per-style: a Home is the same building whatever coat of paint
 * it wears, so appearance data carries no dimensions at all. That guarantees a new style can
 * never ship with a mismatched collider or an unreachable door, and needs no scale tuning.
 *
 * Sized against the island: the walkable grass disc has radius 5.7 (see getGrassTerrainRadius in
 * utils/placementRules.ts), so 3.8 units wide is ~33% of the island's 11.4-unit span — a
 * landmark cottage with room left over for decorations, rather than a house that swallows the
 * island.
 *
 * **Proportion pass:** the plan (3.6 x 3.24) read fine but the building was stocky, so width and
 * depth went up only marginally (~5%) while `height` went up ~14% — the house grows *upward*
 * into a taller, more layered cottage instead of spreading further across the island. Because
 * every dependent number below is a fraction of these three, that edit alone restyles all seven
 * House Styles in proportion: walls, roof rise and pitch, door, window, chimney, collider, entry
 * trigger, pet avoidance and rain roof-splash all follow. Nothing about the silhouettes changed.
 */
export const HOUSE_FOOTPRINT: HouseStyleFootprint = {
  halfWidth: 1.9,
  halfDepth: HOUSE_HALF_DEPTH,
  height: 3.2,
  doorLaneWidth: 0.65,
  doorOffsetZ: HOUSE_HALF_DEPTH + DOOR_APPROACH,
};

/**
 * Fraction of `height` the walls occupy above the plinth; the roof takes the rest.
 *
 * Lives here rather than in HouseModel so the mesh and anything else reasoning about where the
 * walls stop (rain splash, prompt anchor) read one number.
 */
export const WALL_HEIGHT_RATIO = 0.82;

/** Height of the foundation plinth the walls stand on. Constant across styles. */
export const PLINTH_HEIGHT = 0.3;

export interface HouseStyleDefinition {
  id: HouseStyleId;
  /** Display name, e.g. 石磚小屋. */
  name: string;
  description: string;
  /**
   * Catalog item id backing this style in the shop + inventory. Ownership is still plain
   * inventory membership, so purchase/reset/save all keep working unchanged.
   */
  itemId: string;
  /** Shop price. The starter style is not sold, so it carries 0. */
  price: number;
  /**
   * 稀有度 (constants/rarity.ts). Required, like it is on every catalog entry in the game.
   *
   * Grades how much of a STATEMENT the house is, not what it costs — 毛胚屋, 草本屋 and 石磚小屋
   * are the plain shells (普通) while 海景小屋 and 花園小屋 carry elaborate exteriors (稀有), and
   * 現代海景屋 alone is 史詩: it is the only style whose whole idea is a construction the island
   * has never seen (a flat roof terrace over full-height glass), rather than a warmer or wilder
   * version of a cottage. The price ladder happens to run the same way here and that is a
   * coincidence of this shelf, never the derivation: see the never-derive rule in
   * constants/rarity.ts.
   */
  rarity: Rarity;
  /** False for 毛胚屋, which is granted rather than bought. */
  purchasable: boolean;
  roof: RoofKind;
  wall: WallKind;
  /** How much glass. Omitted means `cottage` — see {@link GlazingKind}. */
  glazing?: GlazingKind;
  palette: HouseStylePalette;
  // NOTE: no size/scale field. Every style is built to the shared HOUSE_FOOTPRINT above —
  // appearance varies, dimensions never do. See that constant for why.
  /**
   * Optional exterior decorations the parametric model layers on.
   *
   * These are the third tier of what separates two styles, after roof and wall: a cottage with a
   * porch and a fence reads as a different BUILDING from a cabin with a chimney and a woodpile,
   * even where both happen to sit under a hip roof.
   */
  features?: {
    chimney?: boolean;
    /** Flower box under the side window. */
    windowFlowerBox?: boolean;
    /** Potted plant beside the door. */
    doorPlanter?: boolean;
    /** Trailing vines down a corner post. */
    vines?: boolean;
    /** Stacked firewood beside the door. */
    firewood?: boolean;
    /** Surrounding low picket fence. */
    fence?: boolean;
    /** Raised stilt posts under the plinth. */
    stilts?: boolean;
    /** A covered porch on two posts over the front door. */
    porch?: boolean;
    /** Hinged shutters either side of every window. */
    shutters?: boolean;
    /** A rain barrel under the eave at one corner. */
    barrel?: boolean;
    /** A lit lantern hanging beside the door. Also lights the approach at night. */
    lantern?: boolean;
    /**
     * 小型陽台 — a shallow bracketed balcony high on the front wall, with a railing.
     *
     * Deliberately a Juliet balcony rather than a ground terrace. The Home is a single storey and
     * the player is stopped at `halfDepth + 0.35`, so a deck deep enough to read as a terrace
     * would be half inside ground the player cannot stand on. Up under the eave it is unambiguous,
     * costs no floor area, and gives the front elevation a middle layer between door and roof.
     */
    balcony?: boolean;
    /** 小型遮雨棚 — a small sloped hood on brackets over each front window. */
    awning?: boolean;
    /** Fishing floats on a line, and a net, hung on the end wall. */
    floats?: boolean;
  };
}

export type HouseStyleId =
  | 'starter'
  | 'grass'
  | 'stone'
  | 'forest'
  | 'beach'
  | 'wood'
  | 'garden'
  | 'island'
  | 'country'
  | 'modern'
  | 'grove'
  | 'fisher';

/** The style every Home starts as, before the player buys anything. */
export const STARTER_HOUSE_STYLE_ID: HouseStyleId = 'starter';

/**
 * The inventory item that represents "I own a house but haven't placed it yet". It is granted,
 * never sold, and is consumed the moment the Home is placed.
 */
export const STARTER_HOUSE_ITEM_ID = 'house-starter';

const STYLES_BY_ID = new Map(HOUSE_STYLES.map((s) => [s.id, s]));
const STYLES_BY_ITEM_ID = new Map(HOUSE_STYLES.map((s) => [s.itemId, s]));

/**
 * Resolves a stored style id to its definition, falling back to the starter style so a Home
 * saved with an id from a removed style still renders instead of vanishing.
 */
export function getHouseStyle(id: string | undefined | null): HouseStyleDefinition {
  return (id ? STYLES_BY_ID.get(id as HouseStyleId) : undefined) ?? STYLES_BY_ID.get(STARTER_HOUSE_STYLE_ID)!;
}

/** Resolves a shop/inventory item id to the style it grants, if any. */
export function getHouseStyleByItemId(itemId: string): HouseStyleDefinition | undefined {
  return STYLES_BY_ITEM_ID.get(itemId);
}

/** Whether a catalog item id is a House Style (drives the shop's apply-instead-of-place UI). */
export function isHouseStyleItemId(itemId: string): boolean {
  return STYLES_BY_ITEM_ID.has(itemId);
}

/** Styles the shop should list, i.e. everything except the granted starter. */
export const PURCHASABLE_HOUSE_STYLES = HOUSE_STYLES.filter((s) => s.purchasable);
```

## src/constants/hudLayout.ts

```ts
/**
 * @license
 * SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
 */

/**
 * Screen-space keep-out margins for the world-tracked InteractionPrompt
 * badge (src/components/UI/InteractionPrompt.tsx). The badge is projected
 * from a 3D position each frame and then clamped so it never drifts under the
 * persistent HUD chrome placed by the grid frame (HudFrame.tsx): the left
 * rail (TopBar/MiniMap + SideButtons), the right-side ZoomControl, the
 * top-centre banners, and the bottom NavBar.
 *
 * Centralised here (instead of as magic numbers inside the component) so the
 * clamp stays conceptually tied to the HUD layout — the interactable is
 * always within a few metres of the player, so the projected point is
 * normally well inside this safe zone and these only guard rare edge cases
 * (wide FOV, a door near the frustum edge). Values are conservative upper
 * bounds on each cluster's footprint across breakpoints.
 */
export const PROMPT_SAFE_MARGIN = {
  left: 110,   // clears the left rail (SideButtons column + edge inset)
  // Back to 100 now that 幸運轉盤 (UI/LuckyWheel.tsx) is a ~68px corner icon rather than the
  // 148–224px disc it briefly was: that disc is why this was widened to 180, and it no longer
  // exists — the wheel opens as a modal instead, which is on the z-modal tier and covers this
  // badge outright. The launcher sits inside the bottom/right corner these two margins already
  // reserve for the NavBar dock and the zoom dial.
  right: 100,  // clears the right-side ZoomControl dial + edge inset
  top: 100,    // clears the top-centre banner band
  bottom: 170, // clears the bottom NavBar dock
} as const;
```

```ts
/**
 * @license
 * SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
 */

/**
 * WHAT THE BODY DOES — the posture vocabulary, and the missing layer that made every
 * non-seat interaction in the game look identical.
 *
 * ## The bug this file exists to fix
 *
 * `constants/furnitureInteractions.ts` had ONE table, and it conflated two independent
 * things into a single `InteractionKind`:
 *
 *   what the PROMPT says   「泡澡」「烹飪」「觀星」
 *   what the BODY does     the pose
 *
 * Its `pose` column had exactly two values, `'sit'` and `'lie'`, and every other kind left
 * it undefined. Undefined meant "no pose", and "no pose" was routed in Three/Avatar.tsx to
 * a single hard-coded 0.7 s two-arm reach — so 泡澡, 烹飪, 觀星, 洗手, 許願, 閱讀, 添柴火
 * and eleven others were, frame for frame, the same animation with a different caption. A
 * bathtub could not be anything but "stand beside it and wave", because the vocabulary had
 * no word for what a body does in a bathtub.
 *
 * The kind, then, is the VERB. This file is the BODY, and the two are joined by name:
 * a kind names a posture, an item may override it, and adding 泡澡 to the game is adding a
 * row HERE rather than a branch in the animation file.
 *
 *   Furniture  →  Interaction Kind  →  Posture  →  joint targets  →  Player Animation
 *   (items.ts)   (furnitureInteractions)  (here)   (lib/interactionPosture)  (Avatar.tsx)
 *
 * ## Everything is stated as JOINT NAMES, never as refs
 *
 * A posture is a `BodyPose`: a partial map from {@link RigJointName} to an euler triple. It
 * says "the right arm is at -1.05 pitch", not "write -1.05 into rightArmRef". That is the
 * whole of the model-independence promise (constants/characterRig.ts): the controller drives
 * joints BY NAME, so a model with a different skeleton — one that splits the arm into an
 * upper and a lower segment, say — extends {@link RigJointName} and adds rows here, and not
 * one existing posture, and not one line of the pose maths, has to change. Nothing in this
 * file knows the character is currently a chibi made of capsules.
 *
 * Angles that depend on the character's PROPORTIONS are deliberately NOT here: a seat's leg
 * swing is derived at runtime from the rig and the measured furniture
 * (lib/interactionPosture.ts), for the same reason a seat height is not typed into a pose.
 * What is here is body LANGUAGE — the part that is a choice rather than a measurement.
 */

/**
 * The joints a posture may address.
 *
 * Exactly the rig Three/Avatar.tsx owns today (constants/characterRig.ts). This union is the
 * extension point for a richer model: adding `'leftLowerArm'` here and a row to Avatar's
 * joint map is all a two-segment arm costs, and every posture that does not mention it
 * simply leaves it alone.
 */
export type RigJointName = 'head' | 'torso' | 'leftArm' | 'rightArm' | 'leftLeg' | 'rightLeg';

/**
 * One joint's target, radians, in the joint's own space. Any axis may be omitted — an
 * omitted axis is one the posture has no opinion about and leaves to whatever else is
 * animating it.
 *
 * SIGN CONVENTION, the same one the walk cycle and the swim pose already use:
 *   x  negative swings a hanging limb FORWARD and tips the head UP; positive is back / down.
 *   y  turn about the body's up axis.
 *   z  roll. On the arms it is the elbow going OUT from the ribs: negative on the left,
 *      positive on the right (they mirror, so a single signed number would swing both the
 *      same way across the body instead of opening them out).
 */
export interface JointPose {
  x?: number;
  y?: number;
  z?: number;
}

/** A whole-body posture: every joint it has an opinion about. */
export type BodyPose = Partial<Record<RigJointName, JointPose>>;

/**
 * A repeating motion laid over a posture's held pose — the stir, the scrub, the page turn.
 *
 * This is what stops a posture being a statue. It is a sine rather than a keyframe list on
 * purpose: two of these on the same joint, a quarter cycle apart on different axes, is a
 * circle (see `cook`), which covers nearly every repetitive hand action furniture asks for
 * and costs one multiply per joint per frame.
 */
export interface PostureMotion {
  joint: RigJointName;
  axis: 'x' | 'y' | 'z';
  /** Radians, peak deviation from the held pose. Signed, so two joints can counter-phase. */
  amplitude: number;
  /** Full oscillations across the posture's own duration. */
  cycles: number;
  /** Phase offset in cycles, 0..1. Pair 0 and 0.25 on two axes to trace a circle. */
  phase?: number;
}

/**
 * How the body settles into and out of a posture over its lifetime.
 *
 *   `pulse`  out and back on a half sine — a single gesture, at full extension halfway
 *            through. The reach a fridge used to get, and still gets.
 *   `hold`   in, hold, out — the body arrives at the pose, DOES the thing for most of the
 *            duration, then relaxes. What separates 烹飪 from a wave at a hob.
 */
export type PostureEnvelope = 'pulse' | 'hold';

/**
 * How a posture's root height comes off the anchor it is given. Pairing a rule here with the
 * rig is what lets one catalog number (where the cushion is) serve every character model —
 * see `poseRootHeight` in constants/furnitureInteractions.ts.
 *
 *   `hips`   the body's HIP JOINT rests on the anchor surface. Sitting, and bathing.
 *   `side`   the body is turned onto its side about its feet, so it rests on its own
 *            half-thickness above the surface. Lying.
 *   `stand`  no anchor surface at all: the body stays on the floor it is standing on, and
 *            the posture is played at the piece rather than on it.
 */
export type PostureAnchoring = 'hips' | 'side' | 'stand';

/**
 * What the legs do once the body is on the piece. The three cases are genuinely different
 * GEOMETRY problems, not three sets of numbers:
 *
 *   `reachFloor`     swing down until they reach the floor, or until they clear the piece's
 *                    own front edge — whichever is the wider swing. A dining chair plants
 *                    its feet; a deep sofa lets them hang. Both derived at runtime.
 *   `extendForward`  straight out along the piece, level with the hips. What legs do in a
 *                    bathtub, where there is no floor to reach and the far end is metres away.
 *   `climbOver`      swung up and over an edge while getting on, relaxed once settled. The
 *                    hammock's, and every bed's.
 *   `dangle`         hanging free, straight down from the hip, and left there for the piece's
 *                    own motion to swing. The one case where the legs must NOT be solved: a
 *                    swing seat is 0.70 above the ground against a 0.54 leg, so `reachFloor`
 *                    would peg at "straight down" anyway — but the swing's measured box reaches
 *                    0.90 ahead of the seat (its A-frame straddles the rider), and the "clear
 *                    the piece's front edge" constraint would read that as a metre-deep cushion
 *                    and kick both legs out horizontal. Saying "they hang" is not a shortcut
 *                    past the solver; it is the correct answer that the solver's two
 *                    constraints cannot express.
 */
export type PostureLegs = 'reachFloor' | 'extendForward' | 'climbOver' | 'dangle';

/**
 * How a body answers a piece that is MOVING under it — the second half of the swing rework.
 *
 * A rider is not bolted to the seat. The root goes over with the arc (`follow`), but the legs
 * hang back a beat behind it and the torso leans against it, and those two lags are most of what
 * separates "a person on a swing" from "a mannequin glued to a plank". Both are driven by the
 * piece's own angle, which the controller already has — see lib/outdoorMotion.ts's
 * `suspendedAngle`, the single number this whole mechanism is built on.
 */
export interface PostureRideResponse {
  /** How far the legs trail the arc, radians per radian of tilt. Negative swings them forward. */
  legTrail?: number;
  /** Torso counter-lean per radian of tilt. */
  leanBack?: number;
  /** Arms bracing on the ropes: how far they follow, per radian of tilt. */
  armBrace?: number;
}

export interface PostureSpec {
  /**
   * Whether the player STAYS in it. An occupying posture holds the body until they get up
   * (the prompt turns into 「起身」); a non-occupying one plays for {@link duration} and
   * hands the body back. This is the only structural difference between the two families —
   * everything below is shared, which is what keeps 泡澡 and 洗手 the same kind of thing.
   */
  occupies: boolean;
  anchoring: PostureAnchoring;
  /** Occupying postures only. */
  legs?: PostureLegs;
  /** Occupying postures on a piece that moves. See {@link PostureRideResponse}. */
  ride?: PostureRideResponse;
  /** The characteristic pose, at full extension. */
  hold: BodyPose;
  /** Laid over {@link hold} while the posture is at strength. */
  motion?: readonly PostureMotion[];
  /**
   * The whole body's pitch, radians — positive leans FORWARD. Applied to the character ROOT,
   * so unlike a `torso` entry it carries the arms and legs with it (the torso joint is a
   * sibling of the limbs, not their parent — see Avatar.tsx's CELEBRATE note). This is the
   * axis that makes someone read as leaning over a hob rather than standing at one.
   */
  lean?: number;
  /** Non-occupying postures: seconds. Occupying ones run until the player gets up. */
  duration?: number;
  envelope?: PostureEnvelope;
  /**
   * The sustained idle once an occupying posture has settled — the 「Bathing Idle」 half of
   * the request. Amplitudes are small on purpose: this plays for as long as the player sits
   * there, and anything with a silhouette to it becomes a tic within thirty seconds.
   */
  idle?: {
    /** Root rise and fall, world units. A body in water bobs; a body on a chair does not. */
    bob?: number;
    /** Root pitch rock, radians. */
    rock?: number;
    /** Cycles per second for the bob, the rock and every {@link PostureMotion} in `drift`. */
    rate?: number;
    /** Joints that drift with the bob — hands riding the surface of the water. */
    drift?: readonly PostureMotion[];
  };
  /**
   * Which way the body steps off, as a yaw offset from the direction it is facing. 0 (the
   * default) stands straight up out of a chair and walks forward off a bed. A bath is the
   * case that needs it: you get out of a bathtub over its SIDE, not by wading the two and a
   * half metres out over the taps.
   *
   * WHICH side matters, and the sign is not free. Every piece in this catalog has its front at
   * local +Z (see FurnitureInteraction.facing) and is placed with its back to a wall, so the
   * offset has to come out at +Z once the occupant's own `facing` is added to it. A tub's
   * occupant lies along the piece's local +X (`facing: PI/2`), so stepping out at +Z is
   * `-PI/2` — the OTHER sign lands the body behind the tub, i.e. in the wall it is pushed
   * against, which is exactly where 泡澡 used to put you on standing up.
   */
  exitFacing?: number;
}

/**
 * THE POSTURES. Fourteen rows, and adding a fifteenth is adding a row — nothing downstream
 * branches on the id.
 *
 * The three occupying ones are the body ON the furniture. The eleven acting ones are the body
 * AT it, and the reason there are eleven rather than the one there used to be is that
 * 「按 E → 角色動一下雙手」 is not an interaction: a player should be able to tell what
 * someone is doing from the silhouette alone, with the caption covered.
 */
export const POSTURES = {
  // -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // OCCUPYING — the body goes onto or into the piece and stays there.
  // -------------------------------------------------------------------------

  /**
   * 坐下. Upright on a cushion, hands resting on the thighs. The leg swing is NOT here — it
   * is the one angle that has to be solved per piece, and it is solved from measurements
   * (see `reachFloor`).
   *
   * `lean` is the chibi tax: the skull is 1.17 world units across and a chair seat is 0.6
   * deep, so a body sat bolt upright puts the back of its head through the backrest. A
   * slight forward lean carries it clear — and is also what someone sitting on a chair
   * actually does. (This was `SIT_LEAN`; the value is unchanged.)
   */
  sit: {
    occupies: true,
    anchoring: 'hips',
    legs: 'reachFloor',
    lean: 0.12,
    hold: {
      leftArm: { x: -0.30, z: -0.16 },
      rightArm: { x: -0.30, z: 0.16 },
      leftLeg: { z: -0.06 },
      rightLeg: { z: 0.06 },
    },
    idle: {
      bob: 0.006,
      rate: 0.28,
      drift: [
        { joint: 'leftArm', axis: 'x', amplitude: 0.03, cycles: 1 },
        { joint: 'rightArm', axis: 'x', amplitude: 0.03, cycles: 1, phase: 0.5 },
      ],
    },
  },

  /**
   * 盪鞦韆. THE ONE THE SWING REWORK IS ABOUT.
   *
   * Read against `sit`, which is the posture it is nearest to, because the differences are the
   * whole point — a person on a swing is not a person on a chair that happens to be moving:
   *
   *   the HANDS      grip the ropes, so the arms go UP and slightly out rather than resting on
   *                  the thighs. This is the single most legible thing in the silhouette; with
   *                  the arms down, the pose reads as sitting on a plank.
   *   the LEGS       hang (`dangle`) instead of being solved to the floor. The seat is above
   *                  standing leg length, and the piece's own box is not a cushion — see
   *                  `dangle` for why the solver gets the wrong answer here.
   *   the LEAN       is backward, not forward. You lean back on a swing; you lean forward in a
   *                  chair to keep an oversized head off the backrest, and a swing has none.
   *   `ride`         exists at all. It is what makes the body answer the arc rather than being
   *                  carried by it.
   *
   * The idle is deliberately almost nothing: the piece itself supplies all the movement anybody
   * will look at, and a bob laid on top of a two-and-a-half-second arc just reads as a wobble.
   */
  swing: {
    occupies: true,
    anchoring: 'hips',
    legs: 'dangle',
    lean: -0.06,
    hold: {
      // Hands up on the ropes. `z` opens the elbows out to where the ropes actually are
      // (±0.45 local, about a shoulder and a half apart), mirrored left/right per the sign
      // convention at the top of this file.
      leftArm: { x: -1.02, z: -0.30 },
      rightArm: { x: -1.02, z: 0.30 },
      leftLeg: { z: -0.05 },
      rightLeg: { z: 0.05 },
    },
    ride: {
      // The legs trail the seat: at the back of the arc they are still swinging forward. A real
      // rider's legs lead the arc at the front and trail it at the back, which one signed
      // multiple of the tilt captures well enough at this scale.
      legTrail: -0.55,
      leanBack: 0.22,
      armBrace: 0.14,
    },
    idle: { bob: 0.003, rate: 0.2 },
  },

  /**
   * 躺下 / 休息. Turned onto the side about the feet; the recline angle itself is derived
   * from the rig (`liePitch`), because how far a body has to be tipped off flat to keep an
   * oversized head out of the mattress is a fact about the head, not a taste call.
   *
   * `hold` is empty on purpose. A settled lying body's arms rest against its sides, which is
   * what the rig's neutral already is — the visible work here is all in `climbOver`.
   */
  lie: {
    occupies: true,
    anchoring: 'side',
    legs: 'climbOver',
    hold: {},
    idle: { bob: 0.008, rate: 0.22 },
  },

  /**
   * 泡澡. THE ONE THE REQUEST WAS ABOUT.
   *
   * Down inside the tub with the hips on its floor, reclined back against the end, legs
   * straight out along the length of it (a bath is long in X and shallow in Z — the body
   * lies ALONG it, which is why a bathtub's anchor carries a quarter-turn `facing`), and the
   * arms out wide over the rim.
   *
   * Read against `sit`, which is the posture this is nearest to: the recline is BACKWARD
   * instead of forward, the legs go OUT instead of down, the arms go WIDE instead of onto
   * the thighs, and the whole body bobs. Nothing about it is a sitting body with different
   * hands — which is the point.
   */
  bathe: {
    occupies: true,
    anchoring: 'hips',
    legs: 'extendForward',
    /**
     * Backward — you lean INTO the end of a bath — but only just, and the number is a geometry
     * budget rather than a taste call.
     *
     * The recline pivots about the ROOT, which for a body sitting on a tub floor is 0.33 below
     * that floor, so every radian of it swings the head backward by the head joint's whole
     * height (1.57 world units). At the -0.22 this started at, the back of a chibi skull — 1.17
     * across — came out 0.28 THROUGH the end wall of a 2.53-unit tub. Reclining is the most
     * expensive thing this body can do in a confined space; -0.10 is what the tub affords, and
     * `npm run audit:interactions` fails if a later edit spends more than that.
     */
    lean: -0.10,
    hold: {
      // Floating forward in the water, not resting on the rim: a body sitting on the floor of
      // this tub has its shoulders 0.36 BELOW the rim, so "elbows on the edge" is a pose the
      // proportions cannot reach. Out far enough to read as arms in water, inside the walls.
      leftArm: { x: -0.48, z: -0.34 },
      rightArm: { x: -0.48, z: 0.34 },
      // Chin up, clear of the water.
      head: { x: -0.20 },
      // Apart along the tub floor; the pitch itself comes from `extendForward`.
      leftLeg: { z: -0.10 },
      rightLeg: { z: 0.10 },
    },
    idle: {
      bob: 0.028,
      rock: 0.018,
      rate: 0.36,
      drift: [
        // Hands riding the water, a half cycle apart so they are never symmetrical.
        { joint: 'leftArm', axis: 'z', amplitude: -0.05, cycles: 1 },
        { joint: 'rightArm', axis: 'z', amplitude: 0.05, cycles: 1, phase: 0.5 },
        { joint: 'head', axis: 'y', amplitude: 0.07, cycles: 0.5 },
      ],
    },
    // Over the side, and out the FRONT of the tub. See exitFacing for why the sign is this one.
    exitFacing: -Math.PI / 2,
  },

  // -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // ACTING — the body walks to the piece, does something, and is handed back.
  // -------------------------------------------------------------------------

  /**
   * 使用. The generic one, and the ONLY posture that survives from the old system — where it

   *
   * It stays because a genuinely unclassified "reach for the thing" is a reasonable default
   * for a piece nobody has thought about yet. It is now what an item gets when it asks for
   * nothing in particular, rather than what every item got no matter what it asked for.
   */
  reach: {
    occupies: false,
    anchoring: 'stand',
    duration: 0.7,
    envelope: 'pulse',
    lean: 0.05,
    hold: {
      leftArm: { x: -1.35, z: -0.12 },

    anchoring: 'stand',

    lean: 0.10,

      torso: { y: -0.22 },

  },

  /** 操作. A panel, a dial, a flush lever: one hand, small and precise, eyes down on it. */
  operate: {

    anchoring: 'stand',
    duration: 1.1,

      head: { x: 0.24 },

  /**
   * 烹飪. Leaning over the hob, one hand steadying the pan while the other stirs.
   *
   * The stir is the two-axis trick this file's motion spec exists for: the same joint driven

   */
  cook: {
    occupies: false,
    anchoring: 'stand',
    duration: 2.4,

    occupies: false,
    anchoring: 'stand',

    // Slightly BACK: you tip away from a thing you are looking up through.

   */
  push: {

      leftArm: { x: -1.45, z: -0.15 },
      rightArm: { x: -1.45, z: 0.15 },

    },
    motion: [
      { joint: 'leftArm', axis: 'x', amplitude: 0.44, cycles: 2 },
      { joint: 'rightArm', axis: 'x', amplitude: 0.44, cycles: 2 },
    ],
  },

  // -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // OCCUPYING, added for the outdoor furniture wave — same two families above,
  // no new anchoring or leg mode: both reuse vocabulary `bathe`/`swing` already needed.
  // -------------------------------------------------------------------------

  /**
   * 半躺（躺椅）. `bathe`'s legs and anchoring, `sit`'s reach — this is what tells it apart from
   * both: unlike `lie` (turned onto the side, face down into the furniture) a lounger keeps the
   * body facing forward and the eyes on the horizon, which is the whole point of a deck chair
   * over a bed. Arms rest slightly out on the chair's own arms rather than folded on the chest.
   */
  recline: {
    occupies: true,
    anchoring: 'hips',
    legs: 'extendForward',
    lean: -0.16,
    hold: {
      leftArm: { x: -0.10, z: -0.24 },
      rightArm: { x: -0.10, z: 0.24 },
      head: { x: -0.10 },
      leftLeg: { z: -0.08 },
      rightLeg: { z: 0.08 },
    },
    idle: {
      bob: 0.006,
      rate: 0.20,
      drift: [{ joint: 'head', axis: 'y', amplitude: 0.05, cycles: 0.4 }],
    },
  },

  /**
   * 坐進吊椅. Nearest to `swing`, and the differences say "a chair that happens to hang" rather
   * than "a swing": hands rest low on the seat's own rim instead of gripping a rope overhead, and
   * `ride` is a fraction of the swing's — a hanging chair answers the wind, not a rider pumping it.
   */
  hangSeat: {
    occupies: true,
    anchoring: 'hips',
    legs: 'dangle',
    lean: 0.02,
    hold: {
      leftArm: { x: -0.22, z: -0.18 },
      rightArm: { x: -0.22, z: 0.18 },
      leftLeg: { z: -0.06 },
      rightLeg: { z: 0.06 },
    },
    ride: {
      legTrail: -0.18,
      leanBack: 0.08,
      armBrace: 0.04,
    },
    idle: { bob: 0.004, rate: 0.22 },
  },

  /**
   * 拋擲（飛盤／沙灘球）. A one-arm throw, not the generic two-hand `reach`: the working arm
   * sweeps out to full extension while the torso twists into it, so the silhouette reads as
   * "just let go of something" rather than "reaching for something".
   */
  toss: {
    occupies: false,
    anchoring: 'stand',
    duration: 0.9,
    envelope: 'pulse',
    lean: 0.08,
    hold: {
      rightArm: { x: -1.62, z: 0.42 },
      leftArm: { x: -0.30, z: -0.16 },
      torso: { y: -0.20 },
      head: { x: 0.05 },
    },
    motion: [{ joint: 'torso', axis: 'y', amplitude: 0.10, cycles: 1 }],
  },

  // -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // SOCIAL — not played at a piece of furniture but at another character. Same family as the
  // acting postures (stand, play once, hand the body back), which is why they are rows here and
  // not a second animation path: a player talking to the gardener is the same controller, the
  // same envelope and the same cancel rules as a player opening a fridge.
  // -------------------------------------------------------------------------

  /**
   * 打招呼. The first thing the player does when they start talking to a resident: one hand up and
   * out to the side, waving. Out WIDE rather than straight up — this character's skull is wider than
   * its shoulders, and an arm raised forward past the chin puts the hand through the face.
   */
  greet: {
    occupies: false,
    anchoring: 'stand',
    duration: 1.3,
    envelope: 'hold',
    hold: {
      rightArm: { x: -1.85, z: 0.78 },
      leftArm: { x: -0.12, z: -0.08 },
      head: { x: -0.04 },
    },
    motion: [{ joint: 'rightArm', axis: 'z', amplitude: 0.22, cycles: 3 }],
  },

  /**
   * 聊天. What the player does on every line after the first: a small open-handed gesture and a nod,
   * so pressing the key to hear the next line still reads as the player taking part in the
   * conversation rather than as the resident talking at a statue.
   */
  chat: {
    occupies: false,
    anchoring: 'stand',
    duration: 1.1,
    envelope: 'hold',
    lean: 0.03,
    hold: {
      rightArm: { x: -0.95, z: 0.32 },
      leftArm: { x: -0.3, z: -0.12 },
      head: { x: 0.05 },
    },
    motion: [{ joint: 'head', axis: 'x', amplitude: 0.07, cycles: 2 }],
  },
} as const satisfies Record<string, PostureSpec>;

export type PostureId = keyof typeof POSTURES;

/**
 * The table seen as plain specs.
 *
 * `as const satisfies` above buys two things worth this line: every row is checked against
 * {@link PostureSpec} as it is written, and {@link PostureId} is the exact set of names rather
 * than `string` — so a typo in a catalog row is a compile error rather than a character standing
 * still. The cost is that each row's type is its own literal shape, and a row with no `duration`
 * has no `duration` property to read. This view puts them all back on the same type.
 */
const SPECS = POSTURES as Record<PostureId, PostureSpec>;

export function getPosture(id: PostureId): PostureSpec {
  return SPECS[id];
}

/** Every posture in the table, for audits and for anything that enumerates the vocabulary. */
export const ALL_POSTURE_IDS = Object.keys(POSTURES) as PostureId[];

/**
 * The LONGEST any acting posture runs, seconds. Not read by the runtime — the controller asks
 * each posture for its own duration — but it is what `npm run audit:interactions` bounds the
 * table against, so a posture accidentally given a duration in milliseconds shows up as a
 * failure rather than as a character stuck stirring a pot for half an hour.
 */
export const MAX_ACTION_DURATION = Math.max(
  ...Object.values(SPECS).map((p) => (p.occupies ? 0 : p.duration ?? 0)),
);
```

```ts
/**
 * @license
 * SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
 */

import { ROOM_GRID_SIZE, ROOM_HALF_SIZE, RoomInstance } from './rooms';

/**
 * THE interior room shell: where a room's walls, doorways, floor and ceiling actually are.
 *
 * WHY THIS FILE EXISTS. The shell used to be described in four independent places -
 * BuildingInteriorView's meshes, characterMovement's walkable rectangles, CameraController's
 * wall segments, and CameraController's buildHouseRects - each re-deriving it from
 * ROOM_HALF_SIZE plus its own hard-coded literals (1.5, 0.2, 0.35, 3.4, 4.45, 0.4). The file
 * header on one of those copies said so outright: "left duplicated rather than extracted to
 * avoid touching those already-working code paths". They were not consistent with each other,
 * and the two reported bugs are both that inconsistency rather than a missing collider:
 *
 *   PLAYER SINKING INTO WALLS. Every collision rule was written against ROOM_HALF_SIZE - the
 *   wall's CENTRE LINE - while the mesh is 0.35 thick and carries a baseboard that protrudes
 *   0.22 into the room. The player's centre was capped at ROOM_HALF_SIZE - radius, so their
 *   body surface reached exactly the centre line: 0.175 inside the wall panel and 0.22 inside
 *   the baseboard, i.e. two thirds of the avatar's radius buried in solid geometry. The wall
 *   was never missing a collider; the collider was in the middle of the wall instead of on its
 *   face. Nothing anywhere stated where a wall's *surface* was, so the two could not agree.
 *
 *   CAMERA SEEING THROUGH WALLS. Same cause, one step removed. applyObservationFloor
 *   (lib/cameraCollision.ts) is allowed to push the camera up to CAMERA_COLLIDER_RADIUS past
 *   the geometric limit, and its correctness argument is that every producer of that limit has
 *   already reserved exactly that much clearance to the nearest real surface - so spending it
 *   can at worst put the camera on the surface. The raycast probe honours that (it subtracts
 *   the radius from the hit). The interior's analytic rules did not: walls reserved a
 *   locally-declared 0.55 to the CENTRE LINE, which is only 0.375 of real clearance, and the
 *   ceiling/floor caps reserved nothing at all. Spending 0.5 against 0.375 put the camera
 *   0.125 beyond the wall's inner face with a 0.3 near plane in front of it - the whole 0.35
 *   panel fell behind the near plane and was clipped away, which is the "see the outside of
 *   the house" report. Not a layer-mask or near-plane bug: a margin being spent that was never
 *   actually there.
 *
 * So the fix is one statement of the geometry, consumed by the meshes and by both collision
 * systems. A new room type or a re-styled wall changes these numbers once and the meshes, the
 * player capsule and the camera arm all move together - which is also what makes future rooms
 * "inherit" the collision rules rather than needing their own.
 *
 * WHY SURFACES AND NOT THICKER COLLIDERS. The standoffs below are the real half-thickness of
 * the real geometry plus each agent's own radius, and nothing more. Padding the shell to hide
 * the problem would cost visible walkable floor in a room that is only ROOM_GRID_SIZE across
 * and would still leave the two systems disagreeing about where the wall is.
 */

// --- Wall panel ------------------------------------------------------------------------------

/** Thickness of a SolidWall's main panel. Centred on the room boundary. */
export const WALL_THICKNESS = 0.35;

/** Thickness of the two panels flanking a doorway. Thinner than a solid wall's. */
export const DOORWAY_PANEL_THICKNESS = 0.2;

/** Thickness of the wood baseboard (踢腳線) running along the foot of every solid wall. */
export const BASEBOARD_THICKNESS = 0.08;

/**
 * How far the baseboard's inner face stands proud of the room boundary. It is the deepest thing
 * on the wall - deeper than the panel's own half-thickness (0.175) - which is why it, not the
 * panel, sets the surface below. The mesh derives its centre from this, so the two cannot drift.
 */
export const WALL_BASEBOARD_INSET = 0.22;

/** Height of the crown moulding (線板) capping every wall. */
export const CROWN_HEIGHT = 0.26;

/** Thickness of the crown moulding band. Its inner face lands on WALL_CROWN_INSET. */
export const CROWN_THICKNESS = 0.1;

/**
 * How far the crown moulding's inner face stands proud of the room boundary.
 *
 * Deliberately EQUAL to the baseboard's, and not deeper. The comment on WALL_SURFACE_INSET below
 * is the standing invitation to add a trim's inset to that max, and this is the first trim to
 * take it up - but doing so with a deeper crown would have narrowed the walkable floor of every
 * room in the house by the difference, in exchange for a moulding that sits at head height where
 * nothing walks. Matching the baseboard buys the same silhouette at zero cost to the room: the
 * max below is unchanged, so no collider moves.
 */
export const WALL_CROWN_INSET = WALL_BASEBOARD_INSET;

/**
 * Distance from the room boundary to the innermost solid surface of its wall: the deepest of
 * everything mounted on that boundary. THIS is the plane collision has to respect. Taking the
 * maximum rather than the panel alone is what stops a future trim/moulding from silently
 * re-introducing the sinking bug - add its inset to this max and every system follows.
 */
export const WALL_SURFACE_INSET = Math.max(
  WALL_THICKNESS / 2,
  DOORWAY_PANEL_THICKNESS / 2,
  WALL_BASEBOARD_INSET,
  WALL_CROWN_INSET
);

/**
 * Distance from a room's CENTRE to the inner face of its walls - the actual inside of the room.
 * Every containment rule measures from this, never from ROOM_HALF_SIZE.
 */
export const ROOM_INNER_HALF_SIZE = ROOM_HALF_SIZE - WALL_SURFACE_INSET;

// --- Doorway ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------

/** Half-width of the opening between two adjoining rooms; the flanking panels start here. */
export const DOORWAY_HALF_WIDTH = 1.5;

/** Underside of the header beam (centred 4.4, 1.2 tall): the doorway is clear below this. */
export const DOORWAY_CLEAR_HEIGHT = 3.8;

// --- Floor and ceiling -----------------------------------------------------------------------

/** Walkable floor height. The floor plane is drawn a hair below it to avoid z-fighting. */
export const INTERIOR_FLOOR_Y = 0;

/** Height of the decorative beams hanging below the ceiling plate. */
export const CEILING_BEAM_HEIGHT = 0.12;

/**
 * Underside of the lowest solid thing overhead - the decorative beams, which hang below the
 * ceiling plate at 4.87. The camera has to clear the beams, so they are the ceiling as far as
 * collision is concerned, and the beam meshes are positioned from this rather than the reverse.
 */
export const INTERIOR_CEILING_Y = 4.8;

/**
 * Top of the crown moulding, and why it is here rather than at the top of the wall box.
 *
 * A crown flush with the wall's own top (5.0) would have run straight through two things that
 * are already up there: the ceiling plate, whose underside is at 4.87, and the decorative beams,
 * which hang from 4.8 to 4.92 and cross the room to land on the wall at both ends. Overlapping
 * either is a z-fighting shimmer along the whole top edge of every wall (see audit:zfighting).
 * Capping the moulding at the ceiling limit puts it entirely below both, and reads correctly
 * besides - the beams now sit ON the moulding, the way a beam sits on a wall plate.
 */
export const CROWN_TOP_Y = INTERIOR_CEILING_Y;

/** Thickness of the solid ceiling plate capping every room. */
export const CEILING_PLATE_THICKNESS = 0.12;

/** Centre height of that plate. The mesh is positioned from this, so the two cannot drift. */
export const CEILING_PLATE_Y = 4.93;

/**
 * The plate's UNDERSIDE — the plane something hung from the ceiling actually touches.
 *
 * Deliberately NOT {@link INTERIOR_CEILING_Y}, and the 7 cm between them is the whole reason this
 * constant exists. INTERIOR_CEILING_Y is the underside of the BEAMS: the lowest solid thing
 * overhead, which is the right answer for collision (nothing may pass through it anywhere) and the
 * wrong one for mounting (over most of the ceiling there is no beam, so a pendant hung at 4.8
 * hangs 7 cm below the ceiling in mid-air — exactly the 「懸浮在半空中」 a ceiling mount exists to
 * make impossible).
 *
 * So a mount asks {@link ceilingSurfaceAt} for the surface at ITS OWN position instead, and gets
 * the beam where there is a beam and the plate everywhere else.
 */
export const INTERIOR_CEILING_SURFACE_Y = CEILING_PLATE_Y - CEILING_PLATE_THICKNESS / 2;

/**
 * One decorative beam crossing a room, as an offset from the room's centre and a width.
 *
 * Here rather than as literals in BuildingInteriorView's mesh list, for the same reason every
 * other number in this file is here: the beams are now something OTHER systems have to know
 * about. A ceiling light hung under one has to hang FROM the beam rather than through it, and the
 * mount resolver cannot read a JSX tree. One table — drawn by the meshes, read by
 * {@link ceilingSurfaceAt} — is what keeps 「where the beam is drawn」 and 「where the beam is」 the
 * same sentence.
 *
 * Each beam runs the full width of the room along X, and its underside is INTERIOR_CEILING_Y.
 */
export interface CeilingBeam {
  /** Distance from the room's centre along Z. */
  offsetZ: number;
  /** Extent along Z. */
  width: number;
}

export const CEILING_BEAMS: readonly CeilingBeam[] = [
  { offsetZ: 0, width: 0.25 },
  { offsetZ: -3.0, width: 0.2 },
  { offsetZ: 3.0, width: 0.2 },
];

/**
 * The underside of the lowest solid thing directly above `(x, z)`, or `null` when that point is
 * not under any room.
 *
 * The ceiling's counterpart to {@link buildWallSegments}: the geometry stated once, so the meshes
 * and the placement rule cannot disagree about where the ceiling is. `null` is what makes 「outside
 * the house」 a refusal rather than a lamp hanging over the void — a ceiling mount has no fallback
 * surface the way a floor piece has the ground under it.
 *
 * The area credited to a room is its INNER floor plan ({@link ROOM_INNER_HALF_SIZE}), not the full
 * ROOM_GRID_SIZE the plate mesh spans. The plate reaches to the wall centre lines because it has
 * to meet its neighbour's without a seam; a lamp hung out there would be inside the wall.
 */
export function ceilingSurfaceAt(
  x: number,
  z: number,
  rooms: ReadonlyArray<ShellRoom>
): number | null {
  const inner = ROOM_INNER_HALF_SIZE;

  for (const room of rooms) {
    const dx = x - room.cx;
    const dz = z - room.cz;
    if (Math.abs(dx) > inner || Math.abs(dz) > inner) continue;

    for (const beam of CEILING_BEAMS) {
      if (Math.abs(dz - beam.offsetZ) <= beam.width / 2) return INTERIOR_CEILING_Y;
    }
    return INTERIOR_CEILING_SURFACE_Y;
  }

  return null;
}

// --- Topology --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

export interface ShellRoom {
  cx: number;
  cz: number;
}

export interface RoomNeighbours {
  hasN: boolean;
  hasS: boolean;
  hasE: boolean;
  hasW: boolean;
}

/**
 * Which of a room's four sides open onto another room. Rooms sit on a ROOM_GRID_SIZE lattice,
 * so adjacency is integer grid coordinates - the one place that rounding is done.
 */
export function getRoomNeighbours(room: ShellRoom, rooms: ReadonlyArray<ShellRoom>): RoomNeighbours {
  const gx = Math.round(room.cx / ROOM_GRID_SIZE);
  const gz = Math.round(room.cz / ROOM_GRID_SIZE);

  const has = (nx: number, nz: number) =>
    rooms.some(
      (other) =>
        Math.round(other.cx / ROOM_GRID_SIZE) === nx && Math.round(other.cz / ROOM_GRID_SIZE) === nz
    );

  return {
    hasN: has(gx, gz + 1),
    hasS: has(gx, gz - 1),
    hasE: has(gx + 1, gz),
    hasW: has(gx - 1, gz),
  };
}

export interface WallSegment {
  x1: number;
  z1: number;
  x2: number;
  z2: number;
  /**
   * Unit normal of this face, pointing INTO the room that emitted it.
   *
   * Emitted here rather than inferred by callers, because it is knowable exactly at this point
   * and only approximately afterwards: a segment is a line, and a line has two normals — which
   * of them faces the room is a fact about which side the segment was pushed from, and that is
   * information only `pushSide` has. Anything reconstructing it downstream is reduced to
   * guessing from the room centre, which is the shape "if x > 0 rotate 180" bugs come in.
   *
   * It is what lets a hung object orient itself: a piece mounted on this face turns its local
   * +Z onto this vector, so it faces the room on every wall of every room without a single
   * per-wall case. See lib/interiorPlacement.ts.
   */
  nx: number;
  nz: number;
  /**
   * The span of a doorway opening: solid only above DOORWAY_CLEAR_HEIGHT, where the header
   * beam is. Callers that work in 2D (the build-mode fly camera) treat these as passable.
   */
  isDoorway?: boolean;
}

export interface BuildWallSegmentsOptions {
  /**
   * Emit only the house's outer boundary, skipping the short panels that flank a doorway.
   * For the build-mode fly camera, which is a free edit view rather than a body: colliding
   * with the jamb panels made moving between rooms feel like it snagged, and containing it to
   * the overall footprint is all that view needs.
   */
  exteriorOnly?: boolean;
}

/**
 * The room shell as line segments, placed on the walls' INNER FACES.
 *
 * Each room emits its own four faces, so a wall shared by two rooms produces two segments
 * WALL_THICKNESS apart rather than one on the centre line - which is what makes the wall solid
 * from both sides and is the difference that stops the camera clipping into it. Segments span
 * the full ROOM_HALF_SIZE either way so that a ray leaving diagonally through a corner still
 * meets one of them.
 */
export function buildWallSegments(
  rooms: ReadonlyArray<ShellRoom>,
  { exteriorOnly = false }: BuildWallSegmentsOptions = {}
): WallSegment[] {
  const segments: WallSegment[] = [];
  const inner = ROOM_INNER_HALF_SIZE;
  const span = ROOM_HALF_SIZE;
  const door = DOORWAY_HALF_WIDTH;

  rooms.forEach((r) => {
    const { hasN, hasS, hasE, hasW } = getRoomNeighbours(r, rooms);

    // A side that opens onto another room becomes three segments: the two flanking panels and
    // the opening between them. Closed sides are one unbroken face.
    const pushSide = (
      open: boolean,
      // Maps a position along the wall (`a`) and the wall's own offset (`b`) to world XZ.
      toWorld: (a: number, b: number) => { x: number; z: number },
      offset: number,
      // Unit normal of this face, pointing back into the room. The one caller that knows it.
      nx: number,
      nz: number
    ) => {
      if (!open) {
        const p1 = toWorld(-span, offset);
        const p2 = toWorld(span, offset);
        segments.push({ x1: p1.x, z1: p1.z, x2: p2.x, z2: p2.z, nx, nz });
        return;
      }
      if (exteriorOnly) return;

      const l1 = toWorld(-span, offset);
      const l2 = toWorld(-door, offset);
      segments.push({ x1: l1.x, z1: l1.z, x2: l2.x, z2: l2.z, nx, nz });

      const r1 = toWorld(door, offset);
      const r2 = toWorld(span, offset);
      segments.push({ x1: r1.x, z1: r1.z, x2: r2.x, z2: r2.z, nx, nz });

      const d1 = toWorld(-door, offset);
      const d2 = toWorld(door, offset);
      segments.push({ x1: d1.x, z1: d1.z, x2: d2.x, z2: d2.z, nx, nz, isDoorway: true });
    };

    pushSide(hasN, (a, b) => ({ x: r.cx + a, z: r.cz + b }), inner, 0, -1);
    pushSide(hasS, (a, b) => ({ x: r.cx + a, z: r.cz - b }), inner, 0, 1);
    pushSide(hasE, (a, b) => ({ x: r.cx + b, z: r.cz + a }), inner, -1, 0);
    pushSide(hasW, (a, b) => ({ x: r.cx - b, z: r.cz + a }), inner, 1, 0);
  });

  return segments;
}

export interface WalkRect {
  minX: number;
  maxX: number;
  minZ: number;
  maxZ: number;
}

/**
 * Small overlap between a room's rectangle and the doorway band bridging it to the next room.
 * Without it the two abut exactly and a position on the seam can fail both closed-interval
 * tests at once, which reads as catching on nothing in the middle of an open doorway.
 */
const RECT_SEAM_OVERLAP = 0.05;

/**
 * The shell as the axis-aligned rectangles an agent of `agentRadius` may have its CENTRE in:
 * one per room, inset to keep the agent's body clear of the wall surface, plus one band per
 * doorway so the union stays connected through the openings.
 *
 * The doorway bands are what make this a union rather than a per-room clamp, and they are sized
 * to overlap both rooms' rectangles, so there is no gap for a fast-moving agent to land in.
 */
export function buildWalkableRects(
  rooms: ReadonlyArray<ShellRoom>,
  agentRadius: number
): WalkRect[] {
  const rects: WalkRect[] = [];
  const inner = ROOM_INNER_HALF_SIZE - agentRadius;
  // Half-width of the passage through a doorway, keeping the body clear of the jamb panels.
  const gate = DOORWAY_HALF_WIDTH - agentRadius;
  // The band has to reach from this room's inner limit to the neighbour's, spanning the wall.
  const bandNear = ROOM_INNER_HALF_SIZE - agentRadius - RECT_SEAM_OVERLAP;
  const bandFar = ROOM_GRID_SIZE - ROOM_INNER_HALF_SIZE + agentRadius + RECT_SEAM_OVERLAP;

  rooms.forEach((r) => {
    rects.push({
      minX: r.cx - inner,
      maxX: r.cx + inner,
      minZ: r.cz - inner,
      maxZ: r.cz + inner,
    });

    // Only the +Z and +X neighbours get a band: adjacency is symmetric, so the room on the
    // other side of the same opening would produce an identical one.
    const { hasN, hasE } = getRoomNeighbours(r, rooms);

    if (hasN) {
      rects.push({
        minX: r.cx - gate,
        maxX: r.cx + gate,
        minZ: r.cz + bandNear,
        maxZ: r.cz + bandFar,
      });
    }

    if (hasE) {
      rects.push({
        minX: r.cx + bandNear,
        maxX: r.cx + bandFar,
        minZ: r.cz - gate,
        maxZ: r.cz + gate,
      });
    }
  });

  return rects;
}

/**
 * Adapter for callers holding full RoomInstances. Exists so this module's own functions can
 * stay structurally typed on {cx, cz} and be unit-testable without building room instances.
 */
export function toShellRooms(rooms: ReadonlyArray<RoomInstance>): ShellRoom[] {
  return rooms.map((r) => ({ cx: r.cx, cz: r.cz }));
}
```
