## src/constants/petCare.ts

```ts
/**
 * @license
 * SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
 */

/**
 * 寵物照護 — 「這是一隻正在島上生活的動物」的資料與規則。
 *
 * The data-and-rules half of the Pet Care System, in the same split every other feature in this
 * codebase uses (constants/islandReturn.ts ↔ context/useIslandLife.ts, constants/utilityCards.ts ↔
 * context/useUtilityCards.ts): pure data and pure functions here, no React, no Firestore, no clock
 * of its own. `lib/petRestingSpots.ts` answers where the animal may lie down,
 * `context/usePetCare.ts` owns the one write, Three/IslandPet.tsx turns the decision into movement,
 * and UI/PetCarePanel.tsx is the only place the numbers are ever shown.
 *
 * ## What this is NOT, and must never become
 *
 * It is not a survival simulator. There is no health, no death, no illness, no starvation and no
 * irreversible loss anywhere in this file — the same rule constants/islandReturn.ts is written
 * under, and for the same reason: the game is 島嶼生活, not a creature that punishes you for having
 * a life. Every value here has a FLOOR above zero, every value recovers completely from one feed,
 * and nothing here can gate an interaction, take an item, or cost the player a coin.
 *
 * What poor care produces is exactly one thing: **fewer signs of activity**. The animal moves less,
 * settles more often, and eventually goes and lies down in its own bed — which the player can see,
 * walk over to, and fix. That is the whole consequence, and it is meant to read as 「牠在等你」
 * rather than as 「你輸了」.
 *
 * ## Two numbers, and why they are not seven
 *
 * The brief lists energy / nutrition / mood / lastFedAt / lastActiveAt / resting / currentBehavior
 * as things a pet state COULD hold, and says explicitly not to copy the list. Four of them already
 * exist or must not be stored: `mood` is 離線回歸's (constants/islandReturn.ts), `lastActiveAt` is
 * its `lastSeenAt`, and `resting`/`currentBehavior` are DERIVED — a stored behaviour is one that
 * can disagree with what the animal is visibly doing, and it would have to be written every few
 * seconds to stay true. So the persisted state is two numbers and a timestamp:
 *
 *   nutrition → energy → activity → behaviour → what you see on screen
 *
 * Nutrition is what feeding restores; energy is what nutrition slowly pulls up or down; activity is
 * energy read as a multiplier; behaviour is chosen from activity. Each arrow is one function below,
 * and adding 心情 or 親密度 later is another stored number and another term in {@link petCondition}
 * — not another branch anywhere else.
 *
 * ## Time is measured, never counted
 *
 * Nothing here ticks. {@link settlePetCare} takes a state and 「now」 and returns what that state has
 * become — as a closed form, so settling once after three days and settling a hundred times along
 * the way produce the same answer to within floating point. That is what makes the offline case
 * (brief §16) free: there is no 「離線期間」 code path, because being away is just a larger gap
 * between two timestamps. It is also what keeps this cheap with many pets (§22): a pet's numbers are
 * recomputed when something asks for them, not on a timer per animal.
 */


/* --- Tuning ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- */

/**
 * Every number in the care simulation, in one table.
 *
 * These are PROVISIONAL and are meant to be argued with — the brief is explicit that the balance is
 * not decided yet, so they live here, together, rather than being scattered through the functions
 * that use them. Nothing outside this file may hard-code a hunger time, a decay rate or a floor.
 *
 * The shape they are chosen to produce, for whoever re-tunes them:
 *
 *  - A player who logs in most days never sees any of this. One feed covers about two days, and
 *    energy sits at its ceiling the whole time.
 *  - A few days away and the animal is visibly quieter — it settles more, follows less eagerly, and
 *    starts spending time at its own bed. Nothing is lost.
 *  - Two weeks away and it is mostly resting in the bed. That is the FLOOR: it never gets worse than
 *    「牠在窩裡等你」, and one bowl of food brings it all the way back.
 */
export const PET_CARE_TUNING = {
  /**
   * How much 營養 drains in a day, as a fraction of a full bowl.
   *
   * 0.3 means a full bowl runs down over a bit more than three days, and one serving of the game's
   * actual food (0.55, see 基礎飼料 in constants/items.ts) covers about two. Deliberately slow: a
   * cosy game whose companion needs feeding twice a day is a game with a chore in it, and the
   * brief's §20 rules that out. It is also why there is no 「飢餓時間」 constant anywhere — hunger
   * here is a slope, not a deadline.
   *
   * The shape it produces, which is what to check when re-tuning it: a player who feeds and comes
   * back the next day finds a 悠閒 animal, a week away finds a 懶洋洋 one, and everything past that
   * is the same 懶洋洋 animal — the floor is reached at about three days and nothing gets worse
   * after it.
   */
  nutritionDrainPerDay: 0.3,
  /**
   * How low 營養 is allowed to fall. NOT zero, and this is the single most important number here.
   *
   * A value that can reach zero invites a rule about what happens at zero, and every such rule is
   * some flavour of the death mechanic §6 forbids. Fifteen percent is 「餓了，但沒事」.
   */
  nutritionFloor: 0.15,
  /**
   * The 活動力 a given 營養 level eventually settles at: `energyBase + energySpan × nutrition`.
   *
   * The base is what an unfed animal keeps — a quarter of its liveliness, which is enough to potter
   * about its bed and get up when its owner walks over. Nothing here can drive energy to zero, so
   * 「完全不動」 is not a state this system is able to produce.
   */
  energyBase: 0.25,
  energySpan: 0.75,
  /**
   * How fast energy chases that target, as a half-life in hours.
   *
   * Six hours is the lag that makes the change read as gradual rather than as a switch (§3, §15):
   * feeding a listless animal perks it up over the afternoon rather than in the same frame, and an
   * absence dims it over a day rather than at a threshold it crosses in its sleep.
   */
  energyHalfLifeHours: 6,
  /** The floor under 活動力, for the same reason `nutritionFloor` exists. */
  energyFloor: 0.2,
} as const;

/* --- The persisted state ------------------------------------------------------------------ */

/**
 * 寵物照護狀態 — what is actually written to the save.
 *
 * Stored at `islandState.pet.care` (see `PetLifeState` in constants/islandReturn.ts) rather than as
 * a new top-level profile field, and that is a deployment decision as much as a modelling one:
 * `islandState` is already ONE key in the deployed Firestore ruleset and its `pet` member is already
 * validated as 「a map」, so this whole feature is writable with no rules change. A new top-level
 * field would need a clause in `isValidUser()` and an entry in every write whitelist before a single
 * save could land — see docs/FIRESTORE_RULES.md.
 *
 * Three fields, all required, none optional: an optional field would have to be OMITTED rather than
 * set to `undefined` (Firestore's `updateDoc` throws synchronously on an explicit undefined — see
 * `makePetState`), and there is nothing here a pet can legitimately not have.
 */
export interface PetCareState {
  /** 營養, 0..1. Restored by food, drained by time. Never reaches 0. */
  nutrition: number;
  /** 活動力, 0..1. Chases the ceiling nutrition sets for it. Never reaches 0. */
  energy: number;
  /**
   * ISO of the instant `nutrition`/`energy` were last true.
   *
   * The anchor the whole simulation measures from, and the reason nothing here needs a timer: a
   * value plus the moment it was true IS the curve, so 「離線三天」 and 「分頁在背景放了三天」 are the
   * same arithmetic. Written only when something real happens (an arrival, a feed), never on a
   * schedule.
   */
  updatedAt: string;
}

/**
 * A brand-new companion: fed, rested, and stamped as of now.
 *
 * Full rather than half, because the first thing a player does with a new pet is take it outside —
 * and an animal that arrives already listless is not the thing the shop sold them.
 */
export function newPetCareState(nowMs: number): PetCareState {
  return { nutrition: 1, energy: 1, updatedAt: new Date(nowMs).toISOString() };
}

/**
 * Reads a stored care state defensively.
 *
 * Every field is range-checked rather than trusted, because this value has round-tripped through a
 * document store: an old save, a half-written map or a hand-edited profile must produce a healthy
 * animal rather than `NaN` propagating into the movement code, where it shows up as a pet that has
 * silently stopped existing. Absent — which is every save written before this feature — reads as a
 * brand-new, fully cared-for pet, exactly like one just bought.
 */
export function readPetCareState(raw: unknown, nowMs: number): PetCareState {
  if (!raw || typeof raw !== 'object') return newPetCareState(nowMs);
  const value = raw as Partial<PetCareState>;
  const stamp =
    typeof value.updatedAt === 'string' && Number.isFinite(Date.parse(value.updatedAt))
      ? value.updatedAt
      : new Date(nowMs).toISOString();
  return {
    nutrition: clamp01(numberOr(value.nutrition, 1)),
    energy: clamp01(numberOr(value.energy, 1)),
    updatedAt: stamp,
  };
}

/**
 * Reads the stored per-pet care map, defensively — see {@link readPetCareState} for why every field
 * that has round-tripped through a document store is range-checked rather than trusted.
 *
 * A map rather than one state because a household can hold more than one animal and each has its
 * own appetite (§6, §21). Keys are companion item ids; anything that is not a plain object, and any
 * entry that is not one, is dropped rather than repaired — a garbled key is a pet nobody owns, and
 * inventing a healthy state for it would put a phantom animal in the save.
 */
export function readPetCareStates(raw: unknown, nowMs: number): Record<string, PetCareState> {
  if (!raw || typeof raw !== 'object' || Array.isArray(raw)) return {};
  const out: Record<string, PetCareState> = {};
  for (const [id, value] of Object.entries(raw as Record<string, unknown>)) {
    if (!id || !value || typeof value !== 'object') continue;
    out[id] = readPetCareState(value, nowMs);
  }
  return out;
}

/**
 * The care map with ONE animal's entry replaced — the brief's §21 as a function.
 *
 * Feeding the dog must leave the cat and the bird exactly where they were, and that is a rule worth
 * having a name (and a test) rather than an inline spread at each of the two writers: an inline
 * spread is one forgotten `...` away from a feed that resets the household, and nothing about the
 * resulting save would look wrong.
 *
 * The existing entries are re-read defensively on the way through, so a map that has round-tripped
 * through the document store cannot carry a garbled sibling back into a write.
 */
export function withPetCare(
  cares: unknown,
  petItemId: string,
  state: PetCareState,
  nowMs: number,
): Record<string, PetCareState> {
  return { ...readPetCareStates(cares, nowMs), [petItemId]: state };
}

/* --- Time passing ------------------------------------------------------------------------- */

/**
 * What a care state has become by `nowMs` — the one place time is applied.
 *
 * Closed form on purpose. Nutrition drains linearly and energy eases toward the ceiling nutrition
 * sets for it, both evaluated over the whole gap at once, so this is idempotent in the way that
 * matters: settling after a three-day absence gives the same answer as settling every minute
 * through it, and calling it twice in the same millisecond changes nothing. That property is what
 * lets every reader settle freely — the panel, the behaviour layer, the feed — without any of them
 * coordinating or persisting the result.
 *
 * A clock that has gone BACKWARDS (a wrong device time, a save written on another machine) produces
 * a zero-length gap rather than a negative one, so nothing is ever restored by rewinding.
 */
export function settlePetCare(state: PetCareState, nowMs: number): PetCareState {
  const from = Date.parse(state.updatedAt);
  const hours = Number.isFinite(from) ? Math.max(0, (nowMs - from) / 3_600_000) : 0;
  if (hours <= 0) return state;

  const { nutritionDrainPerDay, nutritionFloor, energyBase, energySpan, energyHalfLifeHours, energyFloor } =
    PET_CARE_TUNING;

  const drainPerHour = nutritionDrainPerDay / 24;
  /** How long until nutrition reaches its floor and stops falling, in hours. */
  const toFloor = Math.max(0, (state.nutrition - nutritionFloor) / drainPerHour);
  /** The part of the gap nutrition was still falling through. */
  const falling = Math.min(hours, toFloor);
  /** The part after it had bottomed out. */
  const flat = hours - falling;

  const nutrition = clamp(state.nutrition - hours * drainPerHour, nutritionFloor, 1);

  // Energy chases the ceiling nutrition sets for it: `e' = k·(target(t) − e)`, with a half-life of
  // `energyHalfLifeHours` and `target = base + span · nutrition`.
  //
  // Solved EXACTLY rather than approximated, and that is the property the whole feature rests on
  // (§16). An approximation — easing toward the end nutrition, or toward the average of the two —
  // gives a different answer depending on how often it is applied, which would mean a player who
  // left the tab open got a different animal from one who closed it. Every reader of this state
  // settles it independently and none of them coordinate, so the answer has to be the same however
  // many times it is asked for. `npm run test:pet-care` pins that against an hour-by-hour walk.
  //
  // The gap is two segments, because the target moves in two ways: it slides while nutrition is
  // still draining, and it is constant once nutrition has hit its floor.
  const k = Math.LN2 / energyHalfLifeHours;
  let energy = state.energy;

  if (falling > 0) {
    // Target sliding as `a − b·t`. The exact solution is `a + b/k − b·t + (e₀ − a − b/k)·e^(−k·t)`.
    const a = energyBase + energySpan * state.nutrition;
    const b = energySpan * drainPerHour;
    energy = a + b / k - b * falling + (energy - a - b / k) * Math.exp(-k * falling);
  }
  if (flat > 0) {
    // Target constant at the floor's ceiling — the ordinary exponential approach.
    const target = energyBase + energySpan * nutritionFloor;
    energy = target + (energy - target) * Math.exp(-k * flat);
  }

  return { nutrition, energy: clamp(energy, energyFloor, 1), updatedAt: new Date(nowMs).toISOString() };
}

/* --- Reading the state -------------------------------------------------------------------- */

/**
 * The named rungs, for COPY AND ICONS ONLY.
 *
 * Behaviour is never switched on one of these — see {@link petActivityResponse}, which is a
 * continuous function of activity precisely so the animal changes gradually (§3, §15) instead of
 * becoming a different pet at a threshold. A band exists because a player reading a panel needs a
 * word, not a number to three decimal places, and because 「牠有點懶洋洋的」 is the honest
 * translation of 0.42.
 */
export type PetConditionBand = 'thriving' | 'content' | 'sleepy' | 'drowsy';

export interface PetConditionBandDef {
  id: PetConditionBand;
  /** Activity at or above which this band applies. The lowest entry must be 0. */
  fromActivity: number;
  label: string;
  /** One line about what the animal is doing, for the panel. Never a warning, never a threat. */
  note: string;
}

/**
 * The four rungs, lowest first.
 *
 * There is no rung below 「懶洋洋」 and there will not be one. The bottom of this ladder is an animal
 * curled up in its own bed — a picture of somewhere it wants to be, not of something going wrong.
 */
export const PET_CONDITION_BANDS: readonly PetConditionBandDef[] = [
  {
    id: 'drowsy',
    fromActivity: 0,
    label: '懶洋洋',
    note: '牠多半待在自己的窩裡，走幾步就想躺下。餵一點東西會好很多。',
  },
  {
    id: 'sleepy',
    fromActivity: 0.45,
    label: '想休息',
    note: '牠比平常安靜，常常停下來坐著，偶爾自己回窩邊待著。',
  },
  {
    id: 'content',
    fromActivity: 0.7,
    label: '悠閒',
    note: '牠在附近晃來晃去，走走停停，看起來很自在。',
  },
  {
    id: 'thriving',
    fromActivity: 0.88,
    label: '活力充沛',
    note: '牠精神很好，跟前跟後，還會自己跑開去探險一下。',
  },
];

export interface PetCondition {
  nutrition: number;
  energy: number;
  /**
   * 活動力 as everything downstream reads it, 0..1.
   *
   * Energy, not a fresh blend of the two: nutrition already reaches the animal THROUGH energy (see
   * {@link settlePetCare}), and mixing it in again here would count it twice and make a freshly fed
   * pet perk up instantly — the abrupt switch §3 asks us to avoid.
   */
  activity: number;
  /** How well looked-after it is overall, 0..1. The panel's summary; nothing behavioural. */
  condition: number;
  band: PetConditionBandDef;
}

/** Everything a screen or the behaviour layer wants to know, from a settled state. */
export function petCondition(state: PetCareState): PetCondition {
  const activity = clamp01(state.energy);
  let band = PET_CONDITION_BANDS[0];
  for (const rung of PET_CONDITION_BANDS) {
    if (activity >= rung.fromActivity) band = rung;
  }
  return {
    nutrition: clamp01(state.nutrition),
    energy: activity,
    activity,
    condition: clamp01((state.nutrition + state.energy) / 2),
    band,
  };
}

/**
 * How activity is allowed to change the animal's MOVEMENT, as multipliers.
 *
 * Continuous, and that is the whole point (§3, §15). There is no activity value at which the pet
 * becomes a different thing; there is a smooth ramp from 「跟前跟後」 to 「走幾步就想坐下」, and every
 * number below is an interpolation along it.
 *
 * These multiply the mood multipliers from constants/islandReturn.ts rather than replacing them —
 * see {@link combinePetMotion}. Two systems describe the same animal (how long you were away, and
 * how well you have been feeding it) and neither may overwrite the other's answer.
 */
export interface PetMotionScale {
  /** Walking pace. Floored well above zero — an animal that stops dead reads as broken (§3). */
  pace: number;
  /** Idle bob, tail, body roll. This is what 「有沒有精神」 actually looks like on screen. */
  liveliness: number;
  /** How strongly it prefers its own resting spot over its owner's heel, 0..1. */
  nestPull: number;
}

export function petActivityResponse(activity: number): PetMotionScale {
  const a = clamp01(activity);
  return {
    // 0.62 at the very bottom: slower than a walk, still plainly walking.
    pace: lerp(0.62, 1.05, a),
    // The widest spread of the three, because liveliness is the channel a player actually READS. A
    // pet at half pace looks like it is lagging; one that also bobs and wags less looks tired.
    liveliness: lerp(0.35, 1.1, a),
    // Only the bottom half of the range pulls toward the bed at all, so an ordinary, slightly
    // peckish animal still follows its owner everywhere.
    nestPull: clamp01((0.55 - a) / 0.55),
  };
}

/** Multiplies two motion scales — 離線心情 × 照護狀態. Neither system overrides the other. */
export function combinePetMotion(mood: PetMotionScale, care: PetMotionScale): PetMotionScale {
  return {
    pace: mood.pace * care.pace,
    liveliness: mood.liveliness * care.liveliness,
    // The STRONGER pull wins rather than the product: both mean 「牠想待在窩裡」, and multiplying two
    // fractions would make an animal that is both long-abandoned and hungry stay home LESS than one
    // that is only hungry.
    nestPull: Math.max(mood.nestPull, care.nestPull),
  };
}

/* --- The behaviour layer ------------------------------------------------------------------ */

/**
 * What the animal is doing with itself right now.
 *
 * A closed union rather than a string, so a behaviour that does not exist is a compile error at the
 * table below rather than a pet that silently stands still. Every one of them is a choice about
 * WHERE the animal wants to be; how it gets there is the mover's business (Three/IslandPet.tsx) and
 * is the same walk in every case.
 */
export type PetBehaviorId = 'follow' | 'wander' | 'idle' | 'goToBed' | 'rest';

/** Where a behaviour puts the animal's target. The mover turns this into a point. */
export type PetBehaviorAnchor =
  /** The follow slot beside its owner — the ordinary companion behaviour. */
  | 'owner'
  /** Its own resting spot, wherever that currently is (lib/petRestingSpots.ts). */
  | 'rest'
  /** Wherever it already is. A stop, not a destination. */
  | 'self';

/** Everything the decision is allowed to look at. Pure inputs — no clock, no scene, no profile. */
export interface PetBehaviorContext {
  /** 0..1, from {@link petCondition}. */
  activity: number;
  /**
   * How strongly the animal is drawn to its own bed, 0..1 — the COMBINED pull of both systems
   * (see {@link combinePetMotion}), so a long absence and a hungry animal both reach the decision
   * through the same number rather than through two competing branches.
   */
  nestPull: number;
  /** How far the owner is from the animal, in world units. */
  ownerDistance: number;
  /** Whether the owner is walking right now. A moving owner is one to keep up with. */
  ownerMoving: boolean;
  /** How far the animal is from its own resting spot. */
  restDistance: number;
  /** Whether the owner is standing near that resting spot. */
  ownerNearRest: boolean;
  /** What it was doing a moment ago. Behaviours are sticky — see {@link PET_BEHAVIOR_STICKINESS}. */
  previous: PetBehaviorId;
}

export interface PetBehaviorDef {
  id: PetBehaviorId;
  label: string;
  anchor: PetBehaviorAnchor;
  /** Extra pace on top of the motion scales — a wander is a potter, a follow is a trot. */
  pace: number;
  /** How far from the anchor the animal is content to drift, in world units. */
  drift: number;
  /** True when the animal is off its feet: legs still, body low. Drawn, never stored. */
  settled: boolean;
  /**
   * How likely this behaviour is in a given context, as an unnormalised weight.
   *
   * Weights rather than thresholds, and this is the mechanism behind 「行為逐漸改變」: at 0.8
   * activity a pet mostly follows and occasionally wanders; at 0.5 it mostly follows but sits down
   * more; at 0.2 it mostly heads for its bed but still gets up sometimes. Nothing flips.
   */
  weight: (ctx: PetBehaviorContext) => number;
}

/**
 * How far the owner may get before following stops being optional.
 *
 * Above this the decision is overridden outright: a companion that stays home while its owner walks
 * to the other side of the island is not resting, it is lost — and the player, who cannot see the
 * numbers, would read it as the pet being broken. Set generously wide so it only fires when the
 * owner has genuinely gone somewhere.
 */
export const PET_LEASH_DISTANCE = 14;

/**
 * How close the owner has to be for the animal to give up on resting and come to them.
 *
 * Deliberately the same idea as constants/islandReturn.ts's PET_NOTICE_RADIUS, and deliberately NOT
 * an import of it: that one is about a pet noticing a returning owner across the island, this one is
 * about a resting pet noticing one standing over it, and tying the two together would mean a change
 * to either silently retunes the other. Both are 「牠看到你了」, at different ranges.
 */
export const PET_NOTICE_DISTANCE = 4;

/** How much a behaviour's weight is multiplied by for already being the current one. */
export const PET_BEHAVIOR_STICKINESS = 2.2;

/**
 * How often the behaviour is re-decided, in seconds.
 *
 * The whole of §22 in one constant: MOVEMENT and ANIMATION run every frame, this does not. A few
 * seconds is slow enough that ten pets cost nothing measurable, and fast enough that a pet notices
 * its owner walking off within a stride. There is deliberately no per-frame path into
 * {@link decidePetBehavior} — the leash override is the one thing the mover checks itself.
 */
export const PET_DECISION_INTERVAL_SECONDS = 3.5;

/**
 * The five behaviours.
 *
 * `goToBed` and `rest` are separate on purpose, and the difference is between a pet that WALKS to
 * its bed and one that appears in it. The brief's §21 rules out the second explicitly; keeping the
 * journey as its own behaviour is what makes the arrival something the player can watch happen.
 */
export const PET_BEHAVIORS: Record<PetBehaviorId, PetBehaviorDef> = {
  follow: {
    id: 'follow',
    label: '跟著你',
    anchor: 'owner',
    pace: 1,
    drift: 0,
    settled: false,
    // Rises with activity, and rises hard the moment the owner is actually walking away: keeping up
    // with a moving owner is the one thing a companion always wants to do. `nestPull` takes at most
    // half of it away — never all, because an animal that stops following altogether is one the
    // player has to go and find, which is the failure mode PET_LEASH_DISTANCE also guards.
    weight: (c) => (0.35 + 1.35 * c.activity) * (c.ownerMoving ? 2.4 : 1) * (1 - 0.5 * c.nestPull),
  },
  wander: {
    id: 'wander',
    label: '四處探索',
    anchor: 'owner',
    // Slower than a follow. Exploring is a potter, and a pet that sprints in circles around a
    // standing owner reads as agitated rather than as curious.
    pace: 0.8,
    /**
     * How far it strays while exploring — about three of its own body lengths. Anchored to the
     * OWNER rather than to the world, so this can never walk the animal off somewhere the player
     * has to go and find it.
     */
    drift: 2.6,
    settled: false,
    // The most 活潑 behaviour, and the only one that needs the owner to be standing still: a pet
    // that wanders off while its owner is walking is a pet being left behind.
    weight: (c) => (c.ownerMoving ? 0 : Math.max(0, c.activity - 0.5) * 2.2),
  },
  idle: {
    id: 'idle',
    label: '待在附近',
    anchor: 'self',
    pace: 0.6,
    drift: 0,
    settled: true,
    // The middle of the ladder — available at every activity, likeliest around the middle, and what
    // a moderately tired pet does instead of trailing its owner across the island.
    weight: (c) => (c.ownerMoving ? 0.15 : 0.5 + (1 - c.activity) * 1.1),
  },
  goToBed: {
    id: 'goToBed',
    label: '回窩裡',
    anchor: 'rest',
    // Unhurried. This is a tired animal walking home, not one fleeing.
    pace: 0.85,
    drift: 0.45,
    settled: false,
    weight: (c) => {
      // Never while the owner is right there — the bed is where it waits for them, so the whole
      // behaviour is pointless (and reads as sulking) with the owner standing beside it.
      if (c.ownerNearRest || c.ownerDistance < PET_NOTICE_DISTANCE) return 0;
      // Already there: `rest` takes over rather than this re-winning every decision.
      if (c.restDistance < 0.8) return 0;
      // Two inputs, one term. `activity` is 「牠沒力氣了」 and `nestPull` is 「牠想回窩」 — a long
      // absence produces the second without the first, which is what makes a well-fed pet whose
      // owner has been gone a fortnight still take itself home.
      return (Math.max(0, 0.55 - c.activity) * 4 + 0.3) * (0.35 + 2 * c.nestPull);
    },
  },
  rest: {
    id: 'rest',
    label: '在窩裡休息',
    anchor: 'rest',
    pace: 0.5,
    drift: 0.25,
    settled: true,
    weight: (c) => {
      if (c.ownerNearRest || c.ownerDistance < PET_NOTICE_DISTANCE) return 0;
      // Only once it has actually arrived. Resting is a thing that happens IN the bed.
      if (c.restDistance > 1.2) return 0;
      return (0.5 + Math.max(0, 0.6 - c.activity) * 5) * (0.35 + 2 * c.nestPull);
    },
  },
};

export const ALL_PET_BEHAVIORS: readonly PetBehaviorDef[] = Object.values(PET_BEHAVIORS);

/**
 * Picks what the animal does next.
 *
 * Weighted choice rather than a priority chain, because a chain gives the same answer every time and
 * a pet that always does the same thing at the same energy is furniture. `roll` is supplied by the
 * caller (0..1) rather than taken from `Math.random()` here, which is what makes this testable —
 * `npm run test:pet-care` walks a fixed roll across the whole activity range and asserts the SHAPE
 * of the distribution rather than one lucky draw.
 *
 * The one hard override is the leash: an owner who has walked off is followed, whatever the animal
 * would rather be doing. See {@link PET_LEASH_DISTANCE}.
 */
export function decidePetBehavior(ctx: PetBehaviorContext, roll: number): PetBehaviorId {
  if (ctx.ownerDistance > PET_LEASH_DISTANCE) return 'follow';

  const weights = ALL_PET_BEHAVIORS.map((def) => {
    const base = Math.max(0, def.weight(ctx));
    return base * (def.id === ctx.previous ? PET_BEHAVIOR_STICKINESS : 1);
  });
  const total = weights.reduce((sum, w) => sum + w, 0);
  // Every weight at zero is possible in principle (a future behaviour table could do it) and must
  // not produce `undefined`. Following is the safe default: it is what a companion is for.
  if (total <= 0) return 'follow';

  let cursor = clamp01(roll) * total;
  for (let i = 0; i < weights.length; i++) {
    cursor -= weights[i];
    if (cursor <= 0) return ALL_PET_BEHAVIORS[i].id;
  }
  return ALL_PET_BEHAVIORS[ALL_PET_BEHAVIORS.length - 1].id;
}

/* --- Resting spots ------------------------------------------------------------------------ */

/**
 * 寵物窩 lives in constants/petHabitats.ts, not here.
 *
 * It used to be declared in this file, back when a resting place was one radius and a label. It is
 * now a KIND (a bed, a house, a cage, a perch) plus the species it accepts plus the posture that
 * follows from the kind — which is a statement about furniture and about which animal is which, and
 * this file is deliberately neither of those things: it is two numbers and how time moves them, and
 * it imports no catalog. See petHabitats.ts's file doc.
 */

/* --- Feeding ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ */

/**
 * What one serving of food may move, and by how much.
 *
 * A RANGE rather than a value, because the amounts belong to the item (constants/consumables.ts):
 * this is the sanity bound every food is checked against by `npm run test:pet-care`, so a mistyped 4
 * in a catalog row cannot quietly become a bowl that fills the animal four times over.
 */
export const PET_FOOD_EFFECT_RANGE = { min: 0, max: 1 } as const;

/**
 * How long the animal visibly eats for after a feed lands, in seconds.
 *
 * The brief's §19 asks the player to FEEL that their pet was looked after, and this is the whole
 * budget for it: the animal puts its head down, bobs while it eats, and a few hearts drift up
 * (Three/IslandPet.tsx). Long enough to read as a small event, short enough that a player feeding
 * three animals in a row is not waiting on an animation.
 *
 * Here rather than in the mover because it is the length of a MOMENT in the feature, not a
 * rendering detail — the toast and the animation are meant to be over at about the same time.
 */
export const PET_FEED_CELEBRATION_SECONDS = 2.6;

/** What a feed actually moved, so the toast can say 「營養 +40%」 rather than guessing. */
export interface PetCareDelta {
  nutrition: number;
  energy: number;
}

/**
 * Applies a set of effects to a care state. The one place food changes an animal.
 *
 * Takes already-resolved AMOUNTS rather than an item, so nothing here imports the catalog and any
 * future source of the same effect (a wheel prize, an NPC's gift, a 功能卡) lands through the same
 * function with the same clamping. The state is settled to `nowMs` first, so feeding always applies
 * on top of what time has already done rather than on top of a stale snapshot.
 *
 * Reports what it actually moved, which is not the same as what was asked for: a nearly full bowl
 * takes only the room it has, and the caller needs to know that to say something true.
 */
export function applyPetCareEffects(
  state: PetCareState,
  effects: { nutrition?: number; energy?: number },
  nowMs: number,
): { state: PetCareState; delta: PetCareDelta } {
  const settled = settlePetCare(state, nowMs);
  const nutrition = clamp(
    settled.nutrition + (effects.nutrition ?? 0),
    PET_CARE_TUNING.nutritionFloor,
    1,
  );
  const energy = clamp(settled.energy + (effects.energy ?? 0), PET_CARE_TUNING.energyFloor, 1);
  return {
    state: { nutrition, energy, updatedAt: new Date(nowMs).toISOString() },
    delta: { nutrition: nutrition - settled.nutrition, energy: energy - settled.energy },
  };
}

/* --- Small helpers ------------------------------------------------------------------------ */

function clamp(value: number, min: number, max: number): number {
  return Math.min(max, Math.max(min, value));
}

function clamp01(value: number): number {
  return clamp(Number.isFinite(value) ? value : 0, 0, 1);
}

function lerp(from: number, to: number, t: number): number {
  return from + (to - from) * clamp01(t);
}

function numberOr(value: unknown, fallback: number): number {
  return typeof value === 'number' && Number.isFinite(value) ? value : fallback;
}
```

## src/constants/petHabitats.ts

```ts
/**
 * @license
 * SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
 */

/**
 * 寵物休息處 — what KINDS of resting place exist, and which animals may use one.
 *
 * The brief's §3 and §24 are one requirement stated twice: 「哪一種寵物該用哪一種窩」 must be an
 * answer the DATA gives, never `if (pet.type === 'dog')` sitting in a component. So there are
 * exactly three things here and nothing else:
 *
 *   1. {@link PetHabitatKind} — the vocabulary of resting places (a bed, a house, a cage, a perch…).
 *   2. {@link PET_HABITAT_KINDS} — what each kind physically IS: how an animal settles into it, and
 *      which species could plausibly use one at all.
 *   3. {@link PetRestSpec} — the field a catalog row declares to BE one of them, for which species.
 *
 * Nothing in the game asks 「這是不是鳥籠」. It asks {@link habitatAcceptsSpecies}, which is one
 * `includes` over data the item wrote about itself. That is the whole of the compatibility system,
 * and it is why a fourth species costs one row in constants/pets.ts, one row here if it needs a new
 * shape of home, and its catalog rows — and no edits at all to the resolver
 * (lib/petRestingSpots.ts), the movers (Three/IslandPet.tsx) or any screen.
 *
 * ## Why the KIND is separate from the item's species list
 *
 * They answer different questions and only one of them is a design choice. A perch is a bar you
 * grip: no dog can use one, ever, and no future catalog row may claim otherwise — that is
 * `suitableFor` below, a statement about the physical world. Whether a particular woven basket is
 * sold for dogs, for cats, or for both is a product decision, and lives on the item. The test
 * (`npm run test:pet-care`) asserts the second is always a subset of the first, so a 「鳥也能睡的
 * 狗屋」 typo cannot ship.
 *
 * ## Why this is not in constants/petCare.ts
 *
 * That file is the care SIMULATION — two numbers and how time moves them. It deliberately imports
 * no catalog and knows nothing about objects standing on the island. This one is about furniture,
 * reads the catalog, and is read by the placement/shop side of the game as well as by the pet.
 */

import { ALL_ITEMS, type ItemDefinition } from './items';
import type { PetSpecies } from './pets';

/**
 * How an animal settles into a resting place.
 *
 * Two postures, because there are two ways an animal is off its feet and they look nothing alike:
 * a mammal LIES DOWN (the body drops and pitches forward — Three/IslandPet.tsx's SETTLE_DROP), and
 * a bird LANDS ON something and grips it (it stops flying and comes down to a bar at a known
 * height). The renderer branches on this rather than on the species, so a future ground bird or a
 * cat that sleeps on a shelf both work without it learning a new animal.
 */
export type PetRestPosture = 'lie' | 'perch';

/**
 * The shapes a resting place comes in.
 *
 * A closed union rather than a free string: a kind that does not exist has to be a compile error at
 * the catalog row, not a bed that silently accepts nobody. Adding one is a member here plus a row
 * in {@link PET_HABITAT_KINDS} — which is the whole cost of 「未來想賣一種水盆窩」.
 */
export type PetHabitatKind =
  /** An open mat or woven basket on the ground. The animal lies on top of it. */
  | 'ground_bed'
  /** A deep round cushion with a raised rim. The animal lies down INSIDE it. */
  | 'cushion_bed'
  /** A roofed home with a doorway — a kennel, a tent, a knitted cat house. */
  | 'enclosed_house'
  /** A raised platform with somewhere to lie, at the top or in a cubby underneath. */
  | 'platform'
  /** A bird cage with a door. The bird flies home into it and settles on the floor bar. */
  | 'cage'
  /** A bare bar or branch a bird grips. Nothing to go inside. */
  | 'perch'
  /** A woven nest a bird sits down into. */
  | 'nest';

export interface PetHabitatKindDef {
  id: PetHabitatKind;
  /** What to call this SHAPE of home on a card — 窩 / 屋 / 籠 / 架 / 巢. */
  label: string;
  /** How the animal is off its feet here. Read by the movers, never by copy. */
  posture: PetRestPosture;
  /**
   * The species that could physically use this shape at all.
   *
   * A statement about the world, not about the shop: no dog will ever grip a perch, whatever a
   * catalog row claims. An item's own `species` list must be a subset of this — pinned by
   * `npm run test:pet-care`.
   */
  suitableFor: readonly PetSpecies[];
  /** One line for the care panel, so a player knows what they are buying. Never a slogan. */
  note: string;
}

const GROUND_SPECIES: readonly PetSpecies[] = ['dog', 'cat'];
const AIR_SPECIES: readonly PetSpecies[] = ['bird'];

export const PET_HABITAT_KINDS: Record<PetHabitatKind, PetHabitatKindDef> = {
  ground_bed: {
    id: 'ground_bed',
    label: '地面窩',
    posture: 'lie',
    suitableFor: GROUND_SPECIES,
    note: '鋪在地上的開放式窩，走過去就能趴下。',
  },
  cushion_bed: {
    id: 'cushion_bed',
    label: '軟墊窩',
    posture: 'lie',
    suitableFor: GROUND_SPECIES,
    note: '有一圈厚邊的圓窩，牠會整隻縮進去睡。',
  },
  enclosed_house: {
    id: 'enclosed_house',
    label: '小屋',
    posture: 'lie',
    suitableFor: GROUND_SPECIES,
    note: '有屋頂和門口的小屋，躺在門邊看得到外面。',
  },
  platform: {
    id: 'platform',
    label: '休息平台',
    posture: 'lie',
    suitableFor: GROUND_SPECIES,
    note: '架高的木頭平台，底層有一個可以窩進去的洞。',
  },
  cage: {
    id: 'cage',
    label: '鳥籠',
    posture: 'perch',
    suitableFor: AIR_SPECIES,
    note: '門一直開著的木籠，牠會自己飛回來停在裡面。',
  },
  perch: {
    id: 'perch',
    label: '鳥架',
    posture: 'perch',
    suitableFor: AIR_SPECIES,
    note: '一根停得住的橫桿，牠會飛過來抓著休息。',
  },
  nest: {
    id: 'nest',
    label: '鳥巢',
    posture: 'perch',
    suitableFor: AIR_SPECIES,
    note: '編出來的小巢，牠會降下來坐進去。',
  },
};

export const ALL_PET_HABITAT_KINDS: readonly PetHabitatKindDef[] = Object.values(PET_HABITAT_KINDS);

/**
 * 寵物窩 — declared by the ITEM, so the animal never looks for a bed by name or by id.
 *
 * The brief's §9 is explicit about the failure mode this avoids: `if (lowEnergy) find('PetBed_01')`.
 * A resting spot is a CAPABILITY a placeable piece declares, exactly as `standable`, `tabletop`,
 * `placement` and `interactions` already are (constants/items.ts) — so a kennel, a cage, a perch or
 * a cat tower becomes one by being added to the catalog with this field, and lib/petRestingSpots.ts
 * finds it without learning anything.
 *
 * It has no `label`: the item's own name is the label. Two names for one object is how a card and a
 * panel start calling the same basket different things.
 */
export interface PetRestSpec {
  /** Which shape of home this is. Decides the posture, and bounds the species list below. */
  kind: PetHabitatKind;
  /**
   * Which species may settle here. REQUIRED — 「所有寵物都能用」 has to be written out as every
   * species rather than left off, because a forgotten field would silently sell birds a kennel.
   */
  species: readonly PetSpecies[];
  /** How close counts as 「到了」, in world units. Roughly the piece's own reach. */
  radius: number;
  /**
   * Where in the piece's OWN local frame the animal settles, in world units before the piece's
   * rotation is applied. Absent means its centre, which is right for a mat or a basket; a kennel
   * whose opening faces +z offsets forward so the animal lies in the doorway rather than in the wall.
   */
  offset?: { x: number; z: number };
  /**
   * How high above the piece's base the animal comes to rest, in world units. Absent means the
   * ground.
   *
   * Only ever non-zero on a `perch` posture: a walking animal reaches its bed by walking, and this
   * game has no climbing — so a dog bed at height 1 would be a bed the dog stands under. A bird has
   * no such problem, because it is already flying. `npm run test:pet-care` pins that rule.
   */
  height?: number;
}

/** Whether a declared resting place accepts a given animal. The whole compatibility system. */
export function habitatAcceptsSpecies(spec: PetRestSpec, species: PetSpecies): boolean {
  return spec.species.includes(species);
}

/** The posture an animal takes in a given resting place. Read by the movers. */
export function habitatPosture(spec: PetRestSpec): PetRestPosture {
  return PET_HABITAT_KINDS[spec.kind].posture;
}

/**
 * Every resting place in the catalog, optionally narrowed to one species.
 *
 * The read the shop's species filter and the care panel's 「你可以買這些」 are both built from, so
 * neither keeps a list of its own to fall out of step with the catalog.
 */
export function getHabitatItems(species?: PetSpecies): ItemDefinition[] {
  return ALL_ITEMS.filter(
    (item) => !!item.petRest && (!species || habitatAcceptsSpecies(item.petRest, species)),
  );
}

/*
 * 「這件商品是給哪一種寵物的」 across BOTH capabilities — a bed's species and a food's — lives in
 * lib/petCompatibility.ts, not here. This file is about resting places; the shop's shelves are
 * filtered by a question that spans food as well, and answering it here would mean this module
 * reaching into `consumable` to do it.
 */

```

```ts
/**
 * @license
 * SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
 */

import type { PetSpecies } from './pets';
import { PET_FEED_CELEBRATION_SECONDS } from './petCare';

/**
 * 寵物怎麼回應玩家 —— 反應的詞彙、三種互動的節奏，與每一種動物玩耍的方式。
 *
 * ## 補的是什麼
 *
 * 寵物照護（constants/petCare.ts）已經決定了牠「想做什麼」（跟著你、四處探索、回窩裡休息），但
 * 玩家**對牠做了什麼**，牠幾乎沒有回應：
 *
 *   摸摸   迷你遊戲點滿之後，寵物在原地以每秒兩圈的速度自轉加彈跳 —— 背對著剛摸完牠的人。點的過程
 *          中牠照樣四處亂走，你摸的是一隻正在離開的動物。
 *   餵食   在牠站著的地方低頭點三秒。沒有碗、沒有走過去、沒有吃完的樣子。
 *   玩耍   不存在。
 *   注意   主人走到窩邊時，牠要等下一次決策（最多 3.5 秒）才起身，而且沒有任何「看到你了」的那一下。
 *
 * 這個檔案是那些回應的**資料**，行為在 lib/petReaction.ts（純數學）與 lib/petActivity.ts（誰正在
 * 做什麼），畫出來的是 Three/IslandPet.tsx。
 *
 * ## 為什麼是「反應」而不是「動畫」
 *
 * PetModel 是一個跟商店圖示、更衣室共用的單位高度模型，沒有頭部關節可以轉。所以寵物的每一個反應
 * 都是寫在**整隻動物的 group** 上的幾個量：跳多高、身體低多少、往前傾多少、左右晃多少、原地轉幾圈、
 * 尾巴搖多用力。一個反應就是這幾個量隨時間的形狀 —— 跟 IslandPet 本來就在寫的 `settle`（趴下）、
 * `eat`（低頭）是同一種東西，只是變成了一張表。
 *
 * 所有幅度都偏小。「有感但不吵」：一隻開心的狗是跳兩下、尾巴猛搖，不是原地轉陀螺。
 */

export type PetReactionId =
  | 'notice' | 'happy' | 'nuzzle' | 'pat' | 'stretch' | 'circle' | 'ready' | 'pickup' | 'drop' | 'pounce';

export interface PetReactionSpec {
  /** 整段多長，秒。 */
  seconds: number;
  /** 跳幾下、每下多高（以動物自己的身高為單位）。 */
  hops?: { count: number; height: number };
  /** 全強度時身體前傾（弧度），正 = 鼻子朝下。 */
  pitch?: number;
  /** 全強度時身體壓低多少（身高的比例）。 */
  drop?: number;
  /** 左右晃：幅度（弧度）與頻率（Hz）。 */
  roll?: { amplitude: number; hz: number };
  /** 整段轉幾圈。 */
  spin?: number;
  /** 尾巴至少搖多用力，0..1（Pets.tsx 的 Tail 讀的是 gait.intensity）。 */
  wag?: number;
  /** 前面花多少比例進入、後面花多少比例退出。預設 0.2 / 0.3。 */
  raise?: number;
  fall?: number;
  /**
   * 會飛的動物用的覆寫。鳥沒有腿可以蹲、沒有地可以跳，同一個「開心」在牠身上是在空中往上竄一下、
   * 翅膀一側往下壓 —— 所以同一列、不同的數字，而不是另一張表。
   */
  air?: Partial<Omit<PetReactionSpec, 'air'>>;
}

export const PET_REACTIONS: Record<PetReactionId, PetReactionSpec> = {
  /** 看到主人了：抬頭、小跳一下、尾巴搖起來。 */
  notice: {
    seconds: 0.9, raise: 0.25, fall: 0.4,
    hops: { count: 1, height: 0.08 },
    pitch: -0.14,
    wag: 0.8,
    air: { hops: { count: 1, height: 0.25 }, pitch: -0.1 },
  },
  /** 很開心（摸完、團聚、玩完）：原地跳兩下、身體左右扭、尾巴全速。 */
  happy: {
    seconds: 1.5, raise: 0.1, fall: 0.25,
    hops: { count: 2, height: 0.18 },
    pitch: -0.06,
    roll: { amplitude: 0.07, hz: 3 },
    wag: 1,
    air: { hops: { count: 2, height: 0.35 }, roll: { amplitude: 0.28, hz: 2 } },
  },
  /**
   * 被摸的時候：往主人手的方向湊、身體壓低一點、慢慢左右蹭。
   * 迷你遊戲進行中每一輪重播，所以它的兩端必須是 0（raise/fall 讓它自己回來）。
   */
  nuzzle: {
    seconds: 1.6, raise: 0.2, fall: 0.2,
    pitch: 0.14,
    drop: 0.08,
    roll: { amplitude: 0.07, hz: 1.2 },
    wag: 1,
    air: { pitch: 0.1, drop: 0.12, roll: { amplitude: 0.12, hz: 1.2 } },
  },
  /** 每點一下「摸摸」：被手壓下去再彈起來的那一下。 */
  pat: {
    seconds: 0.32, raise: 0.25, fall: 0.6,
    drop: 0.06,
    pitch: 0.1,
    wag: 1,
  },
  /** 從窩裡起來：前腳往前伸、胸口壓低，伸一個懶腰。 */
  stretch: {
    seconds: 1.1, raise: 0.3, fall: 0.35,
    pitch: 0.2,
    drop: 0.06,
    air: { pitch: -0.12, hops: { count: 1, height: 0.12 } },
  },
  /** 趴下之前在窩裡轉一圈。 */
  circle: {
    seconds: 1.0, raise: 0.15, fall: 0.2,
    spin: 1,
    drop: 0.04,
    air: { spin: 1, drop: 0 },
  },
  /** 玩具丟出去的那一刻：壓低身體、屁股翹起來、尾巴猛搖，準備衝。 */
  ready: {
    seconds: 0.7, raise: 0.2, fall: 0.3,
    drop: 0.1,
    pitch: 0.12,
    wag: 1,
    air: { pitch: -0.08, hops: { count: 1, height: 0.15 } },
  },
  /** 叼起玩具。 */
  pickup: {
    seconds: 0.4, raise: 0.35, fall: 0.4,
    pitch: 0.35,
  },
  /** 在主人腳邊放下玩具。 */
  drop: {
    seconds: 0.45, raise: 0.3, fall: 0.4,
    pitch: 0.3,
    wag: 1,
  },
  /** 貓撲過去：往前一跳、落地時前傾。 */
  pounce: {
    seconds: 0.6, raise: 0.1, fall: 0.35,
    hops: { count: 1, height: 0.22 },
    pitch: 0.18,
  },
};

/**
 * 餵食的節奏。
 *
 * 碗是真的放在地上的東西，不是一個圖示：主人彎腰把它放在自己面前、朝著寵物的那一邊，寵物走過去、
 * 站在碗後面低頭吃，碗裡的飼料隨著吃掉變少，吃完碗淡出消失。
 */
export const PET_FEED = {
  /** 碗放在主人面前多遠（朝寵物的方向），世界單位。 */
  bowlAhead: 0.95,
  /** 碗出現的時間：主人 `tend` 姿勢彎到最低的時候。秒。 */
  bowlAppearSeconds: 0.75,
  /** 寵物站在碗後面多遠：這個常數加上牠身高的比例（大狗站得遠一點，嘴巴才剛好在碗上）。 */
  standoff: 0.18,
  standoffPerHeight: 0.45,
  /** 走到這個距離以內就算到了。 */
  arriveRadius: 0.16,
  /** 走過去最多花多久。走不到（被家具卡住）就在原地轉向碗開始吃，永遠不會卡在「想吃但到不了」。 */
  approachTimeout: 3.5,
  /** 吃多久 —— 跟吐司訊息與照護系統的「進食」是同一個長度。 */
  eatSeconds: PET_FEED_CELEBRATION_SECONDS,
  /** 吃一口的節奏（秒），每一口一聲很輕的咀嚼聲。 */
  munchEvery: 0.55,
  /** 吃完之後碗停留、淡出的時間。 */
  fadeSeconds: 0.7,
  /** 碗的尺寸（世界單位）。 */
  bowlRadius: 0.2,
} as const;

/**
 * 玩耍：主人丟玩具、寵物去追。
 *
 * 丟出去的方向是主人面向的方向（跟飛盤的 `launch` 同一個道理：方向來自玩家，不是來自世界的某一軸），
 * 落點會被拉回陸地、推出家具與房子，所以球永遠落在寵物走得到的地方。
 */
export const PET_PLAY = {
  /** 丟多遠，世界單位，隨機落在這個區間。 */
  throwMin: 3.0,
  throwMax: 4.2,
  /** 從手上離開到第一次落地，秒。 */
  flightSeconds: 0.8,
  /** 拋物線頂點比兩端高多少。 */
  arcHeight: 1.3,
  /** 丟出去的高度（主人手的高度）。 */
  handHeight: 1.1,
  /** 落地後彈幾下、第一下多高、每下多久，以及每下衰減到剩多少。 */
  bounces: 2,
  bounceHeight: 0.32,
  bounceSeconds: 0.42,
  bounceDecay: 0.45,
  /** 彈跳時順著方向往前滾多遠。 */
  rollOn: 0.35,
  /** 寵物在玩具飛到多遠的時候起跑（飛行時間的比例）—— 在空中就追出去，比等它落地自然。 */
  chaseAt: 0.3,
  /** 追的速度倍率。 */
  chasePace: 1.4,
  /** 離玩具多近算追到。 */
  reachRadius: 0.32,
  /** 叼回來時停在主人面前多遠。 */
  returnAhead: 1.05,
  /** 離主人面前那一點多近算帶回來了。 */
  returnRadius: 0.3,
  /** 整段玩耍的上限。超過就放棄（玩具淡出），寵物回去做自己的事。 */
  maxSeconds: 14,
  /** 主人走得比這還遠，寵物就不追了。 */
  leash: 10,
  /** 玩具淡出的時間。 */
  fadeSeconds: 0.5,
  /** 玩具半徑。 */
  toyRadius: 0.11,
} as const;

/**
 * 每一種動物怎麼玩。
 *
 *   `fetch`   狗：追到、叼起來、帶回主人腳邊放下，然後很開心。
 *   `pounce`  貓：追到、撲上去拍一下，然後慢慢晃回來 —— 貓不撿東西還給你。
 *   `swoop`   鳥：飛過去在玩具上方盤旋一圈，再飛回來。
 *
 * 資料而不是 `if (species === 'cat')`：第四種動物是這張表的第四列。
 */
export type PetPlayStyle = 'fetch' | 'pounce' | 'swoop';

export const PET_PLAY_STYLE: Record<PetSpecies, PetPlayStyle> = {
  dog: 'fetch',
  cat: 'pounce',
  bird: 'swoop',
};

/** 摸摸。 */
export const PET_PETTING = {
  /** 迷你遊戲沒有人點多久，就當作摸完了（玩家把面板晾在那裡走開）。 */
  idleTimeout: 6,
  /** 一次摸摸最長多久。 */
  maxSeconds: 30,
  /** 被摸的時候牠離主人多遠是舒服的距離 —— 太遠就湊過來一點。 */
  closeIn: 1.0,
} as const;

/** 主人走近一隻正在休息的寵物。 */
export const PET_NOTICE = {
  /** 進到這個距離以內，休息中的寵物會抬頭看你。 */
  radius: 3.4,
  /** 離開要再遠這麼多才重新算（遲滯）。 */
  margin: 1.2,
  /** 兩次「看到你了」之間最短多久。 */
  cooldown: 8,
} as const;

/** 在窩裡睡著的呼吸：身體極慢極輕地起伏。 */
export const PET_SLEEP_BREATH = {
  /** 每秒幾次（弧度頻率會乘 2π）。 */
  rate: 0.28,
  /** 起伏幅度，身高的比例。 */
  amount: 0.018,
} as const;
```

## src/constants/petRig.ts

```ts
/**
 * @license
 * SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
 */

import { CHARACTER_ROOT_SCALE } from './characterRig';
import type { AttachmentPoint } from './characterRig';
import type { PetSpec } from './pets';

/**
 * THE PET RIG — where a special cosmetic hangs on a companion.
 *
 * The same contract as constants/characterRig.ts, and for the same reason: a pet cosmetic must
 * not be the thing that knows a 柴犬's head is a 0.29 sphere at y 0.71. It asks for `petHead`,
 * gets a frame, and draws at its own origin.
 *
 * ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 * THE CONVENTION THAT MAKES ONE ORNAMENT FIT NINE ANIMALS
 * ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 *
 * A socket here is **the CENTRE of the body part, and its `scale` is that part's RADIUS**.
 *
 * That one rule is what lets a single bow model sit correctly on a 臘腸's narrow skull, a
 * 紅貴賓's fluffy pom and a 金絲雀's little head without a per-breed model: the cosmetic is
 * authored in UNIT-PART space, where 1.0 is the surface of whatever it is mounted on. A bow that
 * draws its knot at y = 1.0 rests on top of every head on the shelf; a collar drawn as a torus of
 * radius 1.15 clears every neck by 15%.
 *
 * The alternative — a socket at the top of the head — needs the ornament to know how big the head
 * was, which is exactly the coupling the socket exists to prevent.
 *
 * ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 * COORDINATE RULES
 * ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 *
 * Positions are in UNIT-PET space: the space Three/Pets.tsx draws every companion in, where the
 * animal stands on y = 0 with its crown at y ≈ 1 and faces +Z, whatever species it is. The
 * per-breed size is applied afterwards, from `PetSpec.height` (constants/pets.ts).
 *
 * Consequences worth knowing:
 *   - a cosmetic is a child of the pet's own group, so it inherits the walk bob, the idle
 *     breathing and a bird's banking for free. That is section 三's "讓寵物與效果產生一些互動"
 *     obtained by construction rather than by animating an ornament to look like it;
 *   - what must NOT ride along — the spores and petals it emits — is spawned in WORLD space by
 *     the effect runtime, which reads the socket's world matrix. That is why a spore stays where
 *     it was dropped instead of travelling along on the dog's back.
 *
 * Every number below is read off the mesh that draws that part in Three/Pets.tsx. When a breed's
 * model moves, these move with it — there is no way to derive them from the model at runtime,
 * because the "head" of a 紅貴賓 is a pom plus a topknot plus two ear puffs.
 */

/** A pet socket: the centre of a body part, scaled by that part's radius. */
export type PetSocketPoint = AttachmentPoint & { scale: number };

export interface PetAnchors {
  /** Centre of the skull. Hats, bows, anything worn on the head. */
  petHead: PetSocketPoint;
  /** Centre of the neck. Collars — the band encircles the local Z axis. */
  petCollar: PetSocketPoint;
  /**
   * The barrel, at the one place on each animal's back that is actually CLEAR.
   *
   * Not the body's centre, and not the shoulders either. Every companion here is 大頭 by design:
   * a 柴犬's skull is a 0.29 sphere sitting at z 0.26, which shadows its whole shoulder, and the
   * middle of the back is where they all keep their tails. So a pack goes in the gap between the
   * two, and where that gap IS differs per breed — the 臘腸 has a whole long back to choose from,
   * the 紅貴賓 has about 10 cm of it.
   */
  petBack: PetSocketPoint;
}

/**
 * How far the collar band leans back at the top.
 *
 * Every quadruped here carries its neck rising forward (their neck capsules are pitched 0.7–0.8
 * rad), so a band drawn square to the body cuts diagonally through it. Tipping the socket puts the
 * ring perpendicular to the neck it is actually on. Birds get none: a bird's "neck" is a sphere
 * sitting straight on the body, and tilting a collar there just makes it crooked.
 */
const NECK_PITCH = -0.45;

/**
 * 臘腸 — long and low, head held up and well forward of the barrel (z 0.44), which is why its head
 * socket is the furthest forward on the shelf.
 */
const DACHSHUND_ANCHORS: PetAnchors = {
  petHead: { position: [0, 0.75, 0.44], scale: 0.245 },
  petCollar: { position: [0, 0.48, 0.2], rotation: [NECK_PITCH, 0, 0], scale: 0.209 },
  petBack: { position: [0, 0.46, 0], scale: 0.19 },
};

/**
 * 紅貴賓 — no neck mesh at all: the head pom (bottom edge 0.49) and the body (top 0.68) simply
 * overlap. The collar goes at y 0.56, where the BODY sphere's own cross-section is 0.208, so the
 * band is sized to clear that rather than a neck that does not exist.
 */
const POODLE_ANCHORS: PetAnchors = {
  petHead: { position: [0, 0.76, 0.18], scale: 0.27 },
  petCollar: { position: [0, 0.5, 0.12], rotation: [NECK_PITCH, 0, 0], scale: 0.278 },
  petBack: { position: [0, 0.44, -0.14], scale: 0.24 },
};

/** 柴犬 — the broadest head on the shelf (0.29), with prick ears at y 0.93 an ornament sits between. */
const SHIBA_ANCHORS: PetAnchors = {
  petHead: { position: [0, 0.71, 0.26], scale: 0.29 },
  petCollar: { position: [0, 0.5, 0.16], rotation: [NECK_PITCH, 0, 0], scale: 0.243 },
  petBack: { position: [0, 0.47, -0.13], scale: 0.23 },
};

/**
 * All three cats, because they share one body (see CatModel — 橘/虎斑/賓士 are coat patterns, not
 * breeds). Written once and registered under each, so they cannot drift apart.
 */
const CAT_ANCHORS: PetAnchors = {
  petHead: { position: [0, 0.73, 0.24], scale: 0.26 },
  petCollar: { position: [0, 0.53, 0.14], rotation: [NECK_PITCH, 0, 0], scale: 0.226 },
  petBack: { position: [0, 0.5, -0.12], scale: 0.2 },
};

/**
 * Likewise all four birds. A bird's collar sits on the hood sphere at y 0.63, which IS its neck —
 * there is no separate one — and takes no pitch, since it rises straight rather than forward.
 */
const BIRD_ANCHORS: PetAnchors = {
  petHead: { position: [0, 0.76, 0.17], scale: 0.225 },
  petCollar: { position: [0, 0.63, 0.1], scale: 0.21 },
  // The egg body is 0.232 x 0.254 x 0.313; a pack rides the widest part of it.
  petBack: { position: [0, 0.44, -0.08], scale: 0.25 },
};

/**
 * Per-breed anchors, keyed the same way PET_SPECS is — by BREED, because what a socket sits on is
 * the shape of the animal, and on this shelf the cats and the birds each share one body while the
 * three dogs have one apiece.
 */
export const PET_ANCHORS: Record<string, PetAnchors> = {
  dachshund: DACHSHUND_ANCHORS,
  poodle: POODLE_ANCHORS,
  shiba: SHIBA_ANCHORS,
  orange: CAT_ANCHORS,
  tabby: CAT_ANCHORS,
  tuxedo: CAT_ANCHORS,
  budgie: BIRD_ANCHORS,
  javasparrow: BIRD_ANCHORS,
  canary: BIRD_ANCHORS,
  phoenix: BIRD_ANCHORS,
};

/** A breed's anchors, falling back to the cat's — the most average body on the shelf. */
export function getPetAnchors(breed: string | undefined): PetAnchors {
  return (breed && PET_ANCHORS[breed]) || CAT_ANCHORS;
}

/**
 * The companion's canonical root scale — what the effect runtime divides emitter distances by so
 * that "rise 0.3" means 30 cm on a pet exactly as it does on the player.
 *
 * `height` is authored in the AVATAR's local units (see constants/pets.ts), so it needs the
 * character root scale applied to arrive in world units. That is the same conversion
 * Three/IslandPet.tsx makes to size the companion on the island and the dressing room makes to
 * size it on the stage — stated here so the effect system does not restate it a third time.
 */
export function petRootScale(spec: PetSpec): number {
  return spec.height * CHARACTER_ROOT_SCALE;
}
```

## src/constants/pets.ts

```ts
/**
 * @license
 * SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
 */

/**
 * 寵物 — one spec per breed, read by BOTH the shop icon (QVersionIcon's DogIcon) and the 3D
 * companion (Three/Pets.tsx).
 *
 * Shared on purpose: the two are meant to be the same animal, and a player who buys the brown
 * dachshund on the card and gets a grey one standing next to their character has been lied to.
 * Keeping one palette means a breed can only ever be recoloured in both places at once.
 *
 * Adding a breed is this table plus a `pet-<species>-<breed>` entry in constants/items.ts — the
 * icon and the model both key off the id suffix, so neither needs a new branch.
 */

export interface PetSpec {
  /** Main coat colour. */
  coat: string;
  /** Shaded coat, for the far pair of legs and undersides. */
  shade: string;
  /** The breed's light marking — cream mask/socks, pale muzzle, ankle poms. */
  accent: string;
  /** Near-black: nose, and the hanging ears on a dark-eared breed. */
  dark: string;
  /**
   * 鳥 only — the bill, AND the legs with it.
   *
   * One value for both because on every bird here they are the same material and read as the same
   * colour: the 虎皮鸚鵡's olive-grey bill over blue-grey feet, the 文鳥's red bill over pink feet,
   * the 金絲雀's pale horn over pinkish horn, the 鳳凰's gold over gold. A mammal has neither, so
   * this is absent on all six of them.
   */
  beak?: string;
  /**
   * 鳥 only — the one marking the four coat slots above cannot hold.
   *
   * Each bird spends it on whatever its own second signature is: the 虎皮鸚鵡's violet cheek patch
   * and cobalt tail, the 文鳥's pink belly, the 金絲雀's warm orange face and breast, the 鳳凰's hot
   * orange crest and breast. There is no shared meaning beyond "the colour this bird also needs",
   * which is why it is one slot and not a named field per marking.
   */
  mark?: string;
  /**
   * How tall the dog stands, crown to ground, in the avatar's LOCAL units — the same space
   * Avatar.tsx's BASE_HEAD_Y and LEG_LENGTHEN are written in, so these read directly against the
   * character: soles sit at -0.005, the knee is around 0.118, mid-shin around 0.055 and the crown
   * is 0.945.
   *
   * Every mammal stands the same height on purpose. Sizing them by real-world breed size made
   * the 臘腸 — a low dog by definition — the runt of the shelf and hard to even see beside the
   * character; every companion now reads at the same weight, and what distinguishes a breed is
   * its proportions (the 臘腸 spends its size on length, the 紅貴賓 on coat volume) rather than
   * one being a lesser buy than another.
   *
   * The value puts a dog's crown about at the character's knee. Read by eye, not by anatomy: the
   * avatar is 大頭小身, so measured strictly its knee sits at 0.12 — an eighth of its height where
   * a real person's is over a quarter — and dogs built to that number were too small to see.
   *
   * One number per breed, so how big the companions stand is one edit here and nothing else.
   */
  height: number;
}

/**
 * Shared by every 狗 and 貓 — see `height` above.
 *
 * Raised from 0.30 once the companion left the dressing room and started walking the island
 * (Three/IslandPet.tsx). On the stage the pet is a metre from the camera and 0.30 was plenty; out
 * on the island the camera orbits 10–35 units out with the whole terrain in frame, and at that
 * distance a knee-high dog trailing a character is a small brown smudge. This puts its crown just
 * over the character's knee and costs the outfit nothing on either screen.
 */
const PET_HEIGHT = 0.36;

/**
 * 鳥, which are the one thing on the shelf that does NOT stand at PET_HEIGHT.
 *
 * The reasoning above is about companions standing on the floor, where the eye measures them
 * against the character's knee and anything smaller than a knee-high dog is lost. A bird is never
 * down there: it hovers beside the owner's head (see Three/Pets.tsx), so it is read against the
 * face — and at that distance from the camera, a third of the head's height is plainly visible
 * while still obviously a small bird rather than a goose on the wing.
 */
const BIRD_HEIGHT = 0.24;

/**
 * 鳳凰 — the one companion that is not an animal anybody owns, and the only height on the shelf
 * that is set by status rather than by anatomy.
 *
 * The other three are pet-shop birds and are sized against each other; a phoenix measured the same
 * way would be a budgie in red, which is the whole failure mode of putting a mythical bird on a
 * shelf of real ones. Half again as tall as they are is enough that it is plainly the largest thing
 * hovering beside the character without becoming the thing the screen is about — the avatar's
 * outfit still is. Anything past this and its tail plumes start crossing the character's face.
 */
const PHOENIX_HEIGHT = 0.36;

export const PET_SPECS: Record<string, PetSpec> = {
  // 棕色短毛臘腸犬 — spends its height budget on length: long body, legs barely off the ground.
  dachshund: { coat: '#A9682F', shade: '#875123', accent: '#C98B4E', dark: '#6E4019', height: PET_HEIGHT },
  // 杏紅色玩具貴賓 — compact under a coat of pom-poms.
  poodle: { coat: '#E5A277', shade: '#C9814F', accent: '#F3C7A6', dark: '#1F1A17', height: PET_HEIGHT },
  // 赤色柴犬 — the sturdiest build of the three.
  shiba: { coat: '#D97A3D', shade: '#B45E27', accent: '#F7EADB', dark: '#3D2A1C', height: PET_HEIGHT },

  // --- 貓 ---
  // On all three, `accent` is the white or cream the breed's markings are actually made of, and
  // `shade` is what its stripes are drawn in — a cat's pattern is the thing it is recognised by,
  // so the palette is shaped around carrying it rather than around shading a solid coat.
  // 橘貓 — ginger tabby, striped in a deeper ginger.
  orange: { coat: '#E8934A', shade: '#C46A26', accent: '#FFF2E0', dark: '#8A4A18', height: PET_HEIGHT },
  // 虎斑貓 — brown mackerel tabby. Its bars go much darker than the ginger's: narrow stripes at
  // chip size disappear entirely unless they are near-black against the coat.
  tabby: { coat: '#A08765', shade: '#4E3D29', accent: '#F2E7D5', dark: '#3A2E22', height: PET_HEIGHT },
  // 賓士貓 — tuxedo. Not quite black: against this art's dark brown outline a true black loses its
  // own silhouette, and the white markings are what the pattern is read by anyway.
  tuxedo: { coat: '#3C3833', shade: '#2A2724', accent: '#FFFFFF', dark: '#1A1715', height: PET_HEIGHT },

  // --- 鳥 ---
  // All three are drawn from the wild/classic plumage rather than one of the mutation colours the
  // pet trade also sells, because that is the bird a player pictures when they read the name: a
  // 虎皮鸚鵡 is the green one with the stripes (the stripes are what the Chinese name says), a 文鳥
  // is grey with a black hood and a red bill, a 金絲雀 is 金絲 yellow. Sold in a lutino, a white and
  // a red-factor instead, none of the three would be recognisable as what was bought.
  //
  // 虎皮鸚鵡 — wild-type green budgerigar: yellow face and forehead, pitch-black barring edged in
  // yellow over the nape, back and wings, light green body, cobalt tail, blue-violet cheek patches
  // and a row of black throat spots under the mask.
  budgie: { coat: '#86C34A', shade: '#5E9430', accent: '#F2DE55', dark: '#2A241E', beak: '#9A9483', mark: '#5A6BD0', height: BIRD_HEIGHT },
  // 文鳥 — grey upperparts and breast, white-cheeked black head, pink belly, thick red bill with a
  // red eye-ring to match it, pink feet. `dark` is the hood, and it carries the tail too.
  javasparrow: { coat: '#8E9299', shade: '#6C7077', accent: '#FFFFFF', dark: '#26232B', beak: '#E4536B', mark: '#E9AFA4', height: BIRD_HEIGHT },
  // 金絲雀 — the domestic yellow canary, the one whose colour is named after it. `mark` is the
  // warmer orange it carries over the face and breast: a canary painted one flat yellow from bill
  // to tail reads as a rubber duck, and that warmth is the whole difference.
  // `beak` is pushed deeper than a canary's true pale horn: the real colour is a shade off the
  // bird's own yellow, and a bill that vanishes into the face takes the open beak — the whole
  // reason this one is posed singing — with it.
  canary: { coat: '#F4C92B', shade: '#D9A517', accent: '#FDF0B4', dark: '#3B2E18', beak: '#D6A46B', mark: '#F0952E', height: BIRD_HEIGHT },
  // 鳳凰 — the shelf's one mythical bird, and so the one whose palette is not taken from reference.
  //
  // Painted as FIRE, in one hot ramp from crimson through vermilion to gold, rather than as the
  // 五色 (red/blue/yellow/white/black) the classical description gives it. Both are the real bird;
  // this is the one that survives being 64 pixels wide. A five-colour phoenix at chip size is five
  // patches of unrelated hue with no dominant one, and — worse — a red bird with big blue panels is
  // a 金剛鸚鵡, which is another parrot on a shelf that already has one. Everything here is within
  // 40° of hue of everything else, so the whole silhouette reads as one burning thing.
  //
  // `mark` is the hot orange at the crest and the tips of the tail plumes: the ramp needs a rung
  // between the vermilion body and the gold, or the gold reads as a separate yellow bird stuck on
  // the front of a red one.
  //
  // Checked against its own card, not just against cream: this is the game's only 神話 item, so it
  // is the only pet that is ever seen on the magenta plate (constants/rarity.ts, `fieldCore`
  // #EDA8CD). Warm red and gold hold against that pink; a phoenix built on the tier's own magenta —
  // which was the obvious first idea, matching the bird to its frame — vanished into it entirely.
  phoenix: { coat: '#E24B2E', shade: '#B02A19', accent: '#FFD469', dark: '#3B140E', beak: '#F2A31C', mark: '#FF8F2A', height: PHOENIX_HEIGHT },
};

/**
 * Pet ids are `pet-<species>-<breed>`, and the BREED is the key above — one flat table, because
 * what a pet is coloured and proportioned by is its breed, not its species. The species part only
 * decides which component draws it (QVersionIcon's DogIcon/CatIcon/BirdIcon, and the 3D models)
 * and, for 鳥, that it flies rather than stands.
 */
export const PET_SPECIES = ['dog', 'cat', 'bird'] as const;
export type PetSpecies = (typeof PET_SPECIES)[number];

const PET_ID_PATTERN = /^pet-(dog|cat|bird)-/;

/**
 * The species half of an item id, for the few places that genuinely draw or behave differently per
 * species rather than per breed — which component paints the icon, and whether the 3D companion
 * walks on the floor or flies.
 */
export function getPetSpecies(itemId: string | undefined | null): PetSpecies | undefined {
  const match = itemId?.match(PET_ID_PATTERN);
  return match ? (match[1] as PetSpecies) : undefined;
}

/** The breed key for an item id, for the icon and model switches. */
export function getPetBreed(itemId: string | undefined | null): string | undefined {
  if (!itemId || !PET_ID_PATTERN.test(itemId)) return undefined;
  const breed = itemId.replace(PET_ID_PATTERN, '');
  return breed in PET_SPECS ? breed : undefined;
}

export function getPetSpec(itemId: string | undefined | null): PetSpec | undefined {
  const breed = getPetBreed(itemId);
  return breed ? PET_SPECS[breed] : undefined;
}

/* --- 物種資料表 ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- */

/**
 * How a species gets around, and therefore which mover drives it (Three/IslandPet.tsx).
 *
 * A field rather than `species === 'bird'` scattered through the movers, the habitats and the UI:
 * the day a fourth companion arrives that swims or burrows, it declares its locomotion here and the
 * places that branch on it are already asking the right question.
 */
export type PetLocomotion = 'ground' | 'air';

/**
 * 寵物物種 — everything the game needs to know about a KIND of animal, as opposed to a breed.
 *
 * The split is the one {@link PET_SPECS} already states: a breed decides what an animal is coloured
 * and proportioned like, a species decides how it lives. Colour is the flat breed table above;
 * this is the (much shorter) table of the things that are true of every dog, or every bird.
 *
 * It exists because those facts were previously spelled `=== 'bird'` in five unrelated files — the
 * mover picked its branch that way, the interaction badge named the animal from a private
 * `Record<PetSpecies, string>`, and nothing at all knew which resting places or which foods suited
 * which animal. Adding a species is now this table plus its catalog rows; see
 * `docs/pet-care.md` 「新增一種寵物」.
 */
export interface PetSpeciesDef {
  id: PetSpecies;
  /** 狗 / 貓 / 鳥 — the shelf's word for the animal. */
  label: string;
  /**
   * What the game calls one of these when speaking to the player — 小狗 / 小貓 / 小鳥.
   *
   * Separate from `label` because 「摸摸狗」 is not a sentence anybody writes. The badge, the pet
   * panel and the feeding toasts all read this, so an animal is never called two different things
   * on two different screens.
   */
  companionNoun: string;
  /** Which mover drives it, and — through the habitat table — how it settles. */
  locomotion: PetLocomotion;
  /**
   * The shelf its animals are sold on (utils/categoryUtils.ts), so 「去買一隻」 and the species
   * filter on the pet shelves can deep-link without a second lookup table.
   */
  shopCategory: string;
}

export const PET_SPECIES_TABLE: Record<PetSpecies, PetSpeciesDef> = {
  dog: { id: 'dog', label: '狗', companionNoun: '小狗', locomotion: 'ground', shopCategory: 'Dogs' },
  cat: { id: 'cat', label: '貓', companionNoun: '小貓', locomotion: 'ground', shopCategory: 'Cats' },
  bird: { id: 'bird', label: '鳥', companionNoun: '小鳥', locomotion: 'air', shopCategory: 'Birds' },
};

export const ALL_PET_SPECIES: readonly PetSpeciesDef[] = PET_SPECIES.map((id) => PET_SPECIES_TABLE[id]);

/** The species record for an item id, or undefined for anything that is not an animal. */
export function getPetSpeciesDef(itemId: string | undefined | null): PetSpeciesDef | undefined {
  const species = getPetSpecies(itemId);
  return species ? PET_SPECIES_TABLE[species] : undefined;
}

/** 小狗 / 小貓 / 小鳥 — what to call this companion in a sentence. Total: falls back to 寵物. */
export function petCompanionNoun(itemId: string | undefined | null): string {
  return getPetSpeciesDef(itemId)?.companionNoun ?? '寵物';
}

```

## src/constants/placement.ts

```ts
/**
 * @license
 * SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
 */

import { getItemById } from './items';

/**
 * WHAT A PLACEABLE OBJECT ATTACHES TO — the one vocabulary the whole placement system speaks.
 *
 * ## Why this file exists
 *
 * Before it, "where may this go" was answered in two incompatible ways and neither was a
 * property of the item:
 *
 *  1. Indoors, every piece went on the floor. `handleFloorHover` wrote `position: [x, 0, z]`
 *     unconditionally, so a painting was a floor object whose *model* happened to be drawn
 *     1.2 units up (CanvasArtModel's `position={[0, 1.2, 0]}`). Nothing hung on a wall; a
 *     painting was a floating rectangle the player had to eyeball into place, and turning it to
 *     face the room was their problem.
 *  2. `ITEM_LAYERS`, a hand-keyed `Record<itemId, PlacementLayer>` in lib/furniturePlacement.ts,
 *     decided which pieces could overlap which. It was the only place that knew a painting was
 *     "a wall thing", it was keyed by id with an explicit note that the id prefix could not be
 *     trusted (`deco-wall-table` is a console table), and it had no bearing on where the piece
 *     could actually be put — only on what it was allowed to intersect once it was there.
 *
 * So the *capability* ("this hangs on a wall", "this stands on a table") existed nowhere, and
 * adding a wall-mounted item meant editing a collision table and then hoping the player aimed
 * well. This module makes the capability a declared property of the item, in the same spirit as
 * `standable` (constants/items.ts): a flag stating something geometry cannot tell you, with
 * every dimension still measured off the model.
 *
 * ## What is NOT here
 *
 * No sizes, no offsets, no per-item nudges. How far a painting stands off the wall, how wide a
 * shelf is, how high a vase sits on a table — all of it comes from the measured footprint
 * (lib/furniturePlacement.ts). A spec carrying numbers would be a table that can disagree with
 * the model on screen, which is the exact failure `standable` was introduced to end.
 */

/**
 * A kind of surface an object can attach to.
 *
 * - `floor`   — the ground of a room. The default, and what most furniture is.
 * - `surface` — the top face of another placed piece: a table, a cabinet, a shelf, a deck.
 *               Which pieces offer one is declared by `tabletop` in constants/items.ts.
 * - `wall`    — a vertical room face. Position, facing and standoff are all derived from the
 *               wall's own geometry; see lib/interiorPlacement.ts.
 * - `ceiling` — hung from above: a pendant, a chandelier, and in time a hanging plant or a mobile.
 *               Position, drop and clearance all come from the room's own ceiling geometry
 *               (`ceilingSurfaceAt`, constants/interiorShell.ts) and the piece's measured box; see
 *               lib/interiorPlacement.ts.
 */
export type PlacementMount = 'floor' | 'surface' | 'wall' | 'ceiling';

/**
 * Which pieces are even candidates for colliding with each other.
 *
 * A blanket "nothing may overlap anything" rule would ban layouts that are both legal and
 * desirable — a sofa standing on a rug, a chandelier hanging over a table. The rule that holds
 * up is: a piece only collides with pieces on its own layer, because that is exactly the set
 * that occupies the same band of space.
 *
 * `rug` is a layer of its own rather than a free pass: two rugs are flat planes at the same
 * height, so an overlap between them is not merely intersecting, it is *coplanar* — the one
 * case the depth buffer can never resolve at any precision.
 */
export type PlacementLayer = 'floor' | 'rug' | 'wall' | 'ceiling';

/**
 * How high above y = 0 a layer's pieces are drawn.
 *
 * Only `rug` is non-zero, and it exists for the second half of the same bug: a rug is a
 * `planeGeometry` at local y=0 while the room floor is drawn at y=-0.01 (BuildingInteriorView's
 * AnimatedRoom), so a rug used to sit exactly 0.01 above the surface it lies on — far below the
 * depth resolution available at the distances build mode's camera pulls back to. The lift here
 * plus the `polygonOffset` on the rug materials themselves (FurnitureItem.tsx) puts the question
 * beyond the depth buffer's reach entirely.
 */
export const LAYER_Y_OFFSET: Record<PlacementLayer, number> = {
  floor: 0,
  rug: 0.02,
  wall: 0,
  ceiling: 0,
};

/** An item's declared placement behaviour. Absent on an item means {@link DEFAULT_PLACEMENT}. */
export interface PlacementSpec {
  /**
   * Every surface this item may attach to, best first. A one-entry list is the common case;
   * `['surface', 'floor']` is a vase happiest on a table but allowed to stand on the ground.
   *
   * This is what "placement legality must be per-item data" reduces to: nothing anywhere asks
   * whether an item *is* an artwork, or a lamp, or a rug. It asks what the item mounts to.
   */
  mounts: readonly PlacementMount[];
  /**
   * Collision layer, when it is not the one the mounts imply. Only rugs need it: they are floor
   * pieces, but flat coplanar ones that must not be laid over each other.
   */
  layer?: PlacementLayer;
  /**
   * Wall mounts only: how high the piece's centre hangs when the player has not aimed at a
   * height themselves — dropping a piece by tapping the floor near a wall, or the opening
   * position of a freshly picked one.
   *
   * A height, not an offset: it is measured from the room floor to the centre of the piece, so
   * it stays meaningful whatever the model's own origin happens to be.
   */
  hangHeight?: number;
}

/**
 * What an item that declares nothing gets: an ordinary thing that stands on a surface — a table
 * top if it is pointed at one and fits, the ground otherwise.
 *
 * ### Why `surface` is in the default rather than opted into
 *
 * It used to be `['floor']` alone, and the consequence was quiet: the `surface` mount was fully
 * implemented — hit-tested, clamped to the top face, excluded from the overlap check — and NOTHING
 * IN THE CATALOG COULD REACH IT. Not one of the 194 items declared it. So "put the book on the
 * table" had working machinery behind it and was impossible to do, which is the 物品堆疊 report.
 *
 * The fix has to be a rule, because the alternative is a hand-keyed list of "small things" — and a
 * list keyed by item id is exactly what `footprintRadius`, `getCollisionBounds` and `ITEM_LAYERS`
 * each were before they were removed. The rule is: **anything may stand on anything that offers a
 * top, provided it fits on it.** Both halves are already measured off the model —
 * `tabletop` (constants/items.ts) says a piece offers a top, and `clampOntoSupport`
 * (lib/furniturePlacement.ts) answers "does it fit" from the two footprints — so a wardrobe is
 * refused by a nightstand without anyone typing a size, and a new ornament stacks on day one.
 *
 * A piece that does NOT fit on the top it was aimed at falls through to the next surface behind it
 * (lib/interiorPlacement.ts), so pointing a sofa at a side table still puts the sofa on the floor
 * rather than refusing the spot. "Too big for that table" is not an error, it is just not a table
 * you are pointing at.
 *
 * Order matters: `surface` before `floor` is only a tie-break for equal distances — the resolver
 * picks the NEAREST hit along the ray, which is what makes pointing at a table mean the table and
 * pointing past its edge mean the floor behind it.
 */
export const DEFAULT_PLACEMENT: PlacementSpec = { mounts: ['surface', 'floor'] };

/**
 * Where the middle of a hung piece goes by default: a shade above eye level for this scale
 * (the walk band tops out at 1.75, the ceiling at 4.8), which is where a picture reads from the
 * third-person camera. Individual pieces override it — a tall tapestry hangs higher, a small
 * charm lower.
 */
export const DEFAULT_HANG_HEIGHT = 2.1;

/** The item's declared placement behaviour, or the default for anything that declares none. */
export function getPlacementSpec(itemId: string): PlacementSpec {
  return getItemById(itemId)?.placement ?? DEFAULT_PLACEMENT;
}

/** Every surface `itemId` may attach to, best first. */
export function getPlacementMounts(itemId: string): readonly PlacementMount[] {
  return getPlacementSpec(itemId).mounts;
}

/** Does this item accept `mount` as a place to attach? */
export function canMountOn(itemId: string, mount: PlacementMount): boolean {
  return getPlacementMounts(itemId).includes(mount);
}

/** Centre height of a hung piece when nothing has aimed one. */
export function getHangHeight(itemId: string): number {
  return getPlacementSpec(itemId).hangHeight ?? DEFAULT_HANG_HEIGHT;
}

/**
 * Which pieces this one can collide with.
 *
 * Derived from the mounts rather than kept as a second table: a piece that hangs on a wall is on
 * the wall layer *because* that is where it is, and there is no way for the two statements to
 * drift apart. `layer` overrides it only where the two genuinely differ (rugs).
 */
export function getPlacementLayer(itemId: string): PlacementLayer {
  const spec = getPlacementSpec(itemId);
  if (spec.layer) return spec.layer;
  if (spec.mounts.includes('wall')) return 'wall';
  if (spec.mounts.includes('ceiling')) return 'ceiling';
  return 'floor';
}

```
