     a thin border, not saturated gradients/glass — the previous warm
     amber + heavy glass combo read as gaudy. Full design system (radius/
     shadow/font/state/z-index scales, shared component inventory) is
     documented in src/components/UI/DESIGN_SYSTEM.md. */
  --color-island-teal: #2A9D8F;
  --color-island-teal-light: #5FBDAF;
  --color-island-teal-dark: #1F7A70;
  --color-island-navy: #264653;
  --color-island-navy-soft: #4A6169;
  --color-island-navy-dark: #1A2E35;  /* deeper ambient wash, e.g. BuildingInteriorView's non-build-mode backdrop — was a stray bg-[#1a2e35] before this token existed */
  --color-island-cream: #FFFFFF;
  --color-island-cream-2: #F8F6F1;
  --color-island-line: #E1DED4;

  /* Extended for the 2026-07 cozy-furniture-game UI pass (home/build/shop
     surfaces). Keep new panels/cards/icons on this same family instead of
     the old amber gradients + parchment/gilded-plaque look they replaced. */
  --color-island-gold: #E8AA3E;   /* currency only, see feedback-ui-style-preference exception */
  --color-island-coral: #E8836A;  /* danger / delete, muted alternative to rose/red */
  --color-island-sand: #EFE9DC;   /* card inner surface / hover background */
}

/* =========================================================================
   HUD LAYOUT SYSTEM — spacing tokens for the persistent floating chrome.
   =========================================================================
   Single source of truth for how far HUD chrome sits from the viewport edge
   (`--hud-inset`) and how far stacked cards in one rail sit from each other
   (`--hud-gap`). Every persistent HUD element is placed by the shared
   CSS-Grid frame in src/components/UI/HudFrame.tsx and spaced by these
   tokens instead of hand-tuned per-component `top-[Npx]`/`left-N` offsets —
   which is what used to make elements drift into each other across
   resolutions (e.g. SideButtons' old `top-[360px]`, tuned to TopBar's
   height, overlapping it whenever TopBar grew). Change the edge inset /
   inter-card gap here once and the whole HUD follows.

   The frame's own padding is `max(var(--hud-inset), env(safe-area-inset-*))`
   so notched / rounded-corner devices never clip corner chrome (index.html
   opts in with `viewport-fit=cover`). */
:root {
  --hud-inset: 0.75rem; /* mobile — base viewport edge gap */
  --hud-gap: 0.75rem;   /* gap between stacked cards within a rail */
}
@media (min-width: 640px)  { :root { --hud-inset: 0.875rem; --hud-gap: 0.75rem; } }  /* tablet  */
@media (min-width: 1024px) { :root { --hud-inset: 1rem;     --hud-gap: 1rem;    } }  /* laptop  */
@media (min-width: 1536px) { :root { --hud-inset: 1.5rem;   --hud-gap: 1.25rem; } }  /* desktop */

/* =========================================================================
   RESPONSIVE HUD SIZE SYSTEM — four device tiers, one token scale.
   =========================================================================
   The insets above say how far chrome sits from the edge. These say how big
   the chrome itself is, and they step at the SAME four widths so the whole
   HUD changes gear as one piece instead of each card picking its own
   breakpoints (TopBar used to shrink at 1280 while --hud-inset grew at 1280
   and the MiniMap grew at 640 — three components, three different ideas of
   "small screen").

   THE FOUR TIERS — the only widths any HUD sizing may branch on:

     | tier    | range        | Tailwind variant | typical device         |
     |---------|--------------|------------------|------------------------|
     | mobile  | < 640px      | (unprefixed)     | phones                 |
     | tablet  | 640-1023px   | `tablet:`        | tablets, split windows |
     | laptop  | 1024-1535px  | `laptop:`        | 1366x768 … 1440x900    |
     | desktop | >= 1536px    | `desktop:`       | 1080p+ monitors        |

   The `tablet:` / `laptop:` / `desktop:` variants are declared below and are
   min-width, exactly like Tailwind's own — so `text-x laptop:text-y` still
   applies `y` on desktop. They exist so HUD code names the DEVICE TIER it
   means; `sm:`/`md:`/`lg:`/`xl:` stay available for in-panel layout tweaks
   that are about content fitting, not about device class.

   WIDTH IS SIZE, POINTER IS TOUCH. These tiers decide how BIG a control is;
   they never decide whether it is touch-operated. That is `pointer: coarse`
   (hooks/useIsTouchDevice.ts) — a 1180px tablet in landscape lands in the
   `laptop` tier and still needs 44px targets, which is what --hud-tap and
   `.hud-hit` below are for. The JS mirror of this table lives in
   hooks/useHudTier.ts and is checked against this file by
   `npm run audit:hud-scale`.

   HOW TO USE IT. Size a HUD card from these tokens instead of writing
   per-component media queries: padding/gaps from --hud-card-*, glyphs from
   --hud-icon (via `.hud-icon`), copy from --hud-text-* (via `.hud-text-title`
   / `.hud-text-meta`), and the card's own width from --hud-card-w, which is
   deliberately `max-content` on the two small tiers — a compact card is as
   wide as its one row of content, a big one holds a fixed column — with
   --hud-card-max-w as the standing guarantee that neither can run off the
   viewport. */
:root {
  /* --- tier: mobile (base) ------------------------------------------ */
  --hud-card-pad:   0.5rem;     /*  8px - card's own padding             */
  --hud-card-gap:   0.375rem;   /*  6px - between sections in a card     */
  --hud-row-gap:    0.1875rem;  /*  3px - label to the bar under it      */
  --hud-chip-gap:   0.375rem;   /*  6px - between inline chips           */
  --hud-stat-pad:   0.375rem;   /*  6px - inner surface holding the bars */
  --hud-avatar:     2rem;       /* 32px - porthole outer diameter        */
  --hud-icon:       0.75rem;    /* 12px - inline glyph                   */
  --hud-bar-h:      0.375rem;   /*  6px - progress bar thickness         */
  --hud-card-w:     max-content;/* card width: as wide as its own row    */
  --hud-name-max-w: 3.75rem;    /* 60px - name truncates past this       */
  --hud-text-title: 0.75rem;    /* 12px - name, primary numbers          */
  --hud-text-meta:  0.625rem;   /* 10px - labels, badges (never below)   */
  /* Minimum comfortable touch target. NOT tiered — a finger is the same
     size on every screen; only `.hud-hit` (pointer: coarse) applies it. */
  --hud-tap:        2.75rem;    /* 44px */
  /* Hard ceiling so a card can never run off-screen or swallow the view,
     however long a player's display name is. */
  --hud-card-max-w: min(20rem, calc(100vw - var(--hud-inset) * 2 - 1rem));
}
@media (min-width: 640px) {  /* --- tier: tablet --- */
  :root {
    --hud-card-pad:   0.5rem;      /*  8px */
    --hud-card-gap:   0.375rem;    /*  6px */
    --hud-chip-gap:   0.5rem;      /*  8px */
    --hud-stat-pad:   0.5rem;      /*  8px */
    --hud-avatar:     2.25rem;     /* 36px */
    --hud-icon:       0.8125rem;   /* 13px */
    --hud-name-max-w: 5.5rem;      /* 88px */
    --hud-text-title: 0.8125rem;   /* 13px */
  }
}
@media (min-width: 1024px) { /* --- tier: laptop --- */
  :root {
    --hud-card-pad:   0.625rem;    /* 10px */
    --hud-card-gap:   0.5rem;      /*  8px */
    --hud-row-gap:    0.25rem;     /*  4px */
    --hud-stat-pad:   0.5rem;      /*  8px */
    --hud-avatar:     2.75rem;     /* 44px */
    --hud-card-w:     12rem;       /* 192px - fixed column */
    --hud-name-max-w: 7rem;        /* 112px */
  }
}
@media (min-width: 1536px) { /* --- tier: desktop --- */
  :root {
    --hud-card-pad:   0.75rem;     /* 12px */
    --hud-card-gap:   0.625rem;    /* 10px */
    --hud-chip-gap:   0.625rem;    /* 10px */
    --hud-stat-pad:   0.625rem;    /* 10px */
    --hud-avatar:     3.25rem;     /* 52px */
    --hud-icon:       0.875rem;    /* 14px */
    --hud-bar-h:      0.5rem;      /*  8px */
    --hud-card-w:     13.5rem;     /* 216px */
    --hud-name-max-w: 8.5rem;      /* 136px */
    --hud-text-title: 0.875rem;    /* 14px */
    --hud-text-meta:  0.6875rem;   /* 11px */
  }
}

/* The three device-tier variants. Declared next to the table they belong to
   so a reader never has to guess which px value `laptop:` means. */
@custom-variant tablet  (@media (width >= 640px));
@custom-variant laptop  (@media (width >= 1024px));
@custom-variant desktop (@media (width >= 1536px));

/* `short:` — the HUD's only HEIGHT breakpoint.

   Every other breakpoint in this project is a width one, because that is what
   decides how much sits side by side. Bottom-anchored mode chrome has the
   opposite problem: a panel that stacks a toolbar, a header, a category row and
   a card rail (BuildModeOverlay's 建築規劃) is ~660px tall no matter how wide
   the window is, so on a 1366x768 laptop — or a 1080p one at 125%/150% Windows
   scaling — it is TALLER than the viewport. A bottom-anchored stack that
   overflows overflows upwards, which silently ate the toolbar off the top of
   the screen with no scrollbar to get it back.

   So: tighten the paddings, gaps and card size once the window gets short,
   rather than letting the tallest panel decide whether its own controls are
   reachable. 800px is where 建築規劃's full-size layout stops fitting inside
   the HUD insets. Panels using this must ALSO cap themselves (`max-h-full`) and
   scroll their body — this variant buys room, it can't guarantee it. */
@custom-variant short (@media (height <= 800px));

/* BuildingInteriorView draws its own header card ("我的溫馨小窩" / "佈置模式")
   at the top-left of the interior view. It is NOT one of HudFrame's regions —
   it belongs to the view, not the persistent HUD — so HUD chrome in the
   left-rail region has to step around it, which is exactly the "one element
   encodes another's height" coupling the tokens above exist to prevent.
   These two tokens are the single place that card's top offset and height are
   stated: the card itself is positioned/sized from them, and everything that
   must clear it (MiniMap's rail offset, AngelGuide's keep-out) measures from
   them. Change the card's padding or icon size and you change it here once.
   Breakpoint is 640px to match the card's own `sm:` styles. */
:root {
  --interior-header-top: 1rem;  /* the card's distance from the viewport top */
  --interior-header-h: 3.5rem;  /* p-2 + a 40px icon tile */
}
@media (min-width: 640px) {
  :root {
    --interior-header-top: 2rem;
    --interior-header-h: 5.5rem; /* p-4 + a 56px icon tile */
  }
}

/* =========================================================================
   MINIMAP — one size token for the whole instrument.
   =========================================================================
   `--minimap-w` is the outside width of the wheel bezel; everything else about
   the map is derived from it (the map window is a fixed fraction of the bezel,
   MiniMapFrame.tsx) or from `--minimap-h`, which adds the hanging nameplate.
   Stated here rather than inside the component for the same reason as
   --interior-header-*: other chrome has to step around this card — AngelGuide's
   keep-out is measured off these two tokens — and "one element hardcodes
   another's size" is exactly what the HUD tokens exist to prevent. It used to
   be a pair of hand-tuned figures (`pl-[11.25rem]`, `pt-[17rem]`) that could
   only rot the next time the map was resized.

   The map does NOT need these values in JS: it is a follow-camera over a plan
   drawn at a fixed world scale, so it simply shows whatever its window is big
   enough for. Resizing here is the whole responsive story — nothing measures,
   nothing re-lays-out. */
:root {
  --minimap-w: 11.5rem;                          /* 184px — phones */
  --minimap-h: calc(var(--minimap-w) + 1.25rem); /* + the nameplate's overhang */
}
/* Steps on the shared device tiers (see "RESPONSIVE HUD SIZE SYSTEM" above),
   not on breakpoints of its own — the map used to jump to its largest size at
   1280px, i.e. on a laptop, which is the tier that can least afford the
   screen area. It now grows only on a genuine desktop. */
@media (min-width: 640px)  { :root { --minimap-w: 13.5rem; } } /* tablet  — 216px */
@media (min-width: 1024px) { :root { --minimap-w: 14.5rem; } } /* laptop  — 232px */
@media (min-width: 1536px) { :root { --minimap-w: 16rem; } }   /* desktop — 256px */

/* =========================================================================
   GLOBAL Z-INDEX LAYER SYSTEM — single source of truth for the whole app.
   =========================================================================
   Six conceptual layers, low to high. Every `position: fixed/absolute`
   element with a z-index MUST use one of these classes (or a documented
   sub-tier of one) instead of inventing a raw `z-[N]` value or comparing
   two different views' numbers by feel. Plain classes, not @theme --z-*
   tokens: Tailwind v4's `z` utility is a fixed static utility, not one of
   the theme-driven namespaces (unlike `--color-*`), so arbitrary --z-*
   theme keys generate no CSS.

   1. Background   (0)   — the passive 3D scene. Nothing interactive lives
                           here; it never needs to out-rank anything else.
   2. Game View    (10)  — the ONE current full-screen view's own content
                           (Settings/Shop/Fitness/Tracker/DressingRoom/
                           BuildingInteriorView/AuthScreen/BuildModeOverlay).
                           `currentView` is a single enum value, so these
                           are mutually exclusive and never compare against
                           each other — only "below Background? no. below
                           HUD? yes" matters, so they all share one number.
   3. HUD          (20-28) — persistent, always-visible chrome that survives
                           across every Game View (toolbar, nav, top bar,
                           mobile touch controls). Sub-tiers exist ONLY to
                           order HUD pieces against each other; nothing
                           outside HUD should ever need to compare against
                           a sub-value directly.
   4. Floating Panel (30) — a dialog/drawer that BELONGS to a specific Game
                           View but must visually beat the persistent HUD
                           while open (a build-mode toolbar, a furniture
                           drawer, an account panel, an emote tray). THE
                           RULE THAT MATTERS: a Floating Panel must never be
                           a DOM descendant of its Game View's own
                           z-game-view wrapper, because nesting traps a
                           child's z-index below wherever its stacking-
                           context-creating parent landed — no z-index
                           number written on the child can escape that. If
                           a floating panel is ever found "trapped" behind
                           HUD again, the fix is to portal it out to
                           document.body (see BuildingInteriorView.tsx's
                           `PORTAL_ROOT` usage for the pattern), NOT to
                           raise its parent Game View's whole z-index —
                           that was the exact bug that caused MiniMap to be
                           invisible inside the house (BuildingInteriorView
                           was raised to beat HUD, which also lifted its own
                           plain background/canvas above HUD as a side
                           effect). Every view's blocking "are you sure?"
                           style dialogs use z-modal instead (see 6).
   5. Toast        (40)  — short-lived, non-blocking notifications.
   6. Modal        (50)  — blocking, must-acknowledge dialogs (confirm
                           purchase, confirm delete, login bonus, account
                           panel). Kept at 1000, not 50, as a large safety
                           margin so nothing can ever accidentally end up
                           between "the highest real layer" and "modal" by
                           a stray +10.
   7. Loading      (9999) — boot/transition screen. Always absolute top.

   Sub-tier note: within a shared Game View's own content there can be an
   internal, self-contained mini z-scale (e.g. SettingsView's own back
   button above its own scroll body) — that's fine and stays on small raw
   values local to that view, since it never needs to compare against
   anything outside itself. Only cross-view/cross-layer comparisons need a
   class from this table. */
@layer utilities {
  .z-background     { z-index: 0; }
  .z-game-view      { z-index: 10; }

  /* The shared HUD grid frame (src/components/UI/HudFrame.tsx). It is
     `position: fixed`, so it forms ONE stacking context that sits above the
     Game View band and below Floating Panels / Toasts / Modals. All the
     persistent corner chrome lives inside it, and the `.z-hud-*` tiers below
     now order those pieces *within* the frame as a local sub-scale (a
     descendant's z-index can't leak past the frame's context anyway). The
     numbers are unchanged so the relative order is exactly as before; only
     their scope moved from "root siblings" to "inside the frame". Elements
     that must out-rank the frame stay OUTSIDE it as root siblings on their
     own tier: #floating-panel-root (z-floating-panel), corner Toasts
     (z-toast), modals (z-modal), LoadingScreen (z-loading), and
     MobileControls' own full-bleed touch layers (z-hud-touch/controls,
     which must stay below the frame's interactive chrome — the frame is
     mounted after MobileControls in App.tsx's DOM so it wins the tie). */
  .z-hud-frame      { z-index: 20; }

  .z-hud-touch      { z-index: 20; } /* MobileControls touch-capture layer */
  .z-hud-controls   { z-index: 22; } /* MobileControls joystick/action-button visuals */
  .z-hud-toolbar    { z-index: 24; } /* SideButtons, ZoomControl, ControlsHint, MiniMap, InteractionPrompt, BuildModeOverlay */
  .z-hud-navbar     { z-index: 26; } /* NavBar, emote tray trigger */
  .z-hud-topbar     { z-index: 28; } /* TopBar, WeatherToast, PettingMiniGame, AuthScreen */

  .z-floating-panel { z-index: 30; }
  .z-toast          { z-index: 40; }
  .z-modal          { z-index: 1000; }

  /* 管理員測試主控台 (components/UI/admin/). Its own tier because it is the one
     surface that must float over a GAME VIEW's own local sub-scale: ShopView,
     LimitedShopView and friends are z-game-view wrappers whose insides run a
     private z-[60]/[70]/[80] ladder, and a console pinned at z-toast (40) would
     disappear behind the very screen it is there to test. 900 clears all of
     those and the WeatherWidget's z-[100], while staying BELOW z-modal so a
     confirm dialog, a purchase sheet or the reveal still wins — a QA panel that
     could cover a blocking dialog is a QA panel that can trap the tester.
     Rendered only while 管理員測試模式 is on; nothing on this tier exists for a
     normal player. */
  .z-admin-console  { z-index: 900; }

  /* The 史詩/神話 purchase reveal (components/UI/RarityReveal.tsx). It exists
     as its own tier because it is the one thing in the game that must cover a
     MODAL: it plays after a purchase is confirmed, while PurchaseDialog is
     still on screen, and the dialog is the very thing it is revealing past.
     A local `z-[1001]` would have said the same number and none of that, and
     would have been invisible to anyone reading this table for what can sit
     above a modal. Still below LoadingScreen — a reload interrupts everything,
     celebrations included. */
  .z-reveal         { z-index: 1500; }

  .z-loading        { z-index: 9999; }
}

/* --- 管理員測試主控台的版面 ---------------------------------------------

   RWD is a change of SHAPE, not a scaled-down copy of the desktop panel.

   Phone (< 640px)      Bottom sheet. A 320px side panel on a 390px-wide screen
                        is not a side panel, it is a full-screen modal with a
                        sliver of game showing — the exact thing this console was
                        built to stop being. A sheet capped at 72vh keeps the top
                        of the screen (where the character and the profile card
                        are) permanently visible.
   Tablet / landscape   Side panel, min(19rem, 46vw). The vw term is what stops a
   phone (>= 640px)     640px-wide viewport handing half its width to the panel.
   Laptop (>= 1024px)   21rem — ~27% of a 1280px screen, so the game keeps ~73%.
   Desktop (>= 1536px)  25rem, which is the same proportion on a bigger screen
                        rather than the same pixel width squeezed.

   Insets are the HUD's own tokens, so the panel lines up with the rest of the
   chrome and never clips on a notched device. */
/* The 【管理員測試】 handle in the views HudFrame is not mounted for. Inset by the HUD's own edge
   token rather than flush against the viewport, so it lines up with the zoom dial and the 幸運轉盤
   it sits beside in the views that DO have a frame — one shape, one distance from the edge,
   everywhere. (An earlier version cancelled the frame's padding with a negative margin to sit
   flush; that expression did not resolve to the frame's own padding on every breakpoint — it came
   out 16px against a 12px padding on the mobile tier — and a handle 4px off the edge is a worse
   outcome than one that matches the rest of the chrome.) */
.admin-console-handle-floating {
  position: fixed;
  top: 50%;
  transform: translateY(-50%);
  right: max(var(--hud-inset), env(safe-area-inset-right));
}

.admin-console-panel {
  position: fixed;
  left: 0;
  right: 0;
  bottom: 0;
  max-height: min(72vh, 40rem);
  border-radius: 1.75rem 1.75rem 0 0;
}

@media (min-width: 640px) {
  .admin-console-panel {
    left: auto;
    top: max(var(--hud-inset), env(safe-area-inset-top));
    bottom: max(var(--hud-inset), env(safe-area-inset-bottom));
    right: max(var(--hud-inset), env(safe-area-inset-right));
    width: min(19rem, 46vw);
    max-height: none;
    border-radius: 1.75rem;
  }
}

@media (min-width: 1024px) { .admin-console-panel { width: 21rem; } }
@media (min-width: 1536px) { .admin-console-panel { width: 25rem; } }

/* Custom Thin Scrollbar */
@layer base {
  ::-webkit-scrollbar {
    width: 6px;
    height: 6px;
  }
  ::-webkit-scrollbar-track {
    background: transparent;
  }
  ::-webkit-scrollbar-thumb {
    background: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.1);
    border-radius: 10px;
  }
  ::-webkit-scrollbar-thumb:hover {
    background: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.2);
  }

  /* For Firefox */
  * {
    scrollbar-width: thin;
    scrollbar-color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.1) transparent;
  }
}

@layer base {
  body {
    @apply bg-sky-500 overflow-hidden text-white;
    -webkit-tap-highlight-color: transparent;
  }

  /* The React mount point, given a real full-viewport box.

     It has no children in normal flow — App's outermost div is `fixed inset-0`
     — so by default this element is ZERO PIXELS TALL, and that is a live trap
     rather than a tidiness problem. Any `transform`, `filter` or `perspective`
     put on #root makes it the containing block for every absolutely- and
     fixed-positioned descendant, and at that instant every `inset-0` layer in
     the app (App's own root, the 3D scene, a full-screen view, every modal and
     the reveal itself) resolves against a 0-height box and collapses into a
     strip. What the player sees is the whole interface vanishing and this
     file's `bg-sky-500` body filling the screen.

     That is not hypothetical: it is exactly what 神話's screen shake did (see
     `.rarity-shake`, added to #root by RarityReveal.tsx). Buying the 鳳凰 —
     the only 神話 item in the catalog — dimmed the room, span the item in, and
     then flashed a solid blue screen for the 0.56s the shake ran.

     Sizing the box here fixes the whole class of bug at its source, and keeps
     the shake doing what it was written to do: with a box this size, a
     transformed #root still moves its fixed children (the room shakes) but
     they still measure the viewport (nothing collapses). Anything that wants
     to transform the whole app in future is safe by default. */
  #root {
    height: 100dvh;
  }

  /* Keyboard-navigation focus ring. `:focus-visible` only fires for
     keyboard/assistive-tech focus (not mouse/touch clicks), so this is safe
     to apply globally without changing how anything looks for pointer
     users — it just gives keyboard users something to see, which nothing
     in this app currently provides on its own. */
  button:focus-visible,
  a:focus-visible,
  input:focus-visible,
  select:focus-visible,
  textarea:focus-visible,
  [tabindex]:focus-visible {
    outline: 2px solid var(--color-island-teal);
    outline-offset: 2px;
    border-radius: 4px;
  }
}

@layer utilities {
  /* Full-screen scroll-view page insets — comfortable base padding that ALSO
     clears device safe areas (notch, home indicator, rounded corners) so a
     view's content never hides under system UI on phones/tablets. Shared by
     the full-page scroll views (Settings/Tracker/Fitness picker/Shop) so they
     stop each hardcoding their own `pt-12 pb-24 px-6`. */
  .page-shell-y {
    padding-top: calc(3rem + env(safe-area-inset-top));
    padding-bottom: calc(6rem + env(safe-area-inset-bottom));
  }
  .page-shell-x {
    padding-left: max(1.5rem, env(safe-area-inset-left));
    padding-right: max(1.5rem, env(safe-area-inset-right));
  }
  /* A fixed top-right control (e.g. a view's close button) that stays clear
     of the notch / rounded corner. */
  .corner-safe-tr {
    top: max(1.5rem, env(safe-area-inset-top));
    right: max(1.5rem, env(safe-area-inset-right));
  }

  /* RANGE SLIDER — the shared volume/level control (Slider in DesignKit.tsx).

     A thin track is the look we want; a thin ELEMENT is not. A range input hit-tests against its
     own border box, and the thumb's overflow is painted, not grabbable — so styling the control
     itself `h-1` left the player aiming at a 4-pixel-tall strip to start a drag. The element is a
     touch-sized 1.75rem here and the 4px track is drawn INSIDE it by the track pseudo-element, so
     the control looks the same and can actually be taken hold of, including with a thumb.

     `touch-action: none` is the touch half of the same fix: without it the first vertical
     component of a drag is claimed by the page as a scroll and the gesture is cancelled out from
     under the slider. The control is 28px tall inside a scrollable settings panel, so it has to
     claim its own gesture rather than share it. */
  .range-slider {
    height: 1.75rem;
    background: transparent;
    touch-action: none;
  }
  .range-slider::-webkit-slider-runnable-track {
    height: 0.25rem;
    border-radius: 9999px;
    background: var(--color-island-line);
  }
  .range-slider::-moz-range-track {
    height: 0.25rem;
    border-radius: 9999px;
    background: var(--color-island-line);
  }
  /* Re-centred by hand because `appearance: none` drops the browser's own centring: the thumb is
     positioned from the TOP of the track, so half of it hangs below without this. */
  .range-slider::-webkit-slider-thumb {
    appearance: none;
    -webkit-appearance: none;
    width: 1.05rem;
    height: 1.05rem;
    margin-top: -0.4rem;
    border-radius: 9999px;
    background: var(--color-island-teal);
    border: 2px solid #fff;
    box-shadow: 0 2px 6px rgba(38, 70, 83, 0.22);
    cursor: grab;
  }
  .range-slider::-moz-range-thumb {
    width: 1.05rem;
    height: 1.05rem;
    border-radius: 9999px;
    background: var(--color-island-teal);
    border: 2px solid #fff;
    box-shadow: 0 2px 6px rgba(38, 70, 83, 0.22);
    cursor: grab;
    border-width: 2px;
  }
  .range-slider:active::-webkit-slider-thumb { cursor: grabbing; }
  .range-slider:active::-moz-range-thumb { cursor: grabbing; }

  .no-scrollbar::-webkit-scrollbar {
    display: none;
  }
  .no-scrollbar {
    -ms-overflow-style: none;  /* IE and Edge */
    scrollbar-width: none;  /* Firefox */
  }

  .custom-scrollbar::-webkit-scrollbar {
    width: 6px;
  }
  .custom-scrollbar::-webkit-scrollbar-track {
    background: transparent;
  }
  .custom-scrollbar::-webkit-scrollbar-thumb {
    background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.1);
    border-radius: 10px;
  }
  .custom-scrollbar::-webkit-scrollbar-thumb:hover {
    background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.2);
  }

  .custom-scrollbar-brown::-webkit-scrollbar {
    width: 8px;
  }
  .custom-scrollbar-brown::-webkit-scrollbar-track {
    background: rgba(139, 90, 43, 0.05);
    border-radius: 10px;
  }
  .custom-scrollbar-brown::-webkit-scrollbar-thumb {
    background: rgba(139, 90, 43, 0.35);
    border-radius: 10px;
    border: 2px solid transparent;
    background-clip: padding-box;
  }
  .custom-scrollbar-brown::-webkit-scrollbar-thumb:hover {
    background: rgba(139, 90, 43, 0.55);
    border: 2px solid transparent;
    background-clip: padding-box;
  }

  /* Teal-on-cream scrollbar for light card surfaces (e.g. BuildModeOverlay's
     building-item strip, and that panel's own body once a short window makes it
     scroll) — a token-based, reusable replacement for what used to be an inline
     <style> tag with !important overrides hand-rolled in that one component.
     Sized on both axes so the same class works whichever way its element
     scrolls; `.custom-scrollbar` is the dark-surface one and its white thumb is
     invisible on cream. */
  .custom-scrollbar-teal::-webkit-scrollbar {
    height: 6px;
    width: 6px;
  }
  .custom-scrollbar-teal::-webkit-scrollbar-track {
    background: var(--color-island-cream-2);
    border-radius: 9999px;
  }
  .custom-scrollbar-teal::-webkit-scrollbar-thumb {
    background: var(--color-island-teal);
    border-radius: 9999px;
    border: 1px solid var(--color-island-cream-2);
  }
  .custom-scrollbar-teal::-webkit-scrollbar-thumb:hover {
    background: var(--color-island-teal-dark);
  }

  /* "Dock & Signpost" HUD motif (2026-07 pass) — the persistent HUD chrome
     stopped reading as generic rounded-rectangle cards and started reading
     as physical objects a player would find standing on the island: a
     boarding-pass ticket, a signpost, a ship's porthole. Shape carries the
     personality, not color — these stay on the existing island-teal/navy/
     cream/line tokens above, no new hues. See DesignKit.tsx's SignpostTag
     and PortholeFrame, which consume these classes. */

  /* Clipped ticket-stub corner — used on TopBar / AccountPanel headers.

     A CLIPPED ELEMENT CANNOT CARRY ITS OWN SHADOW. `clip-path` clips the
     element's entire painted output, and a `box-shadow` is part of that
     output — so `class="dock-notch shadow-[...]"` silently renders NO shadow
     at all, leaving a hard cut edge where the card meets the 3D scene. That
     read as the "black edge / stray shadow" artifact across the HUD: every
     notched card (TopBar, AccountPanel, the interior header, the NavBar
     plank, every SignpostTag) paired a clip-path with a shadow that never
     drew. Putting the shadow on the same element as a `filter` does not fix
     it either — filters are applied BEFORE clipping, so the blur gets cut
     too.

     Use `.notch-shadow*` on a WRAPPER instead (below). Never re-add a
     `shadow-*` to an element that also clips. */
  .dock-notch {
    clip-path: polygon(0 0, calc(100% - 14px) 0, 100% 14px, 100% 100%, 0 100%);
  }

  /* Shadow for any clipped silhouette (`.dock-notch`, SignpostTag's arrow /
     hanging-plank shapes, the NavBar dock plank).

     Goes on the clipped element's PARENT, where the filter is applied to the
     child's already-clipped rendering — so the shadow traces the cut edge
     (the chamfer, the arrow point) instead of the original rectangle. This is
     the only way to get a shadow onto a clipped shape; see the note above.

     Tiers mirror the navy-tinted box-shadow scale in DESIGN_SYSTEM.md:
     `-sm` for HUD chrome sitting on the scene, `-lg` for panels/modals that
     float above other UI. Keep the blur a little tighter than the box-shadow
     it replaces — drop-shadow traces the silhouette rather than a rectangle,
     so the same numbers read heavier. */
  .notch-shadow-sm {
    filter: drop-shadow(0 3px 6px rgba(38, 70, 83, 0.12));
  }
  .notch-shadow {
    filter: drop-shadow(0 5px 10px rgba(38, 70, 83, 0.14));
  }
  .notch-shadow-lg {
    filter: drop-shadow(0 12px 22px rgba(38, 70, 83, 0.20));
  }
  /* Teal variant, for a clipped element on a teal surface (an active
     SignpostTag) — matches the teal shadow family in DESIGN_SYSTEM.md. */
  .notch-shadow-teal {
    filter: drop-shadow(0 4px 9px rgba(42, 157, 143, 0.34));
  }
  /* Shadow gutter for a HUD region that has to be a scroll container.

     `overflow-y: auto` computes `overflow-x` to `auto` as well, so such a
     region clips its cards on BOTH axes at its own content box — and a card's
     shadow, ring and any deliberate negative margin are all painted outside
     that box. That is what sliced the bottom off the MiniMap's card (its
     `0 14px 34px -8px` shadow was cut to a hard horizontal line, which reads
     as the card itself being cropped) and shaved the left edge the card
     deliberately tucks into the corner with `-ml-*`.

     This reserves a transparent gutter inside the scroll box and cancels it
     again with an equal negative margin, so the region occupies exactly the
     same place on screen while its children have room to paint outside
     themselves. Sized off the largest shadow any rail card uses (MiniMap's,
     ~40px of spill) plus a little slack.

     This is deliberately NOT a MiniMap special case: every card in a scrolling
     rail, now and later, gets its shadow back from the same rule. Pop-outs
     that must escape the region entirely (a tool panel, a dropdown) are still
     a different problem with a different answer — AnchoredPopover. */
  .hud-scroll-gutter {
    --hud-gutter: 2.75rem;
    padding: var(--hud-gutter);
    margin: calc(var(--hud-gutter) * -1);
  }

  /* ---------------------------------------------------------------------
     RESPONSIVE HUD SIZE SYSTEM — the utility half.
     ---------------------------------------------------------------------
     The tokens (:root, top of this file) hold the four-tier scale; these
     three classes are how a component spends them without every element
     growing an `text-[length:var(--hud-text-title)]` arbitrary value.

     Why classes and not Tailwind arbitrary values: an icon needs BOTH the
     CSS box and the SVG's own width/height overridden (lucide writes them as
     presentation attributes), and a token-driven font size wants its
     line-height moved with it. Both are two declarations, which is a class. */

  /* Inline glyph inside HUD chrome. CSS width/height beat lucide's
     `size` attribute, so keep passing `size` as the pre-CSS fallback only —
     same arrangement SideButtons already uses for its vh-scaled tags. */
  .hud-icon {
    width: var(--hud-icon);
    height: var(--hud-icon);
    flex-shrink: 0;
  }

  /* The two rungs of the HUD type scale. `title` is what a player reads at a
     glance (name, primary numbers); `meta` is everything supporting it
     (labels, badges, secondary figures). There is deliberately no third,
     smaller rung: --hud-text-meta bottoms out at 10px, which is the floor
     this HUD is allowed to use. */
  .hud-text-title {
    font-size: var(--hud-text-title);
    line-height: 1.15;
  }
  .hud-text-meta {
    font-size: var(--hud-text-meta);
    line-height: 1.1;
  }

  /* Touch-target floor for a small HUD control.

     A shrunken HUD is only usable if the FINGER target does not shrink with
     it — a 32px avatar on a phone is a perfectly legible picture and an
     unreliable button. This grows the hit area to --hud-tap (44px) with an
     overlay pseudo-element, so nothing about the layout moves; the control
     keeps its drawn size and gains reach. Gated on `pointer: coarse` because
     on a mouse the same overlay would claim hover/clicks from whatever sits
     within 6px of the control. Needs a positioned host, which the class
     itself provides. */
  .hud-hit {
    position: relative;
  }
  @media (pointer: coarse) {
    .hud-hit::after {
      content: '';
      position: absolute;
      left: 50%;
      top: 50%;
      width: max(100%, var(--hud-tap));
      height: max(100%, var(--hud-tap));
      transform: translate(-50%, -50%);
    }
  }

  /* Hover step-up, written as real CSS rather than a `hover:notch-shadow`
     class: these are hand-authored utilities, not registered Tailwind ones,
     so Tailwind cannot generate variants for them and `hover:notch-shadow`
     would silently emit nothing. */
  .notch-shadow-hoverable {
    filter: drop-shadow(0 3px 6px rgba(38, 70, 83, 0.12));
    transition: filter 300ms ease-out;
  }
  .notch-shadow-hoverable:hover {
    filter: drop-shadow(0 7px 13px rgba(38, 70, 83, 0.18));
  }

  /* Stitched divider line, replaces a plain solid border-top between
     sections that used to just be a flat rule. */
  .rope-stitch {
    height: 2px;
    background-image: repeating-linear-gradient(
      90deg,
      var(--color-island-navy-soft) 0 6px,
      transparent 6px 11px
    );
    opacity: 0.3;
  }

  /* Vertical signpost pole rendered behind a column of SignpostTag buttons
     (SideButtons) so they read as one mounted object instead of separate
     floating tiles. Parent must be `relative`; buttons need `relative z-10`
     to sit in front of this (z-0). */
  .signpost-post {
    position: absolute;
    left: 50%;
    top: -14px;
    bottom: -14px;
    width: 6px;
    transform: translateX(-50%);
    background: linear-gradient(180deg, var(--color-island-navy-soft), var(--color-island-navy));
    border-radius: 999px;
    z-index: 0;
  }

  /* MINIMAP TRANSFORMS — the follow-and-face mechanism, as four custom
     properties written once per frame by MiniMapViewport.tsx.

     --mm-tx      \ how far the plan is slid so the player sits on the window's
     --mm-ty      / centre
     --mm-map     how far the plan is turned, from the CAMERA's heading
     --mm-facing  how far the player's arrow is turned, from the CHARACTER's

     The map's rotation and the arrow's are two systems, and this is where that
     separation is actually enforced: `.minimap-plan` and `.minimap-facing` are
     SIBLINGS, never nested, so no amount of map rotation can reach the arrow.
     (Parenting them would be the classic bug — the arrow would silently pick up
     the map's angle on top of its own and point somewhere neither system asked
     for.) Anything that *should* turn with the map — a room, a world-anchored
     NPC pin — is drawn inside the plan and gets it for free instead.

     ORDER MATTERS on .minimap-plan: `rotate(...) translate(...)` translates
     first and then rotates the result, and the element is a 0x0 box parked at
     the window's centre, so its transform-origin IS that centre — which the
     translate has just put the player's own position on. The map therefore
     spins about the player rather than about the middle of the house.

     Deliberately NOT transitioned: the smoothing is done in JS (smoothAngleDeg,
     frame-rate independent and wrapped the short way round the circle). A CSS
     transition on top would fight it, and would turn the 360°→0° wrap into a
     full spin. */
  .minimap-plan {
    position: absolute;
    left: 50%;
    top: 50%;
    width: 0;
    height: 0;
    transform: rotate(var(--mm-map, 0deg)) translate(var(--mm-tx, 0px), var(--mm-ty, 0px));
    will-change: transform;
  }

  /* Keeps a thing drawn INSIDE the rotating plan readable — glyphs, room names,
     the compass letter. Cancels exactly the map's own rotation, so the element
     stays anchored where the map put it but never lies on its side.

     Pivots on the element's own box (`fill-box`, i.e. its bbox for SVG and its
     content box for HTML), NOT the shared viewBox: each of these sits at its
     own spot in a plan-wide coordinate space, so any common origin would swing
     them around the house instead of turning them in place. Note this is the
     opposite choice from .minimap-facing below, for the opposite reason — read
     both before adding a third. */
  .minimap-upright {
    transform-box: fill-box;
    transform-origin: 50% 50%;
    transform: rotate(calc(var(--mm-map, 0deg) * -1));
  }
  /* `0 0` is load-bearing, and `50% 50%` is a trap here.

     An SVG element's transform-origin defaults to `50% 50%` resolved against
     the *viewBox*, and a percentage resolves against the viewBox's SIZE
     measured from user-space (0,0) — it does NOT account for a viewBox whose
     min-x/min-y are negative. The player marker is authored on
     `viewBox="-36 -36 72 72"`, so `50% 50%` pivots on user-space (36,36) — a
     corner well outside the artwork — and the arrow swings itself clean out of
     its own 72px box and disappears the moment it rotates.

     Every marker is authored around its own origin pointing straight up (see
     MiniMapMarker.tsx), so `0 0` IS the marker's centre, in every one of them,
     with no per-marker arithmetic. `fill-box` is wrong here for a second
     reason: the artwork's bbox is not centred on the pivot (the view cone
     extends well above the arrowhead), so pivoting on it would make the arrow
     orbit rather than turn on the spot. */
  .minimap-facing {
    transform-box: view-box;
    transform-origin: 0 0;
    transform: rotate(var(--mm-facing, 0deg));
  }

  /* Circular window-frame bezel for instrument-style HUD pieces
     (ZoomControl, avatar portraits) — layered rings instead of a plain
     border, like a ship porthole. (MiniMap used this too until it became a
     square floor-plan card — see MiniMap.tsx.) */
  .porthole-ring {
    box-shadow:
      0 0 0 3px var(--color-island-cream),
      0 0 0 5px var(--color-island-line),
      0 8px 20px rgba(38, 70, 83, 0.18);
  }

  /* Shop / cozy-panel card system (2026-07 pass) — flat cream cards with a
     thin line border and a soft navy-tinted shadow, teal on hover/selection.
     Replaces the old dark-glass + gilded-parchment shop styling. */
  .store-card {
    @apply bg-white rounded-[2rem] p-4 flex flex-col gap-3 transition-all duration-300 border border-island-line hover:border-island-teal-light shadow-[0_2px_10px_rgba(38,70,83,0.05)] hover:shadow-[0_10px_24px_rgba(38,70,83,0.1)] hover:-translate-y-1 active:scale-[0.98] cursor-pointer relative overflow-hidden text-left;
  }

  /* =====================================================================
     稀有度 (RARITY) — the shop's wordless "this one is special" treatment.
     =====================================================================
     Palette lives in src/constants/rarity.ts and arrives as the
     `--rarity-*` custom properties `rarityStyleVars()` writes on the card;
     only the shapes and the timing are here, so re-tuning a tier is a hex
     edit in one table and never a second copy of this gradient maths.

     MUST come after `.store-card` above. Both are single-class selectors in
     this same layer, and `.store-card` @applies its own border-colour and
     box-shadow (including a `:hover` step), so which one wins is decided by
     source order, not specificity. `.rarity-card:hover` is spelled out for
     the same reason — a bare `.rarity-card` loses to `.store-card`'s
     compound hover selector no matter where it sits.

     Every catalog item declares a `rarity`, so these rules apply to every
     card in the shop. What keeps that from being wallpaper is the per-tier
     layer budget in constants/rarity.ts: 普通 — about three quarters of the
     catalog — spends none of it, so its card is a plate in a hairline ring
     and nothing else.

     The treatment is built as an OBJECT — an enamel plate recessed into a
     turned metal bezel — and not as a tinted panel with effects thrown on
     top. That follows "Making chrome feel expensive" above, whose two
     recorded failures were making a thing heavier and re-tinting the same
     shape; a coloured wash plus rays and sparkles is the second failure
     exactly. Every premium cue below is therefore construction: a graded
     metal ring, a plate sunk by its own inset shadow with a lit bottom lip,
     a sunray grain in the glaze, and light that moves slowly across it.

     Two shadow tiers, never one mid-size blur — same rule as the toolbar. */
  .rarity-card {
    /* The card's own turned edge — the same lit-top-left / shadowed-bottom-right
       ramp the well's bezel is cut from, at roughly a third of its strength.
       The card is a ~320px rectangle and the well is a ~150px disc-in-a-frame;
       carrying the bezel's contrast up to this size stops reading as a mounted
       plate and starts reading as a bevelled 1998 button.

       Held in a custom property so the shadow list below and its `:hover` twin
       are each written once, and so 普通 can blank it to a no-op shadow without
       either rule growing a second copy of the four outer shadows. */
    --rarity-card-ramp:
      inset 0 1px 0 rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.72),
      inset 1px 0 0 rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.34),
      inset -1px 0 0 rgba(38, 70, 83, 0.055),
      inset 0 -1px 0 rgba(38, 70, 83, 0.08);
    /* The two dials the card-scale ladder turns (see the per-tier rules below):
       how deep the tier's colour pools at the foot of the card, and whether the
       paper is engraved. Defaults are 稀有's — the first rung that draws
       anything at all. */
    --rarity-card-pool: 14%;
    --rarity-card-grain: none;
    border-color: var(--rarity-edge);
    box-shadow:
      var(--rarity-card-ramp),
      /* the tier's own hairline ring, kept thin — a fat flat ring reads as a sticker */
      0 0 0 2px var(--rarity-halo),
      /* tier 1: tight contact shadow, what sits the card ON the page */
      0 1px 2px rgba(38, 70, 83, 0.10),
      0 4px 10px -2px rgba(38, 70, 83, 0.10),
      /* tier 2: a wide, soft, coloured bloom, what lifts it OFF the page */
      0 18px 36px -12px var(--rarity-halo);
  }

  .rarity-card:hover {
    border-color: var(--rarity-edge);
    box-shadow:
      var(--rarity-card-ramp),
      0 0 0 2px var(--rarity-halo),
      0 1px 2px rgba(38, 70, 83, 0.12),
      0 8px 18px -4px rgba(38, 70, 83, 0.14),
      0 28px 52px -14px var(--rarity-halo);
  }

  /* =====================================================================
     稀有度 · 整張卡 (2026-09-08) — the tier stops being a frame around a white
     card and becomes the card.
     =====================================================================
     Until this pass a graded card was a coloured hairline, a coloured bloom and
     one lit enamel plate at the top; everything under the plate — name, chips,
     description, price, button — sat on the same white paper a 普通 card sits
     on. So two thirds of the rectangle said nothing about the tier, and the
     grade read as a sticker applied to a card rather than as a property of it.

     The construction, and it is the same rule the plate follows (「change the
     construction, not the colour」 above): the card is a MOUNTED PLATE. Tinted
     paper, cut from the tier's own stone, with the lit plate at its head and a
     hairline mat ruled inside the frame. Every cue below is a piece of that
     object — none of them is the coloured wash with effects thrown on top that
     this section's second recorded failure warns about.

     Where the light comes from is the thing that keeps it coherent: the well is
     the light source (see `.rarity-field`), so the paper is brightest directly
     under it and the tier's colour pools at the foot of the card where the
     light has fallen away. Turn that story around — pool at the top, bloom at
     the bottom — and the card immediately reads as two unrelated gradients.

     The ladder is the same shape as the aura's: 普通 draws NOTHING here (it
     keeps its white paper and its hairline, which is what makes it the floor),
     and each rung above earns another piece of the object rather than a louder
     version of the last one. See the four rules below, in order.

     The alphas are white and navy over the tier's own four values, exactly as
     the plate's are, so a new tier still costs four hexes and no gradient
     maths. `color-mix()` is what lets the saturated `--rarity-field-core` be
     used at a fraction of its strength without a fifth swatch existing purely
     to be its faded twin. */

  /* 稀有 and up — the paper.

     Five layers, front to back: the engraved grain (史詩+, blank here), a
     corner vignette so the sheet falls away at its edges the way the plate
     does, a white bloom directly under the well, the tier's colour pooling at
     the foot, and the flat tinted stock underneath it all.

     `--rarity-field-top` is safe to use at full strength as paper — every
     tier's is a near-white (#EDF6E4 / #EFE7FA / #FCE8E7), and island-navy body
     copy on any of them clears contrast comfortably. `--rarity-field-core` is
     NOT: it is a jewel tone, and a card whose lower half is 稀有's #BCDCA0 is
     a green card, not a card in green paper. That is exactly how the first cut
     of this rule rendered — the pool started at 54% and ran to 26/46%, and 史詩
     and 神話 came out as a lavender card and a pink card with a shop card drawn
     on them. So the pool is held to the bottom quarter and to 14-28%: it is a
     plinth the card stands on, not a wash the card is dyed in.

     The white bloom sits at 50% — directly UNDER the well rather than behind
     it, which is where it was first put and where the plate hides it
     completely. Under is also where it earns its keep twice: it is the light
     spilling off the plate AND the reason the name and the description sit on
     the palest part of the sheet. */
  .rarity-card:not(.rarity-common) {
    background-image:
      var(--rarity-card-grain),
      radial-gradient(150% 108% at 50% 36%, transparent 44%, rgba(38, 70, 83, 0.05) 100%),
      radial-gradient(124% 34% at 50% 50%, rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.72) 0%, transparent 76%),
      linear-gradient(180deg, transparent 68%, color-mix(in srgb, var(--rarity-field-core) var(--rarity-card-pool), transparent) 100%),
      linear-gradient(var(--rarity-field-top), var(--rarity-field-top));
  }

  /* 稀有 and up — the mat.

     A hairline ruled 7px inside the frame, which is the single cheapest thing
     that makes a rectangle read as MOUNTED rather than merely outlined; it is
     what a framed print, a certificate and a museum label all have and what a
     bordered div does not. It lands in the card's own 16px padding, so it never
     crosses a word of copy, and it is `pointer-events: none` because it covers
     the whole clickable card.

     Drawn at 26% of the tier's edge rather than at full strength: the outer
     border is the tier's statement and a second line of equal weight fights it
     for the same job. The mat is the quieter of the two rules, always. */
  .rarity-card:not(.rarity-common)::before {
    content: '';
    position: absolute;
    inset: 7px;
    /* the card's 1.75rem less the 7px it is set in by — a mat that kept the
       full radius would bow away from the frame at the corners */
    border-radius: calc(1.75rem - 7px);
    border: 1px solid color-mix(in srgb, var(--rarity-edge) 26%, transparent);
    pointer-events: none;
  }

  /* 史詩 and up — the paper is engraved.

     A ruled hatch, not the plate's radial grain, and the difference is the
     surface rather than the tier: the well is a machined dial, so its finish
     turns about a centre; the card is a printed sheet, so its finish is ruled
     straight across, the way a banknote or a share certificate is. Running the
     plate's 60-spoke fan out to card size would put a visible starburst behind
     the description and the price, which is the gacha look this whole section
     is built to avoid.

     Navy rather than white — the inverse of the plate's rule and for the same
     reason. The plate can carry white marks because its field is saturated; the
     paper cannot, because it is a near-white, so its grain has to be cut INTO
     it rather than laid ON it.

     0.028 over a 5px pitch, and both numbers are a second cut: 0.04 over 7px
     stopped being a finish and became visible diagonal stripes lying across the
     description. The test is the one the plate's grain is held to — you should
     notice that the paper has a texture, and never be able to count its lines.
     史詩 also deepens the plinth a little over 稀有's, so the rung reads as one
     step and not as 「稀有 plus a pattern」. */
  .rarity-card.rarity-epic,
  .rarity-card.rarity-mythic {
    --rarity-card-grain: repeating-linear-gradient(
      52deg,
      rgba(38, 70, 83, 0.028) 0 1px,
      transparent 1px 5px
    );
    --rarity-card-pool: 19%;
  }

  /* 史詩 and up — a highlight travelling the frame.

     The card-scale twin of `.rarity-metal`, which crawls the well's bezel for
     exactly the same two tiers, and masked to an 8px band around the perimeter
     so it stays ON the frame. A sweep across the whole card would pass over the
     name, the description and the price, and a white band crossing body copy
     reads as a loading shimmer — the one thing a finished object must never
     look like.

     26s, against the bezel's 22s and the glaze's 9s. Three highlights on one
     card must never travel together; coprime-ish periods are what keep the
     three from lining up into a pulse.

     It moves by `background-position` rather than by `transform` because the
     mask belongs to the element: translating the element would drag the mask
     off the frame with it, so the gradient travels inside a mask that holds
     still.

     The band is NOT the bezel's plain white one, and that is the same
     inversion the paper's engraving makes. `overflow: hidden` clips to the
     padding box, so this ring rides the pale paper just inside the border and
     never the saturated border itself — and a white sweep over a near-white
     sheet is invisible, which is exactly how the first cut rendered (the mask
     was right; there was simply nothing to see). So the highlight is cut as a
     real specular instead: a white core with the tier's own colour trailing it,
     and it is the coloured half that does the reading. */
  .rarity-card.rarity-epic::after,
  .rarity-card.rarity-mythic::after {
    content: '';
    position: absolute;
    inset: 0;
    padding: 8px;
    border-radius: inherit;
    pointer-events: none;
    background-image: linear-gradient(
      112deg,
      transparent 36%,
      rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.95) 46%,
      color-mix(in srgb, var(--rarity-edge) 50%, transparent) 55%,
      transparent 64%
    );
    background-size: 280% 100%;
    background-repeat: no-repeat;
    -webkit-mask-image: linear-gradient(#000 0 0), linear-gradient(#000 0 0);
    -webkit-mask-clip: content-box, border-box;
    -webkit-mask-composite: xor;
    mask-image: linear-gradient(#000 0 0), linear-gradient(#000 0 0);
    mask-clip: content-box, border-box;
    mask-composite: exclude;
    opacity: 0;
    animation: rarity-card-sheen 26s ease-in-out infinite;
  }

  @keyframes rarity-card-sheen {
    0%, 74%  { background-position: -70% 0; opacity: 0; }
    82%, 92% { opacity: 0.85; }
    100%     { background-position: 170% 0; opacity: 0; }
  }

  /* 神話 only — the deepest pool, a double rule, and the mat drifting in hue.

     All three are the same three moves the tier already makes on the plate, one
     scale up: more of the tier's colour, one more piece of construction, and
     the one animated hue in the game. The drift is the SAME keyframes and the
     same 12s as `.rarity-mythic .rarity-bezel`, so the card's mat and the
     plate's bezel travel together — two lines on one object turning through the
     same red at different phases would read as a bug.

     `filter` is scoped to `::before` for the reason it is scoped to the bezel:
     it applies to an element and everything inside it, and the mat has no
     inside. Put it a level up and it hue-rotates the artwork, the name and the
     price along with the line. */
  .rarity-card.rarity-mythic {
    --rarity-card-pool: 28%;
  }

  .rarity-card.rarity-mythic::before {
    /* the second rule of the double frame, ruled 4px inside the mat */
    outline: 1px solid color-mix(in srgb, var(--rarity-edge) 14%, transparent);
    outline-offset: -4px;
    animation: rarity-iris 12s linear infinite;
  }

  /* 普通 keeps its white paper, its hairline and nothing else — no ramp, no
     mat, no engraving. It is the floor the other three are measured from, and a
     floor that draws even a little of the treatment turns the rung above it
     into a shade. Spelled as a blanked ramp plus the `:not()` guards above
     rather than as an `unset`, so there is exactly one place to look for what
     普通 does not get. */
  .rarity-card.rarity-common {
    --rarity-card-ramp: 0 0 rgba(0, 0, 0, 0);
  }

  /* The thumbnail form of a tier: border colour and a hint of halo, and NONE
     of the aura.

     Used by every surface that shows an owned item at small size — the
     collection list, the build rail, the furniture drawer, the dressing room.
     Buying something and watching its rarity disappear the moment it lands in
     your inventory says the tier was a price tag rather than a property of the
     object, so the tier has to survive the purchase; what does not survive is
     the five-layer treatment. At 44-64px the 60-line grain collapses into
     moiré and the sparkles land on top of the artwork instead of around it
     (DESIGN_SYSTEM.md's density note is the same failure at a different
     scale). A coloured edge is the part of the treatment that still reads at
     thumbnail size, so it is the only part that gets drawn.

     One shadow tier here, not two: these tiles sit in scrolling lists, and the
     wide coloured bloom that lifts a shop card off the page turns a list into
     a row of glowing lozenges. */
  .rarity-chip {
    border-color: var(--rarity-edge);
    box-shadow:
      0 0 0 1px var(--rarity-halo),
      0 6px 16px -10px var(--rarity-halo);
  }

  /* The well's own 1px border becomes the bezel's dark outer line, with the
     graded metal of `.rarity-bezel` turning inwards from it. */
  .rarity-well {
    border-color: var(--rarity-edge);
  }

  /* The bezel: a ring of turned metal. The plate covers all but its outer
     1.5px, so only the ring is ever seen.

     The light-to-dark ramp is plain white and near-black alphas over the
     tier's own `--rarity-edge`, which is why a new tier needs no extra
     palette entries — every tier is the same object cut from a different
     stone. Lit from the top-left and shadowed at the bottom-right, matching
     the light direction the rest of the card's shadows already imply. */
  .rarity-bezel {
    position: absolute;
    inset: 0;
    background:
      linear-gradient(
        152deg,
        rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.92) 0%,
        rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.25) 32%,
        rgba(10, 20, 30, 0.10) 64%,
        rgba(10, 20, 30, 0.30) 100%
      ),
      var(--rarity-edge);
  }

  /* The enamel plate the animal stands on, set 1.5px inside the bezel.

     `border-radius` is the well's `rounded-2xl` (16px) less its 1px border
     and the 1.5px of bezel it sits inside — a plate that kept the full 16px
     would bulge past the ring at the corners.

     Four backgrounds, front to back: a soft specular on the glaze, a corner
     vignette, the pool of tier colour the animal stands in, then the flat
     base. The vignette is what stops the plate reading as a flat sticker —
     it gives the corners somewhere to fall away to. */
  .rarity-field {
    position: absolute;
    inset: 1.5px;
    border-radius: 13.5px;
    background:
      radial-gradient(66% 52% at 21% 6%, rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.42) 0%, transparent 62%),
      radial-gradient(125% 92% at 50% 112%, transparent 38%, rgba(38, 70, 83, 0.13) 100%),
      radial-gradient(118% 86% at 50% 108%, var(--rarity-field-core) 0%, var(--rarity-field-top) 74%),
      var(--rarity-field-top);
    /* Sunk, not painted on: pressed-in top edge, lit lower lip — the same
       carved-groove construction as the build toolbar's track. */
    box-shadow:
      inset 0 2px 5px rgba(38, 70, 83, 0.16),
      inset 0 -1px 0 rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.7);
  }

  /* 普通 is the one tier whose plate is NOT recessed: a flat panel with a
     hairline, no pressed top edge and no lit lower lip. The recess is a
     premium cue, so the floor of the ladder does not get to have it — that is
     the difference between "this is the bottom rung" and "this is a cheaper
     jewel". Everything above it inherits the carved plate above. */
  .rarity-common .rarity-field {
    box-shadow: inset 0 0 0 1px rgba(38, 70, 83, 0.05);
  }

  /* Sunray grain under the glaze — the brushed radial finish of a watch dial,
     not a starburst. The difference is entirely density: the first pass used
     24 fat spokes, which is the visual signature of a gacha pull screen. At 60
     fine lines it stops reading as "rays" and starts reading as a machined
     surface, which is the whole point.

     Masked to an annulus. The centre MUST be cut out: that is where the lines
     converge to sub-pixel width and turn into moiré mush, and it is also where
     the animal stands.

     Uses the individual `rotate` property, not `transform`: `translate` is
     already carrying the centring here, and the two compose (translate then
     rotate, about the element's own centre) instead of overwriting each
     other the way two `transform` declarations would. */
  .rarity-rays {
    position: absolute;
    left: 50%;
    top: 56%;
    width: 210%;
    aspect-ratio: 1;
    translate: -50% -50%;
    background: repeating-conic-gradient(
      from 0deg,
      var(--rarity-shine) 0deg 1.1deg,
      transparent 1.1deg 6deg
    );
    -webkit-mask-image: radial-gradient(closest-side, transparent 9%, rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.85) 32%, rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.45) 55%, transparent 78%);
    mask-image: radial-gradient(closest-side, transparent 9%, rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.85) 32%, rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.45) 55%, transparent 78%);
    opacity: 0.26;
    /* 90s, not 30s. Premium objects are still; this should never be caught
       moving, only noticed to have moved. */
    animation: rarity-rays-spin 90s linear infinite;
  }

  @keyframes rarity-rays-spin {
    to { rotate: 360deg; }
  }

  /* Four-point sparkles. Positioned and staggered from RarityAura.tsx so the
     scatter is data rather than four more rules here.

     The glow is deliberately `--rarity-edge` and not `--rarity-shine`: a white
     star with a white halo over a pale field is invisible, which is exactly how
     the first pass rendered. Drawing the halo in the tier's own mid-tone puts a
     darker ring under the white core, so the star gets an edge to read against
     and still reads as light rather than as a smudge. Two stacked drop-shadows
     — a tight one for the outline, a wide one for the bloom.

     Thin arms (46.5/53.5, not 43/57) and a long dark interval: each star is lit
     for about a second in every seven, so with four staggered stars roughly one
     is alight at a time. A field of stars all pulsing together is the cheap
     look this is avoiding. */
  .rarity-spark {
    position: absolute;
    background: var(--rarity-shine);
    clip-path: polygon(50% 0%, 53.5% 46.5%, 100% 50%, 53.5% 53.5%, 50% 100%, 46.5% 53.5%, 0% 50%, 46.5% 46.5%);
    filter:
      drop-shadow(0 0 1px var(--rarity-edge))
      drop-shadow(0 0 5px var(--rarity-edge));
    opacity: 0;
    animation: rarity-twinkle 6.8s ease-in-out infinite;
  }

  /* No pop. The first pass scaled 0.35 → 1, which snaps; a jewel catching the
     light changes brightness far more than it changes size. */
  @keyframes rarity-twinkle {
    0%, 100% { opacity: 0; scale: 0.72; }
    7%       { opacity: 0.95; scale: 1; }
    16%      { opacity: 0; scale: 0.8; }
  }

  /* One slow specular pass across the glaze, holding still for most of the
     cycle so it reads as light moving over lacquer rather than as a loading
     shimmer. Inset negatively on both axes so it enters and leaves off-card.

     Broad and weak (a 12%-wide band at 0.55) on purpose — a narrow bright
     streak is a plastic highlight; a wide soft one is a polished surface.

     The band's strength is the element's `opacity` at the peak of the sweep,
     not an alpha baked into the gradient — the animation already owns opacity
     to fade the glint in and out, so putting the strength there keeps it in
     one place and lets the gradient stay a plain two-stop use of the token. */
  .rarity-shine {
    position: absolute;
    inset: -25% -60%;
    background: linear-gradient(
      104deg,
      transparent 44%,
      var(--rarity-shine) 50%,
      transparent 56%
    );
    opacity: 0;
    animation: rarity-shine-sweep 9s ease-in-out infinite;
  }

  @keyframes rarity-shine-sweep {
    0%, 62%  { transform: translateX(-72%); opacity: 0; }
    68%, 92% { opacity: 0.55; }
    100%     { transform: translateX(72%); opacity: 0; }
  }

  /* The half-strength grain. Same 60 lines, same mask, half the opacity — a
     rung below the full finish has to look like LESS OF the same object, never
     like a coarser version of it. Thickening the spokes to make a tier read
     louder is the rejected gacha pass; see the density note above.

     UNUSED since the ladder came down to four tiers (constants/rarity.ts):
     this was 優秀's, the rung that sat between 普通 and 稀有. Kept, with its
     `layers.rays: 0.5` budget value, because it is the right treatment for a
     rung inserted there later and re-deriving it would mean re-deriving the
     paragraph above too. */
  .rarity-rays-half {
    opacity: 0.13;
  }

  /* 史詩 and above: a second specular, this one crawling along the bezel
     rather than across the glaze. It was 傳說's alone until that tier merged
     down into 史詩, and it moved with the items rather than being retired —
     the rung directly below 神話 has to draw more than the middle of the
     ladder does. 22s against the sweep's 9s, so the two never
     travel together and the card never looks like it is loading. Same
     philosophy as the grain's 90s turn — noticed to have moved, not caught
     moving. */
  .rarity-metal {
    position: absolute;
    inset: 0;
    background: linear-gradient(
      118deg,
      transparent 40%,
      rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.85) 50%,
      transparent 60%
    );
    opacity: 0;
    animation: rarity-metal-flow 22s ease-in-out infinite;
  }

  @keyframes rarity-metal-flow {
    0%, 70%  { transform: translateX(-60%); opacity: 0; }
    80%, 90% { opacity: 0.32; }
    100%     { transform: translateX(60%); opacity: 0; }
  }

  /* 神話 only: the one moving hue in the game, and half the reason this tier
     is safely distinct from coral's 危險 despite now being a red itself — a
     static swatch that close could be misread, a colour that drifts cannot.
     (The other half is value: this red is a deep crimson, coral is a pale
     salmon. See constants/rarity.ts.) 12s for a full there-and-back.

     The rotation is NEGATIVE, and that is not a taste call. From the old
     magenta base (~332°) turning +46° travelled toward red, which is where
     this tier has now moved to; turning +46° from red (~357°) instead walks
     the bezel straight through coral (~13°) and parks it on island-gold
     (~40°), the 金幣 colour. So the drift was flipped to run the other way —
     red → crimson → magenta, back across the swatch this tier used to be.

     Scoped to `.rarity-bezel` and nothing else ON PURPOSE. `filter` applies to
     an element and everything inside it, so putting this any higher up would
     hue-rotate the animal standing on the plate (and, on a card, its name and
     price too). The bezel is behind the plate, so only the ring shifts. */
  .rarity-mythic .rarity-bezel {
    animation: rarity-iris 12s linear infinite;
  }

  @keyframes rarity-iris {
    0%, 100% { filter: hue-rotate(0deg); }
    50%      { filter: hue-rotate(-46deg); }
  }

  /* The tier still has to be readable when motion is turned down, so the
     field, the rays and the sparkles all stay — they just stop moving. Only
     the sweep is dropped outright: a glint that never travels is a stray
     diagonal band across the artwork. */
  @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
    .rarity-rays { animation: none; }
    .rarity-spark { animation: none; opacity: 0.9; scale: 1; }
    .rarity-shine { display: none; }
    /* Same rule for the two tier-specific passes: a travelling highlight that
       cannot travel is just a diagonal band lying across the artwork, so the
       bezel's crawl is dropped outright rather than frozen. The hue drift
       stops on its own base colour, which is the swatch in rarity.ts. */
    .rarity-metal { display: none; }
    .rarity-mythic .rarity-bezel { animation: none; }
    /* Card scale, same two calls: the frame's travelling highlight is dropped
       outright (a sheen frozen mid-frame is a white smear lying across one
       corner of the card), and the mat's hue drift stops on the tier's own
       swatch. Everything static — the tinted paper, the pool, the engraving,
       the mat and the double rule — stays, because that is what carries the
       tier when nothing is allowed to move. */
    .rarity-card::after { display: none; }
    .rarity-card.rarity-mythic::before { animation: none; }
  }

  /* =====================================================================
     稀有度揭曉 (RARITY REVEAL) — 史詩/神話 purchases only, the top two of the
     four rungs.
     =====================================================================
     Structure and z-tier live in components/UI/RarityReveal.tsx; this is the
     choreography. Deliberately the loudest thing in the game, and deliberately
     unreachable by ~91% of the catalog: the quiet of every other purchase is
     what this is spending. If buying a 600g budgie also flashed the screen,
     this would mean nothing.

     Runs on ModalOverlay's own scrim (so the fade-in vocabulary matches every
     other modal) with the layers below on top of it.

     ---------------------------------------------------------------------
     THE TIMELINE. Every delay in this block is a row of it, and the one row
     everything else is measured from is the SETTLE at 5500ms — the instant
     the item stops turning and faces front. constants/rarityFx.ts exports
     that number as REVEAL_SETTLE_MS and hangs the confetti, the haptics and
     the shake off it; if you move `.rarity-reveal-spin`'s duration you must
     move that constant with it or the celebration comes apart from the thing
     it is celebrating.

          0ms  screen dims, one short white flash — the 收束
          0ms  the item begins turning in from far away, in silhouette, at a
               fifth of its size, under a whoosh that slows with it
        250ms  rays start bleeding in behind it
      ~2750ms  it is still small (0.62) and still black — the swell that takes
               it to full size is the second half of the track, not the first
      ~3410ms  colour rises into the silhouette as it slows, and the whoosh
               starts RETREATING — it ramps down from here and reaches
               silence exactly on the settle, because a thing you can
               already see does not need a sound telling you it is turning
       5500ms  SETTLE. Everything blooms at once: flash, ground halo,
               energy rings, the tier's gradient, confetti, haptics
       5620ms  the item starts breathing (待機動作), and keeps at it
       5750ms  name, then 類型, then the greeting, then the tags —
               one every ~150ms, each on its own soft bounce
       6800ms  「輕觸繼續」 appears and the overlay becomes tappable
       9000ms  the reveal reports itself finished
       9400ms  the layer has finished fading and is unmounted

     The ARRIVAL is 5500ms of that, and it is the only part that has ever
     changed: 1500 → 3000 → 4500 → 7500 → 5500. The first three moves were the
     turn being asked to be more watchable; the last is the first CUT this
     number has ever taken — 7.5s overshot, and 「音效可以短個兩秒」 took it back.
     Everything after the settle keeps the gap from the settle it always had, so
     the copy still lands on the same beats and the player still gets the same
     ~3.5s to read it. The turn COUNT moves with it every time
     (constants/rarityFx.ts) — changing the track's length at a fixed count
     quietly changes the SPEED instead, which is never what was asked.

     A reveal that runs over nine seconds has to be skippable, which is why
     the hint at 6800ms exists — see RarityReveal.tsx on why it deliberately
     does NOT appear before the copy has landed. */

  /* The whole reveal's envelope, on ModalOverlay itself.

     It exists because the reveal ends by UNMOUNTING: when the last frame has
     played it calls back, the purchase dialog closes and this layer is removed
     from the tree with it. Without an envelope the removal is a hard cut from a
     darkened screen straight to the shop. Fading the layer out over the final
     8% means everything is already invisible by the time it is unmounted, so
     the cut has nothing to show.

     Overriding ModalOverlay's motion-driven opacity is deliberate and legal:
     CSS animations win over inline styles in the cascade. The first 8% here
     performs the same fade-in the motion preset would have. */
  .rarity-reveal-layer {
    animation: rarity-reveal-layer 9.4s linear forwards;
  }

  /* Percentages, not seconds — so they are re-cut whenever the total changes.
     These hold the same ABSOLUTE fade lengths the 5.4s version had (~205ms in,
     ~375ms out); left at 1.8%/96.7% the shorter total would have shrunk both. */
  @keyframes rarity-reveal-layer {
    0%          { opacity: 0; }
    2.2%, 96%   { opacity: 1; }
    100%        { opacity: 0; }
  }

  /* The extra depth under the flash. background-COLOR, never the `background`
     shorthand: a shorthand is not an interpolatable property, so animating it
     in a keyframe silently does nothing at all and the screen never darkens.
     Cost an hour the first time; it fails without an error anywhere. */
  .rarity-reveal-dim {
    position: absolute;
    inset: 0;
    background-color: rgba(12, 9, 15, 0);
    /* Fast: the black has to be fully down before the silhouette is big enough
       to be looked at, or the shape resolves against a room that is still
       fading. */
    animation: rarity-reveal-dim 0.32s ease-out forwards;
  }

  /* Taken all the way to 0.95 — very nearly opaque — and that is doing two jobs.

     **It buries the blue.** ModalOverlay paints `bg-island-navy/45`, and
     island-navy is #264653: a dark BLUE. The reveal renders on one of those
     scrims and the purchase dialog it covers is sitting on a second, so two
     coats of translucent navy over a cream shop is what the screen actually
     was during the spin — a blue wash, not a dark one. Nothing here can win
     that in the cascade (a Tailwind utility out-ranks this file's layer
     whatever the specificity), so it is beaten by opacity instead: at 0.95 the
     navy contributes 5% of the pixel and is gone.

     **And a silhouette is only a silhouette against something dark.** The
     whole opening beat is a black shape turning in from nothing, which needs
     a ground with no colour in it at all. Every earlier value — 0.5, then
     0.62 — left enough of the room showing that the black shape read as an
     icon which had failed to load. */
  @keyframes rarity-reveal-dim {
    from { background-color: rgba(12, 9, 15, 0); }
    to   { background-color: rgba(12, 9, 15, 0.95); }
  }

  /* 光芒的圓心 — where every radial layer below is aimed.

     `--reveal-focus` is a pixel offset from the middle of the screen to the middle of the ITEM,
     measured and published by RarityReveal.tsx. It is negative: the stage is a column with the
     item on top and its name, kind, greeting and tags underneath, and it is the whole COLUMN that
     gets centred, so the item itself rides about half the copy's height above centre — ~110px on
     a phone, and it shifts whenever a line wraps.

     These layers each used to carry their own hand-picked percentage instead (the rays 50%, the
     rings and the settle flash 44%, the gradient 46%), which aimed the light at a point BELOW the
     thing it is meant to be coming off —「商品有點偏光芒中間的上方」. There is now one focal
     point and it is measured, not guessed. **Do not give any of them a percentage of their own
     again**; a layer that looks off is the focus being wrong for all of them.

     The `0px` fallback is the first frame only, before the measurement lands — and the item's
     ground light, its plate and its rim are inside the stage, so they were never affected by any
     of this and still need no offset. */

  /* 「背景切換成符合其稀有度的動態漸層」 — the tier's own colour welling up
     behind the item at the settle, not at the start.

     Held back deliberately: for the first 1.4s the screen is dark and neutral
     so that the silhouette is the only thing being read, and the colour
     arriving WITH the stop is what makes the stop feel like an event rather
     than a background that was always there. The drift afterwards is 14s for a
     single pass — slow enough to be felt rather than watched, which is the
     same rule the 神話 bezel's hue is tuned by.

     A square 200vmax wide and centred, NOT `inset: -20%`. It rotates, and a
     rectangle that only overhangs the viewport a little brings its own corners
     into shot as it turns — which showed up as hard diagonal seams cutting
     across the screen. A square this size has no corner that can reach the
     viewport at any angle. */
  .rarity-reveal-backdrop {
    position: absolute;
    left: 50%;
    top: calc(50% + var(--reveal-focus, 0px));
    width: 200vmax;
    aspect-ratio: 1;
    translate: -50% -50%;
    opacity: 0;
    background:
      radial-gradient(closest-side, var(--rarity-field-core) 0%, transparent 32%),
      conic-gradient(from 210deg,
        transparent 0deg,
        var(--rarity-edge) 90deg,
        transparent 180deg,
        var(--rarity-field-core) 280deg,
        transparent 360deg);
    animation:
      rarity-reveal-backdrop 1s ease-out 5.35s forwards,
      rarity-reveal-drift 14s linear 5.35s infinite;
  }

  /* Raised from 0.28 now that it sits on a near-black dim rather than on a
     half-lit room. The same 0.28 that looked muddy over the old ground reads
     as a third of nothing over this one. */
  @keyframes rarity-reveal-backdrop {
    from { opacity: 0; }
    to   { opacity: 0.4; }
  }

  @keyframes rarity-reveal-drift {
    from { rotate: 0deg; }
    to   { rotate: 360deg; }
  }

  /* The white flash. Short and asymmetric — up in 12% of its life, down over
     the rest — because a flash that fades IN is a lightbulb, not a flash. */
  .rarity-reveal-flash {
    position: absolute;
    inset: 0;
    background: #FFFFFF;
    opacity: 0;
    animation: rarity-reveal-flash 0.5s ease-out forwards;
  }

  @keyframes rarity-reveal-flash {
    0%   { opacity: 0; }
    12%  { opacity: 0.92; }
    100% { opacity: 0; }
  }

  /* The second flash, on the settle. Softer than the opening one (0.55 against
     0.92) and tinted with the tier rather than white, because the two are doing
