```ts
/**
 * @license
 * SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
 */

import * as THREE from 'three';
import { CAMERA_BLOCKER_LAYER } from '../constants/layers';

/**
 * THE camera-collision system. One implementation, shared by every third-person view - the
 * island, the house interior, and anything added later - so "camera feel" cannot drift between
 * scenes and no scene needs its own copy of the rules.
 *
 * It is built around three distances that are deliberately kept as three separate values. Nearly
 * every "the camera zoomed in and never came back" bug is the same mistake: collapsing them into
 * one number, so that avoiding an obstacle *overwrites* the distance the player asked for and
 * there is nothing left to restore.
 *
 *   Desired distance   What the player's zoom setting asks for (uiScale -> distance). Owned by the
 *                      zoom pipeline. NOTHING in this file ever writes to it, so no amount of
 *                      collision can permanently change how far the camera follows.
 *
 *   Collision distance The furthest the camera may sit *this frame* without ending up inside
 *                      something. Recomputed from scratch every frame, always starting from the
 *                      desired distance - it is a per-frame cap, never an accumulator. The moment
 *                      an obstacle stops being in the way it is simply back to the desired
 *                      distance, with nothing to "release" or "reset".
 *
 *   Current distance   Where the camera is actually rendered. Follows min(desired, collision):
 *                      snaps inward instantly (a wall must never be clipped through, not even for
 *                      one frame) and eases back outward smoothly (see CameraDistanceSolver).
 *
 * The Roblox third-person camera behaves exactly this way, and the properties that fall out of it
 * are the ones being asked for here: no fixed delays, no "am I still colliding?" state to get
 * stuck in, no per-object exceptions, and recovery that needs no input from the player.
 *
 * SHORTENING THE ARM IS THE LAST RESORT, NOT THE FIRST. Distance is the one thing the player
 * explicitly chose, so avoidance spends pitch before it spends distance: when the view direction
 * they picked cannot hold a third-person distance, the camera swings UP over the obstruction
 * (see solveAvoidanceLift) and only gives up distance for whatever that cannot solve. Without
 * this, a room barely wider than the follow distance has exactly one answer to "the wall is
 * behind you" - collapse onto the player's head - and the player has to zoom out by hand
 * afterwards. Both the lift and the arm are temporary, both ease back on their own, and neither
 * writes to the player's setting.
 */

/**
 * Radius of the sphere the camera is treated as, in world units. Subtracted from every hit so the
 * camera stops short of a surface rather than with its near plane already inside it - the
 * exterior canvas uses `near` 0.5 and the interior one 0.3 (see Scene.tsx /
 * BuildingInteriorView.tsx), so anything smaller than 0.5 would still let a wall clip.
 */
export const CAMERA_COLLIDER_RADIUS = 0.5;

/**
 * How far off-axis the four extra probe rays start. Approximates a sphere-cast (three has no
 * such primitive) so a pillar or a wall corner that the single centre ray happens to slip past
 * still pushes the camera in. Deliberately smaller than the collider radius: at the full radius
 * the offset origins can start *inside* a wall whenever the player hugs it, which reads as a
 * flicker between "clear" and "fully collapsed".
 */
const PROBE_LATERAL_OFFSET = CAMERA_COLLIDER_RADIUS * 0.7;

/**
 * Hard floor on the collision distance. A camera pinned at exactly 0 sits inside the player's
 * head and its direction becomes undefined; this keeps a sliver of distance so the orbit
 * direction stays well-defined even when the player is jammed into a corner.
 */
export const MIN_CAMERA_DISTANCE = 0.35;

/**
 * The distance below which the shot stops being third person and starts being "the back of the
 * character's head fills the screen". Avoidance treats this as the distance it is trying to
 * PRESERVE, not as a floor it is allowed to clamp to.
 *
 * This is what stops the camera diving onto the player's head. Simply shortening the arm until
 * the sightline is clear is a valid way to avoid geometry, but it is a terrible-looking one in a
 * room barely wider than the follow distance: back into any wall and the answer is always
 * "distance ~0.4", i.e. first person, and the player has to zoom manually to get their view back.
 * When the arm alone cannot keep this much distance, {@link solveAvoidanceLift} looks for room
 * ABOVE instead - see there.
 */
export const MIN_THIRD_PERSON_DISTANCE = 2.2;

/**
 * The camera never renders closer than this while the player's own zoom asks for more, even when
 * the geometry says it should - it is the "reasonable minimum viewing distance" below which the
 * character stops being something you are watching and becomes something you are inside.
 *
 * It is allowed to overrun the geometric limit by at most CAMERA_COLLIDER_RADIUS to hold it (see
 * `applyObservationFloor`), which is exactly the margin that radius exists to provide, so holding
 * it can never expose more than the near plane already clips away. That bound is why this is a
 * floor and not a clamp: it can only ever spend margin that was there for this purpose, never
 * push the camera through a surface.
 */
export const MIN_OBSERVATION_DISTANCE = 1.2;

/**
 * This file imposes no elevation cap of its own: how high avoidance may swing is entirely the
 * `headroom` the caller passes in, and OUTDOORS that is simply the orbit's own polar limit.
 *
 * Outdoors a moderate cap was tried and measured worse where it matters. Lifting makes the arm more
 * oblique to whatever is blocking it, and the standoff a surface demands grows as 1/cos of that
 * obliquity - so the distance a given lift buys back has sharply diminishing returns, and a cap
 * that sounds generous (40 degrees) still left the arm at ~0.9 units against a wall a metre away,
 * versus ~1.6 uncapped. Since the complaint being solved is the camera ending up on the player's
 * head, and the search already takes the SMALLEST lift that works, capping only ever bites in the
 * exact case the lift exists for. The geometry caps itself: past the point where the ground is
 * nearer than the obstruction, more elevation stops buying distance and the search keeps the
 * smaller lift.
 *
 * INDOORS that last sentence is false, which is why CameraController passes a tighter headroom
 * there (MAX_INTERIOR_LIFT_POLAR). A room is closed: full-height walls under a low ceiling mean no
 * elevation ever opens up, so the search climbs to the top of whatever range it is given and the
 * shot ends up looking straight down at the player's scalp. The trade that is right on open ground
 * is the wrong one in a box - see that constant.
 */

/**
 * How many elevations to try between "none" and the limit. The search stops at the first one that
 * recovers the wanted distance, so this is the granularity of "minimum necessary avoidance": too
 * few and the lift arrives in coarse steps that read as the camera jumping as the player walks
 * along a wall. At 8 the steps are ~5 degrees, below what the eye picks out once eased.
 */
const LIFT_SAMPLES = 8;

/**
 * Lift eases in BOTH directions, unlike distance. Distance has to snap inward because a frame at
 * the wrong distance is a frame clipped through a wall; the lift has no such deadline - whatever
 * elevation it is currently at, the distance for THAT direction is solved exactly - so it is free
 * to be smooth, and a camera that swings is far more noticeable than one that dollies.
 */
const LIFT_RISE_RATE = 8;
const LIFT_RETURN_RATE = 4;

const UP = new THREE.Vector3(0, 1, 0);
const liftAxis = new THREE.Vector3();

/**
 * Rotates `dir` in place about the horizontal axis perpendicular to it: positive `radians` raises
 * the camera's elevation, negative lowers it, and the compass bearing is untouched either way.
 *
 * Being an exact, invertible rotation matters: CameraController reads the orbit direction back off
 * the camera each frame, so it undoes the previous frame's lift with `applyCameraLift(dir, -lift)`
 * to recover the player's own direction. Anything approximate here would leak avoidance into the
 * player's aim and accumulate.
 */
export function applyCameraLift(dir: THREE.Vector3, radians: number): THREE.Vector3 {
  if (radians === 0) return dir;
  liftAxis.crossVectors(dir, UP);
  if (liftAxis.lengthSq() < 1e-8) return dir; // already vertical - no bearing to rotate around
  return dir.applyAxisAngle(liftAxis.normalize(), radians).normalize();
}

/**
 * The avoidance half of the system: when the player's own view direction cannot hold a
 * third-person distance, how far up should the camera swing to find one?
 *
 * Sliding up is what a real spring arm does and it is what makes small interiors work. The arm and
 * the lift are solving the same constraint with different resources - the arm trades distance,
 * the lift trades pitch - and the lift is tried FIRST because distance is the thing the player
 * actually set and pitch recovers invisibly.
 *
 * Geometry, not guesswork: `measure` is the same per-direction collision query used for the real
 * direction, so this knows nothing about walls, ceilings, furniture or trees. It just asks "how
 * much room is there if I look from a bit higher?" a few times and keeps the best answer, which is
 * why it needs no per-object or per-scene rules and works unchanged outdoors.
 *
 * @param dir      the player's own orbit direction (unit).
 * @param wanted   the distance worth swinging for - normally MIN_THIRD_PERSON_DISTANCE, capped by
 *                 whatever the player actually asked for.
 * @param headroom how much lift is left before the orbit's own polar limit, i.e. the whole range
 *                 the search may use.
 * @param measure  collision distance along a candidate direction.
 * @param scratch  caller-owned vector, written to. Avoids allocating per frame.
 * @returns the smallest lift that got closest to `wanted`; 0 when lifting does not help.
 */
export function solveAvoidanceLift(
  dir: THREE.Vector3,
  wanted: number,
  headroom: number,
  measure: (candidate: THREE.Vector3) => number,
  scratch: THREE.Vector3
): number {
  if (headroom <= 0) return 0;

  let bestLift = 0;
  let bestDist = measure(dir);

  for (let i = 1; i <= LIFT_SAMPLES && bestDist < wanted; i++) {
    const lift = (i / LIFT_SAMPLES) * headroom;
    applyCameraLift(scratch.copy(dir), lift);
    const dist = measure(scratch);
    if (dist > bestDist) {
      bestDist = dist;
      bestLift = lift;
    }
  }

  return bestLift;
}

/**
 * Extra clearance kept between the camera and a surface ON TOP of the near plane, so a wall the
 * camera is pressed against lands just in FRONT of the near plane rather than exactly on it.
 * A surface sitting exactly on the clip plane is a coin-flip between "wall" and "hole".
 */
const NEAR_PLANE_MARGIN = 0.08;

/**
 * How much of the collider radius may be spent pushing the camera back toward a surface, given
 * the near plane it is rendering through.
 *
 * THIS IS THE 「破圖」 NUMBER. {@link applyObservationFloor} used to spend the WHOLE
 * CAMERA_COLLIDER_RADIUS, on the reasoning that the collision distance has exactly that much
 * clearance reserved - which is true, and which puts the camera exactly ON the surface. A camera
 * on a surface is already through it: the interior canvas clips everything within 0.3 of the
 * lens, so the wall it is resting against is entirely behind the near plane and the player is
 * looking at the outside of their own house. That is the reported 「角色一直往牆壁走時室內視角破
 * 圖」 - it needs the player to be JAMMED into a wall, because only then is the geometric limit
 * small enough for the floor to be spending margin that isn't there.
 *
 * Spending `radius - near - margin` instead keeps the surface a hair in front of the near plane
 * in the worst case, and the whole radius' worth of standoff in every other. Outdoors the near
 * plane IS the collider radius (0.5), so nothing may be spent at all and the floor simply stops
 * where the geometry does.
 */
export function surfaceOverrunAllowance(nearPlane: number): number {
  return Math.max(0, CAMERA_COLLIDER_RADIUS - nearPlane - NEAR_PLANE_MARGIN);
}

/**
 * Raises `distance` to the minimum viewing distance where doing so only spends margin that is
 * actually there - see MIN_OBSERVATION_DISTANCE and {@link surfaceOverrunAllowance}.
 *
 * This is the last thing standing between the player and a camera inside their own head, and it
 * is deliberately not a fixed clamp: it never exceeds what the player asked for, and it never
 * overruns the geometric limit by more than the caller says is safe to spend.
 */
export function applyObservationFloor(
  distance: number,
  collision: number,
  desired: number,
  overrun: number
): number {
  const floor = Math.min(desired, MIN_OBSERVATION_DISTANCE, collision + overrun);
  return Math.max(distance, floor);
}

/**
 * Eases the applied lift, in both directions - see LIFT_RISE_RATE. Rising a little faster than it
 * falls keeps avoidance responsive without the camera hanging high after the obstacle has gone.
 */
export class CameraLiftSolver {
  private current = 0;

  get value(): number {
    return this.current;
  }

  reset() {
    this.current = 0;
  }

  solve(goal: number, delta: number): number {
    const rate = goal > this.current ? LIFT_RISE_RATE : LIFT_RETURN_RATE;
    const t = 1 - Math.exp(-rate * Math.max(0, delta));
    this.current = THREE.MathUtils.lerp(this.current, goal, t);
    if (Math.abs(goal - this.current) < 1e-4) this.current = goal;
    if (this.current < 1e-4) this.current = 0;
    return this.current;
  }
}

/**
 * Rate, in 1/seconds, at which the current distance eases back out once the obstruction clears.
 * Used as `1 - exp(-rate * dt)` so the ease is frame-rate independent - a fixed per-frame
 * fraction (the shape this code used to use) recovers at whatever speed the machine happens to
 * render at, and never actually arrives.
 *
 * ~9 puts a full 7-unit recovery at roughly a third of a second: fast enough that it reads as
 * "the camera came back", slow enough that it is a glide rather than a jump.
 */
const RETURN_RATE = 9;

/** Below this the ease is finished; snapping the last sliver avoids an endless asymptote. */
const SETTLE_EPSILON = 0.001;

/**
 * Resolves Current from Desired + Collision.
 *
 * Inward is instant and outward is smoothed, which is the whole asymmetry: an obstacle appearing
 * must be respected on the very frame it appears (anything else clips), while an obstacle leaving
 * is not urgent and a jump would be jarring. Because the only state kept here is the current
 * distance itself - no "colliding" flag, no timer, no saved pre-collision distance - there is no
 * state that can be left stale, and recovery cannot get stuck: it is always heading for
 * min(desired, collision) as recomputed this frame.
 */
export class CameraDistanceSolver {
  private current = Number.NaN;

  /** The distance the camera was last placed at, or NaN before the first solve. */
  get value(): number {
    return this.current;
  }

  /**
   * Drops the eased state so the next solve() adopts its goal immediately. Call on discontinuities
   * where easing would be wrong (entering/leaving first person or build mode, changing scene) -
   * NOT for leaving an obstacle, which is exactly the case the ease exists for.
   */
  reset(distance?: number) {
    this.current = distance ?? Number.NaN;
  }

  solve(desired: number, collision: number, delta: number): number {
    const goal = Math.max(0, Math.min(desired, collision));

    // First frame (or just reset): adopt the goal rather than easing from nowhere.
    if (!Number.isFinite(this.current)) {
      this.current = goal;
      return goal;
    }

    if (goal <= this.current) {
      // Something is in the way (or the player zoomed in): snap. No interpolation inward.
      this.current = goal;
      return goal;
    }

    // Clear again - glide back out toward the player's own setting.
    const t = 1 - Math.exp(-RETURN_RATE * Math.max(0, delta));
    this.current = THREE.MathUtils.lerp(this.current, goal, t);
    if (goal - this.current < SETTLE_EPSILON) this.current = goal;
    return this.current;
  }
}

/**
 * An upright, Y-axis-rotated box the camera may not sit INSIDE — as opposed to one it may not see
 * past. Outdoors the player's Home is the only one.
 */
export interface CameraContainmentBox {
  /** Centre of the footprint, in world XZ. */
  x: number;
  z: number;
  /** Yaw, radians, matching the placement's own rotation. */
  rotation: number;
  halfWidth: number;
  halfDepth: number;
  /** The solid's vertical extent in world Y. */
  baseY: number;
  topY: number;
}

/**
 * How far the camera may travel along `dir` before it would be standing INSIDE `box`.
 *
 * This is deliberately NOT an occlusion test, and the difference is the whole reason it exists.
 *
 * The raycast probe answers "what is the first thing between the player and the camera", which is
 * the right question for terrain — you cannot be on the far side of a hill. It is the wrong
 * question for a small building on open ground, because it fires on a GRAZE: walking past the
 * corner of the Home swept the roof edge across a 14-unit arm and cut it to a few units, so the
 * character doubled in size and sprang back as the corner cleared, over and over. Placing the Home
 * did the same thing once, hard, the instant the building appeared under an arm that was already
 * there. Neither is the camera avoiding anything — in both the camera is well outside the house
 * and perfectly able to see its owner.
 *
 * What actually had to be prevented (see constants/layers.ts) is the camera ending up in the
 * SHELL: the house is under 4 units across and the arm is much longer, so an arm that runs through
 * the building puts the near plane inside a wall and the player sees straight through their own
 * home. That is a containment condition, and this states it exactly: shorten the arm only when the
 * camera's own position would be inside the box, and by exactly enough to stand it outside.
 *
 * @returns the largest distance ≤ `maxDistance` that keeps the camera clear, or `maxDistance` when
 *          the box does not contain the camera at all.
 */
export function solveBoxContainmentLimit(
  origin: THREE.Vector3,
  dir: THREE.Vector3,
  maxDistance: number,
  box: CameraContainmentBox,
  radius = CAMERA_COLLIDER_RADIUS
): number {
  // Into the box's own frame, where it is axis-aligned and the test is three slabs.
  const cos = Math.cos(-box.rotation);
  const sin = Math.sin(-box.rotation);
  const rx = origin.x - box.x;
  const rz = origin.z - box.z;
  const ox = rx * cos - rz * sin;
  const oz = rx * sin + rz * cos;
  const dx = dir.x * cos - dir.z * sin;
  const dz = dir.x * sin + dir.z * cos;

  // The collider radius is spent by inflating the box rather than by trimming the answer, so the
  // clearance is kept on every face including the roof — trimming only ever reserves it along the
  // ray, which on a shallow approach to a wall is a fraction of the real standoff.
  const hw = box.halfWidth + radius;
  const hd = box.halfDepth + radius;
  const yLo = box.baseY - radius;
  const yHi = box.topY + radius;

  let tEnter = -Infinity;
  let tExit = Infinity;

  // One slab per axis. A ray parallel to a slab either lies within it for all t or misses outright.
  const axes: ReadonlyArray<readonly [number, number, number, number]> = [
    [ox, dx, -hw, hw],
    [oz, dz, -hd, hd],
    [origin.y, dir.y, yLo, yHi],
  ];
  for (const [o, d, lo, hi] of axes) {
    if (Math.abs(d) < 1e-8) {
      if (o < lo || o > hi) return maxDistance;
      continue;
    }
    const inv = 1 / d;
    let t1 = (lo - o) * inv;
    let t2 = (hi - o) * inv;
    if (t1 > t2) [t1, t2] = [t2, t1];
    if (t1 > tEnter) tEnter = t1;
    if (t2 < tExit) tExit = t2;
    if (tEnter > tExit) return maxDistance;
  }

  if (tExit <= 0) return maxDistance;
  // Pivot already inside the box. The player is kept out of the Home's solid by their own collision
  // (characterMovement's resolveHomeCollision), so this is only reachable mid-teleport or while a
  // house is being re-sited around a standing player — and the one thing that must not happen then
  // is the arm collapsing onto their head. Leave it alone; the next frame is outside again.
  if (tEnter <= 0) return maxDistance;
  // The box is further away than the camera, or the arm passes clean through and comes out the far
  // side before the camera sits down. Either way the camera is not in the shell — which is the only
  // thing being asked about here.
  if (tEnter >= maxDistance || tExit < maxDistance) return maxDistance;

  return tEnter;
}

const probeOrigin = new THREE.Vector3();
const probeAxisA = new THREE.Vector3();
const probeAxisB = new THREE.Vector3();
const UP_HINT = new THREE.Vector3(0, 1, 0);
const SIDE_HINT = new THREE.Vector3(1, 0, 0);
// (u, v) multipliers of the two perpendicular axes: the centre ray plus the four "corners".
const PROBE_PATTERN: ReadonlyArray<readonly [number, number]> = [
  [0, 0],
  [1, 0],
  [-1, 0],
  [0, 1],
  [0, -1],
];

/**
 * Scene-driven half of the collision distance: casts from the player outward along the camera's
 * own orbit direction and reports how far it can go before it would be inside something.
 *
 * Completely generic. It knows nothing about houses, trees, walls or furniture - it tests whatever
 * is in the CAMERA_BLOCKER class (see constants/layers.ts), which is declared on container
 * subtrees, so new content inherits its class the moment it is added with no change here. What
 * counts as big enough to go around is a scene-content decision expressed as a class, never an
 * object-by-object test in this file.
 */
export class CameraOcclusionProbe {
  private raycaster = new THREE.Raycaster();
  private hits: THREE.Intersection[] = [];

  constructor() {
    // Layer mask, not a filtered full-scene cast: three skips raycast() entirely for non-matching
    // objects, so the ocean/cloud/grass triangle soup is never touched. See constants/layers.ts.
    this.raycaster.layers.set(CAMERA_BLOCKER_LAYER);
    this.raycaster.near = 0;
  }

  /**
   * @param pivot  where the camera is looking from-behind, i.e. the player's head. Always inside
   *               the playable space, which is what makes casting outward (rather than inward from
   *               the camera's last position) reliable: the ray can never start inside geometry
   *               because the camera drifted there last frame.
   * @returns the largest safe distance along `dir`, never more than `maxDistance` and never less
   *          than MIN_CAMERA_DISTANCE.
   */
  probe(
    scene: THREE.Object3D,
    pivot: THREE.Vector3,
    dir: THREE.Vector3,
    maxDistance: number,
    radius = CAMERA_COLLIDER_RADIUS
  ): number {
    if (!(maxDistance > MIN_CAMERA_DISTANCE)) return maxDistance;

    // Two axes perpendicular to dir. The hint only has to be non-parallel to dir; swapping it near
    // the poles keeps the cross product well-conditioned when looking straight up or down.
    probeAxisA.crossVectors(Math.abs(dir.y) > 0.9 ? SIDE_HINT : UP_HINT, dir).normalize();
    probeAxisB.crossVectors(dir, probeAxisA).normalize();

    let safe = maxDistance;
    let isCentreRay = true;

    for (const [u, v] of PROBE_PATTERN) {
      probeOrigin
        .copy(pivot)
        .addScaledVector(probeAxisA, u * PROBE_LATERAL_OFFSET)
        .addScaledVector(probeAxisB, v * PROBE_LATERAL_OFFSET);

      this.raycaster.set(probeOrigin, dir);
      // Only anything nearer than the best result so far can improve on it, so shrinking `far`
      // each iteration lets three's bounding-sphere test reject most objects outright.
      this.raycaster.far = safe + radius;

      this.hits.length = 0;
      this.raycaster.intersectObject(scene, true, this.hits);
      if (this.hits.length > 0) {
        const hitDistance = this.hits[0].distance;
        // The centre ray starts exactly at the pivot, which is inside the player and therefore
        // always in free space - it is the authority and its hit is always trusted. The four
        // offset rays start PROBE_LATERAL_OFFSET to the side, so when the player is standing that
        // close to a surface those origins can begin *inside* it and report a hit at ~0. Believing
        // that collapses the whole query to the minimum no matter which direction is being asked
        // about, which in turn makes the avoidance-lift search see no way out and give up - i.e.
        // exactly the "camera dives onto the head when you hug a wall" case. Below the offset
        // distance the corner rays know nothing the centre ray does not, so they abstain.
        if (isCentreRay || hitDistance >= PROBE_LATERAL_OFFSET) {
          safe = Math.min(safe, hitDistance - radius);
          if (safe <= MIN_CAMERA_DISTANCE) break;
        }
      }
      isCentreRay = false;
    }

    this.hits.length = 0;
    return Math.max(MIN_CAMERA_DISTANCE, Math.min(maxDistance, safe));
  }
}

/**
 * Clearance reserved around a piece of FURNITURE, as opposed to around a wall.
 *
 * Deliberately smaller than {@link CAMERA_COLLIDER_RADIUS}. That radius is what the room shell
 * reserves, and it is right there: the wall is a plane the camera must never be seen through, and
 * over-reserving costs nothing because the player cannot stand within it either. A wardrobe is a
 * solid standing in the middle of a room the camera has to keep orbiting, and inflating it by half
 * a metre on every face makes it a metre-wider obstacle than it looks — which is how a camera
 * starts moving on its own for pieces it is clearly missing.
 *
 * The floor under it is the near plane (Scene.tsx / the interior canvas both use 0.3): anything
 * less and the camera can rest close enough that the near plane cuts into the piece, which is the
 * "I can see inside the wardrobe" half of the same report.
 */
export const FURNITURE_CAMERA_CLEARANCE = 0.32;

/**
 * Height a piece has to reach before the camera is contained by it at all.
 *
 * The camera cannot descend below `INTERIOR_FLOOR_Y + CAMERA_COLLIDER_RADIUS` indoors, so nothing
 * shorter than that can ever have the camera inside it — and inflating a rug or a doormat by the
 * clearance above would produce a box that technically reaches the camera's floor and shortens the
 * arm for a mat the camera is a metre above. Measured from the piece's own base, so it means "tall
 * enough to be furniture", not "placed high up".
 */
const FURNITURE_CONTAINMENT_MIN_HEIGHT = 0.55;

/**
 * Turns placed furniture into the boxes the camera may not come to rest inside.
 *
 * WHY FURNITURE IS CONTAINED BUT NOT OCCLUDING. Furniture is deliberately absent from
 * CAMERA_BLOCKER (constants/layers.ts) and must stay absent: a raycast blocker fires on a GRAZE,
 * and a room is 12 units across with an arm several units long, so every piece in it would be
 * shortening the arm somewhere almost all of the time — which is what drove the camera onto the
 * player's head the last time this was tried. That reasoning is about OCCLUSION, and it is still
 * correct.
 *
 * It never covered the other half. An arm that passes OVER a sofa is invisible and fine; an arm
 * that ends INSIDE a wardrobe is the camera standing in a solid, and at a 0.3 near plane the piece
 * is cut open and the player is looking at its back faces and through the room behind it. That is
 * 「室內破圖」 and 「Camera 穿過家具」 reported as two things and caused by one. Containment answers
 * exactly it — `solveBoxContainmentLimit` returns the full distance unless the camera's RESTING
 * position is inside the box, so a graze still costs nothing — and it is the same treatment the
 * Home already gets outdoors, for the same reason.
 *
 * Nothing here knows what any piece is. The boxes are the measured footprints
 * (lib/furniturePlacement.ts), so a new item is contained the day it is drawn and a re-modelled one
 * updates itself; there is no table of "tall furniture" to keep in step with the catalog.
 */
export function buildFurnitureContainmentBoxes(
  placements: ReadonlyArray<{ itemId: string; position: readonly number[] | number[]; rotation?: number }>,
  getFootprint: (itemId: string) => {
    cx: number; cz: number; halfW: number; halfD: number; minY: number; maxY: number;
  } | undefined,
  /** The scale the pieces are actually drawn at, since footprints are measured in local units. */
  scale = 1,
): CameraContainmentBox[] {
  const boxes: CameraContainmentBox[] = [];
  for (const placement of placements) {
    const fp = getFootprint(placement.itemId);
    // Not measured yet — exactly one frame after an item type first mounts. Skipping is the
    // honest answer; a guessed box would be worse than none for that frame.
    if (!fp) continue;
    const [px = 0, py = 0, pz = 0] = placement.position;
    const baseY = py + fp.minY * scale;
    const topY = py + fp.maxY * scale;
    if (topY - baseY < FURNITURE_CONTAINMENT_MIN_HEIGHT) continue;

    // The footprint's centre is in the piece's own un-rotated frame, so it turns with the
    // placement — a wall shelf's box hangs off to one side, and that side follows the wall.
    const rotation = placement.rotation || 0;
    const cos = Math.cos(rotation);
    const sin = Math.sin(rotation);
    const ox = fp.cx * scale;
    const oz = fp.cz * scale;
    boxes.push({
      x: px + ox * cos + oz * sin,
      z: pz - ox * sin + oz * cos,
      rotation,
      halfWidth: fp.halfW * scale,
      halfDepth: fp.halfD * scale,
      baseY,
      topY,
    });
  }
  return boxes;
}
```

```ts
/**
 * @license
 * SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
 */

/**
 * CONVEX COLLISION SHAPES ON THE XZ PLANE — the geometry half of the collider rule.
 *
 * ## Why this exists
 *
 * Every collider in the game used to be one axis-aligned box measured around a whole model
 * (lib/furniturePlacement.ts's `Footprint`). A box is exact for a sofa and wrong for everything
 * else, in one direction only — outwards:
 *
 *  - A **round** object gets a square. A 噴泉 is a cylinder 1.58 across; its box reaches 2.24 at
 *    the corners, so 41% of the refusal radius is empty air. Worse, the box turns with the object,
 *    so rotating a rotationally-symmetric fountain changes where it collides.
 *  - A **thin or diagonal** object gets the full sweep of its bounding rectangle: a 樹枝鳥架's
 *    branch, a plank, a leaning surfboard all claim the rectangle they lie across.
 *  - An object **wider at the top than at the bottom** claims its widest slice all the way to the
 *    ground: a 許願井's roof, a bird cage's dome, a parasol. A flower tucked under the eaves reads
 *    as "此處已有其他擺設" although nothing at flower height is within a metre of it.
 *
 * ## The rule
 *
 * A collider is the **convex hull of the solid geometry actually drawn**, taken on the XZ plane,
 * simplified to at most {@link MAX_HULL_POINTS} vertices, and sliced into horizontal slabs so a
 * shape is only as wide as the model is *at that height*. Nothing is typed in per item; nothing
 * branches on an item id. The same three properties fall out for every object in the catalog:
 *
 *  1. it never sticks out past the model, because it is the model's own silhouette;
 *  2. it is round for round things and thin for thin things, because a hull has no preferred axis;
 *  3. it is bounded work, because the vertex cap is a constant.
 *
 * Simplification always *circumscribes* — a removed vertex is replaced by the intersection of its
 * two neighbouring edges, so the polygon can only grow. A collider that is a few percent large is
 * a collider; a collider that is a few percent small lets two models interpenetrate, which is the
 * bug this whole system exists to prevent.
 *
 * ## Padding is not part of the polygon
 *
 * Small pieces need a readability floor and every pair needs breathing room, and both used to be
 * baked into the box's half-extents. Here they are a `pad` the tests add on: the shape is treated
 * as *polygon ⊕ disc(pad)*, which is the exact Minkowski sum with rounded corners rather than a
 * square grown at the corners too. It also means one shape can be re-used at different clearances
 * without being rebuilt.
 *
 * ## Coordinates
 *
 * Points are `(x, z)` pairs, flattened, wound counter-clockwise in the (x → +x, z → +z) plane.
 * World placement uses the same yaw convention as the rest of the game — three.js rotates about
 * +Y as `x' = x·cos + z·sin`, `z' = -x·sin + z·cos`.
 */

/**
 * The most vertices a collider may carry.
 *
 * 12 is where the two costs cross. A circumscribed 12-gon overshoots a circle by
 * `1/cos(π/12) - 1` = **3.5%**, against the 41% a square costs at its corners; going to 16 buys
 * another 1.5% and 33% more work in the per-frame walk loop, and nothing in the catalog is round
 * enough for that to be visible. Shapes with fewer vertices — every box, every plank — are left
 * exactly as they are, so a rectangle stays a rectangle rather than being re-fitted to a polygon.
 */
export const MAX_HULL_POINTS = 12;

/**
 * How far a simplified outline may bulge past the shape it was built from, as a fraction of that
 * shape's half-extent. The collider system's headline number, and the audit's ceiling.
 *
 * An evenly-spaced circumscribed 12-gon costs `1/cos(pi/12) - 1` = 3.5%. Real hulls are not
 * evenly spaced — a model contributes vertices where its geometry happens to have them — so
 * {@link simplifyConvex} can leave a 40-degree span where 30 would be even, and a 40-degree span
 * bulges by `1/cos(20deg) - 1` = 6.4%. Across the whole shipping catalog the worst is 6.3%
 * (木製鳥籠); 8% is that with room to add an item, and it is still five times tighter than the
 * bounding box this replaced, which reaches 41.4% past a round model at its corners.
 */
export const MAX_SIMPLIFY_BULGE = 0.08;

/** A convex collider: a polygon, plus a disc radius it is thickened by. */
export interface ConvexShape {
  /** CCW hull, flattened `[x0, z0, x1, z1, …]`, in the item's own local frame. */
  pts: Float32Array;
  /** Centre of the hull's bounding box — the point `radius` is measured from. */
  cx: number;
  cz: number;
  /** Bounding-circle radius about `(cx, cz)`, INCLUDING `pad`. The broad-phase reject. */
  radius: number;
  /** Half-extents of the hull's bounding box, INCLUDING `pad`. For box-shaped consumers. */
  halfW: number;
  halfD: number;
  /** How far outside the polygon the shape actually reaches. See the module note. */
  pad: number;
}

/* ------------------------------------------------------------------ building */

/**
 * Convex hull of a point cloud on the XZ plane — Andrew's monotone chain.
 *
 * Takes the points flattened, returns them flattened and wound CCW. Duplicate and collinear
 * points are dropped, so a box authored as twelve triangles comes back as four corners.
 */
export function convexHull2D(points: readonly number[]): number[] {
  const n = points.length >> 1;
  if (n === 0) return [];
  if (n <= 2) return points.slice(0, n * 2);

  const idx: number[] = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) idx.push(i);
  idx.sort((a, b) => {
    const ax = points[a * 2], bx = points[b * 2];
    if (ax !== bx) return ax - bx;
    return points[a * 2 + 1] - points[b * 2 + 1];
  });

  // Positive when o→a→b turns left. Exactly zero for collinear points, which the `<= 0` tests
  // below then discard — that is what keeps a rectangle at four vertices instead of carrying
  // every point along its edges.
  const cross = (o: number, a: number, b: number) =>
    (points[a * 2] - points[o * 2]) * (points[b * 2 + 1] - points[o * 2 + 1]) -
    (points[a * 2 + 1] - points[o * 2 + 1]) * (points[b * 2] - points[o * 2]);

  const lower: number[] = [];
  for (const i of idx) {
    while (lower.length >= 2 && cross(lower[lower.length - 2], lower[lower.length - 1], i) <= 0) lower.pop();
    lower.push(i);
  }
  const upper: number[] = [];
  for (let k = idx.length - 1; k >= 0; k--) {
    const i = idx[k];
    while (upper.length >= 2 && cross(upper[upper.length - 2], upper[upper.length - 1], i) <= 0) upper.pop();
    upper.push(i);
  }
  lower.pop();
  upper.pop();

  const out: number[] = [];
  for (const i of lower) { out.push(points[i * 2], points[i * 2 + 1]); }
  for (const i of upper) { out.push(points[i * 2], points[i * 2 + 1]); }
  return out;
}

/**
 * Drops vertices from a convex polygon until at most `maxPoints` remain, growing it as little as
 * possible and never shrinking it.
 *
 * Each candidate vertex is removed by extending its two neighbouring edges until they meet; the
 * triangle that adds is the cost, and the cheapest one goes each round. Because the replacement
 * point is always *outside* the old outline, the result strictly contains the input — a simplified
 * collider can never be smaller than the model.
 *
 * A vertex whose neighbouring edges are near-parallel is skipped: their intersection runs off to
 * infinity, and taking it would turn a gently-curved run of a hull into a spike.
 */
export function simplifyConvex(hull: readonly number[], maxPoints = MAX_HULL_POINTS): number[] {
  let pts = hull.slice();
  let n = pts.length >> 1;
  if (n <= maxPoints) return pts;

  while (n > maxPoints) {
    let bestI = -1;
    let bestCost = Infinity;
    let bestX = 0;
    let bestZ = 0;

    for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
      const p0 = ((i - 1) + n) % n;
      const p2 = (i + 1) % n;
      const p3 = (i + 2) % n;
      // The two edges that would have to meet: p0→p1 and p2→p3.
      const ax = pts[p0 * 2], az = pts[p0 * 2 + 1];
      const bx = pts[i * 2], bz = pts[i * 2 + 1];
      const cx = pts[p2 * 2], cz = pts[p2 * 2 + 1];
      const dx = pts[p3 * 2], dz = pts[p3 * 2 + 1];

      const r1x = bx - ax, r1z = bz - az;
      const r2x = dx - cx, r2z = dz - cz;
      const denom = r1x * r2z - r1z * r2x;
      if (Math.abs(denom) < 1e-6) continue; // parallel — extending them meets nowhere useful

      const t = ((cx - ax) * r2z - (cz - az) * r2x) / denom;
      const ix = ax + r1x * t;
      const iz = az + r1z * t;

      // On a CCW outline an intersection that lies OUTSIDE the edge b→c makes the triangle
      // (b, c, I) wind clockwise, so its signed area is negative. A positive one means the two
      // edges met on the inside — the outline would fold — and that candidate is not a
      // simplification at all.
      const signedArea = ((cx - bx) * (iz - bz) - (cz - bz) * (ix - bx)) / 2;
      if (signedArea > 1e-12) continue;

      // COST IS HOW FAR IT BULGES, NOT HOW MUCH AREA IT ADDS.
      //
      // Area was the obvious measure and it produced visibly uneven results on a circle: the
      // removals bunched up (a 48-gon came back with 41-degree gaps beside 25-degree ones) and the
      // worst bulge reached 8.8% of the radius where an even 12-gon costs 3.5%. Area is
      // height × base, so it lets the greedy take a tall thin bite as readily as a shallow wide
      // one, and taking two tall bites side by side is exactly how the outline ends up lumpy.
      // Bulge is the thing the whole module promises to bound, so it is the thing to minimise:
      // each round takes the shallowest bite available, and a bite next to one already taken is
      // deeper, so they spread out on their own.
      const base = Math.hypot(cx - bx, cz - bz);
      const cost = base > 1e-9 ? (-signedArea * 2) / base : -signedArea;
      if (cost < bestCost) { bestCost = cost; bestI = i; bestX = ix; bestZ = iz; }
    }

    // Nothing removable without folding the outline: stop here rather than damage the shape. The
    // point cap is a budget, not a promise, and a 13-vertex collider costs one more dot product.
    if (bestI < 0) break;

    const next = (bestI + 1) % n;
    pts[bestI * 2] = bestX;
    pts[bestI * 2 + 1] = bestZ;
    pts.splice(next * 2, 2);
    n--;
  }

  return pts;
}

/**
 * Wraps a hull as a {@link ConvexShape}, applying the readability floor.
 *
 * `minHalfExtent` is the smallest a collider may measure across. A 竹製手電筒's stem is a couple
 * of centimetres wide; two of them 1cm apart is legal by the geometry and unreadable on screen. It
 * is applied as `pad` — the shape keeps its true outline and is thickened by a disc — rather than
 * by stretching the polygon, so a thin plank grows a rounded margin instead of becoming a square.
 */
export function makeConvexShape(
  hull: readonly number[],
  minHalfExtent = 0,
  extraPad = 0,
): ConvexShape | null {
  const n = hull.length >> 1;
  if (n === 0) return null;

  let minX = Infinity, maxX = -Infinity, minZ = Infinity, maxZ = -Infinity;
  for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    const x = hull[i * 2], z = hull[i * 2 + 1];
    if (x < minX) minX = x;
    if (x > maxX) maxX = x;
    if (z < minZ) minZ = z;
    if (z > maxZ) maxZ = z;
  }

  const rawHalfW = (maxX - minX) / 2;
  const rawHalfD = (maxZ - minZ) / 2;
  const pad = Math.max(0, minHalfExtent - Math.min(rawHalfW, rawHalfD)) + extraPad;

  const cx = (minX + maxX) / 2;
  const cz = (minZ + maxZ) / 2;
  let radius = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    const dx = hull[i * 2] - cx;
    const dz = hull[i * 2 + 1] - cz;
    const d = Math.hypot(dx, dz);
    if (d > radius) radius = d;
  }

  return {
    pts: Float32Array.from(hull),
    cx,
    cz,
    radius: radius + pad,
    halfW: rawHalfW + pad,
    halfD: rawHalfD + pad,
    pad,
  };
}

/** The rectangle every box-shaped collider reduces to, for callers that only have half-extents. */
export function rectangleShape(
  cx: number,
  cz: number,
  halfW: number,
  halfD: number,
  pad = 0,
): ConvexShape {
  return makeConvexShape(
    [cx - halfW, cz - halfD, cx + halfW, cz - halfD, cx + halfW, cz + halfD, cx - halfW, cz + halfD],
    0,
    pad,
  )!;
}

/* ------------------------------------------------------------------ placing */

/**
 * A shape put down in the world: the same polygon, rotated and translated, written into a caller-
 * owned buffer.
 *
 * Deliberately fills a buffer instead of returning an object. The walk resolve runs this for every
 * placement in reach on every frame, and a per-call allocation there is the one cost that scales
 * with how decorated a player's island is.
 */
export interface PlacedShape {
  /** World-space hull, flattened. Only the first `count * 2` entries are meaningful. */
  pts: Float32Array;
  count: number;
  cx: number;
  cz: number;
  radius: number;
  pad: number;
}

/**
 * Allocates a buffer big enough for any shape this module produces.
 *
 * Twice the vertex cap, because {@link simplifyConvex} treats the cap as a budget and stops early
 * rather than folding an outline it cannot reduce safely. {@link placeShape} clamps to the buffer
 * either way — a silently truncated outline is a collider with a hole in it.
 */
export function createPlacedShape(): PlacedShape {
  return { pts: new Float32Array(MAX_HULL_POINTS * 4), count: 0, cx: 0, cz: 0, radius: 0, pad: 0 };
}

/**
 * Writes `shape`, placed at `(x, z)` and turned by `rotation`, into `out`.
 *
 * `extraPad` is added to the shape's own padding — this is where a pair's clearance goes, so the
 * stored shape stays the object's honest outline.
 */
export function placeShape(
  shape: ConvexShape,
  x: number,
  z: number,
  rotation: number,
  out: PlacedShape,
  extraPad = 0,
): PlacedShape {
  const cos = Math.cos(rotation);
  const sin = Math.sin(rotation);
  const n = Math.min(shape.pts.length >> 1, out.pts.length >> 1);
  for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    const lx = shape.pts[i * 2];
    const lz = shape.pts[i * 2 + 1];
    out.pts[i * 2] = x + lx * cos + lz * sin;
    out.pts[i * 2 + 1] = z - lx * sin + lz * cos;
  }
  out.count = n;
  out.cx = x + shape.cx * cos + shape.cz * sin;
  out.cz = z - shape.cx * sin + shape.cz * cos;
  out.pad = shape.pad + extraPad;
  out.radius = shape.radius + extraPad;
  return out;
}

/* ------------------------------------------------------------------ testing */

/**
 * Do two placed shapes occupy the same ground?
 *
 * Separating-axis test over both outlines' edge normals, with each shape's `pad` subtracted from
 * the gap — which is what makes the disc-thickened shape exact rather than approximated by a
 * grown polygon. The bounding circles are checked first: for two objects that are nowhere near
 * each other, and that is nearly every pair, this is the only arithmetic that runs.
 */
export function shapesOverlap(a: PlacedShape, b: PlacedShape): boolean {
  const dcx = b.cx - a.cx;
  const dcz = b.cz - a.cz;
  const reach = a.radius + b.radius;
  if (dcx * dcx + dcz * dcz > reach * reach) return false;

  const slack = a.pad + b.pad;
  return !hasSeparatingAxis(a, b, slack) && !hasSeparatingAxis(b, a, slack);
}

/** Does any edge normal of `from` separate the two outlines by more than `slack`? */
function hasSeparatingAxis(from: PlacedShape, other: PlacedShape, slack: number): boolean {
  const n = from.count;
  for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    const j = (i + 1) % n;
    const ex = from.pts[j * 2] - from.pts[i * 2];
    const ez = from.pts[j * 2 + 1] - from.pts[i * 2 + 1];
    const len = Math.hypot(ex, ez);
    if (len < 1e-9) continue;
    // Outward normal of a CCW polygon's edge.
    const nx = ez / len;
    const nz = -ex / len;

    let aMax = -Infinity;
    for (let k = 0; k < n; k++) {
      const p = from.pts[k * 2] * nx + from.pts[k * 2 + 1] * nz;
      if (p > aMax) aMax = p;
    }
    let bMin = Infinity;
    for (let k = 0; k < other.count; k++) {
      const p = other.pts[k * 2] * nx + other.pts[k * 2 + 1] * nz;
      if (p < bMin) bMin = p;
    }
    if (bMin - aMax > slack) return true;
  }
  return false;
}

/** Is the world point `(x, z)` inside this shape (its padding included)? */
export function shapeContainsPoint(s: PlacedShape, x: number, z: number): boolean {
  return signedDistanceToShape(s, x, z) <= 0;
}

/**
 * Distance from `(x, z)` to the shape's surface: negative inside, 0 on it, positive outside.
 *
 * One function for "how close is the player standing" (lib/furnitureInteraction.ts's reach) and
 * for "is this point on the deck" — the two used to be a box-distance and a box-contains that
 * could disagree at a corner.
 */
export function signedDistanceToShape(s: PlacedShape, x: number, z: number): number {
  const n = s.count;
  if (n === 0) return Infinity;

  let maxSigned = -Infinity;
  let outside = false;
  let bestSq = Infinity;

  for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    const j = (i + 1) % n;
    const ax = s.pts[i * 2], az = s.pts[i * 2 + 1];
    const bx = s.pts[j * 2], bz = s.pts[j * 2 + 1];
    const ex = bx - ax, ez = bz - az;
    const len = Math.hypot(ex, ez);
    if (len < 1e-9) continue;
    const nx = ez / len, nz = -ex / len;
    const signed = (x - ax) * nx + (z - az) * nz;
    if (signed > maxSigned) maxSigned = signed;
    if (signed > 0) outside = true;

    // Nearest point on this edge as a segment, kept for the outside case.
    let t = ((x - ax) * ex + (z - az) * ez) / (len * len);
    t = t < 0 ? 0 : t > 1 ? 1 : t;
    const qx = ax + ex * t - x;
    const qz = az + ez * t - z;
    const dsq = qx * qx + qz * qz;
    if (dsq < bestSq) bestSq = dsq;
  }

  return (outside ? Math.sqrt(bestSq) : maxSigned) - s.pad;
}

/**
 * Pushes a circle of radius `r` centred at `(px, pz)` out of `s`, writing the result into `out`.
 * Returns true when it moved.
 *
 * Three cases, and the third is the one that matters: a body genuinely inside the outline (spawned
 * there, or shoved in by another resolve pass in the same frame) leaves by the nearest FACE rather
 * than by the nearest point, so it never squeezes out through a corner in the wrong direction.
 */
export function pushCircleOutOfShape(
  s: PlacedShape,
  px: number,
  pz: number,
  r: number,
  out: { x: number; z: number },
): boolean {
  const n = s.count;
  if (n === 0) return false;

  const reach = s.radius + r;
  const dcx = px - s.cx;
  const dcz = pz - s.cz;
  if (dcx * dcx + dcz * dcz > reach * reach) return false;

  const clear = r + s.pad;

  let maxSigned = -Infinity;
  let faceNx = 0, faceNz = 0;
  let bestSq = Infinity;
  let closeX = 0, closeZ = 0;
  let outside = false;

  for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    const j = (i + 1) % n;
    const ax = s.pts[i * 2], az = s.pts[i * 2 + 1];
    const bx = s.pts[j * 2], bz = s.pts[j * 2 + 1];
    const ex = bx - ax, ez = bz - az;
    const len = Math.hypot(ex, ez);
    if (len < 1e-9) continue;
    const nx = ez / len, nz = -ex / len;

    const signed = (px - ax) * nx + (pz - az) * nz;
    if (signed > maxSigned) { maxSigned = signed; faceNx = nx; faceNz = nz; }
    if (signed > 0) outside = true;

    let t = ((px - ax) * ex + (pz - az) * ez) / (len * len);
    t = t < 0 ? 0 : t > 1 ? 1 : t;
    const cxp = ax + ex * t;
    const czp = az + ez * t;
    const dx = px - cxp, dz = pz - czp;
    const dsq = dx * dx + dz * dz;
    if (dsq < bestSq) { bestSq = dsq; closeX = cxp; closeZ = czp; }
  }

  if (outside) {
    const dist = Math.sqrt(bestSq);
    if (dist >= clear) return false;
    if (dist > 1e-6) {
      // Push straight out along the shortest line to the outline. Doing it on this normal rather
      // than on a face normal is what lets a body slide along a sofa instead of sticking to it.
      const inv = 1 / dist;
      out.x = closeX + (px - closeX) * inv * clear;
      out.z = closeZ + (pz - closeZ) * inv * clear;
      return true;
    }
    // Exactly on the outline: leave by the face it is on.
    out.x = px + faceNx * clear;
    out.z = pz + faceNz * clear;
    return true;
  }

  // Inside: `maxSigned` is negative and its face is the shallowest wall.
  out.x = px + faceNx * (clear - maxSigned);
  out.z = pz + faceNz * (clear - maxSigned);
  return true;
}

/** Area of a convex outline. Used by the audits to prove a collider never grew past its model. */
export function shapeArea(pts: readonly number[] | Float32Array, count = (pts.length >> 1)): number {
  let sum = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < count; i++) {
    const j = (i + 1) % count;
    sum += pts[i * 2] * pts[j * 2 + 1] - pts[j * 2] * pts[i * 2 + 1];
  }
  return Math.abs(sum) / 2;
}
```

## src/lib/dailyLoginClient.ts

```ts
/**
 * @license
 * SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
 */

/**
 * 每日登入 — the browser's side of the API, and the only way the client is allowed to change
 * anything about the round.
 *
 * There is deliberately no Firestore write anywhere in this file. Everything else in the game saves
 * itself by writing `users/{uid}` directly; this one asks the server, because the two facts a daily
 * reward turns on — what day it is, and whether this day was already paid — are the two the browser
 * must not be the authority for. See src/server/dailyLoginApi.ts.
 *
 * What this file is responsible for is everything the network can do to a correct server:
 *
 *   - attaching a real identity (a Firebase ID token, refreshed by the SDK, never a uid we chose);
 *   - a stable idempotency key per attempt, so a retry after a lost response is recognised as the
 *     same attempt rather than as a second claim;
 *   - a timeout, because a request that never returns is indistinguishable from one that failed and
 *     the player is left looking at a spinner;
 *   - refusing to let an older response overwrite a newer one.
 */

import { getIdToken } from 'firebase/auth';
import { firebaseAuth } from './firebaseCore';

/** One square, exactly as the server describes it. Snake case: this is the wire shape, not ours. */
export interface DailyLoginRewardDto {
  day_index: number;
  reward_type: string;
  reward_id: string | null;
  quantity: number;
  state: 'future' | 'available' | 'claimed' | 'makeup_available' | 'missed';
  makeup_cost: number | null;
}

export interface DailyLoginStatusDto {
  server_now: string;
  timezone: string;
  anchor_date: string;
  cycle_id: string;
  cycle_number: number;
  cycle_start_at: string;
  cycle_end_at: string;
  current_day_index: number;
  /** 金幣 — what a 補簽 is paid out of. */
  coin_balance: number;
  /**
   * 碎片 — what the round pays.
   *
   * Optional so a client built after the currency split still parses a response from a server that
   * predates it. The panel reads the profile for the balance it displays anyway; this is here so a
   * caller can reconcile against the server's own view.
   */
  fragment_balance?: number;
  /** Which currency every `quantity` below is denominated in. Absent on a pre-split server. */
  reward_currency?: string;
  rewards: DailyLoginRewardDto[];
  /** Server-stamped, monotonic. See {@link isNewerThan}. */
  updated_at: number;
}

export interface ClaimResultDto {
  ok: true;
  replayed: boolean;
  /** How much was granted, in {@link DailyLoginStatusDto.reward_currency} (碎片 today). */
  granted_quantity: number;
  /** What the 補簽 cost, in 金幣. Named for its currency because the payout is no longer in it. */
  spent_gold: number;
  status: DailyLoginStatusDto;
}

export type DailyLoginErrorCode =
  | 'unauthenticated'
  | 'not_configured'
  | 'invalid_request'
  | 'no_profile'
  | 'not_available_yet'
  | 'already_claimed'
  | 'makeup_window_closed'
  | 'insufficient_gold'
  | 'server_error'
  /**
   * The local claim could not be saved.
   *
   * Distinct from `server_error` because no server is involved in it: this is the offline/
   * unconfigured path (context/useEconomyActions.ts, `claimOnProfile`) failing to write the save.
   * It used to report itself as `server_error`, which put 「伺服器忙碌中，請稍後再試」 on screen for
   * a failure that had nothing to do with a server and sent anyone debugging it looking at the API.
   */
  | 'save_failed'
  | 'offline'
  | 'timeout';

export class DailyLoginError extends Error {
  constructor(readonly code: DailyLoginErrorCode, message: string) {
    super(message);
  }
}

/**
 * What each failure says to the player.
 *
 * Held here rather than in the panel so the same wording is used wherever a claim can be started
 * from, and so a new server code cannot reach the screen as a raw identifier.
 */
export const DAILY_LOGIN_MESSAGES: Record<DailyLoginErrorCode, string> = {
  unauthenticated: '請先登入再領取獎勵',
  not_configured: '獎勵服務尚未設定完成，請稍後再試',
  invalid_request: '這個獎勵無法領取',
  no_profile: '找不到玩家資料',
  not_available_yet: '這一天還沒開放',
  already_claimed: '這一天已經領過了',
  makeup_window_closed: '這一輪已經結束，無法補簽',
  // Still 金幣: the only thing this feature charges for is a 補簽, and that is priced in 金幣 even
  // though the reward is 碎片. See constants/dailyLogin.ts's MAKEUP_SURCHARGE.
  insufficient_gold: '金幣不足',
  server_error: '伺服器忙碌中，請稍後再試',
  save_failed: '獎勵沒有存檔成功，請再試一次',
  offline: '目前離線，連上網路後再試一次',
  timeout: '連線逾時，請再試一次',
};

/** Long enough for a cold serverless start, short enough that a dead request is not a hang. */
const REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS = 12_000;

async function authHeader(): Promise<Record<string, string>> {
  const user = firebaseAuth.currentUser;
  if (!user) throw new DailyLoginError('unauthenticated', DAILY_LOGIN_MESSAGES.unauthenticated);
  // `false` — do not force a refresh. The SDK refreshes on its own schedule and a forced refresh on
  // every claim turns one tap into two round trips.
  const token = await getIdToken(user, false);
  return { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` };
}

async function request<T>(path: string, init?: RequestInit): Promise<T> {
  if (typeof navigator !== 'undefined' && navigator.onLine === false) {
    throw new DailyLoginError('offline', DAILY_LOGIN_MESSAGES.offline);
  }

  const controller = new AbortController();
  const timer = setTimeout(() => controller.abort(), REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS);
  let response: Response;
  try {
    response = await fetch(path, {
      ...init,
      signal: controller.signal,
      headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json', ...(await authHeader()), ...(init?.headers ?? {}) },
    });
  } catch (error) {
    if (error instanceof DailyLoginError) throw error;
    // An aborted fetch and a dropped connection arrive the same way; the difference to the player is
    // whether trying again is likely to help, and for both it is.
    const code: DailyLoginErrorCode = controller.signal.aborted ? 'timeout' : 'offline';
    throw new DailyLoginError(code, DAILY_LOGIN_MESSAGES[code]);
  } finally {
    clearTimeout(timer);
  }

  if (!response.ok) {
    let code: DailyLoginErrorCode = 'server_error';
    let message = DAILY_LOGIN_MESSAGES.server_error;
    try {
      const body = await response.json();
      if (body?.error?.code && body.error.code in DAILY_LOGIN_MESSAGES) {
        code = body.error.code as DailyLoginErrorCode;
        message = DAILY_LOGIN_MESSAGES[code];
      }
    } catch {
      // A non-JSON error body means nothing that speaks this API answered: the SPA fallback served
      // its index.html because the route is not mounted, or a proxy returned an HTML 502 because
      // the service is unreachable. That is `not_configured`, not `server_error`, and the
      // difference is load-bearing — the caller (context/useEconomyActions.ts) is allowed to fall
      // back to a local claim when the service is ABSENT, and must not when the service answered
      // and failed. A real 500 from this API carries a JSON body and keeps `server_error`.
      code = 'not_configured';
      message = DAILY_LOGIN_MESSAGES.not_configured;
    }
    throw new DailyLoginError(code, message);
  }

  return (await response.json()) as T;
}

export function fetchDailyLoginStatus(): Promise<DailyLoginStatusDto> {
  return request<DailyLoginStatusDto>('/api/daily-login/status');
}

/**
 * Takes one square.
 *
 * `idempotencyKey` must be STABLE for a given attempt and is the caller's to keep: generating it
 * here would make every retry a fresh attempt, which is the exact case it exists to defend. The
 * panel makes one per button press and reuses it if the request has to be retried.
 */
export function claimDailyLogin(
  dayIndex: number,
  mode: 'free' | 'makeup',
  idempotencyKey: string
): Promise<ClaimResultDto> {
  return request<ClaimResultDto>('/api/daily-login/claim', {
    method: 'POST',
    body: JSON.stringify({ day_index: dayIndex, mode, idempotency_key: idempotencyKey }),
  });
}

/** A fresh key for one user-initiated attempt. Reused verbatim by that attempt's retries. */
export function newIdempotencyKey(): string {
  return typeof crypto !== 'undefined' && 'randomUUID' in crypto
    ? crypto.randomUUID()
    : `k-${Date.now()}-${Math.random().toString(36).slice(2)}`;
}

/**
 * Whether `incoming` is safe to apply over `current`.
 *
 * Two requests in flight can land out of order — a status poll started before a claim can answer
 * after it, and applying it would put a claimed square back to `available` and show a stale
 * balance. Comparing the SERVER's stamp rather than arrival order is what makes that impossible.
 */
export function isNewerThan(incoming: DailyLoginStatusDto, current: DailyLoginStatusDto | null): boolean {
  return !current || incoming.updated_at >= current.updated_at;
}
```

## src/lib/firebase.ts

```ts
/**
 * @license
 * SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
 */

/**
 * Storage facade: one Firestore-shaped API that writes to Firestore for real
 * sessions and to `LocalSaveStore` for local-only guests.
 *
 * ## What changed and why the shape stayed the same
 *
 * This file used to be four things at once — SDK bootstrap, a fake `auth`
 * object that impersonated Firebase's, a hardcoded three-key localStorage guest
 * save, and the Firestore re-exports. The first three have moved out:
 *
 *  - SDK bootstrap  → `lib/firebaseCore.ts`
 *  - authentication → `src/auth/` (AuthenticationManager and friends)
 *  - offline save   → `src/save/LocalSaveStore.ts`
 *
 * What deliberately did NOT change is the exported *shape*: eighteen call sites
 * across the game do `doc(db, 'users', uid)` / `updateDoc` / `onSnapshot`, and
 * rewriting them all was the fastest way to break a working game while fixing
 * login. So this stays a Firestore-shaped port, and the routing decision — real
 * or local — is made in one place, {@link isLocalSession}, instead of by
 * fourteen copies of `localStorage.getItem('is_local_guest') === 'true'`.
 *
 * `auth` is re-exported for the two sign-out buttons that still import it, but
 * it now delegates to AuthenticationManager rather than shadowing Firebase.
 */

import {
  arrayRemove as firestoreArrayRemove,
  arrayUnion as firestoreArrayUnion,
  collection as firestoreCollectionRef,
  doc as firestoreDoc,
  getDoc as firestoreGetDoc,
  getDocFromServer,
  increment as firestoreIncrement,
  limit as firestoreLimit,
  onSnapshot as firestoreOnSnapshot,
  orderBy as firestoreOrderBy,
  query as firestoreQuery,
  setDoc as firestoreSetDoc,
  updateDoc as firestoreUpdateDoc,
} from 'firebase/firestore';

import { authManager } from '../auth/AuthenticationManager';
import {
  localArrayRemove,
  localArrayUnion,
  localIncrement,
  localSaveStore,
} from '../save/LocalSaveStore';
import { recordSaveFailure, type SaveFailure } from './saveStatus';
import { db, isPlaceholderConfig } from './firebaseCore';

export { db };

/**
 * Compatibility shim for the handful of components that import `auth` purely to
 * sign out. New code should use `useAuth()` / `authManager` directly.
 */
export const auth = {
  get currentUser() {
    return authManager.getState().user;
  },
  signOut: () => authManager.signOut(),
  onAuthStateChanged: (callback: (user: unknown) => void) =>
    authManager.subscribe((state) => callback(state.user)),
};

// --- Routing -----------------------------------------------------------------

/**
 * The single routing decision: is the active session local-only?
 *
 * True only for a player whose device could not obtain a Firebase session at
 * all. A signed-in account — including a Firebase *anonymous* guest — is always
 * false, because those have a real uid and belong in Firestore.
 */
function isLocalSession(): boolean {
  return authManager.getState().user?.isLocalOnly === true;
}

/** The namespace a local write belongs to. Never guessed from a path string. */
function localUid(): string | null {
  const user = authManager.getState().user;
  return user?.isLocalOnly ? user.uid : null;
}

/** Tagged references used only in local mode. */
interface LocalDocRef {
  __localDoc: string;
  path: string;
}
interface LocalCollectionRef {
  __localCollection: string;
  path: string;
}
interface LocalQuery {
  __localQuery: string;
  orderByField?: string;
  direction?: 'asc' | 'desc';
  limitTo?: number;
}

function isLocalDocRef(value: unknown): value is LocalDocRef {
  return typeof value === 'object' && value !== null && '__localDoc' in value;
}
function isLocalCollectionRef(value: unknown): value is LocalCollectionRef {
  return typeof value === 'object' && value !== null && '__localCollection' in value;
}
function isLocalQuery(value: unknown): value is LocalQuery {
  return typeof value === 'object' && value !== null && '__localQuery' in value;
}

// --- Reference builders ------------------------------------------------------

export function doc(dbRef: unknown, path: string, ...segments: string[]) {
  if (isLocalSession()) {
    const full = [path, ...segments].join('/');
    return { __localDoc: full, path: full } as LocalDocRef;
  }
  return firestoreDoc(dbRef as never, path, ...segments);
}

export function collection(dbRef: unknown, path: string, ...segments: string[]) {
  if (isLocalSession()) {
    const full = [path, ...segments].join('/');
    return { __localCollection: full, path: full } as LocalCollectionRef;
  }
  return firestoreCollectionRef(dbRef as never, path, ...segments);
}

export function orderBy(field: string, direction?: 'asc' | 'desc') {
  if (isLocalSession()) return { __localOrderBy: field, direction } as never;
  return firestoreOrderBy(field, direction);
}

export function limit(count: number) {
  if (isLocalSession()) return { __localLimit: count } as never;
  return firestoreLimit(count);
}

export function query(ref: unknown, ...constraints: unknown[]) {
  if (isLocalCollectionRef(ref)) {
    const local: LocalQuery = { __localQuery: ref.__localCollection };
    for (const constraint of constraints as Record<string, unknown>[]) {
      if (constraint && '__localOrderBy' in constraint) {
        local.orderByField = constraint.__localOrderBy as string;
        local.direction = (constraint.direction as 'asc' | 'desc') ?? 'asc';
      }
      if (constraint && '__localLimit' in constraint) {
        local.limitTo = constraint.__localLimit as number;
      }
    }
    return local as never;
  }
  return firestoreQuery(ref as never, ...(constraints as never[]));
}

// --- Field values ------------------------------------------------------------

export function increment(n: number) {
  return isLocalSession() ? (localIncrement(n) as never) : firestoreIncrement(n);
}

export function arrayUnion(...elements: unknown[]) {
  return isLocalSession()
    ? (localArrayUnion(...elements) as never)
    : firestoreArrayUnion(...(elements as never[]));
}

export function arrayRemove(...elements: unknown[]) {
  return isLocalSession()
    ? (localArrayRemove(...elements) as never)
    : firestoreArrayRemove(...(elements as never[]));
}

// --- Reads and writes --------------------------------------------------------

/**
 * `object` rather than `Record<string, unknown>`: callers pass declared
 * interfaces (`UserProfile`, `AppSettings`), and TypeScript only grants an
 * implicit index signature to type aliases, never to interfaces.
 */
type DocumentData = object;

export async function updateDoc(reference: unknown, data: DocumentData) {
  const uid = localUid();
  if (uid && isLocalDocRef(reference)) {
    localSaveStore.update(uid, reference.path, data as Record<string, unknown>);
    return;
  }
  return firestoreUpdateDoc(reference as never, data as never);
}

export async function setDoc(
  reference: unknown,
  data: DocumentData,
  options?: { merge?: boolean },
) {
  const uid = localUid();
  if (uid && isLocalDocRef(reference)) {
    localSaveStore.set(uid, reference.path, data as Record<string, unknown>, options);
    return;
  }
  return options
    ? firestoreSetDoc(reference as never, data as never, options)
    : firestoreSetDoc(reference as never, data as never);
}

/** Mirrors `DocumentSnapshot`'s surface as far as this app uses it. */
interface SnapshotLike {
  exists: () => boolean;
  data: () => unknown;
}

export async function getDoc(reference: unknown): Promise<SnapshotLike> {
  const uid = localUid();
  if (uid && isLocalDocRef(reference)) {
    const data = localSaveStore.read(uid, reference.path);
    return { exists: () => data !== null, data: () => data };
  }
  return firestoreGetDoc(reference as never) as unknown as Promise<SnapshotLike>;
}

export function onSnapshot(
  refOrQuery: unknown,
  // Intentionally loose: call sites read either `.exists()/.data()` (documents)
  // or `.docs` (queries), and both back-ends produce those shapes.
  onNext: (snapshot: any) => void,
  onError?: (error: unknown) => void,
): () => void {
  const uid = localUid();

  if (uid && isLocalDocRef(refOrQuery)) {
    return localSaveStore.subscribe(uid, refOrQuery.path, (data) => {
      onNext({ exists: () => data !== null, data: () => data } as never);
    });
  }

  if (uid && isLocalQuery(refOrQuery)) {
    const spec = refOrQuery;
    return localSaveStore.subscribeCollection(uid, spec.__localQuery, (docs) => {
      let rows = [...docs];
      if (spec.orderByField) {
        const field = spec.orderByField;
        const factor = spec.direction === 'desc' ? -1 : 1;
        rows.sort((a, b) => {
          const left = a[field] as string | number;
          const right = b[field] as string | number;
          if (left === right) return 0;
          return (left < right ? -1 : 1) * factor;
        });
      }
      if (spec.limitTo !== undefined) rows = rows.slice(0, spec.limitTo);
      onNext({ docs: rows.map((row) => ({ data: () => row })) } as never);
    });
  }

  return firestoreOnSnapshot(refOrQuery as never, onNext as never, onError as never);
}

// --- Error reporting ---------------------------------------------------------

export enum OperationType {
  CREATE = 'create',
  UPDATE = 'update',
  DELETE = 'delete',
  LIST = 'list',
  GET = 'get',
  WRITE = 'write',
}

export interface FirestoreErrorInfo {
  error: string;
  operationType: OperationType;
  path: string | null;
  authInfo: {
    userId?: string | null;
    email?: string | null;
    isGuest?: boolean | null;
    isLocalOnly?: boolean | null;
    providers?: string[];
  };
}

/**
 * Reports a failed read/write, and RETURNS — it must never throw.
 *
 * This used to end with `throw new Error(JSON.stringify(info))`, which quietly
 * disabled the error handling of every one of its eighteen call sites. They are
 * all shaped like:
 *
 *     try { await updateDoc(...); return true }
 *     catch (e) { handleFirestoreError(e, ...); return false }
 *
 * — so the `return false` was unreachable: re-throwing from inside the catch
 * replaced a handled failure with a rejected promise. What that cost in practice
 * was the entire recovery path. `commitDraft` never returned, so the island
 * editor neither cleared the draft nor reported the problem; the caller's
 * `void commitDraft()` turned the rejection into an unhandled one; and the
 * player got no sound, no message and no change on screen. A save that is
 * refused by the server looked exactly like a click that did nothing, which is
 * why the first-run "place your house" flow could be attempted forever without
 * once telling anyone it was failing.
 *
 * The reason is recorded in `lib/saveStatus.ts` on the way past, so the surface
 * closest to the action can say what actually went wrong instead of guessing at
 * "請稍後再試".
 */
export function handleFirestoreError(
  error: unknown,
  operationType: OperationType,
  path: string | null,
): SaveFailure {
  const user = authManager.getState().user;
  const info: FirestoreErrorInfo = {
    error: error instanceof Error ? error.message : String(error),
    authInfo: {
      userId: user?.uid ?? null,
      email: user?.email ?? null,
      isGuest: user?.isGuest ?? null,
      isLocalOnly: user?.isLocalOnly ?? null,
      providers: user?.linkedProviders ?? [],
    },
    operationType,
    path,
  };
  console.error('Firestore Error: ', JSON.stringify(info));
  return recordSaveFailure(error, path);
}

// --- Startup connectivity probe ---------------------------------------------

if (isPlaceholderConfig) {
  console.info('[firebase] Placeholder configuration detected; running in local-only mode.');
} else {
  // Non-blocking, and failures are expected offline — the local store covers it.
  setTimeout(() => {
    getDocFromServer(firestoreDoc(db, 'test', 'connection')).catch(() => {
      /* offline cache handles this; see docs/AUTH_SETUP.md if it never recovers */
    });
  }, 1000);
}
```

```ts
/**
 * @license
 * SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
 */

/**
 * The one place the Firebase SDK is initialised.
 *
 * Split out of `lib/firebase.ts` so that `src/auth/` and `src/save/` can both
 * reach the SDK without importing each other — `lib/firebase.ts` is now a thin
 * compatibility facade over those two, and it imports this too. Nothing else in
 * the app should call `initializeApp`/`getAuth`/`initializeFirestore`.
 */

import { initializeApp, type FirebaseApp } from 'firebase/app';
import { getAuth, type Auth } from 'firebase/auth';
import { initializeFirestore, type Firestore } from 'firebase/firestore';
import firebaseConfig from '../../firebase-applet-config.json';

export const app: FirebaseApp = initializeApp(firebaseConfig);

/**
 * Long polling is forced because the project has historically run behind proxies
 * where Firestore's streaming transport stalls. Unchanged from the original
 * setup — do not "clean this up" without testing on the deployed host.
 */
export const db: Firestore = initializeFirestore(
  app,
  { experimentalForceLongPolling: true },
  firebaseConfig.firestoreDatabaseId,
);

/**
 * The real Firebase Auth instance.
 *
 * Named `firebaseAuth` rather than `auth` on purpose: the old code exported an
 * object literally called `auth` that *impersonated* this one and rewrote
 * `currentUser`/`onAuthStateChanged` to serve a localStorage guest. Anything
 * that wants "who is signed in" must ask `AuthenticationManager`, not this.
 */
export const firebaseAuth: Auth = getAuth(app);

/** True when the bundled config is still the AI-Studio placeholder. */
export const isPlaceholderConfig =
  firebaseConfig.projectId === 'remixed-project-id' ||
  firebaseConfig.apiKey === 'remixed-api-key';

export { firebaseConfig };
```
